News.title: Rare animal on the brink of extinction is born in UK zoo – but do YOU know what it is?
News.content:
AN EXTREMELY rare animal has been born at a popular UK zoo as a deadly disease pushes the species towards extinction.

It was the size of a ‘grapefruit with legs’ when born weighing just a few hundred grams.



Rana is a babirusa – an unusual species of pig so rare it is only found on four islands in Indonesia.

Tiny Rana was born at Chester Zoo just as a deadly disease threatens to wipe out the species.



Bosses at the zoo said the rare ‘pig-deer’ animals are being wiped out due to African swine fever reaching the Indonesian islands five years ago.

Hannah Owens, assistant team manager at the zoo, said while pig-deers are doing well in captivity, they are “really struggling” in the wild.

“The numbers are radically reducing, and it would be horrendous if they disappeared,” she said.

The species was previously classed as Vulnerable but is set to be uplisted to Critically Endangered following a dramatic decline in numbers.

Rana is the fifth piglet born to mother Matano, an 11-year-old babirusa, who was also born at Chester Zoo.

The animals are known as pig-deers because of their distinctive appearance.



The males feature unusual upper tusks which grow through their snout and curve backwards towards their face.

Hannah added that piglets like Rana were a “lifeline for the species.”

“Rana had ginger fuzz when she was born, but that’s gone now,” she added.

News.title: Brits put off improving their homes, careers and lives because the ‘effort just isn’t worth it’
News.content:
SIX in 10 Brits have put off making improvements to their homes, careers and lives because they feel the “effort just isn’t worth it”.

A poll of 2,000 adults found over a quarter (28 per cent) of these have decided against starting a new fitness routine because it feels like too much of a time commitment.



Another 18 per cent have even put off career changes or applying for a new job altogether, worried it would be too much trouble for too little return.

When it comes to the home, many have delayed making simple improvements, such as decluttering (42 per cent), redecorating (41 per cent), carrying out repairs (39 per cent) or even getting a smart meter (10 per cent).



Others have not switched energy suppliers (19 per cent), improved their home insulation (13 per cent) or opted for energy-efficient lightbulbs (nine per cent), because they believe the hassle will outweigh the reward.

A quarter (25 per cent) say that trying something new has been put on hold because reviews left them doubtful about the outcome.



And a fifth (20 per cent) admit they’ve put things off simply because they assumed it would be too disruptive to fit into their routine.

Yet among those who did eventually take the plunge, 70 per cent said they experienced benefits beyond what they initially expected, while 64 per cent wish they had ignored their assumptions and acted sooner.

TV presenter Anna Richardson, who is backing the research which was commissioned by Smart Energy GB, said: “We’ve all done it, decided something’s going to be a faff before we’ve even given it a go, then let it drag on for months, sometimes years.

“But honestly, more often than not, once you’ve taken that first step it’s much easier and more rewarding than you’d imagined. You get your time back, stop carrying that nagging thought around with you, and often find yourself wishing you’d done it sooner.



“Smart meters are a great example of something that some people put off getting, when in reality they can be quick to get installed and easy to use, helping households better understand their energy use and save money.”

The research went on to find that over half (56 per cent) believe outdated information is a key factor preventing people from making improvements in their lives.

And 22 per cent revealed this has directly influenced their decision about whether to make a change or not.

This may explain why nearly half (42 per cent) regret putting off making an improvement to their home or life.

Eating more healthily (31 per cent), reaching out to people they hadn’t spoken to for a while (26 per cent) and tackling life admin (20 per cent) are among the top things people wish they had done sooner.



Of these, 36 per cent recognised the problem became worse over time as a result, while 34 per cent admitted it caused unnecessary stress.

In fact, 45 per cent regret not taking better steps to manage their energy use at home, suggesting many households wish they had acted sooner, the survey conducted by OnePoll.com found.

As a result, 46 per cent believe they may have paid more than they needed to, while 41 per cent worry they could have wasted energy without realising.

A spokesperson for Smart Energy GB said: “The research highlights how easy it can be to put off changes that could make a positive difference in our daily lives.

“While seven in 10 households now have a smart meter, some people haven’t yet taken up the offer of an installation.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Four in five smart meter owners are already happy with their smart meter, and recent technical fixes and new industry standards introduced in 2026 are helping improve the experience for customers even further.

“Smart meters can help households save money on their energy bills, feel more in control of what they’re spending and put an end to estimated bills.”

News.title: Horror moment screaming cable car riders are trapped in swinging gondola during Colombia quake that killed at least 250
News.content:
THIS is the horror moment cable car riders were left screaming as they dangled mid-air during Colombia’s devastating earthquake.

Tense footage shows terrified passengers gripping onto their seats as the car violently swings from side to side.



Women can be heard screaming and shouting for their lives as the trapped group look at one another in panic.

The horrifying incident in Western Colombia occurred as the country was hit by a 7.4-magnitude earthquake on Monday.



A national disaster has been declared after 254 were killed and nearly 2,600 injured in the disaster, according to local authorities.

The search for life amongst the rubble grew more desperate on Wednesday as time ticked away for victims to be found and rescued alive.



Aid agencies consider the first 48 to 72 hours crucial for retrieving survivors.

Striking at a depth of 64 miles in Chocó province, the quake was felt for hundreds of miles across western Colombia.



Shocking footage shows the moment Colombian news anchor Lina Pulido was live on air when the earthquake struck.

Broadcasting from a local news studio in Bogotá, Pulido remained calm and informed the audience of evacuation protocols as TV screens swung around her.

Shockwaves stretched as far as Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, 750 miles away, and in Ecuador and Panama.



Teams continued to pick through the piles of broken concrete, brick and debris in the hardest-hit cities of Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdo.

More than 3,800 people were reported missing by Monday, as families frantically posted information about loved ones online.

Three people died at the Pereira airport terminal, according to the mayor, as rescuers pulled passengers trapped on the city’s 11,000ft-long gondola lift.



In ​Cali, Colombia’s third biggest city and home to about 2.2 million people, at least 95 people were killed.

One of the first deaths confirmed in Quibdó was Jairson Leonel Valencia, the six-year-old son of a local mayor, The Times reports.

In a grim admission, public health secretary German Escobar said the city’s morgue was now full and authorities were bringing more bodies off the streets.

Official government figures have confirmed 180 deaths – with the toll remaining lower as searches continue.

Small successes have broken through, with rescuers pulling a dust-covered baby through a crack in a concrete wall.



But in many areas the official response has been complicated by deep poverty and civil warfare that has blighted the country for decades.

Colombia’s president Abelardo de la Espriella said 1,000 members of the security forces have been deployed to Cali following reports of looting.

The natural disaster is proving to be an early test for the president who was only inaugurated on Friday.



On Tuesday, he flew to Pereira, accompanied by his wife, the first lady Ana Lucía Pineda, to inspect one of the worst-hit areas.

President de la Espriella said he had mobilised the entire military as well as police to respond to the quake – deploying engineers, rescue workers and search dogs.

The US Department of State described the disaster as “devastating” and pledged £11.5million to help provide emergency shelter and supplies.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The EU is also providing funding and supporting rescue operations, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.

And on Tuesday Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele said his country would send two planes loaded with 100 tons of aid in the coming days.

News.title: Teacher and married mother, 25, arrested after ‘secret meetings and late night vid chats with 14-year-old student’
News.content:
DISGRACED MISS Teacher and married mother, 25, arrested after ‘secret meetings and late night vid chats with 14-year-old student’

A MARRIED teacher accused of secretly meeting a 14-year-old student has been arrested over grooming charges.

Mum-of-one Sadie Flores, 25 was arrested at Graves County Middle School following claims she was having an improper relationship with a student.



On Friday. she was taken into custody on a felony charge of grooming a minor, though it is unclear whether she has entered a plea.

Flores, a Kentucky school teacher, is accused of attempting to “manipulate” the teen by expressing “feelings of love and admiration”, documents obtained by the Daily Mail reveal.



She is the first person charged under Kentucky’s new anti-grooming law, which took effect July 15 and allows law enforcement to intervene before a sexual assault occurs.

According to the court document, the state’s sheriff’s office was notified by the school board after they were contacted by a parent of the teen student.

It is understood the parents discovered multiple exchanges across multiple social media platforms with Flores, court documents suggest.

The court document states: “The messages that were reviewed by investigators were determined… not to be of a legitimate purpose and were not school-related.”



A number of FaceTime calls that allegedly occurred “multiple times in the late evening hours” were uncovered by the parents.

The court document said: “It appears the above [Flores] was attempting to manipulate the minor and expressed feelings of love and admiration more so than just a student-teacher relationship.

“It was also determined that they met in secret before a school function, outside of school, that [Flores] was not directly a part of, but lived in close proximity to the event.”

Flores was married in 2022 and has a baby daughter.

Announcing the pregnancy in 2024, the expectant mother said: “We are so grateful God chose us to be parents to this sweet baby.”



Flores recently shared pictures of her daughter posing in front of church signs, just weeks before she was arrested at her workplace.

It remains unclear at this time if she was still teaching the first grade when she was arrested.

In a statement, the sheriff’s office said: “25-year-old Sadie M. Flores of Mayfield was arrested around 3.30PM at the Graves County Sheriff’s Office on a charge of Grooming a Minor, classified as a Class D Felony.

“Flores, an employee at the Graves County Middle School reportedly was having an improper relationship with a minor student of the district.

“The allegation was initially reported to the Graves County School District Office, who then immediately reported it to the Graves County Sheriff’s Office for an investigation.



“Sheriff’s detectives’ investigation included the seizure of electronic records, interviews, and other related investigative measures.

“Flores was interviewed this afternoon and then arrested.

“She was transported to the Graves County Restricted Custody Center, and later to an out of county detention center.

“The investigation is continuing.”

Graves County Schools Superintendent Matt Madding said: “District administration was made aware of an allegation involving a teacher at Graves County Middle School.



“School officials immediately reported this information to the Graves County Sheriff’s Department for investigation.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We have since been informed that, as a result of that investigation, charges have been filed against this teacher.

“We want to assure our families that the safety and well-being of our students is our highest priority.”

News.title: Disposable barbecues could be BANNED amid heatwave wildfires, Andy Burnham says
News.content:
BURNT OUT Disposable barbecues could be BANNED amid heatwave wildfires, Andy Burnham says

DISPOSABLE barbecues could be banned following raging wildfires across the UK, the Prime Minister has said.

Andy Burnham said he is considering a ban ahead of chairing an emergency Cobra meeting as extreme heat continues to grip parts of the UK.



The PM said today: “People should not be using those barbecues outside at this moment in time”.



Speaking to reporters he continued: “There is obviously a significant problem of wildfires in the south. The New Forest fire is a great concern; we have seen them in northern areas, as well as Suffolk recently.”

He added: “This is a message for the public as well because the wildfires I mentioned, many of them have been created by disposable barbecues.”

Mr Burnham continued: “I do believe we need to get the message out loud and clear. People should not be using those barbecues outside at this moment in time.

“I don’t know yet what the remedy is, but I do want to leave the meeting today with a loud and clear message that we do want people to take the greatest possible care when they are out in the countryside, both in terms of cigarettes, but also those temporary barbecues that we know are causing risk of fires.”

This comes ahead the emergency Cobra meeting to discuss the UK’s response to the extreme heat later today.

Today will be the second Cobra meeting on heatwaves this year after one took place amid high temperatures in June.



Ministers from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), Home Office, and Department for Health will attend, and the Environment Agency will also be present.

A No.10 spokesperson said: “The Prime Minister will chair a meeting of COBR – the government emergency committee – this afternoon on the UK’s ongoing response to extreme heat, wildfires and drought.

“We know how challenging this summer is proving, particularly for firefighters tackling wildfires, farmers working in drought conditions, and NHS staff in busy A&E units.

“We will continue to take the action needed to keep communities safe, protect water supplies and safeguard the environment.”

Several major supermarkets have already started pulling temporary BBQs from their shelves.



Asda, Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Co-op have recently stopped sales following Aldi, Lidl, Waitrose and M&S who have not sold disposable grills since 2022.

Those suspending sales are understood to have acted in line with voluntary guidance from the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC) lasting until next Wednesday as parts of the country face a prolonged heatwave.

Parts of the UK could be set to bake in 38C temperatures later this week as a firefighters’ union chief warned the country faces a “national emergency” over wildfires.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Seve Wright, general secretary of the Fire Brigades Union (FBU), said the UK faces a national emergency “right now” with fires across the country.

Firefighters have responded to 966 wildfires across England and Wales this year, including 185 in the first 10 days of August alone, while July was the busiest month on record for wildfires with 458 incidents, the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC) said.

News.title: Motorcyclist died after ‘massive’ pheasant flew into him in ‘explosion of feathers’ as he took KFC to wife in hospital
News.content:
BIKE TRAGEDY Motorcyclist died after ‘massive’ pheasant flew into him in ‘explosion of feathers’ as he took KFC to wife in hospital

A MOTORCYCLIST died after a “massive” pheasant flew into him as he took KFC to his wife in hospital, an inquest heard.

Andrew Davenport, 47, was riding his BMW bike when the bird hit him in an “explosion of feathers” on the A454 near Bridgnorth, Shropshire.



The bodybuilder and DJ is believed to have been knocked unconscious by the pheasant and went “floppy” over the handlebars, the inquest was told.

Andrew then tragically suffered a fatal head injury when he smashed into a road sign.



Shropshire Coroner’s Court heard there were no drugs or alcohol in his system, visibility was good and there were no adverse road conditions.

His riding was also described as “calm, steady and competent” by a couple who saw Andrew moments before the crash.



The inquest was told Andrew had been taking KFC to his wife on March 1 when the “massive” pheasant hit his left hand side.

Police, paramedics and an air ambulance attended the scene but tragically he could not be saved and was declared dead at the scene.

John Ellery, senior coroner for Shropshire, Telford and Wrekin, said: “There are two incredibly unlucky things that have happened to Andy.

“Firstly, the pheasant and losing consciousness, then colliding with the road sign. It was that which killed him.”



Mr Ellery recorded a conclusion of death as a result of a road traffic collision.

Paying tribute after the hearing, his wife Aine said: “He was loud, always the centre of attention.

“He was full of wisdom. He was a really beautiful man.”

Aine told how she met her husband on Plenty of Fish and was wooed by his “beautiful blue eyes and muscles”.

Andrew was a popular house DJ who had played in Ibiza and was also an entrepreneur who ran events including the Crooked House Festival in Lichfield, Staffordshire.



He also was boss of a bar and once won the Mr Midlands first timer award in a bodybuilding competition.

His mum Linda Osborne said: “In his short life he did an awful lot. He achieved amazing things.”

News.title: Should Andy Burnham’s first Cobra meeting focus on the migrant crisis instead of weather? VOTE NOW
News.content:
ANDY Burnham will chair his first Cobra meeting today in response to the extreme heat – but should the PM be focusing on the migrant crisis?

The 49ft mega-dinghy that made the perilous journey earlier this week laid bare the extent of the Channel chaos, with the average number of migrants per boat increasing tenfold since 2018.



As he emerged from his week-long holiday yesterday, Mr Burnham conceded people will be worried by Monday’s arrival carrying 230 illegal migrants – more passengers than an average EasyJet flight.

The Prime Minister – who has seen 3,003 migrants cross the Channel under his 23-day leadership – admitted he needed to “change tactics”.



It was announced yesterday that a further 13 hotels housing asylum seekers had shut – as Mr Burnham urged middle-class families to “play their part” by accepting accommodation near their homes.

So, as the migrant crisis continues to engulf the PM, much like it did his predecessors, do you think today’s Cobra meeting should focus on migrants rather than the weather?

News.title: Lorry driver dies after HGV smashes through barrier on motorway bridge and plummets 25ft
News.content:
CRASH HORROR Lorry driver dies after HGV smashes through barrier on motorway bridge and plummets 25ft

A LORRY driver has sadly died after their HGV smashed through barriers of a bridge near a major motorway and plummeted 25ft.

Emergency services rushed to the M3 at Junction 14 near Eastleigh following the horror smash shortly before 11pm on Tuesday.



The lorry left the motorway close to the interchange with the M27 before crashing off a bridge on to Chestnut Avenue.

Police raced to the scene and quickly closed off the area.



Crews from Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service, South Central Ambulance Service rapid-response paramedics and a specialist Hazardous Area Response Team attended the scene to launch a complex rescue operation.

Emergency teams worked into the early hours of Wednesday to free the trapped driver as they dealt with the badly damaged HGV.

Pictures from the crash site show the broken bridge barrier where the lorry swerved off the road and onto the tarmac below.

The tipped over lorry lies stuck on its side, with some of its wheels scattered on the road.



It is understood that a specialist heavy-recovery crane will be required to remove the HGV.

A driver from the area reportedly described seeing a lorry “swerving” left and right across the M3 in Hampshire before the incident.

A forensic investigation underway with specialist collision investigators and commercial vehicle officers from Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary to carry out a detailed examination of the crash scene.

It is likely to involve forensic mapping and scanning of the motorway, bridge and vehicle as officers establish how the HGV came to leave the carriageway.

News.title: Simon Levy - live: Sex attack murderer faces jail after first victim tried to warn police
News.content:
Simon Levy, 40, is facing jail for murdering Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, and Sheryl Wilkins, 39, after raping a third woman in a horrific series of attacks

A serial sex attacker is being sentenced today for brutally murdering two women and raping a third. A stream of the sentencing will be available here soon.

Simon Levy, 40, is facing jail after being found guilty at the Old Bailey of killing grandmother Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in March, 2025, and mother-of-four Sheryl Wilkins, 39, in August that year.

He suffocated both women in sexually motivated attacks, with Ms Valencia-Trujillo found in a largely abandoned block of flats on the Aylesbury estate in south-east London, and Ms Wilkins behind a car park wall near Tottenham High Road, north London.

The killings followed a harrowing sex attack on a third woman in January last year in the same car park where Ms Wilkins’ body was later found. Police were told by the victim, who suffered a broken collarbone, that she had been raped and knew where her attacker lived, but she was not formally interviewed until after Levy had killed twice.

News.title: Brits urged to turn off 3 household appliances 'until 8pm' on Wednesday
News.content:
Brits urged to turn off 3 household appliances 'until 8pm' on Wednesday

It comes as Britain looks set for its first solar eclipse in over 25 years

View 3 Images Three everyday chores could wait until later in the day, experts say (Image: Getty Images)

Homeowners will be tempted to carry on with their usual Wednesday routine, but one unusual event means they may have to consider the time they complete some daily chores. An energy expert has issued a reminder to households to hold off on using three appliances until after 8pm as a major solar eclipse is expected to cause a sharp, temporary change in electricity generation.

‌



Justin Nielsen from Wolf River Electric says there's no reason for households to panic or switch everything off, but has suggested moving their more flexible tasks until later in the evening. He specifically highlighted the washing machine, dishwasher and tumble dryer as devices that could easily be delayed.

‌



While saying Wednesday was "not a blackout warning" he explained that electricity system operators know when the eclipse is coming and have been preparing for it. He added that appliances which heat water or air are more worthwhile to postpone than smaller uses such as phone charging or a couple of lights.

‌



View 3 Images A solar eclipse is coming on Wednesday, August 12 (Image: ©2025 George Pachantouris)

The advice comes as the UK prepares for a particularly deep partial solar eclipse on Wednesday, August 12. The Royal Observatory Greenwich says around 90 per cent of the sun will be covered from London, with the eclipse beginning there at 6.17pm, reaching its maximum at 7.12pm and ending at 8.06pm.

‌



It is expected to have an effect on solar generation across Europe, with the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity warning that photovoltaic output could fall by up to 9.7GW under clear-sky conditions. ENTSO-E said the change will be rapid but predictable and that transmission operators have been making preparations to maintain a secure and stable electricity system.

Nielsen said the unusual feature is the speed at which solar generation will change across a large area at almost the same time. He stressed that one household running a dishwasher will not cause a problem, but said the eclipse provides a convenient opportunity to move non-essential electricity use where possible.

View 3 Images The dishwasher is one of the three appliances (Image: Getty Images)

Article continues below

For households following the advice, the three appliances are relatively simple to identify: the washing machine, dishwasher and tumble dryer. Nielsen said delaying them until after 8pm would have little downside, particularly if they were not urgently needed that evening.

The Royal Observatory Greenwich says the eclipse will be visible across the UK and Ireland, although the exact amount of the sun covered and the timings will vary by location. It also advises people never to look directly at the Sun, including during a partial eclipse, and recommends proper eclipse glasses or a solar telescope for safe viewing.

For most households, there is therefore no need to start switching off essential appliances or worry about the lights going out. The expert's advice is simply to consider waiting until after the eclipse period for energy-intensive chores that can easily wait.

News.title: People on doxycycline, diclofenac, amiodarone given 35C heatwave warning
News.content:
People on doxycycline, diclofenac, amiodarone given 35C heatwave warning

Medical scientist give full list of medications which people need to take extra care with in the current heatwave

View Image People need to take extra care in the August heatwave because of the impact if they're taking certain drugs (Image: Getty)

The UK is today being hit by potentially dangerous weather conditions with temperatures of 35C forecast, and up to 38C on Thursday. Rare amber “extreme heat” warnings have been issued by the forecaster for London and parts of the South East, East Midlands, East of England, West Midlands and South Yorkshire from 9am to midnight on Thursday.

‌



The Government urged the public to pay attention to UK Health Security Agency heat health alerts, and advised people should drink plenty of fluids and check in on family, friends and neighbours who may be at high risk. Medical experts have highlighted a number of medications millions take in the UK which can have nasty side effects if the skin is exposed to the blazing sun for too long.

‌



Writing on The Conversation website Nial Wheate, associate professor of the Sydney Pharmacy School, Elise Schubert, pharmacist, and Lisa Kouladjian O’Donnell, research fellow in Geriatric Pharmacotherapy, explained: “There are many medicines that can affect your skin and make you more sensitive to the sun, so it’s important to know which ones to look out for.”

‌



Antibiotics:

The paper said people need to be careful of drugs including doxycycline, ofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, and sulfamethoxazole. They wrote: “The first are the antibiotics. Tetracycline-based drugs are particularly known to cause sensitivity. An example is the drug doxycycline which is used to treat infections, acne, and as a malaria prophylactic (or prevention) for those who are going to a tropical location (lots of sun).

“Other antibiotics known to cause sun sensitivity are fluoroquinolones, like ciprofloxacin, and sulfamethoxazole, which treat a broad range of illnesses such as urinary tract infections, pneumonia or gastroenteritis.”

Antifungals and skin conditions

The antifungals griseofulvin and voriconazole are known to cause sun sensitivity. People may be taking these medicines for skin or nail fungal infections. For people who suffer from skin conditions such as acne, psoriasis, or eczema, the oral retinoid medications including acitretin and isotretinoin and the topical cream pimecrolimus will leave you sensitive to the sun.

‌



New Lansoprazole and Omeprazole warning to anyone who takes them for reflux READ MORE :

Warning issued to millions on atorvastatin for high cholesterol READ MORE :

Anti-inflammatories

Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, like diclofenac, can leave you sun sensitive, especially if applied on the skin, so you need to be sure you adequately protect those areas. The same applies for some opioid-based pain patches, like fentanyl. When you remove the patch, the skin underneath will be sensitive to the sun.

Heart drugs

Amiodarone is a drug used to treat irregular heart beats and azathioprine is an immuno suppressing drug used for people who have inflammatory immune conditions or organ transplants. Both are known to cause sun sensitivity.

Cancer treatment

Finally, a large number of drugs used in cancer chemotherapy will sensitise your skin. These include: 5-fluorouracil, 5-aminolevulinic acid, vemurafenib, imatinib, mercaptopurine, and methotrexate.

‌



The paper said it is important to note that not all people who use one of these medicines will have a sun sensitivity reaction – but extra precautions should be taken.

Remember the five S advice from the Cancer Council:

slip on suitable clothing

slop on sunscreen that is rated SPF30 or higher to exposed skin, especially on your face and arms

slap on a hat

seek shade when you can

slide on sunglasses.

Article continues below

The scientists added: "And if you are concerned a medicine you are taking may be putting you at more risk of sunburn, speak to your pharmacist. They can confirm if your medicine does increase your risk of sunburn and discuss options. This could include having your doctor issue a prescription for a different drug.

"Never just stop taking a medicine because you are concerned about the risk of sun damage or any other side effects; always discuss it first with your health care provider." To read the full article click here.

News.title: Skiathos tourist suffers serious head injuries as plane blasts her during take-off
News.content:
Skiathos tourist suffers serious head injuries as plane blasts her during take-off

A 52-year-old Italian woman was knocked off her feet by the blast from a jet engine as it took off from the airport on the Greek island of Skiathos

View 2 Images Skiathos airport is close to the beach (file) (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

A tourist suffered serious head injuries after being hit by the blast from a jet engine as it took off from a Greek island.

‌



The 52-year-old Italian woman was struck by the jet turbine wash as it left the airport on Skiathos and rushed to hospital. She had been on a road by the airport when the incident happened on Monday.

‌



Many tourists gather to watch planes taking off at a perimeter fence by the runway. Skiathos airport is close to the sea and it provides spectacular views of the aircraft.

‌



The woman was taken to Skiathos' Polyiatreio medical centre, where she underwent a CT scan before being airlifted to Volos General Hospital for further treatment.

View 2 Images The tourist suffered head injuries (file) (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Her condition has been described as serious by the Greek outlet ERT.

‌



It has put the spotlight again on the practice of watching the planes so close up, with people previously caught out by the sudden blasts from the jet engines.

Similar to the famous airport at St Maarten's Princess Juliana Airport in the Caribbean, planes come in to land and take off right over the beach.

In September 2025, people were seen struggling to stay on their feet in footage with a plane overhead and a suitcase was swept into the sea.

Article continues below

"I've been here for 23 years and I've had customers since then, people keep coming all the time to do the same thing and watch," a shop owner in the area said.

Last year, sunbathers were filmed as they were sent flying on a beach by Princess Juliana Airport in St Maarten. The plane took off just 20m above their heads and sent down huge gusts of wind, scattering their belongings and knocking them to the ground.

The incident unfolded on Maho Beach which is located just yards from the runway. There are signs dotted around the area warning tourists to stay away - as the powerful jet blasts can cause 'severe physical harm and/or death'.

News.title: Warning issued to millions on atorvastatin for high cholesterol
News.content:
Warning issued to millions on atorvastatin for high cholesterol

Pharmaceutical expert explained serious side effects when mixed with certain other medications

View Image A pharmaceutical expert has said statins can react badly with other drugs (Image: Getty)

A pharmaceutical expert has explained the side effects and potential issues with other drugs which make some people concerned about taking one of the most prescribed medications in the UK. An estimated 7 to 8 million adults take prescribed statins in the UK, making them one of the most commonly dispensed medicines by the NHS.

‌



Data from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) shows that over 5.3 million people are prescribed these cholesterol-lowering drugs in England alone. A pharmacist has explained the potential impacts of side effects from key drugs like atorvastatin - but emphasised that overall the benefits far outweigh the issues - but also said people need to be wary to watch for potential problems - and go back to their GP immediately if they are spotted - so action can be taken.

‌



Writing on The Conversation website, Dipa Kamdar Senior Lecturer in Pharmacy Practice, Kingston University said: “Like all medicines, statins have side effects. Common ones include headache, digestive upset and dizziness. More serious but uncommon or rare effects include liver inflammation and muscle problems.

‌



“One such condition is myopathy, meaning muscle pain or weakness with raised levels of creatine kinase, an enzyme released when muscle tissue is damaged. In very rare cases, severe muscle breakdown known as rhabdomyolysis can occur.”

However overall among the population taking statins, Ms Kamdar said the main risks lie with other medication being take at the same time: “Large datasets show that most people tolerate statins well. When patients report muscle symptoms while taking statins, there is less than a 10% chance that the statin is actually the cause. Rhabdomyolysis is extremely rare, affecting only a few people per million users. The risk increases at very high doses or when statins are taken alongside medicines that interfere with how they are broken down.”

On blood sugar she explained: “Statins can also cause a small rise in blood glucose, mainly affecting people with prediabetes or diabetes. However, because statins substantially reduce heart attack risk in these groups, the overall benefit outweighs this modest increase. Most side effects are reversible once treatment is stopped, whereas damage from heart attacks or strokes can be permanent.”

‌



Drug interactions

Ms Kamdar said: “Drug interactions are another concern. Statins such as simvastatin and atorvastatin are broken down in the liver by enzymes known as CYP enzymes, particularly CYP3A4. When other medicines block these enzymes, statin levels in the blood can rise, increasing the risk of muscle-related side effects.

“Important interactions include antifungal medications such as ketoconazole, certain antibiotics like erythromycin, immunosuppressants such as ciclosporin, and some heart drugs including amiodarone and diltiazem.

“Even grapefruit can interfere with statin metabolism. It contains chemicals called furanocoumarins, which block CYP3A4 enzymes in the gut, allowing more statin to enter the bloodstream. Not all statins are affected to the same extent, so switching to a different statin could reduce this risk.”

‌



She said that statins are effective - but people need to actually change their lifestyles to handle cholesterol as well - and not just rely on medication. Losing weight it absolutely vital and is a ‘major cardiovascular risk factor’. Ms Kamdar said a review found that combining diet and exercise reduced body weight, improved cholesterol levels and lowered cardiometabolic risk: it reduces factors linked to heart disease and type 2 diabetes.

National guidelines recommend reducing saturated fat intake to help lower LDL cholesterol. Saturated fats are commonly found in butter, fatty meats and processed foods. Replacing them with unsaturated fats, such as those found in olive oil, nuts and seeds, can improve cholesterol levels. Shifting towards plant-based proteins like beans, lentils and soy may also reduce reliance on red and processed meats.

Research shows that higher fibre consumption is associated with better cholesterol levels and lower heart disease risk. Ms Kamdar added: “Ultimately, treatment decisions should be personalised, balancing cardiovascular risk, the proven benefits of statins, potential side effects and what lifestyle change is realistically achievable.

Article continues below

“Statins have transformed cardiovascular care and saved millions of lives. Yet they remain controversial. Addressing poor diet, physical inactivity and obesity remains central to reducing the burden of heart disease in the long term.” To read the full article, click here.

News.title: Simon Levy victim reveals her 'nightmare' as killer sex offender left to roam streets
News.content:
Simon Levy victim reveals her 'nightmare' as killer sex offender left to roam streets

A woman who was sexually assaulted by killer sex offender Simon Levy on the way to Notting Hill Carnival said she suffered 'nightmares' after discovering he was still preying on women

View 4 Images Laura said her nightmare became 'real life' (Image: BBC)

A woman attacked by double murderer Simon Levy has told how her nightmare became 'real life' when she found out he was 'still out preying on vulnerable women' years after her own ordeal.

Laura was one of two women who reported being sexually assaulted by Levy in 2018 after she met him on the way to Notting Hill Carnival. He was jailed for both assaults in 2021 but continued to prey on women following his release in 2023, before his violence escalated to two murders.

Police repeatedly failed to stop him after what a victims' advocacy group described as a "litany of failures", including releasing him on bail and downgrading his risk as a sex offender from high to medium.

View 4 Images Simon Levy, 40, will be sentenced today (Image: Metropolitan Police/PA Wire)

Earlier this year, Levy was convicted of 11 counts of sexual assault between 2022 and 2025, with 10 victims being young women using the Tube and London Overground and the 11th a prison officer he assaulted whilst behind bars. Last week, Levy was found guilty of murdering grandmother Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in March 2025 and mother-of-four Sheryl Wilkins, 39, five months later as well as raping a third woman in a brutal attack in January that year. He will be sentenced today.

In an interview with the BBC, Laura criticised the police's handling of her case, saying she believed she was "doing the right thing" in reporting Levy, adding: "I thought I was doing it to protect other women from someone like that." "I feel really let down by the police. I feel really disappointed," she added.

View 4 Images Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, and Sheryl Wilkins, 40, were killed by Levy (Image: PA)

Laura told the BBC that when she tried to report the crime to police, she was turned away. She claimed that two Metropolitan Police officers told her they "were busy with other, more urgent, things". A female officer eventually took her details, she told the broadcaster. Levy was not arrested for the two attacks in 2018 until the following October, and was formally charged in July 2020. Describing her attacker, Laura who the BBC said has waived her right to anonymity, said: "He's evil. My instincts were right. My instincts not to go and get on trains have always been right then because I just think to myself he's been roaming loose. It's almost like my nightmare is in real life." "What I would think about, dream about, nightmares about was actually happening," she continued. "He was actually still out preying on vulnerable women."

View 4 Images Police have been accused of a 'litany of failings' in the Levy case (Image: PA)

Asked whether there needs to be a change in how the government and society deals with violence against women and girls, Laura said: "They need to look at everything, all of it, because they could have prevented so many women from being hurt. They could have prevented two women from losing their lives." Jobless Levy's crime spree spanned from 2018 to 2025 and included myriad sex attacks and two killings, as the Metropolitan Police, the British Transport Police (BTP) and the courts failed to stop him. The Met, BTP and Crown Prosecution Service have all admitted failings in how they dealt with Levy, who was on bail as his attacks on women escalated to double murder. Laura said the impact of the attack had "never gone away completely" and it had changed her life "completely".

She continued: "I was hysterical. All I remember is crying, and my friend was trying to make sense of what had gone on. There was a lot more things they could have done to make me feel supported."

After last week's conviction, a senior police officer who led the investigation into Levy urged any more survivors of the serial predator to come forward.

Article continues below

Following the verdict, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had served a gross misconduct notice on a Met Police constable and a misconduct notice on a detective sergeant. The Metropolitan Police have been contacted for comment.

News.title: Solar eclipse weather verdict from Met Office as view may be blocked for millions
News.content:
Solar eclipse weather verdict from Met Office as view may be blocked for millions

Some parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland may miss out on the eclipse later today due to a weather front moving in, Met Office forecasters have warned

View 2 Images The solar eclipse will take place later today (stock) (Image: Getty Images)

Some regions may miss out on this evening's solar eclipse, but there should be plenty of Brits who get an "excellent" view.

‌



Although the eclipse should be visible across the UK, cloud cover could obstruct the view. A weather front is expected to push into the northwest later today, with rain on the cards in Northern Ireland and Scotland.

‌



The Met Office published a map showing where is likely to have clear skies between 6pm and 8pm, when the eclipse is due to take place. The event will peak at just after 7pm, although the exact timings vary depending on location - and can be seen here.

‌



The map shows southern parts of England and Wales should have an “excellent” view of the eclipse.

View 2 Images The Met Office's map showing where will have the best view of the eclipse (Image: Met Office)

Solar eclipse glasses sell out on Amazon for Wednesday – four other ways to view READ MORE :

Next solar eclipse in UK after August 12 is in 2027 - every eclipse date listed READ MORE :

North Wales, northern England and southern Scotland can expect “good” conditions, whereas visibility will likely be “low to moderate” in Northern Ireland and the rest of Scotland.

‌



The Met Office has said eastern areas like Aberdeenshire, Angus and Moray are most likely to have clear skies in Scotland. In an updated forecast, it also said there may be breaks in cloud cover in the central belt and southern Scotland.

In total, there are 23 counties in the “excellent” region on the Met Office's map. They are all in either England or Wales.

It states: "Dry and sunny for most with very little cloud around. Patchy cloud and a few showers for northern England and Northern Ireland. Heavier spells of rain for north-western Scotland, possibly thundery."

Article continues below

Warning ahead of solar eclipse

This evening will bring the first near-total eclipse to the UK since 1999, and will be the last chance to see one until 2081.

Safety-approved solar eclipse glasses have been selling out online. And consumers have been warned against using “knock-off” glasses instead. Eye doctors have also urged people to avoid looking directly at the Sun, with even brief exposure causing lasting vision damage.

Only special solar eclipse glasses that are ISO 12312-2 certified for the safest eye protection should be used, experts say. Glasses that do not carry the safety standards, or ordinary sunglasses, should never be used as they reduce glare, making it feel more comfortable to look at the Sun for longer, but still allowing harmful solar radiation to reach the retina.

News.title: Boy swept out to sea survives after using swimming skill he'd learnt only days before
News.content:
Boy swept out to sea survives after using swimming skill he'd learnt only days before

Clayton Garforth, eight, survived after being swept out to sea by a sudden swell off the Mull of Kintyre - he used a lifesaving swimming technique he'd learnt only a few days before

View 2 Images Eight-year-old Clayton Garforth survived by using a lifesaving swimming technique (Image: Maritime and Coastguard Agency)

A quick-thinking eight-year-old boy who was suddenly swept out to sea has told how he stayed alive by using a lifesaving swimming technique he learnt at school only a few days before.

‌



Clayton Garforth was paddling near Westport beach on the Mull of Kintyre on July 18 when a sudden swell took him off his feet and away from shore. He had arrived at the beach with his mum, Dannie, dad, Damon, both 29, and sister Faye, 11, only 10 minutes earlier.

‌



His parents said the sea had been calm until he got in - and have been left suffering "nightmares" about what they saw next.

‌



View 2 Images His family said he had only just entered the water when a sudden swell took him from shore (Image: Maritime and Coastguard Agency)

Clayton, from Tarbert, Argyll and Bute, told the Daily Record: "I was getting further away in the water. I was screaming."

Dannie and Damon said: "We're still having nightmares about it. We aren't good swimmers so if we ended up out there with him, we could've all been in trouble.

‌



"Every time we tried to get to him we got pushed back in and he was pushed further away. He was standing on some shallow sand at one point and we thought he was okay and then it would suddenly get deeper."

People on land immediately called 999 and alerted the Coastguard - but, thankfully, Clayton exactly knew what to do.

The youngster had learned a lifesaving lesson from Tarbert Coastguard Rescue Team (CRT) who had visited his school, Tarbert Academy, at the start of summer.

‌



There, they caught pupils about what to do in an emergency - float to live.

Clayton, who wants to be a medic when he grows up, said: "I remembered to float and not use up my energy."

Damon added: "I was keeping my eyes on him and was shouting for him to float on his back – but he knew what to do before I did."

‌



While Clayton kept himself above water, tracked carefully by his parents from the shore, HM Coastguard sent out a rescue team, and two RNLI lifeboats were dispatched to the scene.

An HM Coastguard helicopter also flew to support. Before the rescuers arrived, however, Clayton was safely helped out of the sea by a father-and-son pair of surfers.

He was taken to hospital, being freezing cold and having swallowed water, but was discharged the next day.

‌



Asked what he would tell other children when heading to the coast this summer, he said: "Be careful near big waves. Stay safe."

David Graham, Coastal Operations Area Commander, said: "Well done to Clayton for reacting so sensibly to such a sudden, scary incident. It shows how quickly an emergency can begin but also the best way to respond.

"I'm very proud of Tarbert CRT for teaching the lifesaving Float to Live advice that kept Clayton safe and gave him the best chance of survival. By saving his energy, he gave time for rescue and for crews to respond to the 999 call."

Article continues below

The Mirror has launched the Save Lives For Sam water safety campaign to tackle the UK's growing drowning crisis. Backed by MPs, Olympic champions, national water safety organisations and bereaved families, the campaign is calling for urgent action to make our waters safer.

That includes compulsory water safety lessons in schools, a nationwide public awareness campaign, better lifesaving equipment at high-risk waterways, the introduction of Sam's Law, and a dedicated Minister for Water Safety. Find out more about the campaign and how you can support it here.

News.title: Three ways to watch the solar eclipse safely without glasses
News.content:
With most online orders not able to arrive in time and shops running out of stock, it may be too late to buy eclipse glasses for Wednesday evening.

But you can still safely watch the spectacle using some household items.

People in the UK will see a partial eclipse - rather than the total eclipse that will be seen in parts of Spain, Greenland and Iceland - but it is the country's most significant eclipse since 1999.

Experts say enthusiasts should not look directly at the Sun without specialist glasses.

And you shouldn't be tempted to try using sunglasses or dark goggles instead.

They often don't give enough UV protection when looking directly at the Sun and you could end up seriously damaging your eyesight, according to The Royal Astronomical Society.

Here are some viewing methods to try instead.

News.title: Woman attacked by Simon Levy feels betrayed he was allowed to attack more women
News.content:
A woman who was attacked by double murderer Simon Levy eight years ago has told the BBC the police made her nightmare "real life" by letting him go on to kill and attack more women.

Laura, whose surname we are not using, said she had been trying to protect other women by reporting Levy in 2018, but feels betrayed by what he was later allowed to do after being released from jail.

Levy was convicted on Friday of murdering Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo and Sheryl Wilkins and raping another woman in London in 2025. He will be sentenced on Wednesday.

He was also convicted earlier this year of sexually assaulting 11 other women, 10 of them on trains and the Tube in London between 2023 and 2025.

Police, prosecutors and the courts made a series of disastrous decisions that left Levy free. He attacked 14 more women before being taken off the streets, despite being a sex offender who was monitored by the Met Police.

Levy was a registered sex offender because he sexually assaulted Laura â and a separate victim - in summer 2018.

Laura says that Levy is "evil" and that his attack "completely changed my life".

But she now realises that what she would "think about, dream about, have nightmares about was actually happening - he was actually still out preying on vulnerable women".

Waiving her anonymity, she said she had been trying to protect other women by ensuring that Levy was jailed.

"I feel like when I reported it, I was doing the right thing and I thought I was doing it to protect other women.

"I feel absolutely devastated for all of those women that have been affected by him â and the families."

Laura says she feels let down by the whole criminal justice system including the Met Police, the courts and judges who bailed Levy, as well as the Crown Prosecution Service.

"They're all as guilty for allowing him to continue to do what he was doing", she says.

"They could have prevented so many women from being hurt.

"They could have prevented two women from losing their lives."

News.title: Burnham to chair Cobra meeting on extreme heat as temperatures surge again
News.content:
The Cobra meeting will be attended by ministers from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, Home Office, and Department for Health, as well as the Environment Agency.

It will be the second Cobra meeting this year on heatwaves, after one took place amid high temperatures in June.

A spokesperson for No 10 said this summer was proving "challenging" in the UK, particularly for "firefighters tackling wildfires, farmers working in drought conditions, and NHS staff in busy A&E units".

"We will continue to take the action needed to keep communities safe, protect water supplies and safeguard the environment," they said.

The hottest weather this week is expected on Thursday across the Midlands, Eastern England, London and south-east England, Yorkshire and Humber.

Temperatures could potentially reach 38C which would equal the highest temperature of the summer so far recorded at Lingwood in Norfolk on 26 June.

This would be the hottest August day since 2003, when 38.5C was recorded.

It is also likely to be the fourth calendar month this year to record 35C or more, which is unprecedented.

On Monday, drought officials declared 71.3% of England in drought, meaning there are a total of 45 million people now living in a drought area, with more than 27 million facing water use restrictions.

Firefighters have responded to 966 wildfires across England and Wales this year, including 185 in the first 10 days of August, and 458 in July, according to the National Fire Chiefs Council.

A fire in the New Forest has been burning since Sunday, which started after a van caught fire on the A31 near Ringwood.

Last week, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the NHS should be "preparing for summer pressures now in the same way we prepare for winter".

She told LBC Radio plans were in place to respond to higher numbers of people coming in to A&E.

On Tuesday, the Met Office said this summer is on course to be the UK's hottest since records began, with the mean temperature currently at 16.48C set to surpass the figure set just last year.

This is in line with evidence that summers are getting hotter and are likely to become drier because of climate change.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski said the Cobra meeting was just a first step, and a "climate emergency" had led to hundreds of deaths and was "stretching our firefighters, health staff and farmers to the limit".

He called for "concrete action" and said he looked forward to hearing how Burnham intended to "prepare for the threats to come".

News.title: Early release scheme risks more serious crimes, probation chief warns
News.content:
The chief inspector of probation for England and Wales has told the BBC the early release of thousands of prisoners could lead to "a serious sexual or violent offence or even murder" because of the demands on probation staff to monitor offenders.

The government is set to release 5,000 offenders from October as part of new laws to create more space in overcrowded prisons.

Probation officers supervise offenders after prison sentences and check they follow the terms of their release, such as sticking to curfews and not taking drugs.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said "protecting the public is our top priority", adding it had invested in probation and hiring trainee officers.

But Martin Jones, His Majesty's Chief Inspector of probation for England and Wales, told the BBC that "ultimately I'm not fully confident that the probation system will be able to cope with this massive work and there's a risk that things will go wrong".

"Probation services are already under unprecedented pressure.

"I mean, they're managing a caseload of 258,000 cases, that's nearly three times the number that are in our prisons, and obviously the early release scheme will be increasing that pressure considerably."

On Tuesday, 50 police chiefs across the UK signed a letter to the prime minister urging him to pursue "every legal option" to prevent the early release of PC Andrew Harper's killers under the scheme.

They called for called for greater consideration of victims when prisoners have their sentences altered, adding: "Families across the country are now facing the distress of learning that offenders may be released earlier than they understood when sentence was passed."

They also welcomed Burnham's intervention on Tuesday, when he said he was "confident" the early release of Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were jailed for 13 years for manslaughter in 2020, in January could be stopped.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp told BBC Breakfast the early release plans had "put public safety at risk as well as disrespecting victims and undermining confidence in the criminal justice system".

He urged Burnham to "pay attention and listen" to the senior police officers, adding he had "never seen every chief constable in the country write to the prime minister directly in this way".

Philip and Nick Timothy, the Conservative shadow justice secretary, wrote to Burnham on Tuesday urging him to introduce emergency primary legislation in September to amend the Sentencing Act 2026.

The letter said grooming gang perpetrators, including those convicted of indecent assault, and those convicted of the manslaughter of an emergency worker should be exempt from the early release scheme.

News.title: Serious failings found in new military crimes unit, leaked report finds
News.content:
A leaked Ministry of Defence (MoD) report, obtained by the BBC, has highlighted serious failings in a new military command set up to investigate the most severe crimes, including rape and sexual assault.

The Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC) was launched after the death of 19-year-old Gunner Jaysley Beck. An inquest found the Army's mishandling of sexual assault and harassment complaints made by Beck contributed to her taking her own life, and exposed "systemic failings".

However, an internal review highlighted ongoing concerns with the unit and warned the military still risks failing victims.

The MoD said the findings had been accepted and significant work has been undertaken since.

The DSCC was created in 2022 to investigate serious crimes independently, outside the military's chain of command.

However, the BBC can reveal that an internal review, which was carried out between 21 August 2025 and 12 November 2025 and overseen by a former senior civilian police officer, concluded that if the DSCC was subjected to scrutiny similar to civilian police forces there would be "a significant risk of (it) being graded as inadequate".

In a statement, the MoD said the review was commissioned "to provide honest challenge, identify areas of improvement and to help ensure the highest standards for victims and witnesses".

It added that following the findings, the DSCC had carried out significant work "including further investment in victim and witness support, strengthening governance and safeguarding arrangements and accrediting investigators to nationally recognised policing standards".

The DSCC was committed to transparency, continuous improvement and ensuring victims receive the support and service they deserve, the statement continued.

News.title: Homes near pylons to get £250 a year off energy bills – first sites revealed
News.content:
UK Energy Minister Michael Shanks told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast the UK's power infrastructure had undergone decades of "woeful underinvestment".

He said he understood the objections of those living nearby, but added the pylons were "crucial" to ensure the National Grid maintained future resilience.

"I totally accept that people might not like that, but it is critical national infrastructure and it has to be built somewhere," he said.

"Building any kind of infrastructure in these communities does cause disruption. But that doesn't mean we shouldn't build any kind of infrastructure and I'm afraid in this country, for too long, we have taken that view, and the result is that we have been held back by not having the infrastructure the country needs."

Shanks added: "Either we go through decades of not upgrading the grid and take the risk that the grid will actually fail, but we also lose the opportunity of cheaper bills, homegrown power connecting.

"We're not prepared to take that risk."

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero says Britain's electricity grid was largely designed for an era when power came from coal and gas-fired power stations, and now needs major upgrades to cope with growing amounts of renewable energy.

Ministers say the lack of capacity means some wind farms are sometimes paid to switch off because there is not enough network infrastructure available to carry the electricity to homes and businesses that need it.

Greg Jackson, chief executive of the UK's biggest domestic energy supplier, Octopus Energy, said the electricity system is inefficient, brittle and expensive.

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the discount scheme was a "positive first step", adding that last year the UK spent more than Â£1bn paying wind farms to turn off on windy days.

"We should just be giving that electricity more cheaply to the people and businesses who live in the areas where we're generating it," he said.

"By doing that, you'd be able to stop wasting that money and instead put the electricity to use cutting bills for those people. But crucially cutting bills for everybody else as well because it's less wasteful."

News.title: Watch: British driver who broke sound barrier sets new speed record
News.content:
A British driver who was the first person to break the sound barrier in a car on land has set a new speed record, this time in a hydrogen-powered vehicle.

Andy Green, a 64-year-old retired Royal Air Force pilot, reached a speed of 406mph (654km/h) at the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah, the fastest a hydrogen-powered car has ever travelled.

Green's record was measured as an average of two runs in a car powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines, with a combined 1,600 brake horsepower (bhp).

In 1997, Green drove the jet-powered ThrustSSC across Nevada's Black Rock Desert at 763mph (1,228km/h), making him the first, and still the only person, to break the sound barrier on land.

News.title: How the weather will affect your viewing
News.content:
One of the most spectacular solar eclipses the UK has seen for decades is taking place on Wednesday 12 August.

From around 18:00 BST, the Moon will begin moving across the face of the Sun, creating a partial solar eclipse across the UK.

At its peak, around 90% of the Sun will be covered from London. In Cornwall, as much as 95% of the Sun could be obscured.

Depending on where you are in the UK, it will peak between 19:02 and 19:16 BST.

News.title: Scotland's public spending deficit falls as tax take rises
News.content:
Scotland's public spending deficit fell by Â£600m last year to Â£25.3bn after an increase in the amount raised in taxes, figures show.

The annual Government Expenditure and Revenue Scotland (Gers) report compares the tax raised in Scotland with public spending for and on behalf of Scotland.

It said that revenue had grown by Â£6.3bn to Â£98.3bn, an increase of 6.9%, while there was a slower growth in expenditure, which rose by Â£5.7bn to Â£123.6bn - an increase of 4.8%.

The largest increases in revenue came from national insurance contributions, which were up by Â£2.4bn, and income tax receipts, up by Â£1.5bn.

The expenditure of Â£123.6bn is the amount spent by the Scottish, UK and local governments north of the border - as well as a share of spending on shared provision such as defence and debt.

News.title: PM admits cost of living help is not enough and hints at further support
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he accepts his announcements aimed at tackling the cost of living are not enough on their own and hinted at further support.

Burnham told BBC's Wake up to Money he will deliver an "accumulation of smaller things" that "combine to take the pressure down" on household budgets.

He spoke of an overhaul of train fares and "more public control" of energy, water and housing but did not give details on how he would bring this about.

Burnham has made a number of announcements to help people with the cost of living since taking office, including the removal of VAT from domestic electricity bills and bringing forward an already planned end to 'subscription traps'.

Asked whether the changes he had announced were not significant to people struggling, he said: "I can accept criticism that this isn't enough, because I wouldn't say it's enough.

"But I take an approach to politics where I do what I can, when I can. Just take that little bit of pressure off and address an issue that you know needs addressing.

"It's not the end of the story," he added.

The prime minister, who is embarking on a tour of the UK while Parliament is in recess, said he believed "more public control of essential services" such as water, energy and housing, "would mean we could get to a more substantial answer to the cost of living crisis".

On water, he said it would not be easy to reverse the privatisation of water companies in England and Wales that took place in the 1980s.

"But very much, I'm looking at what can be done. Same with energy."

He also said that, following the return of rail operators to public ownership, he wanted to "remodel the rail fares so that we can get more public benefit for people".

It comes as the government said on Wednesday that people living within 1,600ft (500m) of new upgraded electricity pylons and substations across Britain will receive a Â£250 annual discount on their bills for a decade.

News.title: Children as young as nine hurt in growing number of e-scooter crashes
News.content:
Most of the incidents in Manchester, Liverpool and Sheffield involved private e-scooters, often on public roads, pavements or footpaths, despite that being illegal.

Private e-scooters are meant only for use on private land, with the owner's permission.

Half of the children injured were aged between 10 and 13. Nearly two-thirds were boys.

Most injuries were sustained by the rider - only 5% were pedestrians that had been hit by an e-scooter - and the most common cause was falling off the e-scooter.

Around 11% were collisions with a vehicle, which was often linked to more serious injuries.

Injuries to the arms and legs were the most common, followed by head or facial injuries.

The doctors say tougher laws are urgently needed. Helmet use is not mandatory in the UK, unlike some other countries.

Some have described the private e-scooter situation in the UK as the "Wild West" with few following any rules.

The researchers told the Emergency Medicine Journal that schools, local councils, youth groups and road safety campaigns all have a role to play.

"Clearly, reporting these accidents is important to influence and change policy, but there must also be an onus on retailers to clearly advise customers of the law, and policymakers to regulate private e-scooters, such as with speed limiters, or mandate helmet use," they say.

To legally rent an e-scooter in the UK, which can be used on roads and cycle lanes, you must be at least 16 and hold a full or provisional driving licence, and the rental company must provide appropriate insurance. Rental e-scooters typically have a limited top speed of around 15mph.

A Department for Transport spokesperson said: "These are concerning findings, and our thoughts are with anyone who has been injured on our roads.

"It is illegal for private e-scooters to be used on roads, pavements or in other public spaces, including by under 16s, and we're bringing forward new laws to make their use safe and legal, including consulting on requirements like helmets."

News.title: Lost village revealed as drought lowers water levels
News.content:
The remains of a lost village that was demolished and flooded to create a reservoir have been revealed as the country continues to face drought conditions.

Low water levels at the Rutland Water reservoir have uncovered buildings, which were once part of the village of Nether Hambleton.

Residents, along with other small villages including Middle Hambleton, were relocated to other areas before the buildings were demolished and the area flooded in the 1970s to create the reservoir.

The creation of the reservoir, which involved damming the Gwash valley near Empingham, was finished in 1976 and flooding took a further three years, Leicestershire and Rutland Wildlife Trust said.

News.title: Poorest areas should not house all asylum seekers, says Burnham
News.content:
Labour has pledged to stop using asylum hotels, a costly form of accommodation that has become a focal point for anti-migrant protests.

The government has sought to house migrants at military sites across the country instead, announcing in June that it planned to open three more including the site in Bicester, Oxfordshire.

The plans have prompted protests there, with residents of nearby Piddington voting to stage a symbolic referendum on leaving the UK.

Burnham said on Tuesday that he would listen to and address the concerns being raised.

"I don't know the issue yet in detail, but in some ways, as I understand it, it is about creating secure space," he said.

"We understand people's concerns and I will look into the issues raised by the good people of Piddington."

But he added: "I do believe all parts of the country need to work, to play their part."

After winning the Makerfield by-election in June, Burnham promised to end "HMO Britain" and said he would change Britain's asylum accommodation system.

HMOs, or houses in multiple occupation, have been widely used by government contractors to house asylum seekers, often in lower income, urban areas.

Speaking on BBC Breakfast on Wednesday morning, immigration minister Anna Turley said the number of hotels had gone from a peak of 400 under the Conservatives to 160 under Labour, and pledged all of them would close by 2029.

Turley said the government had already saved Â£1bn by closing hotels and opening alternative, secure sites for asylum seekers, including two former military bases, student accommodation and former industrial sites around the country.

"I think this is about fairness and we won't be asking anybody to take more than they can, and we won't be asking anyone to take more than their fair share," she said.

"What we've seen in the past is places like Blackpool, and other communities around the country where housing is perhaps cheaper and more plentiful, have had to take more than their fair share of asylum seekers," she added.

"That's put a huge burden on local communities and created real civil unrest, so we want to make sure that we're managing the system much better in a more sustained way that's reducing the impact on local communities.

"It's important that everybody plays their fair share in that, and it's about making sure that no one community is more over-pressured or overburdened than others."

Last week, there were anti-immigration demonstrations in the town of Thetford, Norfolk, with protesters attempting to enter homes where they believed asylum seekers were living.

In response to Burnham's interview, Philp reiterated the Conservatives' policy of leaving the European Convention on Human Rights in order to deport migrants to their country of origin or a safe third country.

"Andy Burnham just doesn't get it," he wrote on X.

"Illegal immigrants should all be deported within a week of arrival - to their country of origin or a safe third country like Rwanda."

Government statistics, external showed there were 97,519 people in receipt of asylum support at the end of March, with 20,885 in hotel accommodation.

The figures added that 72,768 people were in other accommodation, including "dispersal accommodation" - which normally means houses in the community.

The remaining 3,866 people were in receipt of subsistence support only, according to the government.

The regions and nations with the highest number of asylum seekers in receipt of Home Office support included 19,578 in the north-west of England, 13,687 in London, 11,969 in the West Midlands and 8,635 in Yorkshire and the Humber.

The Home Office said the regions with the most supported asylum seekers as a proportion of their overall population were the north-east and north-west of England, with 26 and 25 supported people per 10,000 residents respectively.

It added the local authorities with the highest numbers of supported asylum seekers within them were Glasgow city (3,870), Birmingham (2,142), Liverpool (2,053), Coventry (1,712) and Belfast (1,607).

Burnham, during his time serving as the mayor of Greater Manchester, threatened to block the region from housing any more asylum seekers in 2018.

He complained about the government's dispersal system and said Greater Manchester's public services could not continue to support "disproportionate" numbers of people compared with elsewhere in the country.

Burnham at the time said the north-west of England was hosting 25% of the national population of asylum applicants who require housing and support - with Greater Manchester housing 70% of the region's numbers.

The then-Home Secretary Sajid Javid replied by promising to work towards a fairer distribution.

News.title: Boy, four, taken to hospital after fake squishy toy explodes in his face
News.content:
A mum says she feels "guilty" for buying a fake squishy toy that exploded in her son's face, resulting in him needing hospital treatment.

Jodanna Bevan bought the toys from Shein for her children after seeing them discounted.

Hudson, four, was squeezing his when it "popped and exploded all over his face", with Jodanna describing the filling as a "thick white substance" with a sandy texture.

While his bloodshot eyes "seemed OK" after washing them, Jodanna said by the next morning they were extremely swollen and he was unable to open them, so she took Hudson to hospital.

Shein said it took the claims seriously and the product was no longer available on its platform.

Hudson needed water flushed through each eye to correct their pH balance, and Jodanna, from Bridgend, said it was "horrendous as a parent to watch him go through that".

She said Hudson's vision was damaged but he was given eye drops to fix it.

Hudson, like children across the UK, was drawn to the toys after they became a sensation on TikTok, Instagram and YouTube.

They often resemble dumplings, but children "can't see what's inside the box so they're excited to see which one they get".

News.title: Criticism as thousands of seats empty at Europeans Athletics Championships
News.content:
Nearly 10,000 seats were empty at Birmingham's Alexander Stadium for the European Athletics Championships on Monday evening.

A crowd of 13,623 watched as Britain's 24-year-old sprinter Amy Hunt stormed to her first senior international title, in a stadium that has a capacity of 23,000.

Athletics supporters blamed ticket prices, with some describing them as "extortionate", while BBC commentator Steve Cram commented that spectator numbers were a "little disappointing".

But Birmingham 2026 organisers said they were "delighted" with ticket sales, which have "far surpassed" their targets with "Friday, Saturday and Sunday evening sessions approaching sell-out, with several other sessions close to capacity".

On Monday, Category A tickets for the home straight cost Â£150 with no concessions for juniors.

For the men's 100m final on Tuesday, those same seats cost Â£110, again with no concessions - while a similar ticket for the same final in Rome two years ago was 88 euros (Â£75).

It is Britain's first time hosting the championships in their 92-year history.

News.title: Man guilty of harassing MP Stella Creasy on Tube train
News.content:
A 63-year-old man has been found guilty of harassing the Labour MP for Walthamstow after preventing her from leaving a Tube carriage and behaving in an "abusive and aggressive" manner.

Clifford Wilby, from east London, targeted Stella Creasy on a Victoria line train between Walthamstow Central and Finsbury Park on 15 July last year.

Westminster Magistrates' Court heard how Wilby spoke to Creasy about knife crime and her "failings as a Member of Parliament" before filming her, leading to members of the public intervening.

Deputy Chief Magistrate Tan Ikram found Wilby guilty of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour with intent to cause harassment, alarm or distress.

Wilby and Creasy first met during a Zoom meeting in 2024 as part of her role as an MP.

She said he started to make a complaint about a constituent and she reminded him that she could not discuss somebody else's case.

Creasy said he had "made a series of very serious allegations", became abusive and "referred to the fact he had been diagnosed as a psychopath".

The meeting was stopped because of Wilby's behaviour.
