The Trump administration is facing backlash after transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced 2,000 video gamers have been hired to serve as air traffic controllers.

Duffy first unveiled the plan to meet the national shortfall this spring and recently took to social media with an update revealing the recruitment drive had been a success.

“In April, we launched a NEW CAMPAIGN to recruit video gamers as air traffic controllers – and supercharged the entire hiring process to get the BEST & BRIGHTEST in faster. The results are HISTORIC.”

Duffy said the 2,000 appointments so far was the most in a single year, adding that a further 2,000 were “in the pipeline”. His post was accompanied by a video compilation of testimonials from some of the new hires expressing their excitement about passing their interviews and getting down to work.

open image in gallery Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has announced that 2,000 new air traffic controllers have been hired this year after reaching out to gamers with transferable skills ( Getty )

In announcing the policy, the Federal Aviation Administration explained its reasoning behind the new approach by saying: “With only about 25 percent of controllers holding a traditional college degree, this effort is focused on reaching talented young people pursuing alternative career paths, many of whom are active in gaming.

“Feedback from controller exit interviews reinforces this, with several controllers pointing to gaming as an influence on their ability to think quickly, stay focused, and manage complexity.”

Michael O’Donnell, an aerospace consultant and former FAA official, sounded a note of caution at the time, commenting: “When you bring on someone who has gaming experience, particularly with air traffic control, they have an edge up.

“They’re coming in with a skill set. But it doesn’t replace aptitude, or discipline, or decision making under pressure.”

His concern is now being widely shared in response to Duffy’s announcement about the hiring spree.

“Just one problem…. If they f*** up people die,” one person responded to the secretary’s video. “They can’t just restart a new game.”

“Great thinking,” another said. “One failure mode: Be sure a culture of responsible sleep is created. Don’t want planes falling out of the sky when GTA 6 releases or a new WoW [World of Warcraft] expansion comes out.”

open image in gallery Duffy’s plan to address the national shortfall has been met with public skepticism ( Getty )

Another claiming to have prior experience of working in air traffic control wrote: “As someone with experience in the job, I can tell you that how many you hire doesn’t mean a damn thing.

“It’s how many actually make it through and get certified at their facilities. It’s a very difficult job.”

However, the reaction to Duffy’s post was largely positive, with the more critical commentators shouted down as “Debbie Downers” and “Negative Nellys.”

Among those expressing support for the policy were the billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman and actress Justine Bateman.

“BRILLIANT move to hire YOUNG MEN into stable, well-paying positions,” one person wrote. “As any nation should. Note that it took a Gen Xer to launch this program. A boomer would never.”

“This is creativity in government hiring, love to see it,” applauded another.

The Independent has reached out to the Department of Transportation and FAA for comment.

As millions of Europeans prepare to watch tonight’s solar eclipse, one airline has published a list of the best flights offering passengers a front-row seat.

With Spain falling into the “path of totality”, a narrow corridor where the moon blocks the sun completely, Jet2 has identified 10 scheduled flights operating tonight that promise breathtaking eclipse views.

While views will depend on weather, flight schedules, seat position and final routing, passengers on the following flights are in with a good chance of an impressive show.

The 8.15pm LS1836 service from Ibiza to Bristol is expected to pass closest to the path of totality over northern Spain and the Bay of Biscay, giving holidaymakers one of the strongest chances of seeing the total eclipse from the air, with customers expected to enjoy stunning views.

Passengers on the 7.05pm LS874 service from Faro to Manchester could also fly through a high-coverage eclipse zone, with potential views over western Portugal.

And those boarding the 6pm LS1892 flight from Tenerife South to Bristol could get close to one of the highest-coverage areas as the aircraft travels towards north-west Spain.

Other services listed include:

LS1130 Agadir Al-Massira to Birmingham International, scheduled to depart at 8pm local time

LS274 Alicante to Leeds Bradford, scheduled to depart at 8.25pm local time

LS266 Málaga to Leeds Bradford, scheduled to depart at 8.35pm local time

LS228 Palma de Mallorca to Leeds Bradford, scheduled to depart at 8.40pm local time

LS258 Palma de Mallorca to Leeds Bradford, scheduled to depart at 9pm local time

LS3286 Zante Zakynthos to Liverpool, scheduled to depart at 9pm local time

David Hills, chief customer officer at Jet2, said: “The solar eclipse is already creating real excitement, and some of our customers could be in a very special position to see it from the skies or on their holidays.

“It could be a brilliant once-in-a-lifetime moment for those on board our flights or in some of our destinations, and we cannot wait to see the photos that our customers and colleagues capture.”

Spanish airline Iberia has revealed that it plans to livestream the total solar eclipse from 10,000 metres in the air by chartering a special flight to observe the astronomical event high in the sky.

While the flight is not open to general passengers, footage will be shared from the flight on its social media channels.

An extraordinary case of police mistaking a sex doll in a suitcase for ahuman corpse – complete with lifelike bruises and grazes – has shocked Australia and raised questions about how such a bizarre mistake could have gone unnoticed for more than 20 hours.

Police insisted that investigators followed proper procedures, taking painstaking steps to avoid contaminating the suspected body or the suitcase before reaching their final conclusion.

New South Wales police responded to a call in Oallen, a ⁠town about 200km southwest of Sydney, on Sunday after two members of the public found a suitcase dumped on a roadside. They opened it ⁠and found what they suspected were human remains.

Later that day, police said they believed it was a woman’s body and sent the case for forensic testing, which determined on Monday that the item ⁠was “a lifelike ‌doll wearing clothing, with hair and a nose piercing".

"The item ‌also had markings that resembled bruises and grazes," the police said in ‌a statement.

open image in gallery Police personnel handle a bag covered in plastic containing a lifelike doll ( Reuters )

The police claimed that investigators had decided to examine the bag and its contents at a mortuary and not at the remote Oallen crime scene to avoid potentially losing fragile forensic evidence.

Dr Xanthe Weston, a forensic expert at the University of Newcastle said the roughly 20-hour timeframe was “not extraordinary” and was expected from a forensic perspective.

“So, whilst it seems almost ridiculous that a doll could be mistaken for a human, I can totally see how that could have happened and the police did absolutely the right thing," the expert told the ABC. “Not disturbing that scene and making sure that it wasn’t forensically relevant rather than destroying the scene, suspecting it could be a doll. So they actually followed protocol."

Had it been a body, she noted, disturbing it could have destroyed crucial evidence such as fibres, hair, skin cells, and DNA.

open image in gallery Heads for silicone sex dolls are seen on racks in the production area at a factory for WM Dolls ( Getty )

Modern lifelike dolls were quite convincing as the market demanded realism, Dr Weston said, adding that she had examined both adult and childlike ones professionally.

She cautioned that the “bruise and graze” markings were not necessarily intentional and could simply represent dirt or damage interpreted as injuries by investigators who assumed human remains.

The best practice for potential bodies in containers like suitcases or wheelie bins was not to open them fully – since doing so could destroy fibres, blood or other evidence on zippers – but to X-ray them, Paola Magni, a forensic science associate professor at Murdoch University, said.

In this particular case, she said, examiners would continue checking the doll for traces like semen or DNA in case it was linked to another crime.

“It’s a doll, but if it’s connected to another crime, they can use that opportunity to link it to something suspect,” Ms Magni, an expert in decomposition, told the Guardian.

“Any potentially suspicious situation has to be treated with the best practice in forensic investigation.”

open image in gallery Staff members work with robotic heads for silicone sex dolls at a factory for WM Dolls ( Getty )

Owning an adult-use sex doll is legal in Australia. However, federal and state laws strictly prohibit any sex doll that resembles a minor or a child. Possessing, importing or distributing a child-like sex doll is a criminal offence carrying up to 15 years in prison.

Police said that the doll found in Oallen was not childlike and that investigation into it had concluded.

In 2023, police in the UK closed off a road for two days to investigate a report of a dead body dumped in a wooded area, only to find out that it was a discarded sex doll. The Warwickshire police said it was with “great relief” that a hand and foot seen poking out of undergrowth turned out to be on an inflatable love aid.

News.content:

Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel may soon be equipped with specialized gloves that deliver painful electric shocks designed to force compliance from combative individuals.

ICE aims to spend up to $20 million to obtain thousands of the "conductive distraction and de-escalation devices" for officers and agents by March, according to a notice published Monday by the Department of Homeland Security.

Known as the G.L.O.V.E., an acronym for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, the items are manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC in Lexington, Kentucky, and have been utilized by select police departments and jails in recent years.

Compliant Technologies says the devices function as a normal pair of patrol gloves until officers press a switch to activate their electrical mode ( AP Photo/Ryan Murphy )

DHS said Tuesday that it was working on a response to an Associated Press inquiry and offered no immediate comment. Jeff Niklaus, the founder and CEO of Compliant Technologies, wrote in an email, “Unfortunately, we are unable to speak on this subject.”

The notice said the solicitation for a no-bid contract could be published as early as Friday.

Civil rights advocates expressed alarm at the plan, saying ICE officers already face criticism for their use of force with little oversight or accountability while enforcing President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

Compliant Technologies says the devices function as a normal pair of patrol gloves until officers press a switch to activate their electrical mode. The gloves must be applied directly to someone's skin to deliver a pain stimulus that typically helps an officer gain compliance within seconds, according to the company.

“It’s immediate and sharp, and it will distract you. I call it like a bee sting,” said John Peters, president of the Institute for the Prevention of In-Custody Deaths, who is studying how the device has been used. “If the officer is getting any type of resistance from the person, this is certainly an effective tool.”

Peters said he believed ICE’s planned purchase would likely be the largest from the company to date. He said he could envision ICE officers using the gloves to help remove uncooperative subjects from cars and houses and in and out of detention facilities.

“For smaller officers or weaker officers or older officers, I think it has a great advantage” because it can produce faster takedowns and shorten confrontations, he said.

The manufacturer warns the device should not be used as punishment, against people merely exhibiting “verbal defiance or belligerence” or on high-risk populations such as children, pregnant women or elderly or disabled people.

Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy project director on policing at the American Civil Liberties Union, said the public should have no confidence that ICE officers will use the devices appropriately. She questioned why the devices would be necessary for civil immigration enforcement and noted those getting shocked might have no advance warning.

“ICE spent the last year showing this country they are too quick to use force. Now they will be able to deploy electric shocks with the slight push of a button that maybe nobody else can see them do,” she said. “Introducing gloves that can so easily be used to deliver terrible pain in encounters is a recipe for harm to the public.”

Supporters say the devices are generally used in specific jail and transport situations, rather than broadly to patrol on the streets. They have been used to subdue violent suspects who are refusing to get into squad cars and inmates who are harming themselves and threatening officers, according to Compliant Technologies.

Peters said he expected the devices to be misused by a small number of employees, as with other policing technologies, but he said they are unlikely to cause injuries. He said it would be important for ICE to have robust policies and training in place.

To use the device, officers must complete a course and be recertified every two years, the manufacturer says.

News.title: Secret WhatsApp groups, last-minute ‘drops’ and mystery locations: My bonkers quest to get solar eclipse glasses
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. It all started with an innocent WhatsApp message.

“Has anyone got any spare eclipse glasses? I left it too late and can’t seem to find any!”

Little did I know it but this benign missive, sent to my local community choir group on Monday morning by a nice woman called Sarah, was the unwitting catalyst for what would quickly become a deranged, Race Across the World-style quest to secure a pair for myself. My own personal odyssey, if we want to be culturally relevant.

Within minutes of her original plea, there were multiple replies. “The print shop have got some, I think – heading there ASAP!!!”

“Try the newsagents on Bouverie Road, I got some from there yesterday but they were limited to five pairs per person?”

“This link looks good – currently saying will deliver before Wednesday [prayer hands emoji].”

I’ll be honest – while I’d heard some chatter about the solar eclipse happening on 12 August, prior to this stream of “hot tips” and warm leads I had given it almost zero thought. But the funny thing is, as more messages came pinging in – “sold out online!”; “print shop has run out!”; “newsagent out of stock!” – I suddenly wanted, more than anything else in this solar system, to get my mitts on a pair. The scarcity mindset had officially set in. I struggled to focus on anything else for the rest of the day.

“They’re being stupid – it must be possible to buy them on the internet,” I thought, scornfully. “You can buy anything on the internet. That’s why it’s killing off independent businesses so effectively!”

But, of course, my lovely choirmates weren’t stupid at all. The idiot was me – blithely assuming I’d be able to casually buy a pair two days before the UK’s most complete eclipse event in 27 years.

open image in gallery Persistence pays off: Solar eclipse glasses secured at Old Spitalfields Market ( Helen Coffey/The Independent )

The more I looked online, the more panicked I became. Every single purveyor was either out of stock or advertising a delivery date of Friday 14 August at the earliest, two days after the fact. Yes, even on Amazon Prime. Getting hold of a simple strip of cardboard with black plastic lenses that would ensure I could safely look upon a burning orb 93 million miles away was proving not just tricky but nigh-on impossible.

Still, this was all currently playing out in my humble hometown in Kent. Heading into London to go to the office, I reasoned things would be different there. The Big Smoke, the economic hub of this great nation, would surely be selling specs on every corner.

Alas, the situation in Folkestone was indicative of what was unfolding across the country. A cursory Google search showed that the market in London was just as much shaped by supply < demand and, consequently, the only viable strategy was to comb through a random assortment of Reddit threads and Facebook posts like a detective on the trail of the Zodiac Killer.

Jessops were said to be selling pairs, but whether or not there would be any by the time one arrived was unclear. Greenwich Observatory seemed to be the safest bet, but they warned of limited stocks (and, quite honestly, it was a mission from the City).

open image in gallery Solar Eclipse London is doing strategic ‘drops’ of glasses across London ( Helen Coffey )

There were whispers of some being sold under the counter at a specific bakery by Bond Street tube station, rumours of a single convenience store near Aldgate East that had a fresh batch. Booze and Essential Putney “had 90 pairs this morning”; Snax Wimbledon “just got 300 pairs, apparently”. There was a 2am queue in Whitechapel of insomniac stargazers desperate to get some.

It was while picking through the comments underneath a post from “Muswell Hill Group and Friends” on Facebook in response to the news that Fresh Bakery in Finsbury Park had been flogging them that I realised I had accidentally become part of something – a new tribe of people driven slightly insane by a dearth of resource. “Anybody know if it is open now and if they have two pairs in stock??” wrote one anxious soul. “Driving all the way from Muswell Hill.”

And it was while dissecting a separate social media thread based on the keywords “solar eclipse glasses”, “where”, “buy”, “TODAY, FOR THE LOVE OF GOD” that I happened upon my best, most tangible lead yet: an underground WhatsApp group called Solar Eclipse London.

That’s where things truly got weird. This mysterious enterprise, whose WhatsApp community had only sprung into being on Sunday, seemed to have “ISO 12312-2 certified” eclipse inventory up the wazoo and was deploying it strategically across London. Different locations at different times; limited “drops”, with hype built by trailing cryptic clues about the next ballpark area without details of the exact whereabouts.

I realised I had accidentally become part of something – a new tribe of people driven slightly insane by a dearth of resource

“Finsbury Park, we’re coming soon.”

“We have a big surprise for everyone. There is a location with over 2,000 waiting for you all. Will reveal at 2.30pm.”

“Hint being sent below”, with a picture of the glasses against a backdrop of Big Ben.

And, my personal favourite, “The location rhymes with Chutney??”

The marketing was flawless, as was the entrepreneurial nous; within the space of a few hours, the WhatsApp community had grown from under a thousand-strong to over 7,000 (and by the end of the day it had hit 9,000). And then they hinted Liverpool Street was the next station for a forthcoming “shipment”, which just so happened to be around the corner from my office (#blessed). The exact location, however, would be shared on their Instagram – with instructions to “FOLLOW AND LIKE!”, another excellent marketing ploy for engagement – and pairs would be limited to two per person. Each one would cost £5, cash only. Oh, it was on.

I grabbed two colleagues to ensure we could obtain the requisite number of pairs and headed out into the unknown, refreshing the Insta account every 10 seconds like a woman possessed. Finally, aha! “Old Spitalfields Market”. Still vaguely imprecise, but enough to go on.

open image in gallery See ‘em and weep: solar eclipse glasses have sold out across the UK ( AFP/Getty )

The nearer we got, the more suspicious we felt. Was this all a weird prank? Was someone going to jump out and shout “Punked!” in our faces, like a Noughties Ashton Kutcher, as we stumbled around the precinct?

But any reticence disappeared once we spotted that most British of spectacles: a queue. And not just any queue. This one was long, winding, and stretching into the distance as far as the eye could see. Word had obviously spread quickly and, within minutes, the line had grown so long I could no longer see the end of it.

No point wondering how the heck hundreds of people had arrived before us – witchcraft seemed to be the only plausible explanation – we were in it now.

“This is the second location I’ve tried today,” shared the man directly behind us in the queue, with a mildly manic, desperate air. “Finsbury Park sold out this morning – I’ve just been waiting around for the next drop!”

I briefly wondered whether, if I managed to obtain some and he didn’t, I’d be altruistic enough to give up mine to this more deserving soul. No, came the disconcertingly cold answer from deep within. You snooze, you lose.

This is the second location I’ve tried today – I’ve just been waiting around for the next drop! A desperate man in search of eclipse glasses

Still, there was a conviviality about the whole thing – a curiously carnivalesque spirit. People in the queue caught eyes and smiled shyly, or exchanged tales of their previous attempts to obtain a pair by trekking the width and breadth of London based on little more than hope and hearsay. Perhaps it was being drawn together around the same wholesome event, but a similar feel to that of the World Cup prevailed among these stressed yet jubilant Londoners: we were experiencing another common cause to unite us in these increasingly divided times.

We shuffled forward excruciatingly slowly, every passing minute cranking up the tension another unbearable notch. Unlike some of the other WhatsApp updates, this one had failed to include the number of spectacles on offer. There could be 30, or 300, or 3,000; there was no way of knowing.

After 20 minutes of inching along, we could finally see the front of the line. This, I knew, would be the exact moment they ran out of stock – when we were in first spitting, then touching, distance. The universe’s sick sense of humour all but guaranteed it. We were eight people from the front now. Five. Three. But, wait… They weren’t going to run out! The universe was on our side!

As we arrived at the kiosk, handed over our crisp, £10 notes, joyfully took our strips of cardboard gold and punched the air in triumph, I felt what can only be described as a shot of pure exhilaration.

Sure, it was more work than clicking “next day delivery” on Amazon – but a victory earned through the thrill of the hunt? That tastes all the sweeter.

Most people underestimate how much light a pair of sunglasses blocks out. A typical dark pair removes around 80 to 90% of the visible light reaching the eye.

Safely looking directly at the Sun requires reducing the light reaching the eye by a factor of around 100,000, meaning roughly 99.999% must be removed. Ordinary sunglasses can let around 10,000 times too much visible light through.

That is especially important on Wednesday 12 August, when the Moon will pass in front of the Sun, creating a deep partial solar eclipse across the UK. Timings and the amount of the Sun covered will vary by location. In Bristol, the eclipse begins at about 6.17pm and reaches its maximum at around 7.12pm. Viewers in Cornwall will see roughly 95% of the Sun covered.

Sunlight can injure the eye without causing pain or any obvious warning at the time. Solar retinopathy occurs when intense light damages the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. Symptoms can appear several hours after exposure and include blurred or distorted vision or a dark patch in the centre of your sight. Many people recover over the following weeks or months, but some can be left with lasting changes to their vision.

open image in gallery The safest way to look directly at the eclipse is with proper solar-viewing glasses or a handheld solar viewer that meets ISO 12312-2, ( AFP/Getty )

The safest way to look directly at the eclipse is with proper solar-viewing glasses or a handheld solar viewer that meets ISO 12312-2, the international safety standard for filters designed for looking directly at the Sun. Ordinary sunglasses are covered by different safety standards and are not designed for direct viewing of the Sun.

Solar viewers are thousands of times darker and use filters designed to reduce visible, ultraviolet and infrared radiation to safe levels.

An ISO number printed on the glasses is not, by itself, proof that a pair is safe, because counterfeit products are sold online. Buy from a reputable supplier whose products have been properly tested, and inspect the filter before use. Do not use glasses with scratches, tears or other damage. If you can see ordinary objects through them indoors, do not use them.

About the author Panos Maghsoudlou, NIHR Academic Clinical Lecturer in Ophthalmology, School of Cellular and Molecular Medicine, University of Bristol. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

Put eclipse glasses on before looking towards the Sun and remove them only after turning away. Children should be supervised throughout, particularly if adult-sized frames do not fit securely.

Never look at the Sun through binoculars, telescopes or camera lenses while wearing eclipse glasses. These instruments concentrate sunlight and can damage both the filter and the eye. Any optical equipment used to view the Sun needs a proper solar filter securely fitted over the front of the instrument.

Colander cameras

If you are reading this on the day of the eclipse and local shops have sold out of eclipse glasses, what do you do? Reach for the colander.

A colander does not filter sunlight. Its holes act as tiny pinhole cameras, projecting small images of the Sun onto another surface. Stand with your back to the Sun, hold the colander so its shadow falls onto a sheet of white paper or pale ground, and look at the projected spots of light. During the eclipse, those usually round spots will become tiny crescents. Never look through the holes towards the Sun.

open image in gallery Illustration of camera obscura in Gemma Frisius’ 1545 book De Radio Astronomica et Geometrica ( Leonardo da Vinci, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons )

The method is remarkably old. More than 2,000 years ago, an ancient Greek text traditionally associated with Aristotle described how an eclipse viewed through leaves, a sieve or gaps between the fingers produced crescent-shaped patches of light. Centuries later, the 11th-century mathematician and pioneer of optics Ibn al-Haytham investigated how the image of an eclipse formed when sunlight passed through a small opening into a darkened space. And in 1545, astronomer Gemma Frisius published an illustration showing a solar eclipse being observed using the same camera obscura principle.

If you don’t have a colander, though, a simple eclipse viewer can be made from two pieces of card. Make a small hole in one piece, stand with your back to the Sun and let the sunlight pass through the hole onto the second piece. You will see a tiny image of the Sun, which will become a crescent as the Moon moves across it.

The principle is always the same: keep your back to the Sun and look at the projected image rather than directly at the Sun.

So enjoy the eclipse, but watch it safely. The British Isles will not see an eclipse this close to totality again until September 2081, and the next total solar eclipse visible from the UK will not arrive until 2090. It is a rare sight, and one worth seeing without putting your vision at risk.

One of the UK’s major high street banks has launched a new digital savings arm offering some of the best interest rates on the market.

First Active, created by NatWest, is offering customers the same protections and assurance they would normally have with that company, only without in-branch assistance.

Consumers can secure an interest rate of 4.5 per cent in easy-access savings accounts with First Active, without restrictions on how much cash they can withdraw.

That rate compares favourably with the current market, with Chase (also 4.5 per cent) having previously led the way until a couple of limited 5 per cent recent offerings from Cahoot and Lemfi.

As with most of those rival accounts, there are a couple of factors to note with the First Active offering.

The 4.5 per cent total rate is built with a 3 per cent base rate and a bonus of 1.5 per cent. The bonus lasts for 12 months, after which your account would revert to the lower variable rate – this is the same with Chase, with a present 4.31 per cent offer from the Post Office and Cynergy Bank’s 4.55 per cent account. First Active allows savers to open an account with as little as £1, with a £1m maximum. In comparison, the Cahoot account has a £3,000 limit to earn interest.

Meanwhile, the best easy access savings rates available directly through NatWest are 1 per cent (easy access flexible), 1.15 per cent (cash ISA) and 1.6 per cent (children’s saver). Moneyfacts data shows the average easy access savings rate on 12 August is 2.52 per cent.

While you don’t need to be a NatWest customer to open an account with First Active, those who are already with the high street bank get FSCS protection on up to £120,000 of their total money with each provider, which in this case would include cash held with the new rollout.

Get a free fractional share worth up to £100.

Capital at risk. Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

Get a free fractional share worth up to £100.

Capital at risk. Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

The Independent understands that NatWest wanted to offer customers with different preferences an alternative option, as savers increasingly seek to move their money to where the best interest rates are, rather than merely sticking with a name they know – though First Active is not intended to run as a totally separate brand.

Customers who open an account with First Active will be able to manage their accounts via telephone support, web chat and email, but there is not intended to be any in-branch support.

First Active is a digital offering rather than for those who want in-branch services ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

It is estimated that more than a million current accounts hold over £50,000 in them across the UK, according to research from Spring, while over a fifth of all people (21 per cent) say they keep savings of any amount in their current account – equal to hundreds of billions of pounds.

These accounts often offer no interest at all and which therefore see savings lose real buying value over time, due to the effects of inflation.

British banks launching digital-only services is a common theme, partly to serve different customer bases and also perhaps because the ongoing overhead costs are far lower, which in turn could contribute to them offering the better interest rates often seen.

As well as First Active, NatWest runs the Mettle brand aimed at businesses, while Cahoot is owned by Santander and first direct initially launched as a telephone bank, before becoming HSBC’s digital-only version.

US firms JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs have Chase UK and Marcus respectively, while of course a whole host of digital-only banks have succeeded in the UK including Monzo, Revolut and Zopa.

News.title: Madagascar forced to divide and share mpox vaccine as epidemic takes off
News.content:
Authorities in Madagascar are being forced to split single vaccines into fifths to try to protect as many people as possible during an ongoing mpox outbreak.

The method, known as “fractional dosing”, is authorised by the World Health Organization (WHO) in emergencies when there are critical vaccine shortages, but is not routinely recommended and carries a level of risk.

Madagascar, the African island with a population of roughly 33 million people, is currently battling its largest-ever outbreak of the virus formerly known as monkeypox, with at least 4,000 cases recorded so far.

Another one million people are thought to be at risk of contracting clade 1b mpox, a fast-spreading strain of the virus that emerged from the Democratic Republic of the Congo in late 2023.

High risk groups include sex workers, young children, and people living with HIV/Aids. Medical workers are also at risk.

“Public health authorities in Madagascar have been given too few doses to protect the at-risk population; they were initially given 30,000 doses in May, and a subsequent 30,000 have just arrived at the end of July,” said Akhil Bansal, a doctor of internal medicine working on the mpox response in Madagascar and a policy fellow at the Centre for Global Development.

“However, we need to vaccinate more than one million people, so we have been “fractionally dosing”, or splitting vaccines, into fifths, to stretch the supply as far as we can.

“This is a somewhat established approach for vaccines, but even then, the number of doses we have is insufficient,” said Dr Bansal.

News.title: Sudan exodus threatens humanitarian catastrophe in Chad
News.content:
Trapped in a desert encampment in Chad, Abakar Adam, 70, dreams of returning to his small farm in neighbouring Sudan, nearby to the village where he was born.

But Mr Adam can’t go home.

Hidden from sight, he watched soldiers set fire to his farmhouse and slaughter his livestock three years ago. One month later, after resettling in the city of El Geneina in West Darfur he heard 40mm grenades rain down on hospitals while patients fought for their lives inside and witnessed civilians executed in the street.

Shortly after, a bullet from the rifle of a Rapid Support Force (RSF) soldier ripped through his gut, and he recalls how he struggled to pull his daughter from the blood-soaked sand after her eye was gouged out by a militiaman during their escape from Sudan.

Now, sitting outside his rotting, wooden shelter in eastern Chad, just 20 miles from the border with Sudan, he tells The Telegraph that he can’t forget the faces of the blind and disabled who he witnessed being thrown onto piles of hay and burnt alive.

Adam’s story is not unique and the refugee camp where he finds himself with tens of thousands of others is on the brink of collapse.

News.title: Telegraph Fantasy Football 2026/27: Everything you need to know and FAQs
News.content:
What’s new for 2026/27?





You’ll need to re-register

When signing up to Telegraph Fantasy Football this season you will notice your old logins do not work.

New for this season you will need to register, or login to an existing, telegraph.co.uk account to play.

NOTE: you do not need to subscribe in order to play Telegraph Fantasy Football - it is free to play.

Having trouble making a new account or logging in to an existing telegraph.co.uk account? Click here and look at our troubleshooting guide that can guide you through the process.



We’ve had a makeover and Leagues have moved

Over the summer we changed game provider meaning the site was built again from scratch. We hope you like the new look and feel.

We know nobody likes change, but take your time to get to know the new layout as some aspects of the site may have moved slightly.

The most notable change is that Leagues are now created and joined below your team selection.



Back to basics

With such a short space of time to get the TFF live for this season, the game has been stripped back to basics.

You’ll notice there are no Public Leagues and no prizes for Weekly and Monthly Leaderboard winners. Assistant Manager has also not been integrated for launch.



The Fixture Tracker

Whilst the game has been stripped back to basics, you’ll notice a new fixture tracker above your team selection. This is there to help you make transfer decisions and we hope you like it.

When you see a + in the tracker it indicates how many other games start at that time.



No rule changes.

Whilst some things may have changed, the rules remain unchanged.

Telegraph Fantasy Football is fantasy football at its purest. No gimmicks, no boosts, no captains. Simply pick the best XI players you can.



Assists

However, one exception is this season assists will no longer follow Opta’s “Fantasy Assist” definition and revert back to standard assists.



Did you miss it? League Cup fixtures and five more transfers

In case you missed it last year, this season will also feature League Cup fixtures meaning all competitive domestic football containing Premier League fixtures will count towards your Telegraph Fantasy Football points tally.

Why the change? Well for years the general advice early in the season is to hold onto your transfers and we thought that was getting a bit stale. With League Cup fixtures starting as early as Game Week 3 some seasons, you’d be a fool not to take advantage of some fixture gains against lower-league opposition.

To help with the additional fixtures we have also added five more transfers to your season total.



Paid leagues are no more

Unfortunately Plucky Paid Leagues are not integrated this season.



Three new teams

Ipswich are no strangers to Telegraph Fantasy Football as they both return from relegations in 2025. They bring with them a host of talent including two big names you might recognise, including Jaden Philogene (£2.9m) and Leif Davis (£2.6m).

It has been a fair few years since Hull City (2016/17) and Coventry City (2000/01) last featured in Telegraph Fantasy Football - memories may even flood back of posting in your transfers for the Sky Blues’ players. Both clubs are favourites to go down, but with some exciting signings like Tzolakis (£2.5m) and Thomas-Asante (£2.7m) they will certainly put up a fight.

Start creating your team >



FAQs





When does Telegraph Fantasy Football start?

The 2026/27 edition of Telegraph Fantasy Football will launch in the two weeks leading up to the start of the Premier League. The scoring will commence on Friday August 21, 2026 at 8pm when the Premier League champions Arsenal host Coventry.



How do I register for Telegraph Fantasy Football?

You will need to create a new, or use your existing telegraph.co.uk account in order to play Telegraph Fantasy Football. Simply click “SIGN UP”, then “Continue with Telegraph” and you will be temporarily taken to telegraph.co.uk to login with your existing Telegraph account or create a new account, before automatically returning back to the Telegraph Fantasy Football site.

Note: this account is not the same as your account from previous Telegraph Fantasy Football seasons.

Having trouble making a new account or logging in to an existing telegraph.co.uk account? Click here and look at our troubleshooting guide that can guide you through the process.



How much does it cost to play Telegraph Fantasy Football?

Telegraph Fantasy Football is completely free to play. All managers compete for the £5,000 prize pool as well the chance to challenge friends, family, colleagues and fellow managers in private mini-leagues.



How many players can I pick in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

You only have to pick a squad of XI players in Telegraph Fantasy Football. With no bench to rely on, finding players who get minutes on the pitch is key and we help you out there by allowing transfers right up until every kick-off.



How many teams can I pick in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

You can create up to five teams in Telegraph Fantasy Football with a budget of £50m for each, meaning you have a better chance of being in contention for the prizes come the end of the season if some of your selections prove to be unsuccessful.



How many transfers can I make in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

Up until the first game on Friday August 21, 2025, there is a transfer amnesty, meaning you can make as many changes as you like. After the season has started you have 45 transfers for the whole campaign with a maximum of five per Game Week (00:00 Tuesday to 23:59 Monday).





How do I join a private league in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

Leagues have now moved below your team selection.

This should make it easier for managers to see which league the team is in that they are making changes to.

To join a league click “Join a league” and then add the 6 digit code that the League Chairman will have access to.

To create a league click “Create a league”, name the league and then copy the league code generated to share with your fellow managers.

League Chairmen will have the ability to lock and unlock a league to new joiners.



Do ALL Cup games count in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

Yes. All League Cup fixtures plus all FA Cup games involving Premier League sides count towards your TFF points tally. This adds a great dimension to the game as you will want to load your teams with players who make the latter stages for an advantage over your competitors. However, one thing to note is that penalty shoot-outs do not count towards your score.



How many players are in Telegraph Fantasy Football?

You can expect to compete against more than 100,000 other teams in Telegraph Fantasy Football – a vast but tight-knit community of players where you have every chance of winning one of our many prizes on offer throughout the year.

We aim to include every player in a squad who has a chance of getting some game time. From time to time we may miss a youngster on debut, but rest assured they will soon be added to the player list and feel free to let us know on Facebook or Twitter if you feel someone is missing.

Having technical issues with TFF? Check our Troubleshooting page for help.



What else do I need to know?



Get your strategy right. Getting the balance of your team right can be a tricky business, especially with limited funds, but there are a few tried and trusted methods that will stand you in good stead:



Pick regular starters

Okay, so this isn’t always straightforward in the world of squad rotation where world-class players routinely find themselves sitting on the bench. That said, there are certain players who, if fit, are almost always the first name on the team sheet. Think Bruno Fernandes at Manchester United, Jordan Pickford for Everton and Liverpool’s Virgil van Dijk.



Find a couple of budget ‘gems’

Igor Thiago, Nico O’Reilly and James Garner were among a crop of players who began last term in the ‘unfancied’ category and were must-have ‘enablers’ by the time the season was over. If you’re able to identify one or two of this type of player early in the season, you could be on to a winner.



Be transfer savvy

We’ve all been there – you spend hours selecting your team for the big kick-off then half of them don’t start, the other half have stinkers and your star striker gets a season-ending injury. If you do get off to a slow start, don’t panic. Lurching from one strategy to another could do more harm than good, wasting precious transfers in the process. Trust your instincts, tweak where necessary and the points will come.



Read our weekly Selection Guide

The best advice comes from experts at the Fantasy Football Hub who make our weekly selection guide a prolific source of Telegraph Fantasy Football tips and Telegraph Fantasy Football match facts.

If you subscribe to the weekly newsletter this will hit your inbox on Friday around lunchtime; alternatively it can be found on our social channels or Telegraph Fantasy Football content hub.



Telegraph Fantasy Football Player List

We aim to keep our player list up to date with all comings and goings in the transfer window and the first place to look is our trusted Stats Centre. However, if you fancy yourself as a bit of a Telegraph Fantasy Football expert like the team at Fantasy Football Hub, you can find a player list below in a spreadsheet format so you can do your own analysis.

On the document simply click “file”, then “make a copy” and you will have your own version of the player list at that time to edit as you please.



Download the Telegraph Fantasy Football App

Never miss a chance to make a transfer and download the Telegraph Fantasy Football App which is available on iOS and Android.





You can follow the latest Telegraph Fantasy Football news and discussions throughout the year on Facebook, Twitter and Fantasy Football Content Hub.

News.title: Telegraph Fantasy Football: transfers explained and top transfer tips
News.content:
As the new Telegraph Fantasy Football season approaches, the fantasy football experts at Fantasy Football Hub will continue to bring you the very best in fantasy football knowledge, tips and tools to help you rise up the ranks and win your mini-leagues.

To join the Hub and get access to all their great resources and expert tips you can take advantage of its 50% pre-season discount here.



Transfers explained



A good place to start is by explaining the Telegraph Fantasy Football rules on transfers. First thing to note is the pre-season transfer amnesty, so you can make unlimited changes to your teams right up until the first scheduled kick-off on Friday 21 August, 20:00.

45 is the magic number of transfers you receive during the season, five more than last season to help negotiate the new League Cup fixtures. This equates to a little more than one a week. You can use a maximum of five transfers in any Game Week which run from 00:00 on Tuesdays to 23:59 on Mondays.

Four seasons ago we scrapped the two-hour rule, meaning you can make transfers right up until a game kicks off. However, we don’t suggest you leave it that late as if a transfer is not completed in time you will not gain any points for the game from the player transferred in. Starting XIs are released an hour before kick-off so you have an ample window to implement any changes.

Scrapping the two-hour rule also means that this year you can be more flexible with your transfers each week. Once a player’s game has started you will amass their points for the entire game and are free to transfer them out for another player who may be kicking off while the previous game is being played, thus benefiting from two players’ points.



Top transfer strategy tips



1) Utilise fixture gains



Telegraph Fantasy Football is unique amongst other fantasy games in that you can transfer a player out as soon as they’ve played for a player yet to play that day or match week. So if Haaland (£8.3m) played in the 12.30pm Saturday kick-off, managers can transfer him out for Saka (£6.0m) who plays in the 3pm kick-off, and score points for both. Picking up extra fixtures each time a transfer is made is key to TFF success.



2) Find enablers early and stick



To fit in a combination of Erling Haaland (£8.3m), Bruno Fernandes (£6.5m) and Cole Palmer (£6.2m) or similar, requires TFF managers to find cheaper players to balance teams. Finding those players early into the season, and sticking with them to utilise transfers on the other strategy tips, can ensure avoiding wasting transfers on constant restructuring of squads.



3) FA Cup and League Cup (new for 2025/26)

Players in TFF gain points for the League Cup and FA Cup as well as the Premier League, so often players topping points charts at the season end have progressed far in the competition. When seeing lineups for early League Cup and FA Cup Rounds, if big hitting players who are regulars in the league start against lowly opposition, it’s a prime opportunity to stock up on those assets.

New for this season League Cup fixtures have been included which will make the early stages of the season even more exciting when Premier League teams who are not competing in Europe will gain a fixture against the rest.



4) Favourable fixture runs

Picking players who are playing against weaker opposition often score more points, therefore keeping an eye on the fixtures for teams is important.



5) Balance transfers out over the season

There are ~37 gameweeks in the season, so averaging around one transfer a week is a rule of thumb that keeps managers from running out early. The start of the season is the only time your team is reset, so it’s important to set a structure that works for you so that you don’t need to use too many moves at the start to identify those players who are likely to shine. It’s a marathon, not a sprint, so keeping pace early isn’t a necessity, and often keeping a few extra back until the end run sees TFF managers get a late boost.

News.title: Telegraph Fantasy Football points: a complete guide to scoring
News.content:
How many points for a Goal?

A regular source of goals is often the first thing a manager looks for in a fantasy football team. The highly-priced Erling Haaland is a go-to signing for many, but last season saw the continuation of mid-priced forwards getting in on the action too with the likes of Igor Thiago racking up 22 goals in Telegraph Fantasy Football.

Players get five points per goal scored which, added to starting appearance points (two), mean a regularly starting goal scorer can be a huge asset.



How many points for an Assist?

It won’t take a master tactician to work out that players who rank highly in the goalscoring charts often also feature in the upper echelons of the Assists table.

Bruno Fernandes was head and shoulders above the rest with regard to assist points last season with 21 in total (nine clear of his closest rival).

An assist will earn three points.





What counts as an Assist?

An Assist is the final touch (pass, pass-cum-shot or any other touch) leading to the recipient of the ball scoring a goal.

Outside of fantasy football, if the final touch is deflected by an opposition player, the initiator is only given a goal assist if the receiving player was likely to receive the ball without the deflection having taken place. Own goals, directly taken free kicks, direct corner goals and penalties do not get an assist awarded.

In a change to previous years, Fantasy Assists are not being used.



How many points for a Tackle?

A slightly more nuanced aspect of scoring is the points a player earns for a successful tackle. Managers will need to cast their nets wide to capitalise on tackling points as the highest scorers tend to come from mid-table and even lower-table teams.

Everton’s James Garner was a key beneficiary of tackle bonus points last season with 120 tackles in total. His closest rivals have been very popular this summer with Wolves’ Joao Gomes, now at Aston Villa, and Nottingham Forest’s Elliot Anderson, now at Manchester City. It’s clear from this that deeper lying midfielders are more likely to amass points here.

Players earn a point for every two tackles made during a match and only midfielders are eligible.



What counts as a Tackle?

A tackle is defined as a player connecting with the ball in a ground challenge and successfully taking the ball away from the player in possession. The tackled player must have clearly been in possession of the ball before the tackle was made.

The final destination of the ball (to the tackler, to a teammate, to an opposition player or out of play) is not considered. A tackle will only be deemed unsuccessful if the player tackled retains possession of the ball.

A player cutting out a pass does not count as a tackle.

Players earn a point for every two tackles made.



How many points for a Clean Sheet?

Attainable by goalkeepers and defenders, the top-scorers in the clean sheet category last season mostly came from Arsenal.

There are five clean sheet points on offer for a player who has played at least 60 minutes of a match and two points if the player has played less than an hour where the game has finished with their team conceding zero goals.



How many points for a Save?

In addition to clean sheet points, goalkeepers can earn one point for every two saves made in a match. Much like points for tackling, save points introduce a new angle to team selection with keepers from teams further down the table likely to face more shots than those who generally dominate games.



What counts as a Save?

A save is a goalkeeper preventing the ball from entering the goal with any part of his body when facing an intentional attempt to score by an opposition player.

Saves have the following attributes:

Body part: Hands/Feet/Body

Save type: Caught/Collected/Parried Safe/Parried Danger area/Fingertip

Goalkeeper position: Diving/Standing/Reaching/Stooping

For an exhaustive list of how to score Telegraph Fantasy Football points, take a look at our Game Guidelines.

Whether it’s the Green Jacket, an Olympic medal or the riches that follow a Championship play-off win, there’s always a prize to symbolise a historic victory. Telegraph Fantasy Football is no different – not only are you playing for pride competing against your peers but there is also more than a £5,000 prize pool given out to champions across the season.

Here is a breakdown of all the prizes that can be won.



The Overall League

At the end of the long Premier League season there is a tendency for the cream to rise to the top and duly the highest-scoring Telegraph Fantasy Football managers over the season are handsomely rewarded, with the champion receiving £3,000, the runner-up £1,000, third place £500, fourth £300 and fifth £200.

Managers can only win one of the top three prizes.





Other Leagues prizes

Unfortunately, there are currently no prizes available for winners of the other leagues that used to feature in Telegraph Fantasy Football.





Private leagues

The final prize that you could win is simply priceless. You can set up a private league and compete against your friends, family and colleagues for the ultimate honour of bragging rights for a whole year.

Visit Telegraph Fantasy Football to start your private league and invite your friends to join.



You can follow the latest Telegraph Fantasy Football news and discussions throughout the year on Facebook, Twitter and Fantasy Football Content Hub.

News.title: Arsenal lose second successive pre-season friendly after parading Guimaraes
News.content:
Premier League champions Arsenal continue their preparations for the new season as they take on Borussia Dortmund in the Emirates Cup. Arsenal beat Spanish side Athletic Bilbao 3-0 in the 2025 edition, with goals from Viktor Gyokeres, Bukayo Saka and Kai Havertz sealing victory. These sides met during the 2014/15 Champions League group stages, with both games being won 2-0 by the home side.

Arsenal beat Girona 4-1 just over a week ago but fell to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night. Reflecting on that defeat, Mikel Arteta expressed his frustration at the way his side conceded the goals.

“I am disappointed with the result,” Arteta told Arsenal’s in-house media. “We are here to win football matches. We had some fantastic moments in the first half, the way we played, the way we opened them up. We have to score first, clearly, in the two chances that we had before the score.

“I am very disappointed in the manner that we conceded the first goal, the two giveaways leading to the other two goals. It is true that the finishing quality from them was exceptional, but to win a football match, you have to compete at a different level, especially in those areas of the pitch and that is the learning from today [last Wednesday].”

This is in fact Arsenal’s first game at the Emirates since being crowned Premier League champions, as they sealed the title with a game to spare, with that final match of last season being away at Crystal Palace. After today, Arsenal have two more games, including the Community Shield in a week’s time, before they kick off the defence of their Premier League crown at home against newly-promoted Coventry. The likes of Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Martin Zubimendi are still yet to return after their World Cup exploits.

Dortmund, led by Niko Kovac, finished second in the Bundesliga last season, 16 points off winners Bayern Munich. They have played four pre-season friendlies thus far, winning twice and losing twice. The likes of Karim Adeyemi, Julian Brandt and Niklas Sule have left the club this summer.

Team news to follow shortly.

Sports.title: Footballer declared dead after collapsing in pre-season match ‘wakes up’ in mortuary and is rushed to hospital
Sports.content:
FOOTIE SHOCK Footballer declared dead after collapsing in pre-season match ‘wakes up’ in mortuary and is rushed to hospital

A FOOTBALLER is fighting for his life after sensationally waking up in a mortuary – despite being pronounced dead hours earlier.

Katsina United fans feared the worst when Chinedu Ozor collapsed during the early stages of a pre-season showdown against Niger Tornadoes.



And, having been checked by concerned doctors, the defender was declared dead.

But medics were stunned when Ozor later moved his hand while at the mortuary.



The Nigerian has been rushed to the intensive care unit at Katsina General Hospital, where he is on oxygen as doctors frantically work to revive and stabilise him.

Heartland, who are among Ozor’s former clubs, shocked fans when they released a statement.

It read: “Reliable sources say Chinedu Ozor has been moved from the mortuary to the hospital after reportedly showing signs of movement.

“He is currently on oxygen as medics work to revive him.”

The unexpected update came after Katsina initially headed onto social media to claim Ozor had died.

The statement read: “We mourn the tragic passing of our newly signed player Chinedu Ozor following a medical emergency during today’s friendly match against Niger Tornadoes.



“Our thoughts, prayers and strength are with his family and loved ones. Rest on Warrior.”

Katsina press officer Nasir Gide added: “When we rushed him to a nearby hospital, he was confirmed dead by a doctor.

“We collected a police report and took him back to Katsina General Hospital, where he was also said to be dead.”

The Nigeria Premier Football League and Kano Pillars, who are among Ozor’s ex-employers, paid tribute following news of his passing.

Rivers United general manager Okey Kpalukwu also spoke out when shockwaves were sent through Nigerian football.



He said: “We extend our heartfelt condolences to his family, loved ones and to the management, players, staff and supporters of Katsina United.

“Our thoughts and prayers are with the entire Nigerian football family during this difficult time.”

Ozor only completed a move to Katsina earlier this month as preparations were made for the new season.

Sports.title: Chelsea CONFIRM Pep Chavarria transfer as they sign Marc Cucurella replacement from Rayo Vallecano
Sports.content:
CHELSEA have completed an £18million deal to sign Spanish left-back Pep Chavarria.

The 28-year-old arrives from Raya Vallecano as a replacement for compatriot Marc Cucurella, who joined Real Madrid for over £50m in June.



New Blues manager Xabi Alonso identified Chavarria as a key target early in his reign.

And Chelsea have finally got their man for a bargain fee, having initially been told to meet his £40m release clause last month.



They will pay £16.2m up front, with the rest of the £18m made up in add-ons.

Chavarria, who was playing second-tier football just four years ago, has signed a five-year contract at Stamford Bridge.

The left-sider is capable of playing in a back four, or as a flying wing-back in a five-man defence.

And Chelsea’s new signing claims he’s achieved a lifelong “dream” by signing for one of the “biggest clubs in the world” — under “one of the best coaches” in Alonso.

Chavarria, whose squad number is yet to be confirmed, said: “This is a dream for me as Chelsea are one of the biggest clubs in the world.

“It is a big opportunity but I am prepared and will work hard to help the team achieve success.

Sports.title: Viral footballer who plummeted down hole while celebrating reveals romantic reason he jumped over barrier

THE VIRAL footballer who fell down a pitchside hole was trying to celebrate scoring with his pregnant wife.

In a clip that has been watched by millions, Brazilian player Jacy vaulted the advertising board only to plummet into an abyss.



Thankfully the defender was not seriously hurt in the incident, although he described the sensation as like “falling from a building” in a dream.

To add insult to injury the goal was disallowed following a VAR check.



The Coritiba skipper was able to continue the match following medical treatment, but later went off with an ankle issue.

Explaining what happened, he said: “I scored the goal and wanted to celebrate with my wife because she’s pregnant.

“But then I remembered it was my first goal at Couto Pereira stadium, and I also wanted to celebrate with the fans, but I hadn’t remembered there was a moat there.”

Jacy disappeared down a chute which leads to the dressing rooms at Estadio Couto Pereira.

Ordinarily the tunnel is covered, but it had been opened by ground staff with half-time looming.

Jacy added: “I twisted my foot there. It’s a bit sore, but I’m fine.

Sports.title: Man City boss Enzo Maresca admits the night he sank two England managers in one go is highlight of his playing career
Sports.content:
ENZO MARESCA admits the night he sank two future England managers in one go ranks as the highlight of his playing career.

The new Manchester City boss was part of the Sevilla team who met Steve McClaren’s Middlesbrough in the 2006 Uefa Cup final.



It was the Boro chief’s final game in charge before he left to take the Three Lions job a couple of months later.

His skipper that night in Eindhoven was Gareth Southgate, who stepped up to be Boro boss after McClaren’s departure.



Maresca started the game and scored two late on in a clash that ended 4-0 to the Spaniards.

Former midfielder Maresca, 46, played for 11 clubs over two decades but says that night was one of his most memorable moments.



The Italian recalled: “I got two and I could have had a hat-trick.

“It was a good team. Dani Alves was there and Adriano.

“I remember the Middlesbrough team with Southgate, and McClaren was leaving to go to England.

“Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink also played and he mentioned the game when we worked together at Chelsea.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

“Scoring twice in that final was a career highlight. Then after, when you win that trophy you play against the team that wins the Champions League in the Super Cup.

“Barcelona had beaten Arsenal 2-1 in Paris so we faced them. Messi was there and we beat them 3-0. And I scored again! So the two European finals probably were the best moments.”

Maresca started out as an AC Milan youth-team player and was sad to hear Rossoneri legend Franco Baresi had passed away, aged 66, last month.

He said: “There was never a central defender like him but it wasn’t just him — that team had Marco van Basten, Ruud Gullit, Frank Rijkaard, Roberto Donadoni, Carlo Ancelotti, Paolo Maldini and Alessandro Costacurta.



“They won the Champions League and it was the best team. Arrigo Sacchi was manager and at that time he changed football like Pep Guardiola did in the last 20 years.”

When he looks back on that golden era in Italian football in the 1990s, he finds it hard to believe his home nation have not made an appearance at the last three World Cups.

Maresca added: “The best players, best manager, the best football was in Italy at that time. But now… three World Cups out.

“Now we don’t produce enough players and there are too many foreign players who are not at a high level — but they are cheap.”

Sports.title: What next for Birmingham City? Why Davies is changing his approach
Sports.content:
Birmingham City is a football club transformed. Over 20,000 season tickets have been sold for the forthcoming Championship season, with 14,000 more on the waiting list. Fan parks surround St Andrew's these days. The buzz around the place is palpable.

There are grand plans to reconnect England's second city to the club that bears its name, unlocking its true potential. Supporters clubs are springing up around the world, a product of Tom Brady's presence. And all the talk is of trying to be Premier League ready.

Given this context, with an ambitious ownership and a success-starved support, it is understandable if Birmingham are in a hurry. Excitement brings expectation, not just internally but externally. There is the sense of a club going places. But it takes time.

On reflection, maybe last season was a moment for the club to breathe rather than a case of lost momentum. After all, you must go back 14 years to the 2011/12 season, when Birmingham were in Europe, for a better finish than the 10th-place effort of 2025/26.

"It was our first season back, which people found hard to remember at times," Birmingham manager Chris Davies tells Sky Sports. He is not talking about the club's supporters - "they have been great" - but everyone. This is a man carrying a lot of hopes and dreams.

"One thing I did learn was that I can handle it," he says. "I can handle the ups and downs." There had not been too many of the latter as Birmingham won the League One title with a record-breaking 111 points, their possession football proving utterly dominant.

Last season was more testing. "You can know about the Championship but to feel it is something different." England's second tier asked different questions. Davies and his team did not always have the answers. Plan A worked only some of the time.

"We came up from League One playing total football, having 80 per cent possession with a lot of circulating the ball, a lot of dominating the ball. It was really effective for us because we just controlled games pretty much the whole way through," he explains.

"In the Championship we were very technical in our recruitment of some smaller players, more technical players, and we tried to use that style. It had really good days and it had days where we just didn't have enough punch, especially away from home."

In that context, opening the season with a hard-fought Carabao Cup win at Swansea in which Birmingham scored the only goal having had 39 per cent of the ball was more than just satisfying. It suggested that his Blues side have added different elements to their game.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Carabao Cup first-round match between Swansea and Birmingham

The scorer, August Priske, is a robust young target-man added in January who looks to have benefited from that half-season in the Championship. The 22-year-old Dane also netted the opening goal against Barcelona in front of a packed St Andrew's last month.

"Jhon Solis, Carlos Vicente and August came in at the same time and that little six months that they did have is their initiation to what English football is like, what the Championship is like, and now they are ready to go. They have all done very well."

Vicente, a combative Spanish winger, provided the assist for Priske's goal at Swansea. Solis also scored against Barcelona with the Colombian already proving a popular figure with the fans. He adds presence to Birmingham's midfield just as Priske does up top.

"When I reflected on the season, I thought for us to take the next step and progress, physicality is going to be really important. The game now is a lot of man-to-man pressing, a lot of set-piece emphasis. You need the physical capacity to deal with it."

That thinking has shaped Birmingham's summer too. Supplementing those winter additions, the club have brought in Dael Fry. The expectation is that a 6ft 4in centre-back with nearly 300 Championship appearances to his name will be able to adapt quickly.

The intention is to add to what Davies has already built, rather than pivot completely. "As a team that can keep the ball, it is a lot easier to then move into a more pragmatic or direct style than being a team that only knows how to play pragmatic or direct football."

That change actually began during the closing weeks of the last campaign. Birmingham were in 17th place in mid-April, but Davies used the brief international break in the spring to make some of these adjustments to their style of play. They went more direct.

Image: Christoph Klarer's passing sonar shows how Birmingham have become more direct

"I started thinking about being a little bit more flexible with the shape we were using and how we were positioning ourselves, but focusing more on more direct play, more transitions and more set-pieces if possible. So we sort of finished the season that way."

Birmingham ended the campaign on a five-game unbeaten run, earning that top-10 finish and taking some belief into the summer.

"It is a fine balance because we don't want to lose what we're good at. What I won't come away from is the pressing. I don't think any team last season in the Championship really played through our press consistently. I thought it was really effective for us."

But there will be tweaks once Birmingham win the ball back. "I think that hopefully is something that we can have as a weapon that we can use a little bit more. When we get the ball, just to go forward that little bit quicker, hopefully win more set-pieces."

That explains another addition behind the scenes. Birmingham have brought in a specialist set-piece coach in Scott Fry, with Davies identifying dead-ball situations as an obvious way that his team can become genuine promotion contenders this season.

Solis scored from one against Barcelona. Priske's winner against Swansea came after a set-piece found Vicente and he squared the ball for the striker. In other words, this emphasis on set-pieces is already making the difference. And Davies has been doing his sums.

"We have a set-piece coach and the idea is to score more from them. We needed to score 70-odd goals really to be in among those top teams last season." Crucially, that was the total hit by the top six but not the rest of the Championship. Birmingham scored 57.

The task this time around is to find those extra 13 goals somehow. "If six or seven of those can come from set-pieces and two or three can come from counter-attacks, then you only need another two or three from your general football. So it is absolutely doable."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jude Bellingham discusses his love of Birmingham and his love of cricket

Absolutely doable. That sums up the mood. Last time, they were learning about the Championship. Now they know. "It was not just me, several players had never played in it before. Now they have 40 games in the bank. They know what it is like away at Millwall."

At the training ground, Davies has tried to strip back the buzzwords that once adorned the walls. No more gimmicks is the mantra now. Leaner and meaner, like the squad. The feeling is that there is more continuity now, that this Birmingham are ready to kick on.

Craig Gardner has left as director of football but the club has played down the impact, leaning on the experienced Mike Rigg. Commercially, Birmingham continue to grow, with the biggest revenue of any Championship club not reliant on parachute money.

After storming up and then stabilising, the next step awaits Birmingham City. And now, it feels like everyone is ready for it. "I am confident that we can keep progressing. That is the big thing," says Davies. "We just need to keep moving forward and getting stronger."

Sports.title: Championship play-off changes, new managers & star players - the EFL is BACK!
Sports.content:
The 2026/27 EFL season is here!

We kick off on Friday night with Wolves vs Blackburn Rovers, and every Championship, League One and League Two game is LIVE this weekend!

But what have we got in store for the new campaign? We take a look at some of the key stories...

Championship

From top six to top eight... a new play-off system has arrived!

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Simeon Gholam explains all you need to know on how the play-offs have changed this season in the Championship

The most significant alteration to domestic football in decades has happened over the summer, with the Championship play-offs expanding from a top-six spot to a top-eight position this season, presenting clubs with more opportunity for promotion.

What has (and hasn't) changed?

1st and 2nd are automatically promoted as normal.

3rd and 4th still qualify for the semi-finals.

5th vs 8th and 6th vs 7th in one-off eliminator ties at the home of the side who finishes higher up the league.

The winners of the eliminator ties progress to the semi-finals, to face 3rd and 4th in two-legged ties with the second leg at the home of the side that finishes higher up the league.

One other key thing to note is that, whatever happens, 3rd will face the lowest-ranked team remaining in the semi-finals. So if 8th beats 5th, and 6th beats 7th in the eliminators, 3rd will face 8th and 4th will face 6th. There is no pre-set path for the semi-finals before the eliminators.

in the semi-finals. So if 8th beats 5th, and 6th beats 7th in the eliminators, 3rd will face 8th and 4th will face 6th. There is no pre-set path for the semi-finals before the eliminators. As per usual, the winners of the two semi-finals meet at Wembley for a place in the Premier League.

Are the relegated clubs automatic favourites?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kevin Nolan and Darren Moore tell the EFL Show why Jarrod Bowen is key for West Ham's hopes for an instant return to the Premier League

It did not take long for West Ham and Wolves to be installed as favourites for an immediate return to the Premier League.

The Hammers are playing at this level for the first time in 14 years, and have kept hold of head coach Nuno Espirito Santo and key asset Jarrod Bowen.

Both are familiar with this level, Nuno won the Championship - with Wolves - in 2018, while Bowen played in it with Hull City before he left for east London.

Wolves, meanwhile, replaced boss Rob Edwards with the relatively unknown quantity of Cesar Peixoto in the summer. But the quality in their squad could prove telling - with the likes of Andre, Mateus Mane and Santi and Hugo Bueno sticking about.

They have also added Raul Jimenez and Kieran Trippier to the bank. Experience and class.

It is Burnley where a bit more uncertainty lingers. They have appointed a new head coach in Nicky Hayen, a 45-year-old Belgian who has previously managed Club Brugge and Genk.

But it is worth remembering the Clarets have won promotion in their last two Championship seasons - both times with 100+ points. They are experts at this level.

According to the Sky Sports supercomputer, West Ham and Wolves are the two favourites, with Burnley in fourth just behind Middlesbrough...

Middlesbrough go big to try and get over the line

It was some campaign for Middlesbrough last season. They spent more days in the top two than any other club, but managed to finish fifth.

They were then the victim of the Spygate saga, lost to Southampton in the play-off semi-finals, were reinstated to the final, then lost at Wembley to a stoppage-time Oli McBurnie goal for Hull City.

But any potential hangover looks like it has already been left behind with some of their work in the transfer window.

Owner Steve Gibson has taken his chequebook out and spent serious money to strengthen. Striker Will Lankshear has already made his mark with the winning goal against Wrexham in the Carabao Cup. He scored 11 goals for a struggling Oxford side last season and arrives from Spurs.

Sebastian Berhalter comes in, having last been seen playing for the USA at the World Cup, while goalkeeper Radek Vitek from Manchester United is also an eye-catching addition. He impressed on loan at Bristol City last season.

Kim Hellberg and some Boro fans may be wondering where this backing was in January when they were crying out for reinforcements, but it has certainly led to a swell of excitement at the Riverside about what's possible this season.

Can Southampton escape Spygate scandal?

It was the story that dominated the landscape of last season. A shockwave went around the footballing world when Southampton were expelled from the play-offs after their role in the Spygate scandal.

But the club were quick to back Tonda Eckert, and although an FA charge still hangs over the boss, they have tried to move on and heal the wounds caused by the damage.

Fears of a player exodus have been quelled, with only midfielder Shea Charles departing so far, and the club has brought in goalkeeper Daniel Peretz and striker Cyle Larin permanently, after both starred on loan in the second half of last season.

They will have to overcome a four-point deduction. But they came from a long way back last season with a remarkable run in the second half of the campaign, and they certainly have the quality to challenge.

Managerial changes in the Championship

There are also a few other managerial changes to make a note of. Tony Mowbray is back at Blackburn Rovers four years after he left the club, while Watford have brought in Alessio Dionisi.

Elsewhere, Michael Skubala left Lincoln City after leading them to promotion to join Bristol City. While his exit opened the door for the Imps to make the unique move of appointing joint-managers in the role. Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw take the reins at Sincil Bank.
