World.title: Patients, health workers lament deplorable condition of Ebonyi health centre
World.content:
…No beds, medical equipment as staff quarters decay

By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki

ABAKALIKI — Patients and health workers have raised the alarm over the deplorable condition of the Umuebe/Amaovo Primary Health Centre in Amovu Community, Ohaukwu Local Government Area of Ebonyi State.

An investigation showed that the health centre was in a state of disrepair, with inadequate medical facilities, deteriorating staff quarters, lack of electricity and poor environmental sanitation threatening healthcare delivery at the facility.

Patients visiting the centre were seen sitting on benches due to a lack of adequate chairs and beds, while the staff quarters had reportedly become dilapidated and infested with rodents and reptiles.

The facility was also surrounded by overgrown bushes, while erosion and indiscriminate dumping of refuse posed additional environmental and health risks.

An indigene of the community, Mr Ekene Onwe, lamented that the health centre, which was the nearest medical facility for many residents, especially indigent pregnant women, had become a shadow of its former self.

He said the deteriorating infrastructure, absence of basic medical equipment, lack of electricity and poor maintenance had crippled healthcare services and put patients at risk.

“The health centre has collapsed completely due to negligence at the local government level and lack of monitoring and supervision from the state Ministry of Health.

“When this health centre was established by the government of Dr Sam Egwu, patients came from far and near to access healthcare services at the facility. Women visited the health centre for antenatal care and child delivery, but the reverse is now the case as the place is a ghost of itself.

“I know that this health centre saved many women and helped reduce maternal mortality. Before now, old men and women received treatment here. Some emergency cases were also handled here before patients were referred to the teaching hospital, which is no longer possible because of the decay in the facility,” Onwe said.

He appealed to Governor Francis Nwifuru and the state Ministry of Health to urgently intervene and rehabilitate the health centre.

“We are losing our pregnant women and other patients here due to inadequate medical equipment and lack of drugs,” he added.

A patient’s relative at the facility, Mrs Ngozi Ogbadu, said the health workers were willing to work and remained at their duty posts but lacked the basic equipment needed to provide effective healthcare.

She said the deteriorating staff quarters and poor working conditions had discouraged some patients from patronising the facility, forcing them to seek treatment elsewhere, including from unqualified practitioners.

Ogbadu said the centre lacked essential medical equipment needed to provide quality healthcare, particularly for pregnant women, nursing mothers and children.

A health worker, Mrs Chinyere Eze, said the facility had no hospital beds, patient chairs, delivery couches, examination equipment and other critical medical tools required for effective healthcare delivery.

She also lamented the absence of electricity, saying health workers faced serious challenges attending to emergencies and conducting deliveries at night.

The Officer-in-Charge of the health centre, Mrs Ogochukwu Uto, confirmed that the facility was operating under difficult conditions.

According to her, although the centre provides antenatal care, immunisation, child delivery and other primary healthcare services, health workers are often forced to improvise because the available equipment is outdated and grossly inadequate.

She also decried the deteriorating environment, attributing the situation to severe erosion and indiscriminate dumping of refuse around the premises.

Uto warned that the environmental challenges posed serious risks to public health and the safety of patients and health workers.

Healthcare experts have consistently described primary healthcare centres as the bedrock of Nigeria’s healthcare system, particularly in rural communities where they serve as the first point of contact for medical services.

They warned that inadequate investment in infrastructure, equipment and personnel could undermine efforts to improve maternal and child healthcare.

The health workers appealed to the Ebonyi State Government, Ohaukwu Local Government Council, development partners and public-spirited individuals to urgently rehabilitate the facility, renovate the staff quarters, provide modern medical equipment and restore electricity.

They also called for urgent measures to control erosion and clear the refuse and overgrown vegetation around the health centre to create a safer environment for patients and health workers.

World.title: U.S deports 3 million foreign nationals in 15 months
World.content:
US President Donald Trump speaks after signing executive orders in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on August 7, 2026. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP)

By Nkiruka Nnorom

The Donald Trump administration said it has completed 15 consecutive months without releasing a single illegal alien into the United States, while carrying out more than 3 million deportations and tightening visa and citizenship rules.

In a fact sheet released by the Department of State, the administration said the measures were part of efforts to put Americans first and restore the immigration system after what it described as record-shattering illegal immigration under the previous Biden administration.

“President Trump has delivered on his promise to fix the immigration system, prioritize American citizens, and protect U.S. citizenship. The border is sealed. The results are undeniable,” the statement said.

According to the administration, more than 3 million illegal aliens have been deported since President Trump returned to office, including thousands convicted of violent crimes.

It said the government also launched an unprecedented denaturalization surge targeting persons who fraudulently obtained U.S. citizenship. To date, claims have been filed against 88 individuals found to be ineligible for citizenship.

The administration further stated that it has terminated taxpayer-funded benefits for over 1.4 million illegal immigrants improperly receiving public assistance and banned them from more than a dozen taxpayer-funded healthcare programs.

As part of the crackdown, the administration said it paused visa processing for 75 high-risk countries to protect the homeland and deter overstays, and strengthened screening procedures for existing visa programs.

It also said it has moved to purge tens of thousands of illegal aliens from voter rolls in multiple states, arguing that voting was a right reserved only for American citizens.

In addition, the citizenship test was reformed to “better assess aliens’ understanding of American history, government, and values, and better ensure aliens meet all eligibility requirements.”

The statement recalled that in his first week back in office, President Trump signed an Executive Order invoking a crisis at the Southern Border and taking immediate action to end illegal entries.

“For 15 straight months, no illegal aliens have been released into the country,” the administration said.

Recall that the U.S Mission in Nigeria has repeatedly warned Nigerian visa applicants and holders to strictly comply with U.S immigration laws or risk revocation and deportation.

In posts on its official channels, the Mission said visas would be revoked for criminal activity, overstay, fraud, and for engaging in conduct that threatens public safety.

It urged Nigerians to use their visas for the purpose for which they were issued and to depart the U.S before their authorized stay expires.

Immigration remains a central issue in U.S politics ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, with the Trump administration projecting its policies as a restoration of law, order and fiscal discipline.

World.title: How Ridima Is Changing the Way Nigerians Buy, Sell and Think About Gift Cards
World.content:
Ask ten Nigerians what a gift card is, and most will describe the same thing: something you receive from someone, redeem at a store, and forget about. That description made sense ten years ago. It does not describe how gift cards in Nigeria work today.

Gift Cards Are No Longer Just Gifts

The traditional idea of a gift card is that it is a present. Someone buys it for you, you spend it at one brand, and the story ends there. Digital commerce has quietly rewritten that story.

Today a gift card in Nigeria might arrive from a cousin in Houston, or it might be something you bought for yourself ten minutes ago because you needed to pay for a subscription. It might sit in your notes app for six months because you do not shop at that brand. It might become cash in your bank account before the end of the day.

That is a very different object from a birthday present. A gift card now behaves like digital money with a brand attached to it. It can be bought, used, held or turned into Naira. Once you look at it that way, a lot of what is happening in the Nigerian gift card market starts to make sense.

Why Nigerians Buy Gift Cards

Nigerians buy gift cards because they solve a real payment problem, not because a birthday is coming.

The most common reason is access. Plenty of international brands and services do not accept Nigerian cards cleanly, or the payment fails at checkout for reasons nobody explains. A gift card removes that friction. You load the value, you pay, you move on.

The other reasons stack up quickly:

Gaming, where credit for consoles and in-game purchases is often sold as a card

Online shopping on international stores

Digital subscriptions for music, streaming and software

Paying for tools and services that need an international payment method

Gifting friends and family, which is still a real use, just no longer the main one

Simple convenience, because a card is faster than sorting out a card issue with your bank

None of this is occasional behaviour. For a large group of Nigerian consumers, buying gift cards is now a routine part of paying for things online, closer to buying airtime than to shopping for a present.

And Why Nigerians Sell Them

Nigerians sell gift cards because not every card that lands in your hands is useful to you.

You might receive a card for a brand you have never shopped at. You might get a denomination that does not match anything you actually want to buy. You might simply prefer the money. Somebody sends you a $100 card as a gift, and what you need this week is Naira in your account, not store credit.

So the question comes up: what do I do with a gift card I do not need?

For years, the answer was uncomfortable. You asked around your WhatsApp groups to find someone willing to buy it. You dealt with a stranger who promised to pay after you sent the details. You tried a platform you had never heard of and hoped for the best. People got burned often enough that a lot of Nigerians just let cards expire rather than take the risk.

That experience is what dedicated gift card services have been fixing. Selling a gift card should not require you to find a person you can trust. It should just be a transaction.

Ridima Is Simplifying Both Sides

Ridima works as Nigeria’s leading platform for buying and selling gift cards by acting as the service provider on both sides of the transaction, not as a middleman between two users.

That distinction matters more than it sounds.

When you want to buy a gift card in Nigeria on Ridima, you buy it from Ridima. When you want to sell a gift card, you sell it to Ridima and get paid in cash. There is no other user on the other end of the trade.

That is not a small design detail. The biggest worry people carry into a gift card transaction is whether the payment will actually come once the code has left their hands. When the platform is the buyer, that risk sits with the company instead of with you, and the transaction becomes something you can finish on your own schedule rather than someone else’s.

The whole flow reduces to two sentences. Need a gift card? Buy it from Ridima. Have a card you do not need? Sell it to Ridima.

For anyone who has spent time in the older world of informal gift card trading in Nigeria, that is a meaningful change. The uncertainty in those transactions was never really about the cards. It was about the people you had to trust to complete them.

Trust Matters More Than Ever

Trust decides whether a gift card platform gets used at all, because everything being traded is digital and hard to verify by eye.

Consumers who buy and sell gift cards ask the same questions every time. Is this platform real? Will I actually receive the card I paid for? Will my card be accepted when I sell it? How much am I getting? How fast will the money land? And if something goes wrong, is there a human being who will respond?

Answering those questions is not a marketing exercise. It is infrastructure.

KYC checks exist so that both sides of a transaction know who they are dealing with, which is the base layer of any financial service. Fraud detection matters because stolen and already-redeemed cards are a real problem in this market, and screening them out protects honest sellers from being lumped in with bad actors.

Transparent rates deal with the oldest complaint about informal trading, which was never really that the rates were bad. It was that nobody knew what the rate was supposed to be. Seeing what your card is worth before you agree to anything turns the transaction from a negotiation into a decision.

Fast verification and payouts are there because a promise of money is not money. And support over email and live chat matters for a simple reason: a platform is still there tomorrow when you have a question, which is more than you could say for the stranger in the group chat.

Ridima runs all of this because the alternative, asking Nigerians to trust a platform on vibes alone, does not work anymore. People have been burned too many times.

Changing the Meaning of “Value”

A gift card has one printed value and several real ones, depending on who is holding it.

Take a $100 card. To one person, that is $100 of shopping at a brand they already use, so the card is worth exactly its face value and they will spend it. To another person, the same card is locked. It is worth $100 on paper and nothing in practice, because they do not shop there and never will.

Both people are right. The face value is fixed. The usefulness is personal.

What platforms like Ridima do is unlock the second one. When you can turn gift cards to Naira reliably, the card stops being useless just because the person who sent it picked a brand you do not use. Whoever is holding the card decides what it is for, and a gift card rate calculator means you can see that number before you commit to anything.

That is the real shift in behaviour. Gift cards used to be something you received and spent, or received and wasted. Now they are something you can buy, use or cash out, and the choice belongs to whoever is holding the card.

Convenience Is Reshaping the Industry

Convenience is now the main competitive pressure in gift card trading in Nigeria, because that is the standard every other digital service has already set.

Nigerians moved money instantly, opened accounts from their phones, and got used to services that work in under two minutes. That expectation carried over. Nobody wants a gift card exchange process that involves long back and forth, unclear rates, or a payout that arrives whenever it arrives.

The demand is simple. Tell me what my card is worth. Let me complete the transaction. Pay me. The platforms that make those three steps easy are the ones people keep using, and the ones that do not are steadily losing customers to the ones that do.

Where Gift Cards Go From Here

Gift cards are likely to become a bigger part of how Nigerians pay for international products and services, not a smaller one.

As more commerce, entertainment and software moves online, the payment gap that gift cards fill is not closing quickly. What will change is the quality of the experience around them. Expect more pressure on speed and payout times, wider selections of cards on offer, clearer rates, stronger security, and better tools for checking what a card is worth before you sell it. Expect consumers to get sharper too, because people who transact regularly learn quickly what a fair rate looks like.

The question is already moving. It used to be “what is a gift card?” It is now “what can I actually do with this value?”

Whether you are looking to buy a gift card or turn one you do not need into cash, Ridima makes the process simple, secure and straightforward.

World.title: Only 40% of births registered in Nigeria — NPC
World.content:
By Folarin Kehinde

ABUJA — The National Population Commission, NPC, has raised the alarm that only about 40 per cent of births in Nigeria are currently registered, despite more than five million children being born in the country annually.

The Commission disclosed this in Abuja during the commemoration of the 2026 Africa Civil Registration and Vital Statistics, CRVS, Day.

Speaking at the event, Chairman of the NPC, Dr Aminu Yusuf, said the low registration coverage, particularly of births and deaths, remained a major challenge to Nigeria’s efforts to build a comprehensive and reliable national population database.

Yusuf, however, said the Commission had taken a major step towards closing the gap with the nationwide launch of a fully digital Civil Registration and Vital Statistics system on the Vital Rights Platform on July 1, 2026.

According to him, the launch marked the end of manual registration and the beginning of a new era of technology-driven civil registration in Nigeria.

He said the digital system would enable the country to securely and promptly record births, deaths, marriages and other vital events, while providing reliable data for governance, planning and sustainable development.

The NPC chairman explained that the digital platform would improve the storage and security of vital records, reduce duplication through automated verification and unique identifiers, and facilitate interoperability with health institutions, identity management agencies, planning bodies and statistical institutions.

He said: “More than five million children are born in Nigeria every year. According to the most recent Nigerian Demographic and Health Survey, only about 40 per cent of births are registered, while death registration coverage remains unacceptably low.

“These statistics underscore the urgent need to accelerate registration coverage through sustainable public awareness, stronger partnerships and increased community participation.”

Yusuf said the Commission was also decentralising registration services to bring them closer to Nigerians, particularly those living in rural and underserved communities.

He disclosed that digital registration services had already been extended to about 4,000 of the 8,809 wards across the country, with plans to achieve nationwide coverage.

The NPC chairman further revealed that more than 4,000 functional registration centres had been established across the 774 local government areas, while the Commission had commenced an expansion programme aimed at increasing the number to about 8,000 centres nationwide.

He said the expansion would reduce the distance, cost and time involved in accessing registration services and help ensure that no child or vital event was excluded because of geographical barriers.

Yusuf said the Commission had also strengthened partnerships with the Association of Local Governments of Nigeria, ALGON; National Identity Management Commission, NIMC; UNICEF; and BAMFOR Technologies Limited through a partnership compact signed in January 2025.

He added that the NPC was working with the National Primary Health Care Development Agency, state governments and health institutions to integrate birth registration into routine health services, allowing children to be registered as close as possible to their point of birth.

Also speaking, UNICEF Nigeria’s Chief of Child Protection, Natalie McCauley, described birth registration as a fundamental child right and the state’s first legal recognition of a child.

McCauley said a birth certificate provided proof of identity and laid the foundation for access to healthcare, education, social protection and legal protection throughout a child’s life.

She commended Nigeria’s progress in expanding digital birth registration, noting that services were now available in more than 4,000 wards across the country, including rural, hard-to-reach and humanitarian settings.

She urged the government and stakeholders to focus on three priorities as Africa enters a new CRVS decade: integration, decentralisation and digitalisation.

According to her, civil registration systems must work seamlessly with health, identity management, social protection and education systems, while services must be brought closer to families, especially those in remote communities.

“Every registered birth strengthens child protection. Every registered child becomes more visible to the systems designed to serve and protect them,” she said.

McCauley assured that UNICEF would continue to support the Nigerian government and its partners to strengthen birth registration systems, increase awareness and ensure that no child was left behind.

World.title: 10 types of foreigners who lost their U.S. visas as 175,000 canceled
World.content:
The United States Department of State has revoked more than 175,000 visas under President Donald Trump as part of an intensified effort to identify foreign nationals who violate U.S. immigration rules, commit crimes or pose risks to public safety and national security.

According to the department, the majority of the visa revocations followed law enforcement encounters involving criminal offences. Assault, driving under the influence, theft and drug-related crimes were among the leading reasons for the cancellations.

Other cases involved reckless driving, sexual assault, child abuse, fraud and embezzlement, among other offences.

The State Department said the revocations are part of its ongoing vetting process designed to ensure that visa holders comply with the conditions attached to their visas and do not pose a threat to Americans.

Here are 10 categories of foreign nationals whose visas have been revoked or who have faced deportability determinations:

1. People charged with sexual assault

The State Department revoked the visa of a foreign national charged with felony rape and sexual battery, including an alleged offence involving a mentally disabled victim.

2. People accused of kidnapping and child exploitation

Another foreign national faced charges including felony kidnapping, human trafficking and sexual exploitation of a minor.

3. People arrested for domestic violence and violent conduct

Visa revocations also involved foreign nationals arrested for offences including disorderly conduct, resisting arrest with violence, drunk driving and domestic violence.

4. Birth tourists

A U.S. embassy in North Africa revoked more than 100 visas belonging to parents accused of travelling to the United States primarily to give birth so their children could obtain U.S. citizenship.

5. People accused of child sexual offences

The department cited cases involving foreign nationals charged with offences including sodomy of a child, aggravated sexual battery and possession of child sexual abuse material.

One individual was reportedly charged with more than a dozen counts related to possession of such material.

6. Drug and dangerous-driving offenders

The State Department also cited a foreign national who was arrested while driving with heroin and a blood alcohol level more than three times the legal limit.

7. Foreign nationals accused of endorsing violence

Multiple foreign nationals who celebrated the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk also had their visas revoked, according to the department.

The cases included individuals who made comments appearing to praise the killing or express support for violence.

8. People involved in major healthcare fraud

One foreign national accused of operating a legitimate business helping vulnerable patients access healthcare was allegedly involved in a Medicaid fraud scheme involving more than $5 million in fake services.

9. People accused of fraudulently obtaining visas

The department also cited a foreign national accused of building a company around false claims, deceiving investors and defrauding clients of millions of dollars.

According to the State Department, the individual allegedly used fabricated claims and forged letters to fraudulently obtain a U.S. visa.

10. Foreign nationals considered deportable on foreign policy grounds

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also determined that several foreign nationals are deportable on foreign policy grounds.

The cases cited by the department include a Cuban national linked to an alleged influence operation connected to Cuba’s communist regime, Iranian nationals with alleged connections to the Iranian government, a Laotian child sex offender who received a pardon from Minnesota Governor Tim Walz, and a Kuwaiti national accused of expressing a desire for violence against the U.S. president and referring to Americans as his “enemy.”

The State Department said the Trump administration will continue to identify, investigate and revoke visas belonging to foreign nationals it considers threats to Americans.

The department stressed that a U.S. visa is a privilege rather than a right and said it would continue using available measures to protect communities from people who violate the conditions of their entry or pose public safety and national security concerns.
