A major one is the administration’s threat to have the US Postal Service not deliver mail ballots for states that don’t comply with its demand that they hand over their voter lists. This is a request that even many red states have rejected, citing privacy concerns.

Democrats are much more likely to use mail ballots, which Trump has baselessly connected to widespread fraud. So curtailing them could greatly help Republicans.

(Federal courts have blocked this Trump executive order, and the administration recently appealed to the Supreme Court.)

Trump has also gone to great lengths to try to substantiate his still-baseless claims of widespread fraud. That includes the administration seizing 2020 ballots in Fulton County, Georgia, and Trump’s recent primetime address about election security that some read as a statement of intent — a pretext for more direct federal involvement in elections, which are run by states.

President Donald Trump speaks about election security during an address to the nation from the East Room of the White House on July 16. Saul Loeb/Pool/Reuters

Ty Cobb, who served as White House counsel in Trump’s first term, said he interpreted the speech last month as a “predicate that he needs to declare an emergency.”

And Trump has occasionally said things, like he did in the new interview, suggesting he would like to take control of US elections.

Back in February, he urged his party to “take over the voting in at least 15 places,” adding: “The Republicans ought to nationalize the voting.”

The Washington Post also reported in March that pro-Trump activists were circulating a potential executive order that claimed Chinese interference in the 2020 election gave Trump emergency authorities over the 2026 election. And Trump’s primetime address focused on China, despite the tenuous evidence.

Trump’s intense focus on the “SAVE America Act,” which has never appeared to have a chance to pass but Trump has said is vital, could also be read as part of building the case for more drastic action.

But whether Trump could take over elections himself, as Root posits, is far from certain.

As CNN’s Marshall Cohen and Michael Williams reported in February, the Constitution makes it difficult for Trump to truly “nationalize” elections. Courts have overwhelmingly upheld the principle that states are in charge of elections.

Presidents generally have more authority to act unilaterally when national security is involved — hence the significance of invoking China — but some experts are skeptical that Trump’s effort would pass legal muster.

World.title: Iran’s supreme leader elevates military veterans willing to confront the US
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has boasted that his war in Iran has led to a “very rational,” “very different,” and “much more reasonable” leadership in Tehran. But the elevation of six hardliners to top security positions this week suggests the Islamic Republic’s new command may be neither moderate nor inclined to compromise.

The men now rising through the security establishment have spent their careers confronting enemies abroad and suppressing dissent at home.

The announcement of the senior appointments, purportedly made by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Monday, followed the naming of a new national security chief, Mohsen Rezaie, a day earlier.

Experts say the changes mark a shift in approach compared to the more cautious tone under Mojtaba’s father, Ali Khamenei, who was supreme leader until assassinated by Israel at the start of the war.

An image of “Team Mojtaba” featured on the front page of the Hamshahri newspaper on Tuesday. Hamshahri

It is both more aggressive toward external enemies and more vigilant toward internal dissent.

There are two parallel priorities, says Hamidreza Azizi at the Clingendael Institute, a think tank in the Netherlands: preparing the state for a more confrontational external environment and further securitizing the domestic sphere.

“The emphasis on offensive operations, unified command, and faster decision-making suggests that the leadership wants to move from Ali Khamenei’s traditionally more cautious approach to deterrence toward what could be described as offensive deterrence,” Azizi told CNN.

Most of the appointees have a background in intelligence, according to Saeid Golkar, associate professor of political science at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga.

“The picture we are seeing is the Islamic Republic moving toward a security-dominated bureaucratic regime,” he told CNN.

The reshuffle reinforces the regime’s “current maximalist and hardline positions,” according to the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, “including absolute Iranian control of the Strait of Hormuz, the removal of US troops from the region, and the development of Iran’s nuclear program.”

Rezaie has long called for resistance against the United States while acknowledging a place for negotiation.

In March he warned that “if the United States strikes Iran’s electricity infrastructure, this time the equation will not be ‘an eye for an eye’; rather, it will be a head, hands, and feet for an eye.”

And last month he claimed: “The United States has been trapped, it has fallen into the trap of Iran, but we will not let it go.”

Targeting Trump through the ballot box

Rezaie belongs to a faction of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) that believes “the only way to get concessions from the US is the continuation of fighting, exerting pressure on the US and a steady dose of pain on Donald Trump,” said Sina Azodi, assistant professor of Middle East politics at George Washington University.

His elevation feeds into the overall Iranian strategy of prolonging the conflict with the US and ensuring that Trump’s allies face defeat in the midterm elections, Azodi told CNN.

“The current leadership in Tehran is far more risk-taking,” according to Vali Nasr, author of “Iran’s Grand Strategy.”

That leadership believes that Iran’s “weak” response to the killing by the US in 2020 of Qasem Soleimani, the leader of Iran’s elite Quds Force, was one reason Trump escalated pressure in his second term, according to Nasr.

Soleimani was targeted by a US missile in Baghdad at the end of the first Trump term. Iran did not retaliate directly, despite furious rhetoric.

This new group of leaders is more willing to use “Iran’s own military capabilities directly, and challenge adversaries without the same level of restraint,” says Israeli analyst and Iran-watcher Danny Citrinowicz.

“This shift should be especially concerning when it comes to the nuclear issue. A significant number of voices inside Iran believe that Ali Khamenei’s strategy of maintaining a strategic ‘limbo’ – avoiding both escalation and resolution, ultimately weakened Iran more than it protected it,” Citrinowicz posted on X.

‘Granular’ domestic security strategy

One of the new appointments brings back a veteran intelligence figure as the head of the Basij volunteer militia, which is under the Guards’ control and was heavily involved in the brutal suppression of protests in January.

Hossein Taeb – a close ally of Mojtaba Khamenei – “was a particularly controversial and divisive figure during his tenure as head of IRGC Intelligence, closely associated with the hardline security apparatus’s repression of dissent,” wrote Sina Toossi, senior fellow at the Center for International Policy, on X.

The United States sanctioned Taeb in 2010 for his involvement in suppressing protests the previous year after a presidential election widely thought to have been rigged.

His new mandate “calls for strengthening the Basij’s ‘public intelligence network,’ exploiting modern technologies, and expanding neighborhood organization” of the militia, Toossi said.

In a picture obtained by AFP from the Iranian news agency Tasnim, Hossein Taeb attends a meeting in Iran’s capital, Tehran, on June 24, 2018. Hamed Malekpour/Tasnim News/AFP/Getty Images

This amounts to “an attempt to make intelligence and internal security much more granular: pushing collection, detection and early warning deeper into neighborhoods, local social networks and mosques,” according to Babak Vahdad, an independent researcher.

That is significant “after a war in which penetration, covert networks, sabotage and intelligence failures became one of the Islamic Republic’s most serious vulnerabilities,” he added.

In part, the appointments could be an effort by Khamenei – who has not been seen or heard from directly since being chosen as supreme leader in March – “to instal allies in influential positions in case growing economic pressures prompt another public uprising,” according to Golkar.

Given his long absence from public view, analysts are unsure whether Khamanei is indeed the architect of the new set-up.

But the combination of Taeb, Rezaei, Ahmad Vahidi – now commander of the IRGC – and other security veterans “indicates a leadership increasingly relying on experienced intelligence and military figures to consolidate the system after the war,” Azizi told CNN.

“It is not a complete break with Ali Khamenei’s approach, but it does represent a harder and more explicitly confrontational version of it.”

CNN’s Aida Karimi contributed to this article.

World.title: Thailand tightens gun controls after deadly school shooting
World.content:
Bangkok —

Thailand is suspending new gun permits and tightening its firearm controls after last week’s deadly school shooting, in which a 14-year-old boy killed eight people before turning the gun on himself.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul issued the directive on Tuesday, ordering government officials to “urgently elevate firearm control measures across the entire system,” according to a statement from his office.

The measures include temporarily suspending the issuance of gun purchase permits, re-reviewing all permits still pending approval, and suspending new “welfare gun” programs – which allow eligible public officials, including civil servants and politicians, to buy discounted weapons.

Government agencies will also now inspect gun dealers nationwide and verify sales records; inspect ammunition at shooting ranges to check that they’re following regulations; and “accelerate crackdowns on illegal firearms, rigorously prosecute offenders, and request maximum penalties from the court,” the directive read.

The statement also lays out broader reforms that will take longer to legislate, such as increasing penalties for offenders, tightening ammunition controls for gun dealers and ranges, and requiring that gun permits be renewed on a more frequent basis.

An initial compensation of 1 million baht (about $30,166) has been approved for six of the deceased victims, the statement said.

Officials prepare to pay their respects at the Tem Rak Samakkhi Buddhist temple in Nonthaburi, north of Bangkok, on August 11, 2026, in front of the caskets of the grandparents shot dead by their 14-year-old grandson, before he killed six others at his school and then turned the gun on himself. Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty Images

The mass shooting has shone a new spotlight on Thailand’s high levels of gun ownership, both licensed and unlicensed.

Last Friday, the 14-year-old gunman first killed his grandparents at their home, where he also lived, before opening fire at a secondary school and killing six people there. He then killed himself. It was the country’s worst mass shooting since 2022.

Police said on Sunday the gunman had previously had an air gun confiscated by a teacher last year, and had watched violent content online, using social media to learn how to use a firearm. The firearm he used is believed to have been his grandfather’s.

Thailand has the highest rate of civilian gun ownership in Southeast Asia, with around 15 guns per 100 people. Its firearm death rate is similarly elevated, second in the region only to the Philippines.

Countries with higher gun ownership rates tend to see correspondingly higher firearm death rates. Multiple studies link easy access to firearms with more frequent gun-related deaths, including through suicide, homicide and unintentional injury.

As well as reigniting debate about gun control in Thailand, the shooting has put a focus on mental health for students and young people.

The Ministry of Education said it would develop new safety protocols in the coming months, including mental health screenings and a system to refer at-risk people to specialists, drills for emergency response plans, a drive to stamp out bullying and better detection to stop items from being taken into schools.

Mass shootings elsewhere in the world have often led to stricter gun control measures. Serbia and New Zealand, two nations with comparatively high gun ownership rates, both tightened rules and brought in gun amnesty drives following horrific massacres in recent years.

The outlier remains the United States, where gun violence and rates of mass shootings are among the highest in the world, with little progress made on tighter laws in the face of strong lobbying and constitutional protections.

World.title: Liberia: Five LDEA Leadership Changes in Two Years—Senator Konneh Warns Liberia Cannot “Change the Figurehead” and Cure the Cancer
World.content:
MONROVIA— President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s decision to replace the leadership of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency marks the latest turn in a revolving door that has seen the agency change hands five times in just over two years.

By Obediah Johnson, [email protected] and Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The appointment of retired Major General Daniel Dee Ziankahn, Jr. as Director General-designate comes as the LDEA and Liberia’s wider security establishment face perhaps their most serious credibility crisis in years.

But for Senator Amara Konneh, the latest change raises a question that goes beyond the credentials of the incoming director: Can Liberia fix a deeply troubled security institution simply by repeatedly changing the person at the top?

Konneh’s answer is no.

“Changing the leadership at LDEA does not automatically fix the cancer eating away at our security system,” the Senate Public Accounts and Audit Committee chairman warned Tuesday.

His argument goes to the heart of Liberia’s ongoing cocaine crisis. The country has recorded cocaine seizures valued at more than US$336 million, including an approximately US$317 million shipment intercepted in the VOA Community in Paynesville and a roughly US$19 million consignment seized at Roberts International Airport.

The investigations have generated allegations involving individuals connected to the security and law-enforcement establishment, triggered internal investigations and produced leadership changes.

Now, President Boakai has turned to Ziankahn, a retired military general and former Defense Minister, to restore stability and credibility to an agency that has experienced extraordinary leadership turbulence.

But the question remains whether another change at the top can address what critics describe as deeper institutional weaknesses.

Five Changes, One Troubled Agency

The significance of Ziankahn’s appointment is best understood against the backdrop of the leadership changes that preceded him.

Since taking office in January 2024, President Boakai has overseen five changes involving the top leadership of the LDEA—three director-general-level appointments and two periods in which officials served as Officer in Charge.

The revolving door is striking, particularly because the fight against illicit drugs was one of Boakai’s prominent campaign commitments.

After his inauguration, Boakai moved quickly to appoint Abraham Kromah, a veteran security officer who had previously served as Deputy Commissioner of Police for Operations under former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf.

Kromah arrived with a reputation as a tough law-enforcement officer, and his appointment was initially welcomed by many Liberians who expected him to bring a more aggressive approach to the fight against drugs, particularly the synthetic drug commonly known as Kush.

Instead, his tenure became embroiled in an internal management crisis.

A public confrontation involving Kromah and his deputies, Hassan Fadiga and Gbawou Kowou, escalated into a physical altercation and resulted in their suspension. The administration subsequently ordered an investigation, and following the submission of the report, Kromah and his deputies were removed.

But the report was never made public. That unresolved issue continues to hang over the agency. For the public, the unanswered question is simple: What did the investigation find? The absence of a public explanation has contributed to a recurring problem within the LDEA—major decisions are announced, but the underlying findings are often kept from public view.

Peters Leaves With a Warning

Following Kromah’s removal, Christopher K. Peters Sr. was appointed Officer in Charge of the LDEA on June 4, 2024. Peters’ tenure was brief.

Although he pointed to drug seizures worth more than US$4 million and lengthy prison sentences secured against traffickers, he resigned only months after taking office.

His resignation letter, addressed to then-Minister of State Sylvester M. Grigsby (now deceased), offered perhaps one of the clearest diagnoses of the agency’s institutional weaknesses.

Peters argued that winning the war on drugs required strategic reforms, enhanced training, additional personnel, adequate funding and sustained support from key partners. He also stressed the need for leadership capable of promoting calm, maturity and teamwork within the agency.

His resignation became effective October 31, 2024. Whether his recommendations were fully acted upon remains an open question.

Souh Returns—Then Leaves

Peters was succeeded by Anthony Souh, another experienced law-enforcement officer and former LDEA Director General during the Ellen Johnson Sirleaf administration, when Boakai served as Vice President.

Souh returned to the agency with institutional experience and familiarity with Liberia’s drug-enforcement challenges.

But his return did not produce lasting stability. About a year later, the Boakai administration removed Souh and other senior LDEA officials, paving the way for another restructuring.

Again, the cycle continued.

Then Came Biago

The next major leadership arrangement brought Fitzgerald T. M. Biago, a Deputy Commissioner of Police, into the agency’s leadership.

On August 28, 2025, President Boakai appointed Biago, a Deputy Commissioner of the Liberian National Police, as Officer-In-Charge. He led an interim management structure alongside Ernest T. Tarpeh of the National Security Agency and Patrick B. Kormazu of the LNP following the removal of Souh and other senior officials.

Nearly a year later, his leadership was thrown into controversy after activist Martin K. N. Kollie alleged that Biago had received a vehicle as a gift from Leroy Harris, a suspect in the US$317 million cocaine investigation.

Biago denied involvement in the drug allegations and stepped aside to make himself available for investigation.

A Ministry of Justice review did not establish his involvement in narcotics trafficking. But the government said the review identified ethical concerns, prompting President Boakai to indefinitely suspend Biago from the Liberia National Police and order a more detailed investigation.

Again, the distinction is important: the government did not establish that Biago was involved in the narcotics trade, but it found ethical concerns serious enough to warrant further action. And again, the LDEA was left with a leadership problem.

Now comes Ziankahn.

The retired major general brings perhaps the strongest national-security credentials of any of the recent LDEA appointees.

He became the first post-war Liberian Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of Liberia, appointed in 2014 after the restructuring of the military following the civil war. He had enlisted in the newly restructured Armed Forces of Liberia in 2006 and rose through the ranks before becoming Chief of Staff, a position he held from 2014 to 2018.

He subsequently served as Liberia’s Minister of National Defense under former President George Weah and later became Military Advisor to President Boakai.

Analysts say his appointment represents a significant shift in the profile of LDEA leadership. The administration appears to be betting that Ziankahn’s military and national-security experience can bring discipline, stability and strategic direction to an agency that has repeatedly struggled with internal turmoil. But that is precisely where Konneh’s warning becomes relevant.

A Revolving Door at the LDEA

Ziankahn’s appointment marks what amounts to the fifth leadership change at the LDEA in roughly two years under President Boakai—three director-general-level appointments and two individuals who have served as Officer in Charge.

The frequency of those changes raises a fundamental institutional question: If leadership keeps changing but the underlying vulnerabilities remain, is the problem really the person at the top?

The “Self-Policing” Problem

Senator Konneh argued that institutions implicated in allegations surrounding a major criminal investigation should not be left to investigate themselves.

“Institutions with heavy corruption and cartel allegations cannot investigate themselves,” he said, calling for an open, credible and independent inquiry into high-ranking individuals allegedly connected to the narcotics network.

That demand strikes at the heart of the cocaine investigations.

The magnitude of the seizures has transformed the issue from an ordinary drug-enforcement matter into a national security question.

A shipment valued at hundreds of millions of dollars does not move through international supply chains, ports, airports and local communities without sophisticated organization, financing, logistics and access.

That inevitably raises questions about whether criminal networks operated entirely outside the state—or whether individuals with access to official systems may have facilitated, enabled or shielded elements of the trade.

Those questions cannot be answered merely by replacing one agency director with another. They require investigators capable of following the evidence wherever it leads. And that means senior officials cannot be treated differently from ordinary suspects simply because of their positions.

Ziankahn’s Appointment: A Strong Man for a Weak System?

There is little doubt that Ziankahn brings considerable experience to the position. The retired major general previously served as Liberia’s Minister of National Defense and, more recently, as Military Advisor to President Boakai.

His background gives him significant exposure to national security operations and strategic decision-making. That experience could prove valuable to an agency that has been battered by leadership instability and public distrust.

But experience alone does not answer the central problem.

The question is whether Ziankahn will inherit an agency capable of functioning independently—or an institution whose credibility has been damaged by allegations that reach beyond its current leadership.

Konneh acknowledged Ziankahn’s credentials while making clear that his appointment does not erase the unresolved questions.

“We wish Gen. Ziankahn success in his Senate confirmation and in his tenure, but we will observe closely,” he said.

That may ultimately become the defining test of the new LDEA leadership.

Ziankahn will not merely be judged by the number of drug seizures under his watch. He will be judged by whether his tenure produces an agency in which investigations are insulated from political influence, evidence is protected, officers are held accountable, and no official is considered untouchable.

World.title: Liberia’s Drug Crisis: Accountability Must Begin Within the Security Sector
World.content:
Senator Amara Konneh’s latest intervention raises an important question that Liberia can no longer afford to avoid: Can the government effectively fight transnational drug trafficking while simultaneously confronting allegations of corruption within the very institutions responsible for fighting it?

By E. W. Cooper, contributing writer

I believe the answer must be yes—but only if the government is prepared to apply the same standard of accountability to everyone.

This is not about protecting the opposition, defending the government, or creating political scapegoats. It is about protecting Liberia’s national security.

The reported US$317 million cocaine seizure is not an ordinary criminal matter. It involves alleged transnational criminal networks, international partners, substantial financial resources, and allegations involving individuals within Liberia’s security architecture. That requires an investigation that is professional, evidence-driven, and insulated from conflicts of interest.

I therefore agree with Senator Konneh on one fundamental principle: there must be no sacred cows.

But accountability must be based on evidence.

If an officer is accused of accepting money, investigate the financial trail.

If an officer claims he was instructed to escort a shipment, examine the communications records.

If someone is alleged to have facilitated communication between detained suspects and an international network, examine the phones, financial transactions, surveillance footage, and other available evidence.

If an official is accused of interfering with an investigation, determine exactly what action was taken, when it occurred, and whether it violated the law.

And if allegations are made against the Inspector General or any other senior official, those allegations should receive the same objective scrutiny.

Recusal Is About Integrity

This is where my position remains consistent.

When serious allegations begin pointing toward an official who has a significant role in overseeing an investigation, recusal can be an act of institutional integrity rather than an admission of guilt.

The objective is not to remove someone because they have been accused. The objective is to ensure that the person being questioned is not simultaneously in a position to influence the investigation into those questions.

If the official is innocent, an independent process can establish that.

If the allegations are unsupported, the official’s credibility can be restored.

And if evidence establishes wrongdoing, the law should apply.

That is precisely why an impartial process matters.

International Assistance Should Strengthen, Not Replace Liberia

There is another important point.

International involvement in a case of this magnitude should not be interpreted as evidence that Liberians are incapable of investigating their own country. Liberia has capable law-enforcement and security professionals.

International partners can provide specialized expertise, intelligence, forensic capabilities, financial investigations, and transnational investigative connections that are particularly valuable in organized-crime cases.

But Liberian institutions must remain part of the process.

The objective should be partnership—not institutional surrender.

The President’s Test

President Boakai now faces an important test of leadership.

The public does not simply need arrests. It needs to see a process that is credible.

The President must demonstrate that accountability is not determined by rank, political affiliation, personal relationships, or institutional loyalty.

If someone is innocent, clear them.

If someone violated administrative rules, discipline them.

If someone committed a crime, prosecute them.

And if the evidence leads to someone at the highest level of government or security institutions, follow the evidence there as well.

That is what the rule of law means.

The government should not fear the truth. The truth, properly established through evidence and due process, ultimately protects legitimate institutions.

The greatest danger would be for Liberia to investigate this matter selectively—protecting some, sacrificing others, and allowing public pressure rather than evidence to determine the outcome.

This investigation should not be about Cocaingate as a political slogan.

It should be about establishing exactly who knew what, who did what, who benefited, who facilitated the operation, who attempted to obstruct the investigation, and whether anyone within Liberia’s security apparatus compromised the Republic for personal gain.

Follow the evidence.

No sacred cows. No scapegoats. No selective justice.

Just truth, accountability, due process, and the rule of law.E. W. Cooper is a Law enforcement supervisor, Homeland Security & Emergency Management professional, and a Criminal Justice scholar.

World.title: U.S. Signal to Liberia’s Drug War Carries Extra Weight After Record Busts — and a Cloud Over Its Chief Enforcers
World.content:
The U.S. Embassy meeting between Chargé d’Affaires Joe Zadrozny and Liberia’s top police officials — Inspector General Gregory Coleman and EPS Director Sam Gaye — comes at a fraught moment: a $19 million cocaine bust in July was followed by a record $317 million seizure implicating senior police officers themselves, some now facing charges. Coleman has also faced unproven allegations of ties to the trafficking network, making the embassy’s emphasis on “accountability” read as pointed encouragement rather than blanket endorsement.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia- By any measure, U.S. Chargé d’Affaires Joe Zadrozny’s meeting with Liberia National Police Inspector General Gregory O.W. Coleman and Executive Protection Service Director Sam Gaye should have been a routine diplomatic courtesy. Instead, it lands at one of the most consequential moments in Liberia’s modern anti-narcotics effort — and its timing, coming just as President Boakai reshuffles the LDEA’s leadership for the third time in two years, makes it read as something closer to a signal than a formality.

Why the timing matters

The meeting follows two extraordinary seizures in the space of a few weeks. In July, security personnel intercepted six cargo boxes at Roberts International Airport disguised as textiles and seasoning cubes; inside were nearly 200 compressed blocks of cocaine, ultimately valued around $19 million — a case that drew public criticism after delays in identifying suspects raised fears that individuals connected to the shipment had already fled the country. Weeks later came a seizure of a different order of magnitude entirely: nearly four tonnes of cocaine, worth an estimated $317.7 million, recovered from what investigators described as an organized, sophisticated, and well-funded trafficking network that may have operated in Liberia for more than six years. Authorities later incinerated 4.2 metric tons of the drug, sending what Coleman called a message that Liberia was no longer “a place of comfort” for traffickers.

What has made the second bust politically explosive, however, is who it implicated. Coleman confirmed that Liberia’s chief of highway patrol and the head of the major crimes unit face charges, with a deputy police commander at the main airport also under suspicion — meaning the very institution now meant to lead enforcement, the Liberia National Police, has senior officers accused of facilitating the trafficking it is supposed to stop.

The credibility problem the U.S. visit runs into

That is precisely why Zadrozny’s meeting cannot be read purely as encouragement. Coleman himself has become a subject of serious, if unproven, allegations. In a July 15 letter to Zadrozny, CDC Secretary General Jefferson Koijee requested U.S. backing for an international investigation, alleging that Coleman took vehicles from a drug cartel and distributed them to President Boakai, Vice President Koung, and the presiding officers of the Legislature, and separately that the 2024 removal of former LDEA head Abraham Kromah was orchestrated by Coleman to protect a cartel he was allegedly connected to, and that Coleman later maneuvered Fitzgerald Biago — his own deputy at the police — into the LDEA’s top job. Koijee’s broader argument was structural: that repeatedly installing senior police officers atop the drug agency has blurred the LDEA’s independence and concentrated excessive influence within Liberia’s security apparatus.

Notably, Boakai’s own government has now partly validated that structural critique without validating the corruption allegation. Monday’s Executive Mansion release states that the Justice Ministry’s probe into Biago “did not establish any involvement… in illegal narcotics trafficking” but did identify unspecified “ethical concerns” — landing in a gray zone that neither clears the LDEA leadership pipeline of suspicion nor confirms the most serious claims against it. Biago’s own departure now repeats the very pattern Koijee flagged: a police-to-LDEA pipeline replaced, once again, by another appointee — this time a retired general rather than a police officer, which may itself be read as an attempt to break that cycle.

What the U.S. statement does — and doesn’t — say

Read against this backdrop, Zadrozny’s language is carefully calibrated. It reaffirms partnership and frames Liberian institution-building as serving “regional stability” and the “enduring friendship” between the two countries — standard diplomatic register. But it also pointedly addresses itself to “law and order” and “a just and accountable legal system,” phrasing that functions as quiet pressure on Coleman and Gaye specifically to see the investigations — including into their own ranks — through to a credible conclusion, rather than as an unqualified vote of confidence in current leadership.

The U.S. has skin in this game beyond diplomacy: earlier reporting has linked American law enforcement, including the Department of Justice, to the broader trafficking investigation tied to the record cocaine seizure, and West Africa’s role as a transit corridor — now carrying an estimated 30 percent of Europe-bound cocaine, according to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime — makes Liberia’s enforcement capacity a matter of direct interest to Washington and European partners alike, not just Monrovia.

The stakes for the investigation ahead

For Ziankahn’s incoming LDEA leadership, the practical effect of the U.S. engagement is likely to be twofold: continued technical and possibly intelligence-sharing support for dismantling the trafficking network behind the record bust, paired with implicit international scrutiny of whether Liberia’s own police leadership — the officials the U.S. just met with — can be trusted to police itself.

Whether Coleman and Gaye emerge from the ongoing probes as central figures in prosecuting this case, or as subjects of it, may do more than any embassy statement to determine whether Liberia’s “war on drugs” produces lasting institutional reform or simply another rotation of the same personnel through different chairs.

World.title: Guinea Border: Time for Government to Level with the Liberian People
World.content:
Since February, Liberia’s border with Guinea has seen repeated incursions, a flag removal, troop deployments, and the displacement of thousands of residents in Lofa County. President Boakai has pursued the right diplomatic path — tripartite summits, joint technical commissions, a special envoy — but the public has received only sporadic updates since. This editorial argues that quiet diplomacy without public transparency risks eroding trust at home and, given West Africa’s history, could let a manageable dispute harden into something far more dangerous. It calls on the government to communicate more regularly and plainly with affected communities, not just with counterparts in Conakry.

FOR NEARLY a year now, communities along Liberia’s border with Guinea have lived with a question their government has not fully answered: what exactly is happening on our land, and what is being done about it?

PICTURE A FAMILY in Sorlumba, in Foya District, going about an ordinary morning — tending a farm plot, walking to a river crossing they’ve used their whole lives — when armed soldiers from across the border appear and declare the ground beneath their feet belongs to someone else. That is not a hypothetical. It is close to what residents there say happened earlier this year, when Guinean soldiers reportedly crossed into Liberian territory, seized construction equipment from a Liberian road contractor, and — most provocatively — ordered the removal of the Liberian flag that had flown at the riverbank for decades, even through the years of civil war. ￼ For people who lived through that war, watching their flag come down was not an abstract diplomatic incident. It was personal.

THE BARE FACTS, as they have trickled out through news reports rather than official candor, are troubling enough on their own. Alleged incursions in February sent panic through border communities. Guinea responded to the rising tension not with reassurance but with troop deployments to the frontier, and Liberia’s own rights commission later found that the affair had displaced thousands of residents and exposed serious gaps in both border protection and regional diplomacy. Thousands of displaced people is not a statistic to file away — it is thousands of individual decisions to grab what could be carried and walk away from home, uncertain when, or whether, it would be safe to return.

TO ITS CREDIT, the Boakai administration did not let the crisis spiral into confrontation. President Boakai joined his Guinean and Sierra Leonean counterparts in Conakry in March for a tripartite summit that produced commitments to dialogue, joint technical commissions on border delimitation, and a pledge to convene a full Mano River Union summit within a month to “revitalize” the organization. In June, Information Minister Jerolinmek Piah reaffirmed that Liberia remained committed to resolving the dispute through diplomacy, and that a special presidential envoy had been dispatched to follow up on the Conakry commitments.

THESE ARE THE RIGHT instincts. Nobody serious wants Liberia and Guinea shooting at each other over a riverbank in Foya.

BUT GOOD INSTINCTS are not the same as good governance, and here is where the government’s approach has fallen short: the Liberian public still does not know, in any real detail, where things stand. The promised MRU summit, floated for July, has come and gone without a clear public accounting of whether it happened, what it produced, or why it may have slipped. The joint technical commissions on border delimitation — the actual mechanism that would settle, once and for all, whose land is whose — have operated largely out of public view. The people of Lofa County did not get to choose whether their homes sat on contested ground. The least they are owed is honesty about what their government is doing to protect them.

THIS MATTERS for reasons beyond transparency as a good-governance principle. West Africa has spent the better part of four decades relearning, at enormous human cost, how quickly a border dispute can metastasize into something far worse. Liberia’s own seven-year civil war and Sierra Leone’s decade of conflict were not born in a vacuum — porous, poorly governed borders and cross-border grievances were accelerants for both. Analysts tracking the current tensions have noted that all four Mano River Union countries have emerged from civil conflict, yet peace remains fragile due to weak border governance, contested territorial claims, and shifting political transitions ￼ — a diagnosis that should concentrate minds in Monrovia as much as in Conakry.

THERE IS ALSO a very human political risk in silence. When government communication goes quiet, the space fills with rumor, opposition point-scoring, and — as nearly happened in Foya, where young residents reportedly moved to confront Guinean soldiers directly rather than wait for diplomacy to work — with ordinary citizens deciding to defend their own communities because no one has told them help is coming. A government that explains its strategy clearly gives frightened people a reason to trust the process instead of taking matters into their own hands.

WE ARE NOT calling for saber-rattling, nor for the kind of “inflammatory rhetoric” the government has rightly said it wants to avoid. We are calling for the opposite: more information, delivered more often, in language ordinary Liberians in Foya and Vahun can understand and act on — not just diplomatic communiqués aimed at regional bodies and foreign audiences.

PRESIDENT BOAKAI has said, correctly, that this is “not a matter for confrontation, but for calm, facts and sustained engagement.” We agree entirely — provided that “facts” reach the farmers, traders, and families living along that border, and not only the diplomats in closed-door rooms in Conakry. Liberia has been here before. The region does not need reminding of what happens when land disputes are left to fester unexplained. Let this government show, through consistent and honest public communication, that it has learned that lesson.

World.title: Police officers directed to be professional -Musamba
World.content:
Inspector General of Police, Graphel Musamba, has directed all police officers to discharge their duties with professionalism, integrity, neutrality and respect for the constitution, ahead of the August polls.

In a statement issued to the media, Mr Musamba, says the Police have enhanced crime detection operations and Rapid Response Teams across all provinces, in a bid to ensure that every eligible citizen can vote freely and peacefully, without intimidation.

Mr Musamba further directed the police officers to exercise respect for human rights while dealing with criminal conduct, protect every citizen equally and arrest all individuals who commit crime, regardless of political affiliation.

He said that the Police and Electoral Commission of Zambia have coordinated measures to safeguard electoral materials, polling stations, election officials and integrity of the electoral process.

“Every voter, every candidate and every election official will be protected without fear, favour or political consideration,” said Mr Musamba.

Mr Musamba said that the Zambia police service has progressively implemented its 2026 electoral security plan with additional police officers deployed across the country to strengthen police visibility, improve response times and reassure communities.

Mr Musamba also urged members of the public to play a part in safeguarding peace by returning home, to work or continue with lawful activities after casting their votes and avoid loitering around polling stations, unless as accredited by the ECZ.

He also urged members of the public to obtain election results only from official and authorised sources and to avoid circulating or relying on unverified information, rumours and speculative announcements on social media.

Mr Musamba further urged the public to expect increased police presence and snap security checkpoints on selected roads, as a preventive measure that is intended to enhance public safety.

World.title: Poll staff deployed-Kanchibiya
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) has commenced the deployment of poll staff in Kanchibiya District ahead of this week’s general elections.

Kanchibiya District Electoral Officer (DEO) Augustine Chanda says the deployment follows briefings conducted for various stakeholders, including uniformed personnel, the media, Non-governmental Organisations (NGOs) and faith-based organisations.

He said the commission also conducted briefings for poll staff in preparation for their deployment to various polling stations across the district.

Mr Chanda said the deployment exercise will begin with staff assigned to the furthest areas, including Cheweshimfwamba to ensure that all personnel are in their respective areas before polling day.

He expressed hope that the deployment of all poll staff in the district will be completed by midday tomorrow.

And Mr Chanda has said that poll staff were also taking oaths of affirmation as part of the requirements for their engagement with the ECZ and the electoral process.

He urged all stakeholders who had been briefed by the commission to participate in the electoral process in accordance with established guidelines.

Mr Chanda said the guidelines and stakeholder engagements were aimed at ensuring effective coordination of operations among all players during the elections.

He also challenged the media to disseminate accurate information to members of the public who may not have an opportunity to witness activities taking place at various polling stations.

He added that police are expected to maintain peace and protect voters.

And Mr Chanda said the commission’s priority was to maintain voter confidence and ensure that the electoral process was free, fair and inclusive to all eligible citizens.

World.title: Liato family thanks President Hakainde Hichilema
World.content:
Family of the late former Cabinet Minister, Austin Liato, has expressed profound gratitude to President Hakainde Hichilema, for having accorded Mr Liato a National Mourning.

Family representative, Jonathan Liato, also thanked the church, political leaders, friends and members of the public for standing with them during the period of National Mourning.

speaking during the burial ceremony at Leopards Hill Memorial Park today, Mr Liato said the support and presence of mourners demonstrated the love and respect that people had for the late Mr Liato.

He said the family was particularly humbled by the presence of the President of the Republic of Zambia, through his representative, saying it was a demonstration of solidarity with the family during its time of grief.

Mr Liato also thanked serving and former Members of Parliament, ministers, civic and government leaders for standing with the family and honouring the life and service of the late Mr Liato.

He further expressed gratitude to church leaders and men and women of God for their prayers, words of comfort and for giving the bereaved family hope through the Christian message of resurrection.

Mr Liato also commended the church, service family, friends, choir, organisers and all those who assisted the family from the time of the late Liato’s death, saying their support helped ensure that the funeral proceedings were conducted with dignity and care.

He said Mr Liato lived a life dedicated to God and the people of Zambia, adding that the family would continue to remember and honour the late Mr Liato for his service to the nation and the people.

World.title: President Hichilema speaks infrastructure development in Matero
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has assured residents of Matero and Lima constituencies of more infrastructure development if voted for the second term of office, in the August 13 general elections.

Speaking when he addressed multitudes of Matero and Lima residents at Chunga grounds, President Hichilema committed to work on township roads in both constituencies, saying he wants all the township roads to be upgraded to bituminous standard.

He indicated that most of the township roads in Matero and Lima constituencies are in a deplorable state.

And President Hichilema further assured the people in the two constituencies of improved water supply once voted back into office, in the August 13 polls.

The Head of State said he was aware that water supply was a challenge in the two constituencies, pledging to work on the drainage system in Matero and Lima, noting that during the rainy season the said areas often experience floods.

President Hichilema said the improved drainage system will allow water to flow freely without causing flooding.

Meanwhile, President Hichilema has promised to build additional health facilities in the newly created Lima constituency.

The President said his goal is to ensure that women give birth in a safe facility.

President Hichilema also announced at the same community engagement that skills training centres for the youths will be constructed in Matero and Lima constituencies.

The President has since urged the people of Matero and Lima constituencies to also vote for the UPND candidates in the forthcoming general elections, saying voting for UPND candidates who include Councillors and Members of Parliament will enable him to easily deliver development.

World.title: Nakonde ballot papers verified
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) in Nakonde District, in Muchinga Province has completed the verification of ballot papers ahead of Thursday’s general elections.

The verification exercise was conducted in the presence of stakeholders and representatives from the United Party for National Development (UPND) and the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP).

Nakonde District Electoral Officer Donald Mwanza says that ballot papers from Nsonde and Mukumbe polling stations, drawn from 2 wards under 2 constituencies, were sampled during the exercise.

He stated that the stakeholders expressed satisfaction with the process and confirmed that everything was in order.

Mr Mwanza further disclosed that the dispatch of polling officials to hard-to-reach areas has commenced today.

He said 10 polling stations will receive officials and election materials in this first phase of the dispatch.

The District Electoral Officer added that both transport and personnel are ready and that the district is fully set for the poll scheduled for Thursday, August 13th, 2026.

World.title: ECZ conducts ballot verification in Mpika
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) in Mpika says it remains committed to ensuring transparency, credibility and fairness in the electoral process ahead of tomorrow’s General Elections.

The Commission made the assurance following a ballot paper verification exercise conducted at the Mpika Town Council Chambers in Mpika District in Muchinga Province.

The exercise was witnessed by various election stakeholders who participated in the verification process.

Mpika District Electoral Officer Samuel Musenga said the verification exercise was necessary and conducted in accordance with Zambia’s electoral processes and procedures.

Mr Musenga said the exercise was important as it helped to dispel any doubts among stakeholders ahead of the general elections.

He expressed satisfaction with the active participation of stakeholders in the exercise, saying their involvement was key to promoting transparency, accountability and credibility in the electoral process.

Mr Musenga further disclosed that the deployment of poll staff had commenced in Mpika District and that all poll staff would be fully deployed by today.

He said the ECZ was working tirelessly to ensure that all logistical arrangements were completed ahead of polling day.

Meanwhile, stakeholders have expressed satisfaction with the ballot paper verification exercise conducted in Mpika District.

Mpika District Southern Africa Centre for the Constructive Resolution of Disputes (SACCORD) Coordinator Tresfold Chifwalo said the verification exercise was conducted smoothly without any problems.

Mr Chifwalo said the exercise had given stakeholders confidence in the credibility of the forthcoming elections.

“ECZ must continue engaging all stakeholders as it promotes the true meaning of democracy and transparency,” he said.

And Mpika North Constituency Returning Officer Donatello Singa disclosed that all poll staff in Mpika District would be deployed using road transport.

Mr Singa said arrangements for the deployment of election materials and personnel to polling stations across the district were underway.

“Residents of Mpika District should turn out in large numbers and exercise their civic right to vote on August 13,” he said.

World.title: ECZ ballot-marking contradiction sparks fresh integrity concerns
World.content:
The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) is facing pointed questions over a contradiction in its own guidance on how voters should mark their ballots, after officials reportedly told political parties, journalists and voters that a tick is acceptable alongside the commission’s long-standing public instruction that the correct mark is an “X”. The discrepancy has emerged just a day before the country votes, against a backdrop of public allegations concerning pre-marked ballot papers.

Governance analyst Kanyanta Chanda Kapwepwe, writing in The Mast, said the commission’s current public voter education material states plainly that the correct mark is an X, and that this is the message Zambians have been officially given throughout the campaign. Yet ECZ officials are now said to be telling stakeholders that a tick, provided it remains within the box, will also be accepted.

“Yet ECZ officials are now telling political parties, journalists and voters that a tick is also acceptable provided it remains within the box. This creates an obvious and deeply troubling contradiction,” Kapwepwe wrote. The recent actions have raised further integrity concerns about the ECZ.

The concern has been sharpened by circulating public allegations that additional ballot papers were printed in Tanzania with the intention of benefiting the incumbent government, and that people hired to pre-mark those papers were allegedly given incorrect instructions on which symbol to use, resulting in ballots marked with a tick rather than an X. Tanzania’s own ballots use a tick. The allegation goes further, claiming that because it was too late to order fresh ballots once the error was discovered, the commission subsequently allowed the tick as an acceptable mark to avoid discarding the disputed papers.

Kapwepwe was careful to describe these as serious but unverified claims. “These are not trivial allegations. These are serious allegations touching the very foundation of the electoral process and bordering on electoral integrity. They demand answers from ECZ, not silence, ambiguity or contradictory instructions,” he wrote.

He argued that if no pre-marked ballots exist, the commission should have nothing to fear from issuing a clear, unequivocal clarification. If the allegations are false, he said, ECZ can and should decisively put them to rest. But if irregularities are present, he said Zambians have a right to know before entering polling stations tomorrow.

The piece calls on the commission to issue an immediate written statement matching its existing public voter-education message, warning against any scenario in which presiding officers apply inconsistent standards from one polling station to another.

“There must be no situation in which one presiding officer accepts a tick while another rejects it, or where voters in one polling station are subjected to a different standard from voters elsewhere,” Kapwepwe wrote, adding that any clarification must be published before polling begins rather than left to individual officers to interpret on the day.

This is not the only anxiety around process integrity to surface in the campaign’s closing days. Independent presidential candidate Given Katuta separately urged Zambians to guard their votes jealously, saying the electorate should not hand ballots to ECZ and walk away, arguing this creates room for what she described as underhand methods at polling stations and tallying centres.

“The electorate must not hand over ballots to the Electoral Commission of Zambia and walk away, as doing so will create room for underhand methods at polling stations and tallying centres. ECZ, in its current form, cannot conduct free and fair elections because of interference from government,” Katuta said.

Tonse-PF Pamodzi Alliance running mate Makebi Zulu made a related point, saying protecting a vote does not end with casting it, and that protection must begin at community level where people are able to vote freely without intimidation or coercion. Socialist Party national campaign manager Bob Sichinga urged all SP candidates, members and polling agents to remain vigilant throughout the process, warning that “anything is possible” once counting and transmission of results begin.

Not every party voice struck a suspicious tone. UPND media director Mark Simuuwe said his party would protect its vote in a peaceful manner consistent with what he described as the party’s hallmark approach throughout the campaign.

ECZ has not yet issued a formal public response to the marking-instruction contradiction as flagged in Kapwepwe’s analysis. With polling stations opening at 06:00 hours tomorrow and closing at 18:00 hours, the window for the commission to clarify its position before voters begin casting ballots is narrowing.

World.title: State House warns leaders: incitement to kill is not political rhetoric
World.content:
State House has issued a stern warning to political leaders across the divide, saying threats of violence cannot be dismissed as ordinary campaign talk and that every leader carries moral responsibility to reject inflammatory language before the country votes tomorrow. Chief communications specialist Clayson Hamasaka said the warning follows weeks of tension around a video in which Tonse Alliance presidential affairs chairperson Binwell Mpundu was alleged to have said he was ready to die or kill during the election.

Hamasaka said in a statement that no political disagreement is worth a single life, and that words spoken by leaders carry consequences that go beyond the individual who utters them.

“Zambia is bigger than any candidate, any party and any election. Let us protect our peace and, above all, protect human life,” he said.

The controversy over Mpundu’s remarks has shifted in tone over recent weeks. When the video first surfaced, it was initially suggested the footage had been generated using artificial intelligence, an explanation that circulated for several days before Mpundu himself acknowledged the recording was genuine. Hamasaka said this sequence of events was itself troubling, arguing that leaders should not use technology as cover for statements they are ultimately responsible for.

“Artificial intelligence did not put those words on the national stage. Leaders did. And artificial intelligence cannot take responsibility. Only leaders can do that,” Hamasaka said.

State House said the moral responsibility to reject inflammatory language rests with every political leader regardless of party affiliation, and that where statements amount to criminal incitement, the law provides for serious consequences. Hamasaka called on leaders across the political divide to lower the political temperature in the closing hours before voting.

“This is not the moment for political games or contradictory explanations. It is the moment for every political leader, without exception and regardless of party, to lower the temperature, reject inflammatory language unequivocally, and ensure that no citizen is placed in danger for the sake of political power,” he said.

Hamasaka expressed confidence that the election would pass peacefully, saying Zambians had largely rejected the culture of electoral violence, intimidation and hate speech that scarred previous contests. He said the peace built over recent years must now be protected through the final hours of voting.

The Electoral Commission of Zambia has already acted in the specific case connected to the video, revoking Mpundu’s accreditation to access the National Results Centre on security grounds. Chief electoral officer Brown Kasaro said the commission considers statements of that nature a serious concern, given their potential to incite violence and undermine the peaceful conduct of the process.

Inspector-General of Police Graphel Musamba echoed the call for restraint, directing officers to remain professional, neutral and impartial while enforcing the law during and after voting. He said police would act firmly against anyone found committing electoral offences or disturbing public order, regardless of political affiliation, and warned that unlawful assemblies, road blockages and attacks on individuals would attract immediate intervention.

Traditional leaders have also weighed in on the broader question of political conduct this campaign season. Chiefs Chisunka and Chimense of the Ushi people in Mansa District said the period had been largely peaceful compared with previous elections, which they recalled as marked by bloodshed and serious political violence.

“During the last regime, we saw a lot of bloodshed, people were hacked with pangas, people killing each other especially during campaigns,” Chisunka said, adding that the current administration’s term had seen a marked reduction in such incidents.

Hamasaka’s appeal was not limited to any single party or figure. He said the message applied equally to every leader, urging that calls for peace be matched by concrete restraint in language used at rallies, on social media and in interviews during the final stretch of campaigning.

The Independent Broadcasting Authority has separately reinforced the same message to media houses, warning broadcasters against airing unverified claims or speculative content that could inflame tensions as results begin to emerge. Director-general Webster Malido said stations must handle developing events, live interviews and sensitive stories with extra caution so as not to spread misinformation or fuel tension.

With polling opening early tomorrow morning, State House’s appeal represents one of the final formal interventions from government ahead of the vote, aimed at ensuring that whatever political differences exist among candidates and their supporters, no citizen is placed at risk in the process of choosing the country’s next leadership.

World.title: Africa: As Funding Shrinks, Africa's SRHR Movement Vows Not to Retreat
World.content:
Mombasa, Kenya — As funding shrinks, civic space narrows and opposition to sexual and reproductive rights grows across Africa, advocates are gathering in Mombasa with a simple message: progress cannot be taken for granted.

More than 250 advocates, policymakers, youth leaders, healthcare providers, researchers, civil society organisations and community leaders from across the continent have converged for the MenEngage Africa SRHR Learning and Exchange Symposium, PROGRESS 2026, a three-day gathering focused on defending bodily autonomy, advancing sexual and reproductive justice and finding new ways to push forward in the face of growing resistance.

The symposium, organised by Sonke Gender Justice and MenEngage Africa held under the theme Reclaiming Autonomy, Advancing Sexual and Reproductive Justice in the Face of Resistance, and comes at a critical moment for the region's SRHR movement. Activists across the continent are confronting shrinking civic space, rising opposition to SRHR, patchy delivery of Comprehensive Sexuality Education, and persistent barriers facing adolescents, women, persons with disabilities, LGBTQIA+ persons, and other marginalised groups. These challenges are compounded further by conservative policy shifts, climate-related crises, and the growing threat of technology-facilitated gender-based violence.

But speakers at the gathering argued that the response cannot be retreat.



They called for stronger solidarity, greater youth leadership and a renewed commitment to organising with men and boys positioned as critical partners in challenging harmful gender norms and advancing equality.

Runyararo Mutariswa, Regional Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights Coordinator at Sonke Gender Justice, described the gathering as far more than a conference or symposium - a continental movement in the making.

"Progress 2026 is more than just a conference. It is more than a symposium," she said. "We are opening a continental movement."

She said the meeting should be a space not only to share knowledge, but also to listen, learn and imagine together what the future of SRHR and sexual and reproductive justice could look like.

Mutariswa urged participants not to limit themselves to asking what they were learning over the coming days, but to forge connections and collaborations, and to consider what becomes possible when individuals stop working in isolation and start seeing themselves as part of a wider movement.

For Mutariswa, the theme is also an invitation to think boldly about the kind of movements needed to respond to those challenges.

She called for movements that are intergenerational and create meaningful space for young people to participate as leaders and co-creators, that treat feminist leadership, men's engagement, social norms work, research, advocacy, and community organizing as interconnected parts of one larger ecosystem rather than separate silos. She encouraged participants to remain open to unexpected possibilities, including new relationships, ideas, collaborations, and new ways of approaching their work. She called on them to also bring their curiosity, their questions, their lived experiences, and the lessons carried from the different corners of their movements and, crucially, to leave space for the unexpected.

Movements are built out of passion

Sonke Gender Justice's regional SRHR specialist, Jude Thaddeus Njikem, echoed that commitment. He said that Sonke and MenEngage Africa remain focused on strengthening African-led, intersectional, and inclusive responses to SRHR challenges. He described PROGRESS 2026 as an essential space to deepen collaboration, amplify youth voices, and drive transformative action so that "no one is left behind."

Njikem recalled that when the movement gathered in Nairobi for PROGRESS 2024, organizers made a deliberate choice to skip 2025 and return in 2026 stronger, bolder, and more united. It was an ambitious plan, he said, one made without knowing how much would go wrong in the year in between. The intervening years brought growing uncertainty for organisations working on sexual and reproductive health and rights.

He described 2025 as a year that tested the movement in ways few had anticipated.

Funding for sexual and reproductive health and rights, for bodily autonomy, gender justice, HIV programming, and comprehensive sexuality education was hit hard. This forced many programs that had contributed enormously to community organizing and rights protection to shrink or fundamentally rethink how they operated. That uncertainty, he said, shadowed the entire planning process for this year's symposium and left the organizing team - spanning Sonke Gender Justice and MenEngage Africa - grappling with funding restrictions, shifting priorities, and difficult decisions at every turn.

But rather than retreat, the challenges reinforced the need to bring the movement together.

He framed this year's gathering as proof that movements are not built only when resources are plentiful, but out of passion and as a reminder to choose courage over fear and solidarity over isolation. The organisers asked themselves whether they could speak about reclaiming autonomy while retreating from the fight for it, and whether they could call for stronger movements while allowing opposition to SRHR to weaken their own.

Njikem expressed his gratitude to the partners who also stayed the course despite experiencing similar restrictions, some losing donors, others closing offices. He thanked UNESCO, UNAIDS, and other partners for keeping the movement alive. He reaffirmed the movement's core commitments to dignity, bodily autonomy, sexual and reproductive health and rights and justice, comprehensive sexuality education, and youth leadership. He said women, girls, persons with disabilities, LGBTQI+ communities and people living with HIV must continue to have their rights, care, protection and freedom recognised.

The movement is operating in a difficult environment, he said, with misinformation growing and communities being pushed back into silence, shame and fear. But the gathering itself, he said, demonstrates that the movement remains active despite the challenges.

"This room tells us that even when resources are reduced, our resolve must not be reduced," said Njikem. "We are still here, still organising, still learning, still existing, and still building."

Progress must be sustained

Bafana Khumalo, Co-Executive Director and co-founder of Sonke Gender Justice, said the gathering in Mombasa was itself evidence that progress can continue despite the political and financial challenges facing the SRHR movement.

Khumalo said that the difficult global context described current geopolitics as a backlash against gains achieved through years of work by activists and organisations represented at the symposium.

"As people of resilience, we say we still have to register progress because, despite everything, we are still here. We are still organising. We are still working very hard," he said.

Khumalo described PROGRESS 2026 as a space where dignity "must never be negotiated nor compromised," and pushed back against rising misinformation and resistance to equality, autonomy, and abortion rights: "We cannot afford to give up now or later because the future, especially for our youth, is bright."

He called movement-building itself an act of resilience - one that amplifies the courage of women and girls, reminds the sector that "inclusion without access is not inclusion" for persons with disabilities, and strengthens communities having difficult conversations about power, culture, and sexuality. Progress, he said, "must be protected through relationship building that is based on trust, accountability, and solidarity."

He also stressed that sexual and reproductive justice cannot be left to individual organisations, sectors or countries, thanking partners including MenEngage Africa, the Kenya MenEngage Alliance, UN agencies, diplomatic partners, civil society and other movement partners for supporting the convening. He said progress requires more than discussion. It must be sustained through organising and protected through relationships built on trust, accountability and solidarity.

"When we leave Mombasa, I ask that we leave with renewed courage, stronger partnerships, and practical commitment to reclaim the space for our communities, for organisations, and for movements," he said.

He ended with a message of optimism despite the challenges confronting the movement: "Another world is indeed possible."

'Anything for the girls without the girls is not for the girls'

MenEngage Africa co-chair and founding director of Shamwari Yemwanasikana (Friend of the Girl Child), Ekenia Chifamba, said the symposium was intended to help turn regional discussions into a more coordinated and practical response to threats facing SRHR and marginalised communities.

She said that young people must be at the centre of decisions affecting their lives. She warned that policies and programmes cannot claim to serve young people if they are developed without their meaningful participation.

She said the symposium comes at a critical time as resistance to gender equality and sexual and reproductive health and rights grows across Africa and other parts of the world.

"We are witnessing a growing resistance to gender equality and sexual and reproductive health rights. Civic space is shrinking... funding streams are also becoming increasingly constrained." She said that the symposium is a space for solutions, not just diagnosis. "We will not simply discuss these problems, but we will definitely also come up with solutions and the way forward."

"Every person has the right to bodily autonomy, dignity, information, and also the freedom to make decisions about their own lives" - a principle she said applies equally to women and girls, young people, persons with disabilities, and people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities. Engaging men and boys, she added, remains essential to that vision: "Healthy masculinities, accountable allyship, and leadership are not optional."

She draws on her own experience empowering young girls and women in Zimbabwe through Shamwari Yemwanasikana, a community-based, non-governmental organization.

"Anything for the girls without the girls is not for the girls" - a principle she extended to young people generally, insisting they sit "at the center" of PROGRESS 2026 rather than at its margins.

She also challenged participants to consider whether the continent has the courage, coordination and commitment needed to accelerate progress towards the African Union's Agenda 2063 and the Sustainable Development Goals ahead of 2030. She urged participants to carry those voices beyond institutional boundaries. She said that the success of the gathering would depend not only on the quality of its conversations but also on the relationships and alliances built during the symposium.

Men must be partners in advancing gender equality

Wilson Muthemba Nzau, the Chairperson of Kenya MenEngage Alliance (KEMEA), said lasting progress on sexual and reproductive rights and gender equality cannot be achieved without meaningfully engaging men and boys.

"Men are not only part of the problem, but we must be a part of the solution," said Nzau.

Nzau also called for greater support for women's leadership. "Women's leadership is not a threat to men... men must be willing to use their influence, open doors for women, challenge discrimination, support women's participation, encourage women's leadership."

He said KEMEA's work focuses on challenging harmful social norms, promoting positive masculinities, preventing violence and creating safer families and communities. He grounded that philosophy in KEMEA's on-the-ground work from its Dad and Daughters program, which helps fathers build stronger relationships with their daughters, to partnerships with traditional and religious leaders, including training pastors and vicars to challenge violence against women and girls from the pulpit. He also pointed to KEMEA's work with men's mental health, and with institutions such as the Kenya Police Service, where he said the alliance found sexual harassment "rampant... especially where the power dynamics are tilted towards our male brothers."

"Change does not happen through one organization or one centre. Change happens through partnership, through deep community connections, and we must have responsible systems," he said.

Drawing on KEMEA's work with community, faith and traditional leaders, he said lasting change requires partnerships and stronger local networks.

He urged participants to use PROGRESS 2026 not only to exchange ideas but to build relationships that continue beyond the symposium.

"The question we must ask ourselves is, when we return home, what will we do differently?" said Nzau.

He called for men and boys to be treated as important partners rather than an afterthought. He ensured that women and girls remain at the centre of efforts to advance equality and that young people have space to lead.

Progress requires people willing to defend it

Dr Remmy Shawa, Senior Programme Specialist for Education for Health and Well-Being at UNESCO's Regional Office for Southern Africa, said PROGRESS 2026 comes at a critical time as the development, gender equality and human rights space faces growing pressure.

He said shrinking civic space and challenges to international norms and funding make gatherings such as the Mombasa symposium increasingly important because they remind activists and practitioners that progress remains possible. "Despite the setbacks we face as activists, practitioners and human rights defenders, there still is hope," said Shawa.

He left delegates with three commitments to hold onto, adding that these values must remain the non-negotiable guardrails.

First, that adaptation to context must never mean abandoning core values: "Dignity, equality, inclusion, bodily autonomy, self-determination... these values must remain the non-negotiable guardrails."Second, that education remains one of the most powerful tools for transformation, given the more than 300 million children and adolescents in school across sub-Saharan Africa, for equipping young people with the skills to challenge harmful norms and seek out services. Third, that collective action must place young people at its center, pointing to the Eastern and Southern African Ministerial Commitment on Education, Health and Well-Being as a model - one that depends on governments, civil society, communities, and "fundamentally... young people themselves."

"Progress is not and is never inevitable. It requires people willing to stand for it, to work for it, and when necessary, to defend it," he said.

Sweden's Ambassador to Kenya, Håkan Åkesson, said the PROGRESS 2026 symposium comes at a critical moment. "We do see pressure on civic space and less money set aside for sexual and reproductive health and rights. We see organized resistance to gender equality."

He said these pressures have real consequences, affecting young people's access to accurate information, women's access to healthcare, survivors' access to services and justice, and people's ability to live free from stigma and discrimination. For Sweden, he said, SRHR is "a matter of health and rights, of course, but also equality and dignity."

He said that Sweden's partnership with Sonke Gender Justice dates back to 2012 and has helped expand MenEngage Africa's gender-transformative work across the continent. "Engaging men and boys must always strengthen, never replace feminist leadership and women's rights," he said.

Åkesson said defending SRHR and gender equality also requires protecting civic space so that civil society organisations, health workers, journalists and human rights defenders can organise, advocate and hold institutions accountable.

Close 

He said PROGRESS 2026 provides an opportunity to move from commitments to implementation, confront misinformation, learn from setbacks and build stronger partnerships.

"Progress is never automatic. It must be protected, financed and built together," said Åkesson.

He reaffirmed Sweden's commitment to working with partners defending rights, strengthening health systems and advancing gender equality, adding that "we should never give up."

Young people are driving social change

Maria Røysamb, First Secretary at the Royal Norwegian Embassy in Nairobi, reaffirmed Norway's commitment to sexual and reproductive health and rights. She said that progress depends on people willing to challenge discrimination and push for change. She said young people are increasingly at the forefront of that change, using community networks, digital platforms, art, culture and new forms of activism to advance rights.

She said Norway's embassy had spent the past year listening directly to young people in Kenya, who are organising through community networks, digital platforms, art, and culture in ways that often look nothing like traditional civil society structures.

"Many do not call themselves human rights defenders, yet they are defending rights every day," said Røysamb.

She said consultations with young people had made clear that they want to participate in shaping their societies rather than simply survive within them. "We want to live, participate, and be heard, but not survive."
