World.title: Merz’s deal with the Taliban alarms Afghan dissidents in Germany
World.content:
Under pressure from the rising far right, Berlin is letting Taliban officials staff Afghan missions in exchange for more deportations. Activists say the arrangement puts them at risk.

Zarmina Paryani and her four sisters fear they may soon have to again face the persecutors they fled from in Afghanistan — and this time inside Germany.

Paryani and her sisters were imprisoned twice in Kabul for protesting against the Taliban after the Afghan militants retook the capital in 2021, the 27-year-old said. After going into hiding for several months, the family eventually made their way to Germany in search of safe haven.

But now, Berlin has struck a Faustian bargain that allows the Taliban to deepen its diplomatic foothold in Germany in return for cooperation on deporting Afghan migrants back to Afghanistan. For Paryani and other Afghan activists who resisted the Taliban at home, the arrangement is giving their former persecutors new leverage over their lives in exile.





“It’s hard to accept that my fate and my affairs are being discussed with the very same representatives whose oppression, prisons, whippings and violence I fled from,” Paryani, who worked as a midwife in Kabul and now lives in western Germany, told POLITICO.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government first struck a deal with the Afghan government announced last October that gives Taliban officials control of diplomatic missions in Berlin and Bonn in exchange for permission to return Afghan migrants directly to Afghanistan. That cooperation was deepened early this summer with a deal that allows more Taliban officials to work in Germany in return for cooperation on additional deportation flights — now up to three per month.

Under the new deal, Germany has expanded deportations to include not only Afghan men convicted of crimes, but also, more broadly, Afghan men with no protected status or legal right to remain in Germany.

The agreement with the Taliban makes Germany an outlier in Europe, making it the first EU country to allow Taliban-appointed officials to work in diplomatic missions inside the country. Before the agreement, Western-oriented Afghan officials representing the former government in Afghanistan had remained in charge.

The arrangement comes as Merz’s government grapples with rock-bottom approval ratings and the rise of the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, now the country’s most popular political force, according to polls. The AfD’s surge comes ahead of two elections in the former East Germany, where the far-right party is ahead in polls by wide margins. In one of those states, Saxony-Anhalt, the party may take real governing power for the first time since it was founded in 2013, a result that would serve as a great humiliation for the conservative Merz, who was elected chancellor last year partly on a promise to crack down on migration.





The AfD’s rise is piling pressure on the chancellor to deliver on his election pledge to deport more migrants — even as he insists that working with the Taliban does not legitimize a regime notorious for its human rights abuses. Overall, Afghans are the third-largest group of refugees or people who have fled war to come to Germany, behind Ukrainians and Syrians.

“We are not extending a hand to this Taliban regime,” Merz said in the German parliament in June. “Rather, we are seeking cooperation at the necessary technical level, which is in our country’s national interest.”

‘Nightmares’ and ‘psychological distress’

For Afghan rights activists in Germany, one of the worst consequences of Berlin’s deal with the Taliban is that it may particularly put at risk some 35,000 Afghans who came to Germany under special humanitarian programs for people deemed especially vulnerable to the Taliban. They include Paryani and her sisters in addition to thousands of human rights activists and Afghans who worked with the German military during its nearly two-decade presence in the country.

Paryani and others fear they will have to face the Taliban when attempting to renew their Afghan passports — which they need to extend their humanitarian visas — at Afghan diplomatic missions. Another 321,000 Afghans live in Germany as refugees or with other forms of protected status. They do not necessarily need Afghan passports, unless they want to apply for a permanent residence status.

More generally, activists and refugees also fear the Taliban, with their growing presence in Germany, could gain access to personal information held in databases in German missions, including details about their families, making them susceptible to blackmail and extortion.

Afghan activists speak at a protest camp at Berlin’s Alexanderplatz on Aug. 15, 2025, the fourth anniversary of the Taliban takeover. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images

“Given my personal history and my stance on extremism, I am concerned for my safety and that of my family,” one former teacher from Afghanistan granted anonymity due to his fear of retribution from the Taliban told POLITICO.

The former teacher, who lives in Germany with a humanitarian visa, said German immigration officials have asked him to renew his expired Afghan passport, a request that he fears will force him to deal directly with his persecutors.

“This situation continues to cause me significant psychological distress,” he said. “Sometimes I wake up at night because of nightmares related to the Taliban and this situation.”

‘Vulnerable to blackmail’

With its handling of the Taliban, Merz’s government is setting a precedent that will be closely watched by other EU countries. Government officials in Austria and Belgium have said they’re watching Germany’s cooperation with the Taliban closely. Taliban officials also held talks focused on deportations with the EU Commission in June in Brussels.

But Hamid Nangialay Kabiri, the former head of the Afghan consulate in Bonn, who quit last September in protest over the initial deal allowing Taliban officials to serve in diplomatic missions in Germany, warned that the German government’s decision to cooperate with the Afghan regime would come back to haunt it — and that the Taliban would use their new leverage over Germany to advance their interests in Europe, including by building networks that intimidate dissidents.

“They are destroying my country, and now they are coming here,” he said. “They are not thinking of diplomacy. They have a lot of plans in their mind.”





It’s a sentiment politicians inside the left-leaning opposition also share.

“The German government has made itself vulnerable to blackmail,” Schahina Gambir, a lawmaker for the Greens who was born in Kabul, told POLITICO. “We’re seeing recognition through the back door. The Taliban are being granted access to embassies, they’re being granted immunity, they’re given channels for dialogue — and at the same time, the situation for women and girls in Afghanistan is getting worse and worse.”

There are already signs that the Taliban are exercising their newfound leverage.

Last May, Kabul unexpectedly halted a deportation flight at the last minute, seemingly seeking to extract additional concessions from the German government. A couple of weeks later, Berlin announced the terms of the latest agreement allowing additional Taliban-appointed officials to work at diplomatic missions in Germany.

Officials in Berlin depicted the new deal as a victory and a practical necessity, allowing for more deportations.





“To increase the number of repatriations, more passports must be issued, more identities must be verified, and so on,” Martin Giese, a spokesperson for Germany’s foreign ministry, said at the time. “To this end, it will also be necessary for more consular officials to be involved.”

But Paryani, the Afghan midwife who fled to Germany with her four sisters, said the Taliban would use their new power to torment them in the country they had sought safety in.

“A Taliban member once wrote to me: ‘Just wait until our embassy in Germany reopens. Then we’ll find you there,'” she said of a comment that had surfaced under one of her social media posts about two years ago. She then deemed it irrelevant because it seemed so unrealistic.

“Today, I feel as though that threat has become a reality,” she said.

World.title: Zelenskyy’s Balkan fumble
World.content:
Since Zelenskyy’s visit, Vučić threatened to physically redirect the Iber River that runs from Serbia to Kosovo in retaliation for Kosovo demolishing Serb-owned houses along the reservoir’s shore. Such a move would drain the reservoir supplying much of Kosovo’s water and crucial cooling capacity to its largest power plant.

In addition, Serbian Foreign Minister Marko Djurić and Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama exchanged barbs on X, with the latter accusing Serbia of being in “a political bubble” and being in denial over the fact that “Serbia lost Kosova” long ago.

Kosovo was an Albanian-majority southern province of Serbia for most of the 20th century. Its people held broad political rights under socialist Yugoslavia until a decade-long Serb crackdown on dissent led to the armed conflict of 1998-99. A three-month NATO bombing campaign drove Serbian forces out and made the province a U.N. protectorate.

Kosovo declared independence in 2008 and, to date, it is recognized by over 100 nations, including the U.S., U.K. and 22 of the 27 EU member countries. It is also a potential EU candidate country, submitting its application in December 2022.

The country’s status has long been a favorite talking point for Russian President Vladimir Putin, who has used it to justify invading Georgia in 2008 and annexing Crimea in 2014. Kosovo’s Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca said he took note of Zelenskyy’s views “with regret” and that such rhetoric echoes “Russia’s attempts to invoke Kosova as a precedent.”

As for why Ukraine’s leader would wade into the intractable Balkan issue at all, it likely comes down to weaponry.

World.title: Farage vs. Binface: Inside the Clacton by-election circus
World.content:
The feeling that the town has been made to look daft was apparent even among those preparing to vote once again to return the Reform UK leader to parliament. And it’s not the rival candidate wearing a trash can on his head that they’re holding responsible for the “farce.”

Thursday may not be the end of the matter, either. A parliamentary investigation into Farage’s alleged failure to declare millions of pounds of donations in the run-up to his 2024 election could mean yet another by-election — and a tougher battle for the right-wing populist next time around.

Bid for absolution

This self-inflicted campaign is taking place because of Farage’s decision to resign his parliamentary seat and put his fate in the hands of Clacton’s residents.

Ordinary punters, he argued, should be the ones to have their say as he faced mounting questions over undeclared donations. The gamble was that such a vote would absolve him of wrongdoing in the eyes of the public, regardless of the findings in two parliamentary probes — one over a £5 million donation from a crypto-entrepreneur, and the other into support from a convicted fraudster. Farage has denied wrongdoing in both instances, arguing that help was given in a personal capacity.

Reform UK Party Leader Nigel Farage gestures as he speaks during a press conference on a plan to deport foreign prisoners on August 10, 2026 at Royal Horseguards Hotel in London. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images

But Britain’s main political parties took one look at this ploy and opted out. That’s how Count Binface, one of the most enthusiastic inheritors of a rich British tradition of standing as a satirical candidate in elections, ended up as Farage’s most high-profile rival.

Others risking their £500 deposit to get their names on the 90-cm-long ballot paper include rival jokesters with names ranging from Howling Laud Hope, Nick the Incredible Flying Brick and Baron Von Thunderclap. Broadcast rules mean the 34-strong candidate list needs to be read in full at every mention of Farage’s by-election on TV.

World.title: Breakfast looks a lot more expensive under new EU pesticide plans
World.content:
Even under more plausible scenarios envisioned by the researchers, in which external growers get on board to varying degrees, consumer prices would rise and EU agricultural imports decline. Though that would in turn boost domestic production, with exact numbers depending on producers' willingness to adapt.

The findings lay out an unpalatable political choice for Brussels: Keep angry farmers' tractors off the streets, or hit consumers' wallets as they fulfill basic needs at the grocery store.

The proposed residue ban, which is part of the food and feed safety simplification package, is popular with European farmers seeking a level playing field with foreign growers — after all, it was partly designed to appease their ire over the EU's trade deal with the Mercosur bloc of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay. In order to avoid leaving any residue on fruits and vegetables, producers would essentially have to stop using the substance in question.

However, critics say it clashes with global trade rules, as it essentially imposes EU rules on foreign producers, which is known as a mirror clause.

A wide range of international producer groups argue that the proposed ban goes beyond existing health protections in order to push a one-size-fits-all approach, ignoring the reality that growers around the world face different pests, climates and farming conditions.

“The choice is between berries that are available all year round — healthy, safe and at a fair price — or limited production at a high price,” said Amine Bennani, president of the Moroccan Association of Red Fruit Producers.

World.title: Europe has officially delayed the roll out of the ETIAS travel permit indefinitely
World.content:
Europe’s much-delayed travel permit for visa-free visitors has hit yet another roadblock, with the European Union now pushing back the launch of the European Travel Information and Authorisation System (ETIAS) indefinitely.

 

The system, which will eventually require travellers from countries including the UK, US, Canada and Australia to apply for pre-travel authorisation, was previously expected to launch in 2027. Now, even that timeline is uncertain, as technical problems with Europe’s new border system continue to cause headaches.

For travellers, the message is simple for now: don’t apply, and don’t pay anyone claiming to offer ETIAS applications.

Last month, UK-based newspaper The Financial Times reported that the scheme was likely to be postponed and, on its website, the EU made the decision official, writing: "ETIAS is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorizations are collected at this point.”

“The European Union will inform about the specific date for the start of ETIAS several months prior to its launch,” the statement added.

The move comes following chaos surrounding Europe’s new electronic entry/exit system (EES), which has seen passengers face huge airport queues and missed flights over the busy summer holiday season. That scheme was initially supposed to launch in 2022, but faced countless pushbacks.

When ETIAS does eventually launch, it’s set to cost €20 and grant access to 30 European countries in the Schengen Zone, as well as Iceland, Norway, Liechtenstein, and Switzerland. Children under 18, adults over 70, and some family members of EU citizens will reportedly be exempt from the charges.

It will be valid for three years or until your passport expires, and it will allow holders to stay in the Zone for up to 90 days within any 180-day period.

Based on the US ESTA program, which has operated since 2008, applicants will need to complete an online form and provide personal information. They’ll also need to answer security questions and undergo pre-travel screening, with most applications expected to be approved within minutes.

According to reports, ETIAS officials are expected to put forward a revised ETIAS timeline next month and, while there are rumours it could still come into force this year, it seems more likely that a 2027 launch will be the case.

World.title: Russian strikes kill two in Kherson overnight, Ukraine retaliates
World.content:
Russian overnight strikes on Kherson, in southern Ukraine, killed two and injured two others.

 

Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia's Novorossiysk, in Crimea, killed two people and injured eight, including an eight-year-old child, the regional governor said on Wednesday after the latest exchange of air attacks between the warring countries.

Ukraine has increased its strikes on Russia in what it says is fair retribution for Moscow's own daily strikes on Ukrainian cities that force people into shelters and kill civilians across the country.

Russia's Krasnodar — a southern region home to several tourist hotspots — saw a barrage of "several hundred" Ukrainian drones, regional governor Venyamin Kondratyev said.

"An eight-year-old child died in Novorossiysk... Eight people, including one child, were also wounded and have been hospitalised," Kondratyev said on Telegram.

He added that debris from drones damaged 21 buildings in the port city, with unverified images on social media showing blocks of flats with blown-out windows and charred cars.

Naval base targeted

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Kyiv had "carried out a unique operation targeting the naval base in Novorossiysk — the last major stronghold of the Russian fleet in the Black Sea, more than 300 kilometres from the front line."

"Hits on air defence positions, piers, and seaport infrastructure have been confirmed," he said on social media.

He posted a video from Russian social media showing the attack unfolding — streaks of orange flashes of air defence and blue counter-drone laser beams being shone into the sky — and a thick grey cloud billowing over the city after dawn.

Another person was killed in the Krasnodar region when drone debris fell into the garden of a private house in the village of Volna.

Two people were also wounded in the resort town of Gelendzhik on the Black Sea coast.

Russia shot down 502 Ukrainian drones across its territory and the Black Sea overnight, its defence ministry said in a statement.

Ukraine's air force, meanwhile, reported that Moscow attacked with missiles and 138 drones, 112 of which were shot down or intercepted, launched mostly at its southern Odesa region and Sumy in the northeast.

Russian drones killed two people in the frontline city of Kherson in southern Ukraine, the city chief said, including a woman whose house was hit.

Civilians are frequently killed in the city, with Russian troops based on the opposite side of the Dnipro River, which snakes through southern Ukraine.

World.title: Spotify to label AI-generated artist personas with new ‘AI Persona’ badges
World.content:
Music streaming giant Spotify has announced that from September it will begin adding an “AI Persona” badge to some artist profiles, helping listeners identify when an artist’s music may have been generated using artificial intelligence.

 

AI Personas will also be excluded from Spotify’s editorial and algorithmic recommendations, in an effort to give greater visibility to music made by genuine human musicians and artists.

Spotify will give artists the option to disclose whether they consider themselves an AI Persona. The platform will also conduct its own reviews to identify profiles that appear to be AI-generated identities.

Listeners will also be able to report artists they believe should be reviewed by Spotify’s team.

"Although there’s a broad spectrum in how artists use AI as a creative tool, the question of whether a profile represents an actual human is one where Spotify can help make a clear determination," reads a press release from Spotify.

It adds: "This badge is about the artist’s public identity, not about how the music was made."

Growing concerns over AI music

The move comes at a time of growing concern across the music industry over the volume of AI-generated musical slop flooding streaming platforms.

In June, French music streaming service Deezer reported that uploads of AI-generated tracks had, for the first time, exceeded half of all daily new music deliveries.

Following the milestone, the platform said it would remove generative-AI tracks being used to generate fraudulent streams, as well as tracks that had not been streamed for six months or more.

Spotify has faced a similar problem. Last year, the platform revealed that it had removed 75 million spam tracks over a 12-month period, as AI tools contributed to a flood of low-quality and fraudulent music.

The alarming success of AI-generated music

The Velvet Sundown provided an early glimpse of how easily AI-generated artists can break through into the mainstream. The psychedelic rock project appeared on Spotify in 2025 and quickly amassed more than a million monthly listeners, releasing two albums in June.

Its supposed four members - complete with names (led by vocalist and “mellotron sorcerer” Gabe Farrow), photographs and elaborate biographies - appeared to present the band as a genuine four-piece from the US.

AI-generated image of the fictitious band The Velvet Sundown Credit: The Velvet Sundown

But doubts soon emerged. Reddit users started questioning the band’s authenticity after their music began appearing in listeners’ Spotify Discover Weekly playlists, while the group's imagery and promotional material appeared clearly artificial.

The band’s own social media accounts initially denied the allegations, insisting that the music had been created by “real” people using “real instruments, real minds, and real soul”.

Eventually, The Velvet Sundown’s Spotify profile was updated to acknowledge the truth. The band described itself as a “synthetic music project guided by human creative direction”, with its music, voices, lyrics and imagery created with the assistance of AI.

The group still has more than 100,000 monthly listeners and several of their tracks have over one millions streams.

The phenomenon has also begun to spill into more traditional measures of musical success with the AI-generated country project Breaking Rust reaching No 1 on Billboard’s Country Digital Song Sales chart with “Walk My Walk”.

The viral track now has close to 30 million streams on Spotify.

World.title: Germany’s best viewpoints from above: Scenic walks, mountain peaks and sky-high bridges
World.content:
An expansive country of bustling cities plus calmer forests, alpine summits and rivers, Germany offers plenty of ways to experience its landscapes.

 

But for a different perspective on the country: look up.

Some of the country’s best panoramic viewpoints are from the country’s treetop walks, viewing platforms and dramatic suspension bridges that put its forest canopies, river valleys and coastal cliffs at centre stage.

See the top of Germany from the Zugspitze on the Austria-Germany border

Germany’s highest mountain stands 2,962 metres tall and is home to the country’s last remaining glaciers: the Nördliche Schneeferner and the Höllentalferner.

Situated on the border between Germany and Austria, this mountain peak’s summit offers scenic views of 400 surrounding mountain peaks across Germany, Austria, Italy and Switzerland.

The Zugspitze is a hotspot for mountaineers, skiers, snowboarders and toboggan enthusiasts alike and is accessible via a choice of three cable cars, including an almost 100-year-old cogwheel train.

Views beside Hercules in Kassel

Europe’s largest hillside park, covering a total area of 560 hectares and at a height of 530 metres, is located in the city of Kassel.

Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe in Kassel is famed for its array of trees, plants and architectural waterwork attractions that date back to the 18th century, joining UNESCO’s World Heritage Site list in 2013.

For the best views of Kassel, visitors should stand beside the park’s 8.3-metre-high statue of Hercules. From there, views include Wilhelmshöhe Palace and Löwenburg Castle in the distance and, on a clear day, the Harz and Rhön Mountain ranges on the horizon.

Stand sky-high in Berlin

Got some extra time in Berlin? Add the Berlin Gasometer in the Schöneberg district to your itinerary for a different perspective on the German capital.

The former low-pressure gas tank, first established in 1913, has lived several lives, serving as an advertising space, event venue and television studio.

Rising to almost 80 metres into the sky, the structure houses a Sky Lounge with a roof terrace located at a height of around 66 metres above ground. For those with a head for heights, the elevated vantage point leaves the entire city at your feet, with sights including the Zoological Garden, the Reichstag government building and Victory Column on offer as far as the eye can see.

Walk along the treetops of Black Forest in Bad Wildbad

Bad Wildbad is home to a walkway that stretches 1,250 metres and leads to a 40-metre high observation tower that rewards visitors with unmissable panoramic views of the Black Forest mountain range and Enz Valley river.

The route winds over the course of one to two hours to get to the top, where visitors can see The Nature Park Schwarzwald Mitte/Nord – the country’s third largest nature park. On especially clear days, visitors might be lucky to even see as far as the Stuttgart TV Tower and the Swabian Jura mountain range.

Sights fit for a king on Rügen Island

Germany’s largest island, the Baltic Sea island Rügen, houses the “King’s Chair”.

Known locally as Königsstuhl, the 118-metre high King's Chair is the highest point of Rügen's famous chalk cliffs located within the Jasmund National Park.

From the top of the viewing platform, visitors are rewarded with a sweeping view of the endless blue Baltic Sea, coastal formations, white chalk cliffs and lush green beech tree forests.

See Saxony from Bastei Bridge in Lohmen

This 76.5-metre-long and 305-metre-high stone bridge rises above the Elbe River in Germany in the heart of Saxon Switzerland Park.

This historic bridge peaked local interest for its tourist potential as early as 1824 as a site of sandstone rock formations. Today, it leads visitors through the rocky ravine of the Mardertelle to the ruins of the 13th-century Neurathen medieval rock castle.

The monument is open to the public year-round, but for travellers keen to skip the crowds, it’s best to either arrive early in the morning or in the evening to catch the sunset.

World.title: Fake videos and false allegations target candidates in French 2027 presidential election
World.content:
France's presidential election is set for the spring of 2027, and it is already attracting instances of misinformation and alleged foreign interference that have since sparked criminal proceedings.

 

Researchers from the bot-tracking network AntiBot4Navalny have detected a campaign linked to Matryoshka, a covert influence and disinformation operation aligned with Russia.

At first, these posts focused on Gabriel Attal, the former prime minister of France who is running to succeed current president Emmanuel Macron.

Attal filed a criminal complaint with French authorities "alleging foreign interference originating from Russian networks", after fabricated videos impersonating French news outlets targeted him online.

Fake videos bearing the logos and visual identity of well-known French news outlets such as Le Figaro and Libération circulated online, attempting to smear Attal by linking him to political scandals.

Some attempted to throw Attal's health into question, with one false headline claiming he'd been hospitalised, and another claiming he had Parkinson's disease.

These false headlines claim Attal's health has deteriorated. Euronews

Somewhat paradoxically, various false posts even alleged that Attal had launched a campaign against "nonexistent" Russian disinformation to try and block social media platform X.

Others said that he had paid news outlets to spread disinformation about him, and that he had considered fabricating an assassination plot against himself to try and blame Russia.

News agency AFP, which reports having seen Attal's complaint, said that the former prime minister's lawyers said the fake content could undermine the integrity of the upcoming election.

They added that France's Secretariat-General for Defence and National Security (SGDSN) and Viginum, its foreign interference watchdog, had warned Attal about the disinformation campaign targeting him.

Attal's office did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.

A selection of false social media posts spreading disinformation about Attal. Euronews

Following the disinformation campaign against Attal, researchers noted that the Matryoshka network shifted its focus to Édouard Philippe, another former prime minister and a contender in the presidential election.

Posts against him follow a similar pattern to those against Attal, mimicking respected media outlets such as Le Monde and AFP to mix real-life circumstances with distorted claims.

For example, one of the posts falsely claims a politician admitted Phillippe orchestrated corruption in an investigation involving the association LH French Tech.

Philippe is currently under investigation over alleged financial wrongdoing, but there is no evidence that Stéphanie de Bazelaire, who is also implicated in the investigation, made these claims, despite what the post suggests.

The probe centres on a four-year agreement worth €2.154 million between the Le Havre metropolitan authority and LH French Tech to run the city's digital innovation hub while Philippe was mayor of Le Havre.

Financial prosecutors are investigating him for the alleged embezzlement of public funds, favouritism, illegal conflict of interest and financial misconduct by a public official.

He has consistently denied wrongdoing and says he is cooperating fully with the investigation.

Other posts claim that Philippe had apologised for referring to the inhabitants of France's former colonies as "scum", and that a company owned by his wife had supplied toxic components for the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine.

However, there is no credible evidence to support either claim, nor any record of the news outlets impersonated in the posts having published these reports.

It's not the first time the Matryoshka network has targeted elections. A parallel campaign using the same methods has also aimed at candidates in Germany's upcoming September state elections.

Here, the campaign has sought to exploit historical tensions between Germany's East and West,an effort researchers say seeks to aggravate existing grievances and ultimately deepen political polarisation.

World.title: Pyongyang tests another missile within one week and ahead of US-South Korean military drills
World.content:
North Korea conducted its second ballistic missile test in less than a week on Wednesday, South Korean media reports, in what is believed to be a protest against the upcoming military exercises between Seoul and Washington, which Pyongyang sees as a practice for an invasion.

 

A ballistic missile fired from the North’s eastern coastal Wonsan area around 6 a.m. flew more than 700 kilometres, South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said.

South Korea’s military condemned the test and warned it remains ready to repel any provocation by Pyongyang in cooperation with the United States. South Korea’s national security council called North Korean ballistic missile launches “acts of provocation” and urged the North to halt them immediately.

The Japanese Defense Ministry also reported detecting the launch, saying the weapon landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone, between the Korean Peninsula and Japan.

Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told reporters that Japan strongly protested the North Korean launch through their embassies in Beijing. “It’s a serious problem that affects the safety of the Japanese people,” he said.

A TV screen shows a file image of North Korea's missile launch during a news program at Seoul Railway Station in Seoul, South Korea, Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. (AP Photo/Ahn Yo Ahn Young-joon/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

The launches, within days of each other, were seen as part of North Korea’s extended run of weapons tests as the country has refused to return to talks with the US and South Korea for years.

It also came two days after South Korea and the United States announced they will kick off their annual large-scale military drills on 17 August to beef up readiness against North Korean threats.

North Korea has previously responded to the Ulchi Freedom Shield training and other major South Korea-U.S. military exercises with provocative weapons tests and harsh rhetoric, although experts believe Pyongyang often uses its rivals’ military training as a pretext to boost its own testing activities. The US and South Korea have repeatedly said their training is defensive in nature.

After last year’s Ulchi Freedom Shield training exercises began, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un said the drills showed the US and South Korea’s “will to ignite a war” and claimed they have grown more provocative than before, which has prompted North Korea to respond with “proactive and overwhelming” countermeasures.

Last week, on 6 August, South Korea, the US, and Japan detected the launch of a short-range ballistic missile from North Korea in what was the North’s first ballistic weapons testing activity since late June.

Pyongyang didn’t confirm the reported launch, though it usually releases details of weapons tests a day later.

World.title: Morocco accuses Spain of assaulting migrants crossing into Ceuta and claims sovereignty over enclave
World.content:
Morocco's National Human Rights Council (CNDH) has once again pointed the finger at Spain. In a preliminary report released on 8 August, the council accuses the Spanish security forces of having assaulted and ill-treated some of the migrants who entered Ceuta on 30 and 31 July, when around 80,000 people crossed the border in just 48 hours.

 

According to the document, the Council's monitoring team gathered testimonies from migrants who had already been returned to Morocco and who all reported assaults by Spanish officers, "especially in places beyond the reach of cameras", in their own words.

The report also refers to minors who are said to have suffered insults and beatings at the hands of "extremist groups" as they passed through the city, and criticises the authorities in Ceuta for failing to provide adequate care, particularly for children and young people.

The CNDH goes further and blames the "local authorities" for the closure of restaurants and shops in the city, even though that decision in fact came from business owners themselves, following a recommendation from the local employers' association.

The council has also traced the role of social media in triggering the influx: it says it had already identified misleading content on migration on 8 July on pages with more than 90,000 followers, and that it has analysed 23 Facebook groups with more than a million members between them.

Morocco already accused Spain in 2022

This is not the first time that the same Council has targeted Spain. In 2022, after the storming of the Melilla border fence that left at least 23 people dead, it pinned responsibility on the Spanish authorities for keeping the gates closed.

Although Morocco's public prosecutor eventually closed the case citing "absence of evidence of a crime", the ruling was controversial precisely because reports suggested it had been Moroccan officers who relaxed controls at the border, allowing sub-Saharan migrants to cross.

Morocco claims Ceuta and Melilla

The report also comes alongside a diplomatic front that Morocco has chosen to reopen. Justice Minister Abdellatif Ouahbi told pan-Arab channel 'Asharq News' that Rabat is keeping its historic claim to Ceuta and Melilla alive, and that the issue "remains on the table" whenever representatives of the two countries meet.

He spoke of a "long-term" strategy to reclaim what he considers Moroccan territory through dialogue, and took the opportunity to press another demand: the repatriation of unaccompanied Moroccan minors who remain in centres in Spain, whose responsibility, he says, also lies with the Spanish authorities.

It is worth recalling that neither Ceuta nor Melilla has ever been Moroccan territory, despite being in Africa. Ceuta came under Spanish sovereignty in 1580 during the Iberian Union, while Melilla has been Spanish since 1497, when it was seized by the Crown of Castile.

World.title: Germany news: Cabinet approves intelligence service reforms
World.content:
Published 08/12/2026 Published August 12, 2026 Cabinet passes controversial intelligence agency reform

The foreign intelligence agency (BND) is headquartered in Berlin's Mitte district Image: NDR

The German Cabinet has approve a more than 700-page package of laws granting much greater powers to both the domestic intelligence agency (BfV) and the foreign intelligence agency (BND).

The package will allow the agencies more latitude in the gathering and storage of information and data, along with new options to actively combat acts of sabotage and hacking attacks.

The government says the package aims to enable the agencies to operate more effectively in the face of a myriad of hybrid security threats.

"We will not look on passively as foreign interference, sabotage and threats to the pillars of our constitution and our free society continue to grow," chancellery head Nina Warken told the daily Rheinische Post.

"Our [intelligence] services can only take targeted action against these hybrid attacks if they have more liberties and up-to-date measures" at their disposal, she said.

However, the planned reform has also met with considerable criticism from those who see the extended powers as a threat to civil rights.

The leader of the Free Democrats (FDP), Wolfgang Kubicki, accused Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of "breaking a taboo."

"It can hardly be imagined that the Constitutional Court will not intervene here," he told the Augsburger Allgemeine daily.

"I do not want any secret police in Germany," he said. "I want full court control in the case of attacks on basic rights and a state that understands that you don't defend liberty by curbing it."

World.title: EU packaging rules: Why small firms are sounding the alarm
World.content:
The EU has introduced new rules targeting packaging waste and "forever chemicals." Although the changes will be phased in slowly, some small sellers have already paused shipments due to the additional red tape.

What changes from Wednesday?

In a drive to cut waste and improve public health, new European Union rules take effect on Wednesday, banning high levels of PFAS "forever chemicals" in packaging.

Under the EU's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR), any new packaging products entering the market will now have to meet tighter standards if designed to come into contact with food.

PFAS have been linked to increased risks of certain cancers and other health conditions.

Although the amount of material people are exposed to from food packaging is usually low, scientists are worried about the long-term effects.

After all, PFAS are highly persistent chemicals and accumulate in the body and the environment.

PFAS are used to make paper and cardboard packaging both grease- and water-resistant and are found in everything from pizza boxes to TV dinners.

Packaging with lower PFAS reduces the risk of these persistent chemicals migrating into food or the natural world when thrown away.

The new rules are in addition to curbs onbisphenol A (BPA) in food-contact materials, which took effect across the EU last month.

Recycling rates in the EU are rising, but lower than the increase in packaging waste Image: Robert Michael/dpa/picture alliance

Under PPWR, businesses will not be required to recall or destroy packaging or goods that were already on the market before Wednesday.

While consumers won't notice any difference, businesses have fiercely criticized the changes, which also require packaging to meet new sustainability standards.

Are the new packaging rules too complicated?

Many small businesses and online traders believe the additional cost and red tape are too cumbersome.

They complain that they now have to register their packaging in multiple EU states, often with fees.

"Instead of facilitating cross-border trade, the new rules threaten to make it significantly more difficult," warned Händlerbund, the German online retailers' association.

Händlerbund warned its members : "There is no minimum quantity and no exception for small businesses."

EU lawmaker Elisabeth Dieringer of the far-right Freedom Party of Austria has warned that PPWR would mean five-figure costs for medium-sized firms.

"While corporations have their own departments for this [red tape], the Mittelstand [medium-sized firms] has little choice but to 'eat or die,'" she wrote on X on Tuesday.

Several businesses, from sole traders to medium-sized firms, said they had paused deliveries to and within the EU due to the new rules.

"Under these rules, I would need to appoint an authorized representative in every single EU country I send to," wrote the owner of a small online store, Monstaas Workshop, in an Instagram post.

"The cost is around €300 ($346) per country, per year ... these costs are simply not affordable."

From pollution to progress: Tackling PFAS across continents To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Swedish embedded electronic devices maker iLabs Electronics said it would halt web shop orders from EU countries.

"The cost and administrative burden [of PPWR] is now out of proportion to our direct sales volume," iLabs wrote on its website.

A petition on change.org had been signed by more than 45,000 people by Wednesday morning, calling on Brussels to "stop destroying EU micro-businesses."

How bad is the EU's packaging waste problem?

According to the European Commission, the bloc's executive arm, EU countries have witnessed a 20% increase in packaging waste over the last decade.

Without PPWR, Brussels says, discarded packaging was set to rise by another 19% by 2030, driven by the boom in online shopping and convenience food.

EU data shows that 178 kilograms (392 pounds) of packaging waste was generated per person across the bloc in 2023. Of this, 35.3 kg was plastic packaging, only 42% of which was recycled.

At 215 kg per capita (in 2023), Germany's waste from packaging is much higher than the EU average.

Scientists are worried about long-term exposure to 'forever chemicals' in food packaging Image: Tobias Steinmaurer/photosteinmaurer.com/IMAGO

Each EU resident generates the equivalent of roughly half a kilo of packaging waste every day, data from Eurostat, the EU's statistics agency, shows.

According to Brussels, the volume of waste has grown faster than recycling rates over the past decade.

Packaging also ⁠accounts ⁠for about 40% of plastic consumption in Europe, an EU official told reporters at a briefing on Tuesday.

What are the EU's long-term waste targets?

Although PFAS is the main focus of this initial phase of PPWR, the EU has set binding targets to cut packaging waste by 5% by 2030 and 15% by 2040.

From 2028, packaging manufacturers will be required to carry standardized labels that clearly show the materials used and how it should be recycled or disposed of.

Some stores, particularly restaurants and cafes, will be required to offer customers reusable packaging as an option, often at no extra charge.

Deposit-and-return schemes for plastic bottles and soda cans, such as those operational in Germany and the Netherlands, will be rolled out across the EU by 2029.

Then from 2030, all packaging placed on the EU market, including single-use plastic bottles, must be designed to be recyclable.

Packaging will also be required to be kept to a minimum to protect the product and fulfill its function.

This measure is meant to reduce the overuse of packaging for marketing purposes.

Meanwhile, single-use plastic packaging for fresh produce will be banned from 2030.

EU states will be able to set their own penalties for non-compliance, with German authorities allowed to impose fines of up to €200,000 ($230,000) for more serious breaches.

Edited by: Kristie Pladson

World.title: AI helping create popular mobile sports games
World.content:
After the World Cup and before the domestic season, many football fans still crave more. Amateur coders are helping to fill this gap.

After the World Cup and before the domestic football season begins, the world's most popular sport tends to enjoy a relatively quiet period. For some though, the need for football remains.

This summer that demand has been met by the creation of a raft of mobile sports games in which players can dive into nostalgia and storytelling. This craze has seemingly been inspired by the viral 82-0 basketball game in which players can draft an all-time NBA starting five by spinning a random wheel for teams and decades.

Inspired by this, Deniz Sancar, a hobbyist coder who works in advertising, created 38-0-0. Sancar told "mobilegamer.biz" that despite having no previous coding experience, he built the game overnight with Claude Code, an advanced AI assistant that is designed to help with coding. The game was number one in the UK App Store games charts in June.

Destiny Eleven: From TikTok to France and the world

Another example is Destiny Eleven. Maxence Pigne, a PSG fan and a project manager, was inspired by a game he saw on TikTok that allowed players to play out the career of a professional footballer. After the 2026 World Cup, Pigne released his version, also created with the help of AI assistant Claude, which took the original idea further by offering more variety and choices in the career.

The man who specializes in computer science told French weekly "Le Point" that the decision to publish the free game earlier than planned paid off because by the end of July, the game had over one million players with 14 million careers having been created. Leverkusen striker Martin Terrier is reportedly a fan of the game, which has seen many variations in different languages emerge in the weeks since its arrival.

Mobile games are big business

It's clear mobile games have come a long way since Nokia released "Snake" back in 1997. They are now big business. According to digital market intelligence platform Sensor Tower, approximately 50 billion mobile games were downloaded in 2025, generating $82 billion (€71 billion) in in-app purchases. According to "Game, the German Games Industry Association," revenue in Germany in 2025 was approxiamtely $3.12 billion, with 28.1 million players.

"This clearly indicates that mobile gaming in Germany is no longer a niche topic, but rather a serious genre with significant purchasing power," Kyle Kuscu, chairman of the German Mobile Gaming Association (DeMoGa), told DW.

"This is also relevant for the esports sector: Germany has a broad player base, and mobile gaming is the largest platform in the country in terms of user numbers."

This summer, the emergence of sports-drafting games has clearly benefited from a World Cup summer but also because of game design.

"The World Cup or tournament effect only amplifies this, but it doesn’t fully explain the hype on its own," Kuscu said.

"Such games satisfy a fundamental human need shared by many users: control, optimization, and imagination in a very compact format—in other words, the feeling of having it all in your own hands, of building the perfect team or career, without a long learning curve or complex controls."

What counts is the 'idea and final execution'

AI has been involved in video game creation for years, but with smarter and faster AI in 2026 comes an even more financially efficient approach for game developers. This is particularly important in the tough economic conditions in which free-to-play mobile games operate.

"The trend toward smaller, faster-to-develop games with AI support is likely to continue and may even grow. But I don’t believe that every viral success story will be repeated," Kuscu said.

"Based on our own experience and confirmed by external sources, we know that AI has long been used extensively and intensively in game development, especially for coding, prototyping, research, and repetitive tasks. At the same time, many people remain skeptical about quality, dependencies, and creative limitations. Even if we advocate for the use of AI-assisted programming, what ultimately counts is the idea and the final execution of a game, and that won’t change."

Short shelf life a key problem in a competitive market

The challenges for such games to maintain their success remains a major challenge though, especially given the overall gaming market remains a far from profitable industry. More teams can release more games, but that makes competition stiffer than ever.

"The biggest hurdle is no longer just production, but the business model behind it: Mobile games are extremely dependent on user attention, repeat usage, and, above all, in-app purchases," Kuscu said.

"A viral launch does not yet equate to a viable, let alone successful, business. They must get a handle on session duration, community building, update frequency, and monetization very quickly. This is precisely where the crux of the matter lies, because otherwise the hype will fizzle out before the game can become a sustainable title."

Whether it's the immersive storytelling nature of these games or the ease with which a virtual world can be reached, it's clear that these games have found a gap in the market. History suggests they might not be popular for long, but even if this summer is their moment in the sun, their emergence appears a significant reminder of the challenges the mobile game industry will face with the increased involvement of AI.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

World.title: Key issues in Zambia's 2026 general election
World.content:
Economic recovery, youth turnout, women's representation and judicial independence are among the issues shaping Zambia's vote on Thursday.

Zambia's general election on Thursday will be fought on economic recovery, governance reforms and a sweeping change to the country's parliamentary map.

Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema, leader of the United Party for National Development (UPND), is seeking a second term against 14 opponents.

His principal challenger is Brian Mundubile, a former ally of the late President Edgar Lungu, who has surged to the front of a fragmented opposition after being backed by a coalition of rival parties.

The Electoral Commission announced in April that 70 new constituencies would be added, raising the number of parliamentary seats from 156 to 226, creating smaller, more local voting districts. Up to 8.7 million voters are expected to take part in the elections, a majority of whom are women.

Economic issues dominate election campaign

Economic issues dominate voters' concerns. Official data shows that over 70% of the population lives on less than three dollars a day, and many households survive on salaries between $60 and $100 (€52 and €87) a month while grocery prices keep rising.

"I would like the new government to increase our salaries. [Maize meal] is very expensive. Everything is expensive," said security guard Lucky Mutelo.

Rebecca, a market shopper, echoes the sentiment, noting that "the cost of living is still too high."

Incumbent Hakainde Hichilema faces Brian Mundubile, a former ally of late president Edgar Lungu Image: Brian Mundubile media team

The government has been making significant gains on these issues.

Hichilema's government has secured a landmark debt restructuring agreement, restoring an International Monetary Fund program and supporting economic growth. Inflation fell to 6.5% in June this year.

The administration has also rolled out free education and an expanded Constituency Development Fund, which allocates public money directly to each of the country's constituencies to finance community-driven local development projects and infrastructure.

Nevertheless, a historic drought that crippled agriculture and forced severe hydro‑power load‑shedding has strained household finances.

Election demographics amid a fragmented electoral field

To become president, a candidate must secure 50% plus one of the total votes cast. If no contender reaches this threshold, the two highest‑scoring candidates will face off in a second round — a mechanism designed to ensure that the president enjoys a clear popular mandate.

There are 14 names on the ballot, so even small swings in support across the ten provinces could determine whether the election goes to a second round.

Our time is now: Zambia's youth running in elections To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Analysts say the election's outcome would hinge on urban centers such as Lusaka and the Copperbelt, where cost‑of‑living pressures are most acute, while rural provinces traditionally follow established party loyalties.

Rural voters in the Southern, Western and North‑Western provinces historically back the UPND, whereas the opposition targets the Northern, Luapula and Eastern provinces.

Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported that the high youth turnout that propelled the current president Hakainde Hichilema to a landslide victory in 2021 is expected to be a decisive factor again, especially in the densely populated urban districts.

Nearly half of registered voters are aged between 18 and 35, making young people a potentially pivotal bloc, Institute for Security Studies researcher Zenge Simakoloyi told AFP.

Can women swing this election?

Gender representation is another prominent theme. In this election, there is one female candidate for president, and four female running mates.

Mwaka Nyirenda is one of a handful of women contesting for a parliamentary seat.

"Politics is still a man's world. People doubt you, underestimate you and try to intimidate you," she told DW, noting that the financial bias still favors male candidates.

Women comprise roughly 51% of Zambia's population but hold only about 15% of parliamentary seats, and fewer than 20% of political leadership positions.

Leah Diana Mitaba, publicity secretary of the Non‑Governmental Coordinating Council, warns that these figures "demonstrate that Zambia remains far from achieving the 50:50 gender representation envisaged in the Constitution, the SADC Protocol on Gender and Development, the African Union Agenda 2063 and the UN Sustainable Development Goals."

Girls Gone Political, a civil‑society group, campaigns for greater female participation. Its leader, Dorothy Mtanga, thinks more civic education is needed. "There's the need for sustained democratic civic education to ensure that more women are elected into office," she said.

Judicial independence called into question

This election also raises questions about the independence of Zambia's judiciary.

Can Zambia trust election referee? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2024, President Hichilema suspended three Constitutional Court judges who ruled in favor of his rival, former President Edgar Lungu.

Lawyer Linda Kasonde argued that "judicial independence is the ability to adjudicate on any matter, without fear or favor, regardless of the stakes involved in the case." In practice, opposition lawyers think the executive is trying to interfere with justice delivery.

Kasonde identifies two recent concerns. First, an executive‑approved salary increase for judges that bypassed the constitutional emoluments commission.

"The government increased salaries for judicial officers in 2025 outside the proper procedure, raising questions about whether the process was independent," she told DW.

Second, the appointment of 16 new judges in early 2026, many of whom hail from the incumbent's strongholds.

"These appointments call into question whether any decisions that will be made regarding the elections will be done independently," lawyer Kasonde concluded.

Amnesty International says Zambian laws, including the Public Order Act and cybercrime legislation, have been weaponized to restrict dissent, opposition gatherings and freedom of expression. It also warns that the increasing use of criminal charges against government critics could have a chilling effect on political expression.

Chief Justice Mumba Malila recently reassured the public.

"The judiciary stands ready to discharge its constitutional responsibility, independently, professionally and within the strict timelines established by the law," he said. Critics, however, maintain that true independence requires full structural and financial autonomy from the executive.

Continuity or change?

Zambia's status as one of the region's stable multi‑party democracies in the Southern African Development Community (SADC) means that this election will influence regional democratic norms.

The country's ability to host a peaceful transition or renewal of power is a barometer for neighboring states, especially after recent defeats of incumbents in Botswana and Malawi.

Polls will be open from 6:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Zambians will elect a president, National Assembly members, mayors, councilors, and council chairs.

This election holds the potential to either consolidate President Hichilema's reform agenda or usher in a new administration.

This article was compiled from several DW video reports covering Zambia's 2026 general election

World.title: Solar eclipse: What to look forward to
World.content:
The last solar eclipse visible from the European mainland was in 1999. Here's what to expect, and how to prepare for this rare occasion.

On Wednesday, about 980 million people across parts of the Northern Hemisphere will have the chance to observe this upcoming solar eclipse.

They will be joined by hosts of researchers who will be taking advantage of the fleeting minutes when the sun's corona is visible from Earth to test specialized instruments and capture rare images. With them, they hope to gain a deeper appreciation of the material above the sun's surface .

What's going to happen?

During a solar eclipse, the moon orbits between Earth and the sun during the daytime, casting a shadow which temporarily darkens the sky and appears to blot out the sun. At the height of an eclipse, the moon's disk appears to align with the sun, revealing the sun's corona — its outermost atmosphere that flares outward like a crown (hence the name).

As the moon approaches and the sky darkens, you might also notice the temperature dropping, shadows appearing crescent-shaped, the wind beginning to shift and animals behaving unusually.

Eclipse fever sweeps Spain ahead of rare spectacle To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Solar panels will be able to produce less energy in this time. In Germany, this is expected to lead to a brief surge in electricity prices.

Right before the eclipse reaches its maximum point, known as totality, watch out for Baily's beads. These are the final rays of sun reaching Earth through valleys on the moon's surface. They appear as white specks encircling the moon like a string of pearls.

As night closes in during totality, keep an eye out for the stars that appear. Some might even be able to catch a glimpse of auroras or passing meteors.

Where will the eclipse occur?

If you live in Greenland, Iceland, northern Russia, northern Spain or northeastern Portugal, you're in luck! Viewers in these locations will be able to observe a total solar eclipse.

In most of Western Europe, as well as parts of northern Africa and northern America, astronomy enthusiasts will still be able to watch a partial solar eclipse.

And this is just the first of two eclipses in August. The second will take place on August 27-28, when Earth moves between the sun and the moon to create a lunar eclipse.

The next solar eclipse will happen February 2, 2027, over much of Africa, South America, as well as parts of Antarctica.

While eclipses themselves are fairly frequent occurrences, it's not that often that a total solar eclipse is visible on inhabited parts of the globe. The last solar eclipse visible for most of mainland Europe, for example, was in 1999.

What time is the eclipse happening?

The spectacle will begin at 15:34 GMT, with the moon slowly dimming the sun's light as it creeps into position. About two hours later, at 17:46 GMT, the eclipse will reach totality for about two minutes.

But where on the globe you are watching from will make a difference. While Icelanders will be able to observe the eclipse's totality at 17:48 GMT, viewers in Spain will have to wait until 18:27 for their chance.

Where can I watch the eclipse?

Since the eclipse is happening relatively late in the day, viewers are recommended to watch from high places to catch a good view of the sun as it dips toward the horizon. Most west-facing hills, towers and (safe) rooftops with an unobstructed view should do the trick.

If you're the kind who prefers crisper images, NASA is also offering a livestream .

Can I wear normal sunglasses to watch the eclipse?

In short, no. Looking directly into the sun can cause permanent damage to the retina at the back of your eye. Ordinary sunglasses, even polarized ones, are far too weak to provide enough protection.

Instead, you'll need certified ISO 12312-2 glasses, available at most pharmacies and opticians. Most are sold out already, but there are plenty of directions online for building a pinhole camera to safely watch the eclipse with small children.

You can also use a kitchen colander, or any other tool with small holes, to project tiny crescent-shaped shadows onto a safe surface.

Whether or not you are wearing eclipse glasses, never look at the sun through a camera, telescope or binoculars without a specialized filter, as the concentrated light can cause serious damage to your eyes.

World.title: India news: IndiGo engine failure triggers airport emergency
World.content:
08/12/2026 August 12, 2026 Food safety, hygiene issues plague India's quick commerce firms

In Mumbai, authorities suspended the license of a Blinkit facility after finding a large-scale cockroach infestation, improperly stored food and expired or tampered products [FILE: February 10, 2023] Image: Debajyoti Chakraborty/NurPhoto/picture alliance

India's quick commerce sector, especially grocery delivery services, is in the doldrums as authorities flag serious food safety and hygiene violations.

Authorities in the southern Karnataka and western Maharashtra states sealed a Zepto warehouse on Tuesday and suspended the license of a Blinkit facility after inspections found serious violations, reports said.

In Karnataka, a Zepto warehouse near Bengaluru was sealed by the food safety department after finding unhygienic food handling and storage conditions, improper labelling and misbranding.

Zepto said in a statement that it had cooperated with officials and was taking steps to address their observations, the Hindustan Times reported, adding that it remained committed to food safety and hygiene standards.

In Mumbai, authorities suspended the license of a Blinkit facility after finding a large-scale cockroach infestation, improperly stored food and expired or tampered products.

Food was also found on rusted racks, while cold-storage areas lacked adequate cleanliness.

The facility has been barred from selling or distributing food or conducting any food business during the license suspension, authorities said.

World.title: Pakistan says 3 nationals killed in Houthi Red Sea attack
World.content:
Pakistan's foreign minister has said Islamabad "strongly condemns" Houthi attacks on commercial vessels while offering condolences to the families of the dead.

At least three Pakistani nations were killed in an "incident involving an attack on a commercial vessel in the Red Sea," Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on Wednesday.

Another Pakistani national had sustained injuries.

"Pakistan strongly condemns the Houthi attack on a non-combatant commercial vessel. Such attacks endanger innocent lives, constitute a violation of international law, and pose a serious threat to freedom of navigation, maritime security, and the safety of commercial shipping in the Red Sea," the minister said in a post on X.

Pakistan's Foreign Ministry was in contact with Saudi Arabia and Yemen to ascertain further details of the incident, Dar said. Meanwhile, the Pakistani Embassy in Riyadh was coordinating the retrieval and repatriation of the mortal remains of their deceased nationals.

Vessels under attack amid Middle East conflict

On Tuesday, the US and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels reported separate attacks on shipping as peace negotiations between Washington and Tehran seemingly stagnated once again.

At the southern end of the Red Sea, a suspected Houthi attack on a small cargo vessel killed four crew members, Yemen's Transport Ministry said. It was not immediately clear is this was the same vessel Dar was referring to.

Commercial shipping and seafarers passing through the Middle East have increasingly come under attack by both the US and Iran since the conflict began earlier this year.

Indian seafarers pay the price in US-Iran war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: Australia approves new rules benefiting gig delivery workers
World.content:
Delivery drivers in Australia are to be guaranteed "world-leading" higher pay and insurance cover on the job. The move could be a model for other countries.

Food and grocery delivery workers in Australia will be paid at least A$31.30 (€19.15, $22.11) an hour and be given accident insurance on the job under new rules approved by Australia's industrial relations tribunal.

The hourly rate, set out in an order issued by the Fair Work Commission (FWC) on Tuesday, is above Australia's minimum wage of A$26.44.

The FWC's order, which could serve as a precedent for other countries, has been hailed by the Transport Workers Union (TWU) as "a landmark moment for the Australian gig economy." The union called the new rules a "world-leading set of standards."

What rights and protects did the FWC give gig delivery drivers?

The minimum hourly rate will be paid for "engaged" time, i.e. the time between taking on a delivery job and completing the commission.

The order, which takes effect on August 17, also requires companies to provide a "reasonable minimum level of cover" ​for personal accident insurance on the job, without specifying exactly how much.

The workers will, however, still be responsible for maintaining ⁠third-party ⁠insurance for the vehicles used for deliveries.

Unions and workers in Australia ​have long sought ⁠reforms benefiting gig workers.

They have previously not been covered by many of the protections given to other employees, being classified as "independent contractors."

The new rules are expected to affect some 250,000 workers.

Gig workers worldwide encounter exploitative work conditions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

UN moves to protect gig workers

The FWC's order comes after the United Nations' International Labour Organization (ILO) in June adopted a new global treaty for decent working conditions in the gig economy.

The standards laid down in the treaty, the first global treaty of its kind, still need ratification by governments.

In Australia, the parliament passed legislation in 2023 and 2024 under the center-left Labor government that granted gig workers more negotiating rights over minimum pay and working conditions.

Those laws gave the FWC the power to set rules for pay and insurance.

World.title: 16 pueblos españoles que piden manga larga cuando cae la tarde
World.content:
Vielha (Lleida). La gran baza de los pueblos seleccionados radica, sobre todo, en la posibilidad de tener que taparse para descansar, algo que se ha convertido en todo un lujo durante la canícula. Es un requisito que cumple Vielha, a la vera de los ríos Garona y Nere, con su casco histórico construido a la manera aranesa, a golpe de piedra, pizarra y madera. Sus mínimas descenderán hasta los 12ºC la noche del domingo; las máximas alcanzarán picos de 33ºC en las horas centrales del jueves y viernes, pero bajarán a los 24ºC (y con probabilidad de lluvias) el lunes, según la Aemet. La capital del Valle de Arán se presenta como un buen campamento base para conocer este territorio del Pirineo catalán, con sus 33 núcleos de población, sus algo más de 10.000 habitantes y sus iglesias románicas. Es recomendable acercarse a la cascada Saut deth Pish, probablemente la más bonita de la zona. Más información: visitvaldaran.com/descubre-la-val-daran/pueblos/vielha/.

Toni M (GETTY IMAGES)

World.title: Arranca el mayor escaparate de las estrellas del mundo
World.content:
24 de los 52 jugadores convocados para la final del Mundial y 18 campeones juegan en LALIGA. Ninguna de las grandes ligas europeas supera el dato. La competición arranca este viernes con nuevas caras y viejos conocidos que elevan el nivel del torneo

No hay que esperar cuatro años para volver a ver a las mejores estrellas del fútbol mundial: en LALIGA, juegan cada fin de semana. La temporada 2026/2027 arranca este fin de semana con un dato que refleja el talento del fútbol profesional español: 24 de los 52 jugadores convocados por España y Argentina para la final del Mundial juegan en la máxima competición del fútbol español, así como 18 campeones que contribuyeron a que en la camiseta de la selección española figuren ahora las dos estrellas.

totales en 3.318 Goles

totales en 601 Asistencias

totales en 377 Edad media 26,42 años El XI de los Campeones del mundo con más partidos en LALIGA Unai Simón 237 Eric García 145 Aymeric Laporte 186 Marcos Llorente 270 Pedri 201 Marc Cucurella 143 Ferran Torres 211 Álex Baena 173 Mikel Oyarzábal 349 Nico Williams 157 Borja Iglesias 291 *Se incluyen datos de LALIGA EA SPORTS y LALIGA HYPERMOTION.

Fuente: LALIGA / Transfermarkt

El logro del trofeo más prestigioso del fútbol ha propiciado que la primera jornada se haya dividido para esperar la vuelta de las merecidas vacaciones de los campeones. Entre el sábado 15 y el miércoles 19 de agosto se disputarán siete partidos de LALIGA EA SPORTS. Los tres restantes, aplazados para que los equipos puedan contar con todos sus futbolistas, se disputarán a finales de mes: el Valencia-Real Betis, el día 25; el Real Madrid-Real Sociedad, el 26 y cerrará la jornada el 27 el FC Barcelona-Athletic Club, dos de los equipos que más jugadores aportaron al combinado español con 11 estrellas. Por su parte, el pistoletazo de salida a LALIGA HYPERMOTION será el viernes 14 con el duelo que enfrenta al filial de la Real Sociedad contra el CD Castellón, una de las revelaciones de la pasada campaña que se quedó a las puertas del ascenso.

Como cada temporada, los equipos ultiman sus plantillas. Llegan nuevas caras y viejos conocidos que elevan el nivel de LALIGA EA SPORTS. Nombres como el de Sergio Canales, que regresa al R. Racing Club tras una estancia en México; Anthony Gordon, estrella de la selección inglesa que llega al FC Barcelona o el de José Mourinho, en su vuelta al banquillo del Real Madrid.

Nuevas caras y viejos conocidos en LALIGA EA SPORTS José Mourinho REAL MADRID El portugués José Mourinho releva esta temporada a uno de sus alumnos más aventajados, Álvaro Arbeloa, en el banquillo madridista. En su anterior etapa (2010-2013) dirigió al conjunto blanco en 114 partidos –84 victorias– en LALIGA EA SPORTS y logró el título liguero en la campaña 2011/12. Foto: Diario AS Diomande REAL MADRID El fichaje del extremo costamarfileño, titular en el pasado Mundial con su selección, llega para reforzar el ataque del Real Madrid. Ya disputó diez partidos con la camiseta del CD Leganés (dos goles y una asistencia) en la temporada 2024/25. En la imagen, montaje elaborado por el Real Madrid para anunciar su fichaje. Foto: Real Madrid Canales R. Racing Club El canterano racinguista debutó en LALIGA EA SPORTS el 10 de octubre de 2008 con el equipo santanderino. Pasó por el Real Madrid, el Valencia CF y la Real Sociedad; brilló en el Real Betis (164 partidos ligueros, 30 goles y 25 asistencias) y ahora vuelve a su tierra tras tres años en la liga mexicana. Foto: Diario AS Grimaldo Atlético de Madrid A sus 30 años, el campeón del mundo (en la imagen, con el trofeo) tiene un nuevo reto en su carrera: debutar en LALIGA EA SPORTS. Se formó en La Masía, jugó en el Benfica y del Bayer Leverkusen. Con el filial del FC Barcelona jugó 75 partidos (4 goles, 9 asistencias) en LALIGA HYPERMOTION entre 2011 y 2015. Foto: Getty Images Anthony Gordon FC Barcelona El internacional inglés, fichado del Newcastle, llegó a las semifinales en la pasada Copa del Mundo y ahora llega a LALIGA EA SPORTS para reforzar el ataque del FC Barcelona. En la imagen, su presentación como nuevo futbolista culé. Foto: Diario AS Aissa Mandi Levante UD Un veterano (34 años) que vuelve a LALIGA EA SPORTS tras dos años en la Ligue 1. Mandi, internacional con Argelia en 114 ocasiones y capitán, jugó 206 partidos en la máxima categoría del fútbol profesional español entre 2016 y 2024, primero en el Real Betis y luego en el Villarreal CF. En la imagen, el central, en una disputa con Lionel Messi durante el Mundial. Foto: Getty Images Yeremay RC Deportivo El extremo canario (22 años) y canterano deportivista fue una de las sensaciones de LALIGA HYPERMOTION en las últimas dos temporadas: 77 partidos, 25 goles y 15 asistencias. Ahora, llega a LALIGA EA SPORTS pese al interés de equipos de la Premier League y la Serie A italiana. En la imagen, durante uno de los entrenamientos de pretemporada. Foto: Diario AS Dubasin CA Osasuna El hispano-belga nacido en La Seu d'Urgell (Lleida) jugó en el Albacete Balompié, en el FC Basilea suizo, en el Real Oviedo y en el Real Sporting. Con 138 partidos en LALIGA HYPERMOTION –34 goles y 21 asistencias– Dubasin llega al CA Osasuna para debutar en LALIGA EA SPORTS. En la imagen, el extremo (a la izquierda), durante la preparación veraniega. Foto: Diario AS Álex Calatrava RCD Espanyol de Barcelona Cala, como le conocen los aficionados del CD Castellón, fue uno de los pilares del conjunto blanquinegro que llegó el año pasado a los PLAYOFFS DE ASCENSO. En la categoría de plata anotó 14 goles, repartió 8 asistencias en 42 partidos. Ahora, el fichaje del RCD Espanyol de Barcelona tiene la oportunidad de hacerse un hueco en la élite. Foto: Diario AS Chupe, Larrubia y Joaquín Málaga CF El tridente ofensivo del Málaga CF la pasada temporada: entre los sumaron 43 goles y 17 asistencias para devolver al equipo donde se formaron a la élite nueve años después. Salvo Joaquín Muñoz, que disputó cuatro partidos en LALIGA EA SPORTS con el Atlético de Madrid entre 2019 y 2020, Chupe y Larrubia debutarán en la máxima categoría. Foto: Diario AS

La guía para disfrutar de la emoción de LALIGA

LALIGA EA SPORTS se emite en los dos canales oficiales, Movistar LALIGA y DAZN LALIGA, cada uno, con cinco encuentros por jornada. Habrá, además, tres jornadas exclusivas aún por definir que solo se podrán seguir por el primero. Ambos canales se pueden ver a través de los operadores oficiales: Movistar Plus+, Orange y DAZN. Esta temporada, habrá también un partido por jornada que se dará en abierto a través de la señal de Teledeporte.

La jornada empieza en el bar

Los aficionados que quieran vivir el fútbol en un ambiente diferente también pueden hacerlo en los miles de bares que cuentan con los paquetes oficiales de retransmisión. Con un doble valor añadido: los futboleros que decidan acudir a su establecimiento de confianza contribuyen al crecimiento y a la dinamización del sector HORECA y refuerzan, con su visita, la cultura de la previa y el pospartido, lo que demuestra que el fútbol también puede ser una experiencia social que va mucho más allá de los 90 minutos.
