Además, a lo largo de la temporada, LALIGA llevará a las pantallas de los bares oficiales concursos, sorteos y premios exclusivos, ofreciendo a los aficionados nuevas formas de participar y disfrutar de la competición mientras viven el partido en su segunda grada.

Hazte fan de LALIGA y participa en sorteos para ganar premios

Ampuero, la primera activación de LALIGA BARES Tras 14 años de ausencia, el regreso del Racing a LALIGA EA SPORTS (domingo 16, 17.00 horas) servirá para la primera activación de la temporada de LALIGA BARES , la plataforma que pone a los bares en el corazón del fútbol profesional. Con motivo del partido, LALIGA se desplazará a Ampuero (Cantabria), localidad natal del capitán santanderino Íñigo Sainz-Maza, con el objetivo conectar el fútbol profesional con historias que entrelazan la identidad del territorio y la hostelería. Sainz-Maza, protagonista del segundo episodio de 42 Legados , un proyecto audiovisual de PRISA y LALIGA, no solo es uno de los vecinos más queridos de su puebluco, sino que personaliza la resistencia y la humildad que caracterizan a la afición santanderina. La activación guarda, además, una sorpresa: la presencia de una leyenda del club montañés.

World.title: Dos senderos idóneos para explorar el Valle de Arán en verano
World.content:
En la zona occidental de la comarca pirenaica esperan la Artiga de Lin y la Val de Toran. Cascadas, mariposas, pequeños pueblos y antiguos caminos para el contrabando que se disfrutan sin multitudes

Que levanten la mano quienes hayan estado en Baqueira, Salardú o Artíes. ¡Hala, cuánta gente! Ese es el Naut Aran (el Alto Arán, en aranés), al que más de un millón de personas acuden en invierno a esquiar. Que la levanten ahora quienes hayan estado en Es Bòrdes o en Canejan. Ni la décima parte. Esta zona occidental del Valle de Arán, por la que corren el río Garona y la carretera N230 poco antes de entrar en Francia, no es tan famosa como la oriental, pero por eso mismo está rodeada de montañas silenciosas, virginales, sin remontes ni aparcamientos para 1.600 vehículos.

Cuando la nieve se retira, aquí se ven flores, mariposas y cascadas. Hay dos senderos idóneos para explorarla: el que recorre el pasmoso valle de la Artiga de Lin, donde surgen a chorros las aguas del glaciar del Aneto después de circular casi cuatro kilómetros bajo tierra, y el camino del Contrabando, entre Canejan y Sant Joan de Toran, por el que los vecinos traficaban durante la posguerra con café y azúcar de la vecina Francia.

Los Ojos de Júpiter, del Diablo o del Judío

La Artiga de Lin es el paraje natural más espectacular de la comarca. En este valle glaciar hay dos lugares difíciles de creer: a 1.370 metros de altura, se encuentra la surgencia de los Uelhs deth Joèu (­los Ojos de Júpiter, del Diablo o del Judío, que de las tres formas lo traducen), donde brotan 1.580 litros de agua por segundo —y hasta 10.000 en pleno deshielo—. Cien metros más arriba, a 1.470, está el Plan dera Artiga, una gran pradera alpina rodeada de hayedos, abetales y escarpadas montañas calizas a casi 3.000 metros de altura donde lindan el Valle de Arán y el de Benasque, Lleida y Huesca, Cataluña y Aragón.

Surgencia de los Uhels deth Joèu, en la Artiga de Lin. Andrés Campos

A diferencia de lo que ocurre en la zona oriental del Valle de Arán, aquí no se puede aparcar a pie de pista porque no hay ninguna. Tampoco hay atascos porque los meses de mayor afluencia de visitantes en esta zona, los estivales, es obligatorio estacionar junto a la ermita dera Mair de Diu dera Artiga de Lin, tres kilómetros antes de llegar al final de la estrecha carretera que sube culebreando por el valle desde el pueblo de Es Bòrdes. Luego se puede continuar subiendo por el asfalto en un trenecito turístico o hacerlo a pie por el camino del Agua, que es una senda ribereña fácil y preciosa.

Siguiendo el camino, antes de una hora se verá la surgencia de los Uelhs deth Joèu. “¿De dónde sale tanta agua?“, se preguntan todos los que examinan por primera vez este nacedero torrencial, porque aunque su caudal medio se reduce en verano a 250 litros por segundo, sigue siendo mucha fuente. Pues resulta que sale del Aneto, el techo de los Pirineos, en la vecina Huesca. Y se sabe porque, en 1931, el espeleólogo francés Norbert Casteret vertió 60 kilos de colorante inocuo en el Forau d’Aigualluts —un sumidero kárstico del valle de Benasque donde las aguas recién fundidas del glaciar del Aneto desaparecen bajo tierra después de pegar un buen salto—, y comprobó que estas aparecían teñidas en los Uelhs. Así que estas aguas nacidas al sur de los Pirineos, en vez de ir al Ebro y al Mediterráneo, que sería lo lógico, corren cuatro kilómetros bajo las montañas para engrosar el río Garona y acabar en el Atlántico.

Indicador de rutas en la Artiga de Kin, en el Valle de Arán. Andrés Campos

Flores mil, más de 150 mariposas y dos guías excelentes

Al pie de la cascada tumultuosa, hay una pasarela metálica que permite cruzar el río Joèu para seguir subiendo por el abetal de la margen contraria y acabar saliendo, tras dos horas de paseo, al Plan dera Artiga de Lin. Es un rellano glaciar bellísimo, presidido por la mole rocosa del Malh dera Artiga (2.711 metros) y alfombrado de prados llenos de flores —gencianas, astrancias, violetas de los Pirineos, geranios silvestres, consueldas mayores, malvas moscadas…— y mariposas de montaña: la apolo, la mnemosine, la colias alpina, la erebia oeme, la común, la dentada…

Para distinguir las más de 150 especies que viven en este Shangri-La de las mariposas, es sumamente útil la guía ilustrada que ha publicado el Conselh Generau d’Aran. Otra guía excelente para explorar la Artiga de Lin es Sara Arjó, bióloga que dirige la empresa de ecoturismo y educación ambiental Verd e Blu y que es la autora de Parpalhòles dera Val d’Aran, un juego didáctico de papiroflexia con 14 recortables de mariposas de siete especies, las más llamativas del lugar.

Mariposa zygaena osterodensis en la Artiga de Lin. Andrés Campos

Todo es bonito en la Artiga de Lin, hasta el espléndido refugio donde Arjó se toma un refresco y algún tentempié con sus clientes, dejándolos disfrutar un rato largo de este paisaje embobador antes de acercarse al siguiente lugar destacado de la ruta: la cascada de Pomèro. En esta última, a solo 300 metros del refugio, les presenta la amapola amarilla (Papaver cambricum), una flor rara en España, pero muy abundante y estimada en las islas británicas, a tal punto que la usa como emblema Plaid Cymru, el partido nacionalista que ahora gobierna en Gales. Una microcentral eléctrica produce en este florido salto la energía de la que se abastece el refugio, que es grandecito, con habitaciones para 27 montañeros y un buen restaurante para cualquiera que pase.

Vista al Aneto desde el mirador de Vilamòs

Desde el refugio se baja cómodamente por la carretera asfaltada hasta la ermita donde se aparcó al principio. Como no se tarda mucho en completar la vuelta a pie (la ruta circular descrita, de algo menos de ocho kilómetros, lleva hacerla unas tres horas, cuatro con paradas contemplativas y de refresco), hay tiempo para acercarse en coche al mirador de Vilamòs, que está a solo siete kilómetros de la Artiga de Lin en línea recta, pero a 17 por una carretera loca (la LV5055) que sube desde El Pont d’Arròs trazando 16 revueltas. El mirador no está señalizado en la carretera, pero sí en Google Maps.

Vista del refugio de la Artiga de Lin, en el Valle de Arán. Andrés Campos

Desde aquí, con la ayuda del móvil y de la aplicación AR AlpineGuide (disponible en Google Play y en Apple Store), pueden identificarse las montañas que se alzan alrededor de la Artiga de Lin, arropando su formidable recuenco glaciar: la doble cima de la Forcanada, el Malh dera Artiga, la Tuca Blanca de Pomèro… Detrás de esta última cumbre asoman las nieves perpetuas y los riscos estratosféricos del macizo de la Maladeta, señoreados por el Aneto (3.404 metros).

Después de este atracón de montañas, apetece bajar a El Pont d’Arròs para darse otro de cocina aranesa en el restaurante del hotel Peña. Este es un cuatro estrellas cómodo y hogareño a más no poder, al que solo le falta aire acondicionado en las habitaciones para ser extraordinario. Pronto lo instalarán: el cambio climático obliga. Luego, un baño en la piscina climatizada y a la cama, que mañana hay que madrugar para explorar otra cara oculta de Arán, su rincón más desconocido y solitario: la Val de Toran.

Republicanos, judíos, maquis y contrabandistas

En Puntaut, poco antes de que el río Garona se cuele en Francia y de que la carretera N230 española se convierta en la N125 gala, se desvía a la derecha otra muy estrecha, sin eje central y sumamente virada que se adentra en la recóndita Val de Toran. Seis kilómetros y 38 curvas más arriba, se llega a Canejan, un pueblecito-balcón que domina desde su altura un inmenso panorama ­de las montañas donde España y Francia se besan.

Una cruz occitana en en suelo de la Plaça dera Castra, en Canejan. Andrés Campos

En la Plaça dera Castra, la mayor y más cuidada, la del Ayuntamiento, de pavimento decorado con una gran cruz occitana —la enseña aranesa—, dos paneles informativos recuerdan que por Canejan pasaban a Francia no pocos republicanos que huían de la represión franquista tras la Guerra Civil y judíos que escapaban en dirección contraria, de la Europa ocupada por los nazis, durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial. También recuerdan que esta fue la primera localidad atacada y tomada por los guerrilleros antifranquistas en octubre de 1944 durante la llamada Operación Reconquista de España, que pretendía deponer al dictador y restaurar la República. No dicen nada, en cambio, de los contrabandistas que trajinaban aquí en los años del hambre y del racionamiento, entre 1939 y 1952. Para decirlo, están los vecinos. No es que haya muchos en la Val de Toran (unos cien), pero casi todos están en Canejan. Una de ellas, Generosa Marqués, cuenta al que quiera oírla el caso de sus padres, Pedro y Palmira, que una vez al mes iban a la comuna gala de Fos y volvían cargados de café y azúcar, productos que escaseaban en el mercado regulado español y por los que sacaban un buen pico. Hasta que una noche los sorprendieron y pasaron las 15 siguientes entre rejas.

Difícil saber qué caminos usaban los contrabandistas para cruzar la raya. Como dice Generosa, “el tiempo, el del reloj y el atmosférico, los ha borrado”. Sin embargo, se conservan bien algunos de los que seguían para trapichear en este valle fronterizo, como el histórico que une Canejan, Porcingles y Sant Joan de Toran. Para andar por él solo hay que subir a lo más alto de Canejan y salir del pueblo siguiendo la calle Era Cau, que pronto se hace de tierra, asciende dejando a la derecha unas rústicas bordas y se vuelve prácticamente llana. Para más señas, hay indicadores de dirección y marcas de pintura blanca y roja a lo largo de todo el recorrido, pues coincide con el sendero GR-211. Y se puede consultar el mapa y descargar el track de la ruta en Wikiloc.

La soledad de Porcingles y Sant Joan de Toran

Tras una hora de paseo por este camino alto y horizontal, contemplando cómo desde una terraza el callejón sin salida montañoso de la Val de Toran, se entra en Porcingles, una aldea fantasma con solo dos casas temporalmente habitadas, calles impracticables y un lavadero cuyas aguas llevan tanto tiempo sin reflejar a un humano, que las mariposas (los sátiros del bosque y los ocelados, por citar dos especies que aquí se ven), se posan sobre las manos del recién llegado, sin saber qué es. Las ruinas de Porcingles son un recuerdo escalofriante de cuando a la Val de Toran llegó para quedarse una muchedumbre de 500 personas poseída por la fiebre del oro o, más bien, del zinc y del plomo, que eran lo que se sacaba de las minas de Liat, en la cabecera del valle, durante el siglo XIX y a principios del XX. Había incluso un teleférico de 13 kilómetros que transportaba todo lo extraído valle abajo, hasta el lavadero de mineral de Puntaut.

El camino, bastante llano hasta Porcingles, gana luego altura, cruza el barranco de Gotèrs y la pierde para llegar, al cumplirse dos horas de marcha, a Sant Joan de Toran. Tampoco es un lugar donde viva una multitud: solo tres personas. Pero junto a los prados que alguien se ha tomado la molestia de segar, hay una iglesia con macetas floridas a cada lado de la puerta y una docena larga de casas y bordas tradicionales de piedra en perfecto estado, en cuyos tejados de afilado caballete no falta una sola losa de pizarra: señal de que aquí viene a pasar cortas temporadas gente harta del mundanal ruido, que sabe lo que es bueno y que puede permitírselo. En este pueblo de postal se encuentra uno de los pocos negocios turísticos de la Val de Toran, el restaurante Estupendet, buen sitio para tomarse una ensaladilla rusa de verdad y una cerveza artesanal Refu. Este pulcro pueblecito rodeado de prados y montañas es lo más encantador del Valle de Arán, con permiso de la Artiga de Lin.

World.title: Roberto Martinez front-runner to be next Netherlands head coach
World.content:
The Dutch football association KNVB is reportedly lining up Roberto Martinez to take over from Ronald Koeman as coach of the national men’s team,.

The 53-year-old Spaniard emerged as a surprise contender after candidates such as former Feyenoord and Liverpool manager Arne Slot, former Ajax and Manchester United coach Erik ten Hag and PSV boss Peter Bosz ruled themselves out.

The KNVB held talks at the weekend with under-21 coach Michael Reiziger, but there have been no further discussions since Sunday, the Telegraaf reported on Wednesday.

Louis van Gaal also sent an open application to Zeist last week saying he was ready to step in for a fourth spell in charge, but the KNVB has not followed up with the 75-year-old former Ajax trainer.

Martinez was in charge of Portugal during the recent World Cup in North America, resigning after the team lost 1-0 to eventual winners Spain in the round of 16.

Previously he coached Belgium for six years, reaching the World Cup semi-final in 2018. He would be the first foreign manager to coach Oranje since Ernst Happel in 1978.

World.title: Uncertain future for Dutch bike brands after Accell goes under
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Netherlands’ largest bicycle manufacturer, Accell, has been declared insolvent, leaving an uncertain future for major brands such as Batavus, Sparta and the British-based bike maker Raleigh.

A court appointed curators last week when Accell applied to suspend payments to its creditors, the last step before insolvency in the Netherlands.

In a statement, the curators said they would explore all options, including a relaunch for Accell’s Dutch operations, based in Amsterdam. The company’s other European branches remain in business.

CEO Jonas Nilsson said: “Every realistic option for the future of the business has been tirelessly explored, and none has resulted in a solution to continue the group in its current form.”

Irish media reported that Quanta Capital, a Dublin-based investment firm founded by former road race cyclist Mel Sutcliffe, was preparing a bid with a number of other investors. Sutcliffe sold Eurotrek Raleigh Ireland to Accell 10 years ago.

Pandemic buyout

Accell was bought by a consortium led by New York-based private equity firm KKR for €1.8 billon in 2022 following a surge in demand for bicycles during the coronavirus pandemic.

But the company struggled to produce bikes fast enough and its costs rose after it ordered too many components in anticipation of a sustained rise in sales that never materialised.

By the time supply chains recovered after lockdown, Accell was left with a mountain of unsold bikes that it had to sell at a discount to limit its losses. Revenues fell 22% in 2024 to just over €1 billion.

Accell closed the Netherlands’ last remaining bike factory, the Batavus plant in Heerenveen, last year, shifting production to Hungary and shedding 160 jobs.

Babboe recall

The company was also hit by the mass recall of 22,000 Babboe cargo bikes after it received hundreds of complaints about the frames breaking on the road, which cost it tens of millions of euros as well as severe reputational damage.

The consumer standards agency NVWA briefly banned Babboe from selling new bikes and launched a criminal investigation amid allegations that the company had tried to cover up the flaws.

The collapse of Accell leaves the Netherlands with only one major bike maker, Gazelle, based in Dieren, as well as a handful of smaller manufacturers such as Kruitbosch (whose brands include Cortina) and Azor.

The consumer protection agency Consumentenbond has advised owners of Accell-made bikes to check the status of their guarantee with the shop or retailer where they bought it. Some replacement parts are still available because they were made by other companies.

World.title: Fire station break-ins soar as criminals steal rescue gear
World.content:
Break-ins at Dutch fire stations, which have risen sharply this year, are threatening life-saving work, the police have said. Criminal gangs are stealing the cutting equipment crews use to free people trapped in crashed cars, which they can be used for robberies.

There were 17 break-ins or attempted break-ins at fire stations in 2024 and 18 in 2025, broadcaster NOS reported. So far this year there have been 50. Stations in Maassluis, Aalsmeer and Ten Boer were all targeted in the past week.

The police, the fire service and the public prosecution department have begun working together nationally to stop the thefts. “One way or another, we are going to put a stop to this,” Jos van der Stap of the national police told NOS.

Police believe experienced criminals have discovered a market for the specialist tools. Van der Stap said they are being used in raids on jewellers and, abroad, to break open cash machines, and have turned up in several places across Europe.

Steven van der Looij of Brandweer Nederland, the national fire service organisation, said staff who work day and night at stations find it terrible thatpeople are coming into the buildings. Both quiet rural stations and busy city ones staffed around the clock have been hit.

Locking the equipment away is not straightforward. Everything on a fire engine is laid out so it can be grabbed at speed, Van der Looij said, and every extra lock has to be undone again. “Every second counts.”

Security cameras are being installed at some stations and windows are being replaced with mirrored glass.

World.title: Mental health services lose track of 62,500 people, says report
World.content:
A quarter of adults with a severe mental illness in the Netherlands – an estimated 62,500 people – are receiving no or insufficient care and have dropped out of sight of mental health services altogether, according to a report from the sector body de Nederlandse GGZ.

The organisation puts the total number of adults with a severe mental illness at around 250,000. What goes wrong, it says, is rarely the treatment itself but the handover – the point at which someone leaves a clinic, moves house or finishes a prison sentence.

“A discharge from a clinic, a house move or the end of a period in detention must not become the moment at which someone loses their support,” GGZ chair Ruth Peetoom said in a statement on Tuesday. “A psychological vulnerability does not disappear when a care pathway or an assessment comes to an end.”

Nowhere to go

The housing crisis is one of the biggest obstacles in helping patients through the transition out of care. The report calculates that 3,980 social housing units are needed each year for people leaving sheltered accommodation, but only 1,320 came free in 2023.

Around 33,000 people aged between 18 and 65 were registered as homeless at the start of 2024.

The pattern is similar for people leaving prison. Of the roughly 5,000 people released each year after more than three months inside, 27% are homeless or have no known address immediately afterwards, and almost half reoffend within two years.

Outreach

The report calls for assertive outreach – teams that actively go looking for people who are not asking for help – to be made a statutory duty for councils again.

It has not been one since social care was devolved in 2015, and funding is now split between health insurers, councils and central government, on top of the pressure on waiting lists that has already prompted legal action against the state.

Debate about severe mental illness in the Netherlands is dominated by figures on nuisance and public safety, the report says. It puts the number of people who pose a safety risk to others at around 1,500, against 24,000 to 60,000 who are a risk to themselves, through self-neglect, homelessness or avoiding care.

If you are struggling with your mental health, support is available. The MIND Hulplijn offers free, anonymous advice on 0900-1450, on weekdays from 9am to 9pm, or via mindhulplijn.nl. In a crisis, contact your family doctor or call 113.

World.title: NEC close in on Champions League after knocking out Olympiacos
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

NEC Nijmegen are one step away from reaching the Champions League group stages after a hard-fought 2-1 win against Olympiacos.

After a 0-0 draw in Piraeus last week, NEC fell behind straight after half-time when Ayoub El Kaabi fired the 48-time Greek champions in front.

Bryan Linssen equalised with a lunging volley in the 70th minute to take the match to extra time.

The fans in the Goffertstadion thought they were celebrating a winner when Kaj Sierhuis headed the ball into the net in the 93rd minute, but his effort was ruled out for offside.

But with Olympiacos reduced to 10 men following the sending-off of Kostas Fortounis just before the end of regular time, NEC found the breakthrough when Emre Mor dispatched a loose ball in the penalty area.

Standing between NEC and the lucrative Champions League group is Norwegian side Bodø/Glimt, who reached the last 16 of the competition last season.

Bodø/Glimt also needed extra time to overcome Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise 3-2 in the home leg for an aggregate score of 6-5.

The first leg will be played in Nijmegen on August 19, with NEC travelling to the Arctic Circle for the return leg on Tuesday, August 25.

World.title: Visser bags second Dutch European athletics gold in photo-finish
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Nadine Visser won the Netherlands’ second gold medal at the European athletics championships in a dramatic final of the 100 metres hurdles.

Visser, 31, was awarded the victory on a photo-finish after edging out her Polish rival Pia Skrzyszowska with her lunge for the line.

Both athletes were awarded the same time of 12.67 seconds, but Visser was adjudged to have got there first by 1/1000 of a second.

It was a first outdoor title for Visser, who has two gold and two silver medals for 60 metres hurdles at the European indoor championships.

“I’ve been to so many championships but there was always something that got in the way,” she said. “But I didn’t want to think about it too hard, because that puts you under pressure.”

In other events, Elvis Afrifa reached the men’s 100 metres final, but just missed out on a medal in fourth place.

Koster sixth

Afrifa finished 0.03 seconds behind the bronze medallist, the fast-finishing German Owen Ansah. Gold and silver went to the British pair of Romell Glave and Jeremiah Azu as the defending champion, Italy’s Marcell Jacobs, pulled up halfway through the race with an injury.

Maureen Koster finished sixth in the women’s 5000m after leading the field in the closing laps, before being overtaken in the last 200 metres by a string of fast finishers led by Italy’s Nadia Battocletti.

Just behind her in seventh place was 23-year-old compatriot Amina Maatoug, running in her first European championships, while Jennifer Gulikers finished 13th.

Femke Broeders-Bol cruised through her heat of the 800 metres, winning in a time of 1:59.96 seconds. The 26-year-old, who switched from the 400 metres hurdles this season, will run again in the semi-finals on Thursday.

World.title: Biggest eclipse in 27 years to darken Dutch skies tonight
World.content:
The biggest solar eclipse over the Netherlands in 27 years will take place on Wednesday evening, when around 90% of the sun will disappear behind the moon.

The eclipse begins at about 7.15pm and reaches its peak around 8.10pm, when the moon appears to take its largest bite out of the sun. The two then set together roughly an hour later.

Because the sun will already be low in the sky by then, anyone hoping to watch will need a clear view towards the west or north-west. Forecasters expect a warm, largely clear evening, with some thin high cloud in the north that should not obscure the view.

Eye specialists have warned against looking directly at the sun. Sunglasses, welding goggles and CDs offer no protection and can cause permanent damage to the retina. Only eclipse glasses meeting the ISO 12312-2 safety standard are considered safe.

A simple alternative is to make a pinhole in a sheet of paper and project the image of the sun onto a white surface.

Public viewings have been organised around the country. The Radboud University observatory in Nijmegen will be open, and the Copernicus observatory in Haarlem is taking telescopes fitted with solar filters to the seafront at Bloemendaal. Eclipse watches are also planned on the Frisian islands.

Only in Iceland, northern Spain and a small part of Portugal will the sun vanish completely.

The last time this much of the sun was covered over the Netherlands was in August 1999 – an event that regional broadcaster L1 recalls was largely spoiled by cloud in much of the country. A comparable eclipse is not expected again until 2081, and the next total eclipse visible from the Netherlands will come on October 7, 2135.

Anyone still outdoors later has a second chance. The Perseid meteor shower peaks overnight into Thursday, and with a new moon the sky will be unusually dark.

World.title: Amsterdam transport chief hid €850m bridge costs before election
World.content:
Amsterdam’s former transport chief, Melanie van der Horst, knew before March’s local elections that a planned cycle and pedestrian bridge over the IJ would cost up to €850 million – more than double the sum set aside – but did not tell the city council, documents released under a freedom of information request show.

Van der Horst, who is now the city’s head of economic affairs and was also lead candidate for the social-liberal party D66 at the elections, had been told by officials that the estimate for the Oostbrug had risen to between €650 million and €850 million, compared with the €325 million budgeted. The papers were obtained by Amsterdam broadcaster AT5.

Officials circulated the final estimate internally around December 2 and, according to AT5, explicitly gave Van der Horst the choice of making the figures public before or after the vote. At a meeting on February 12 it was decided to keep the older, lower amounts in the city’s official investment note.

Eight days before the elections Van der Horst was given a presentation setting out how the new range had been calculated. During the campaign she cited the IJ crossings as one of her administration’s achievements.

The new estimates only surfaced in early June, when the city published the documents handed to coalition negotiators.

The bridge, which at 1.2 kilometres would be one of the longest in the country, is being paid for jointly by the council and the regional transport authority Vervoerregio Amsterdam.

Emergency debate

Seven opposition parties – PvdD, Volt, JA21, Denk, BIJ1, CDA and SP – said in a joint statement they were shocked by the revelations but were not yet drawing conclusions, and an emergency debate has been requested. The coalition party PRO and D66’s own council group have also said they want answers.

Van der Horst declined to comment, referring questions to Elise Moeskops (D66), who took over the transport brief. Moeskops said the provisional estimates carry wide margins and could still change, that work on the design is continuing and that a final figure is not expected until early next year.

Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians. The figures also show that the overall number of registered foreign workers has risen more than 8% over the last year, a faster rate of growth than in recent years. However, the government official responsible for migration strategy says this is because stricter government measures have pushed some employers to register previously uninsured workers. The ZUS data, reported by Dziennik Gazeta Prawna (DGP), a leading daily, show that there were 1.34 million foreign workers registered in ZUS at the end of June, up from 1.24 million at the same point last year. That 8.2% increase is larger than the growth rate of around 6% seen in each of the previous two years, notes the newspaper. Maciej Duszczyk, the deputy interior minister responsible for migration, commented that the rise actually reflects the government’s tougher migration strategy, which he said “forces employers to report for insurance those who arrived earlier” but were working unregistered The official pointed to recent data showing that, in fact, in the first half of this year, Poland issued 50% fewer work permits to foreigners than in the same period of 2025. Dane ZUS pokazują dokładnie to co zakładaliśmy w Strategi Migracyjnej. Radykalny spadek liczby wydawanych, nowych zezwoleń na pracę (ponad 50% rok do roku) wymusza na pracodawcach zgłaszanie do ubezpieczenia, tych którzy przyjechali wcześniej. Tylko w pełni legalne zatrudnienie! — Maciek Duszczyk (@MaciekDuszczyk) August 11, 2026 Ukrainians remain by far the largest group of registered foreign workers, with 901,000 now in the system, a 10.1% rise from a year earlier. Belarusians (144,000, up 4.9%) remain in second. But two non-European migrant groups whose numbers have been growing rapidly in recent years now occupy third and fourth place: Indians (25,500, up 4.9%) and Colombians (23,000, up 31%, which was the fastest growth of any national group). Georgians, who had previously been the third-largest group, saw their number fall by 17% to 22,000, meaning they are now in fifth, ahead of Filipinos (15,400, down 2%), Moldovans (14,200, down 1%), Nepalis (13,400, up 8.3%), Vietnamese (12,200, up 6.1%), and Russians (11,800, down 2.5%). Latin American migration to Poland is booming, with 45,000 work permits issued last year, five times more than in 2022@Gosia_Tomczak looks at what is driving this trend and what challenges and opportunities it has created for both the migrants and Poland https://t.co/tl1wUTCaC0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2025 ZUS’s data also show that foreign workers are increasingly establishing their own businesses in Poland, which Dziennik Gazeta Prawna notes is a sign that they are establishing longer-term ties with the country but also a result of an easier online system for registering businesses. In 2021, only 22,700 foreigners had a registered business in Poland, a figure that now is now almost five times higher, at 102,000. The rise has been driven in particular by Ukrainians, many of whom are legally entitled to establish companies in Poland under the same terms as Polish citizens. As a result, 7.6% of foreign workers now run their own business, up from 6.7% a year ago and from 2.7% before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which led to a wave of Ukrainian refugees settling in Poland. Ukrainian refugees boosted Poland’s GDP by 2.7% last year while not raising unemployment or lowering wages, finds a report by the UN @Refugees agency and @Deloitte "Whoever thinks refugees are a burden on the economy should think again," says @UNHCRPoland https://t.co/rOvtOvBNwG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2025 Over the last decade, even before the war in Ukraine, Poland has experienced a wave of migration unprecedented in its history and among the largest anywhere in Europe. For six years running, between 2017 and 2022, it issued more first residence permits to immigrants from outside the European Union than did any other member state. Much of the surge in immigration came during the rule of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government from 2015 to 2023, despite its strong anti-migrant rhetoric. The current government, a more liberal coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, came to power pledging to reduce immigration, which it said had got out of control under PiS. Under Tusk’s government, in 2024, Poland issued the lowest number of residence permits to non-EU immigrants in a decade. In 2025, the government introduced tougher entry requirements for foreign workers and students. It has also stepped up deportations of foreigners who have broken the law. However, Duszczyk notes that the current government still sees “selective and responsible migration” as a way to “maintain the competitiveness of the economy without limiting wage growth”. ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Mother bear and cubs spotted on busy hiking trail in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. A female brown bear and her three cubs have been spotted in Poland’s Tatra mountains crossing a popular trail filled with hikers, with the animals coming unusually close to people. According to an official from Tatra National Park, where the incident took place, the behaviour could be a survival strategy by the mother to protect her young from male bears, which can kill cubs but tend to avoid humans. In a video posted on Sunday, the mother and three cubs were seen crossing the Chochołowska Valley trail in broad daylight, as crowds of people looked on Videos of the bear family have appeared increasingly often on social media, prompting questions about whether the animals are becoming less wary of people. But park officials say the female’s behaviour may have a biological explanation. “As we know, male brown bears are infanticidal. They kill not only other bears’ cubs, but their own as well. So the females, to avoid contact with the males, tend to stay closer to people,” Tomasz Zwijacz-Kozica, a park official, told local newspaper Gazeta Krakowska. “Females sense this instinctively and generally use the presence of people as a sort of shield to defend themselves against these males,” he added. The park staff hope to gather more detailed data on the female bear’s movements and behaviour in the future by possibly fitting her with a telemetry collar. They note that similar behaviour has been seen before. Around 20 years ago, a female bear drew attention when hundreds of tourists photographed her. They advise visitors to remain calm if they encounter a bear and to follow several basic rules, including staying calm and not running or making sudden movements, which may trigger a pursuit; not approaching the animals; and not attempting to take close-up photographs or use a flash. If a bear is encountered, visitors should slowly retreat in the direction from which they came while maintaining eye contact with the animal. Particular caution is required when cubs are present. Visitors should also avoid feeding bears or leaving rubbish behind. The smell of food can attract animals to trails and encourage behaviour that brings them into dangerous contact with people. A woman has died after being attacked by a bear in a forest in southeastern Poland. Such incidents are extremely rare, with the last fatal bear attack in the country reported in 2014 https://t.co/sAC2MPAvfh — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 23, 2026 Estimates of Poland’s brown bear population vary between 120 and 400, with most found in the southeastern Bieszczady mountains as well as the Tatras and Beskids further west. The population is thought to be growing, with a rise in reports of encounters with humans. In April this year, a woman was killed in a bear attack, Poland’s first such fatality since 2014. Another bear attack earlier in the year in the same region left a man with head and limb injuries. In March, the government launched a new 16 million zloty (€3.7 million) scheme aimed at both protecting bears and ensuring the safety of their human neighbours. It includes the creation of a special force to monitor and respond to bear sightings, including fitting the animals with tracking collars. In 2022, the town of Zakopane, located at the foot of the Tatra mountains, installed bear-proof rubbish bins to prevent animals from foraging in them – and thereby coming closer to areas of human population Poland has launched a new programme to protect brown bears and ensure the safety of their human neighbours, amid growing reports of encounters. World.title: Kaczyński appeals to President Nawrocki to unify Poland’s right-wing opposition ahead of elections
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has called on opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections. His appeal comes as PiS, which for the last two decades has dominated the Polish right, is in crisis, amid falling polling numbers, a split by a breakaway faction, and a growing challenge from far-right parties that have long been critical of PiS. That has created a fragmented opposition, with parties competing against one another as much as or more than with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition. Some on the right hope that Nawrocki, who enjoys good relations with various parts of the opposition, could act as a unifying figurehead bridging those divides. 🔴 Jarosław Kaczyński ujawnił, o co osobiście poprosił Karola Nawrockiego. Podczas miesięcznicy smoleńskiej prezes PiS odniósł się do podziałów na prawicy i przyznał, że widzi dla prezydenta wyjątkowo ważną rolę: ma pomóc scalić zwaśnione środowiska. „Ja prezydenta swego czasu… pic.twitter.com/qwXhmccun2 — Super Express (@se_pl) August 10, 2026 Speaking on Sunday at a monthly commemoration of the 2010 Smolensk air disaster that killed his identical twin brother, then-President Lech Kaczyński, Jarosław was reported by a variety of Polish media outlets as saying that he had asked Nawrocki to act as a “patron” for a unified right. “I asked the president some time ago, and I hope he will do it,” said Kaczyński, quoted by newspaper Fakt. “It would be very good if the president took up this matter energetically.” “We could continue to develop – as we did during our years of government – not only in terms of achieving GDP growth, but also by undertaking major investments, by undertaking everything that would truly change Poland.” Kaczyński was referring to the period between 2015 and 2023 when a PiS-dominated coalition, known as the United Right (Zjednoczona Prawica), ruled Poland. In the latter year, it was ousted from power by a more liberal coalition led by Tusk, Kaczyński’s great rival. Since then, the landscape on the Polish right has changed dramatically. One of PiS’s partners in the United Right, the hard-right Sovereign Poland (Suwerenna Polska), merged with PiS in 2024. The other, the centre-right Agreement (Porozumienie), is now defunct. Meanwhile, support for PiS itself has collapsed. Having won 35% of the vote at the 2023 elections, it now averages only around 20% in polls – the party’s lowest figures for almost 20 years. To make matters worse, last month, around a fifth of the party’s MPs formed a breakaway group in parliament led by PiS deputy leader and former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki. They plan to soon form their own, separate party, Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), with a more moderate, centre-right agenda than PiS. At the same time, PiS has found itself challenged by a growing far right. Confederation (Konfederacja), which won 7% of the vote in 2023, is now polling around 12-13%. The even more radical Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), which broke away from Confederation last year, is at 9%. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 That has resulted in a much more fragmented right, with four separate entities not only opposed to Tusk’s government but also competing with one another for overlapping electorates. With parliamentary elections scheduled for autumn 2027, there have been questions over whether and to what extent the opposition should seek to cooperate with one another. One option would be an agreement not to stand candidates against one another for seats in the upper-house Senate, which are contested on a single-member-district system rather than through the proportional representation that decides the share of seats in the more powerful lower-house Sejm. Parties in Tusk’s current ruling coalition themselves formed such a “Senate pact” at the 2019 elections, helping them win control of the upper house, then repeated that in 2023, when they retained control. Although the Senate has a limited legislative role, it would be a significant prize for Nawrocki and the opposition, especially if Tusk’s coalition wins the Sejm, because the Senate has the power to approve or reject national referendums proposed by the president. An even more ambitious plan that has been rumoured is for some elements of the right-wing opposition to run joint electoral lists for the Sejm. That would require a far greater degree of programmatic consensus and longer negotiations over how to distribute places on lists. The government's majority in the Senate has, for the second time, rejected a proposal by opposition-aligned President Nawrocki to hold a referendum on whether Poland should continue implementing the EU's climate policies, which he argues are too costly https://t.co/Idm6dnzQEH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 6, 2026 Nawrocki is seen as key to any such plan coming to fruition. He was elected last year to the presidency as an independent, but with the formal backing of PiS. Ahead of the second-round run-off vote, he also received endorsements from defeated first-round rivals Sławomir Mentzen, one of the leaders of Confederation, and Grzegorz Braun, the leader of KKP. Since taking office, Nawrocki has continued to cultivate good relations with PiS and Confederation, as well as with Morawiecki’s new breakaway faction. However, he has kept his distance from Braun, whose anti-Americanism, antisemitism and sympathy towards Russia makes him something of a pariah. The European Parliament has again voted to strip Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face further charges for Holocaust denial as well as various antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT incidents during last year's presidential campaign https://t.co/4EHVEuSDnM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 26, 2026 Media reports have suggested that Nawrocki is planning to play a role in creating a “broad patriotic camp” among the opposition ahead of next year’s elections. Last week, during an event celebrating the first anniversary of his swearing in, the president also hinted at this role. He noted he will, in the coming months, be presenting “a presidential development strategy”, which “I believe will become a point of reference in the upcoming parliamentary elections for all those who aspire to govern Poland, a real plan for the future of the republic”. The strategy would be aimed in particular at “patriotic forces” who are “ready for dialogue between the offices of the president and future prime minister”. Given that Nawrocki and Tusk’s government are bitterly opposed to one another, that was a clear reference to opposition parties. A report on Sunday by Newsweek Polska, based on unnamed inside sources, claimed that Kaczyński is hoping to form a single electoral list for the Sejm elections compromising PiS, Development Plus and all or parts of Confederation, under the patronage of Nawrocki. 💥 Nowa obsesja Jarosława Kaczyńskiego, w jaki sposób odzyskać władzę. Prezes PiS naciska na Karola Nawrockiego, by prezydent stworzył "listę Nawrockiego" prawicy do Sejmu. To najbardziej ryzykowna, ale też o ogromnej stawce, decyzja prezydenta.https://t.co/sqRPFUuiZ7 — Jacek Gądek (@JacekGadek) August 9, 2026 Other leaders on the right have expressed varying degrees of willingness to work with one another. Speaking to broadcaster TVN on Saturday, Krzystof Bosak, another of Confederation’s leaders, expressed support for the idea of a Senate pact. On Friday, Morawiecki said that he can “fully imagine working with Sławomir Mentzen”, who “I believe is absolutely part of the patriotic camp”. However, Mentzen himself quickly ruled out the idea, tweeting that he’d rather “quit politics than join this gang leading Poland to disaster”, adding that Tusk, Kaczyński and Morawiecki are “one and the same”. Whereas Bosak represents a nationalist faction of Confederation seen as more compatible with PiS, Mentzen represent’s a libertarian wing that is bitterly opposed to the former PiS’ government’s high social spending, support for Ukraine, and the restrictions it introduced during the COVID-19 pandemic. Demonstrations took place in around 25 Polish cities on Sunday against a “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. The protests came after police data showed a significant increase in reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland so far this year, including a number of high-profile incidents of verbal and physical aggression. Sunday’s demonstrations, which took place under the slogan “Do Not Be Indifferent”, were organised by the Committee for the Defence of Democracy (KOD), an NGO, with support from other groups, including Amnesty International. “[This is] a nationwide campaign aimed at expressing opposition to the growing wave of hate, xenophobia, nationalism and violence directed against Ukrainians and members of other minorities,” wrote KOD ahead of the events. On Sunday, hundreds gathered on Warsaw’s Castle Square carrying Ukrainian and Polish flags and many waving signs saying “With U”, with the letter “U” coloured in Ukrainian national colours. #Siódemka Plac Zamkowy w Warszawie, protest w ramach: 🛑 NIE BĄDŹMY OBOJĘTNI! WSPÓLNIE PRZECIWKO NIENAWIŚCI! W wielu miastach Polski wyszliśmy na ulice, żeby jasno powiedzieć: nie ma zgody na hejt, przemoc i agresję wobec Ukraińców. W ostatnim czasie coraz częściej słyszymy… pic.twitter.com/kOfq4zBuGT — Piotr #FBPE Fijałkowski (@piotr4913) August 9, 2026 In Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, local media reported that around 150 people attended a demonstration, carrying placards saying “Let’s defend our neighbours from the aggression and stupidity of others” and “Putin is the enemy, Ukraine is our neighbour”. In Gdańsk, on Poland’s northern coast, around 300 people gathered, according to local media. However, they were also met with a small counter-demonstration of around a dozen people, led by the New Hope party that is part of Poland’s far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) opposition group. The counter-protesters held a banner declaring “Solidarity with victims of mass immigration” and “Down with Bandera”, a reference to historical Ukrainian nationalist leader Stepan Bandera, who in Poland is associated with the massacres of around 100,000 Poles by Ukrainians during World War Two. Separately, on Friday, a group of NGOs organised a demonstration against anti-Ukrainian violence outside the prime minister’s chancellery, during which they delivered a petition, signed by over 11,000 people, calling for the government to take “decisive action against xenophobic attacks”. Police data published last month showed that the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025. Among those incidents have been a number of high-profile cases, including two 11-year-old Ukrainian girls being verbally abused by a man on a bus in the city of Bielsko-Biała and a violent attack on young Ukrainians by a group of Polish teenagers in Warsaw. Ukrainians are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group, with around 1.6 million living in the country. While Poland welcomed Ukrainian refugees in 2022, there has been growing negative sentiment towards them recently, indicated in polls and through anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from prominent politicians. Tenions have been stoked further by a diplomatic crisis that began in May, when President Volodymyr Zelensky named a Ukrainian military unit after a group responsible for massacring Poles during World War Two. That prompted Polish President Karol Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 In particular, two far-right opposition parties, Confederation and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have used anti-Ukrainian rhetoric, while the largest opposition group, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has recently taken a tougher line towards Ukraine. Last week, PiS announced that, if it returns to power, one of its first actions would be to deport Ukrainian conscription-age men who are not in legal employment. At one of Sunday’s protests, in Kraków, a demonstrator responded with a placard declaring “Deport xenophobia”. Poland’s more liberal ruling coalition has condemned anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from the right-wing opposition. Last month, Prime Minister Donald Tusk called for a “war against this violence”, saying that “thugs and hooligans have gained courage, audacity and political patronage” from the opposition. Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative PiS, has called for Ukrainian men of conscription age who are not legally working to be deported to Ukraine. World.title: Remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII exhumed in Ukraine
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The remains of a further 55 victims of massacres of Poles by Ukrainian nationalists during World War Two have been exhumed in Ukraine. Around half were children, and most show signs of brutal deaths, including skulls pierced with farming tools (as pictured above). The announcement comes amid ongoing tensions between Poland and Ukraine over the so-called Volhynia massacres, sparked by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s recent decision to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which was responsible for leading the killings of around 100,000 Poles. However, both sides have expressed hope that continued exhumations of victims – most of which are believed to still remain buried in unmarked mass graves in Ukraine – can ease that path towards reconciliation. 📣 Zakończenie tegorocznych prac ekshumacyjnych ofiar Zbrodni Wołyńskiej w Ostrówkach i Woli Ostrowieckiej ❗ Od 13 lipca do 7 sierpnia br. pracownicy Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej, przedsiębiorstwa „Wołyńskie Starożytności” oraz specjalista z zakresu medycyny sądowej z… pic.twitter.com/iDJR5NmdEn — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) August 7, 2026 The new findings were made in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka, two neighbouring former villages, now depopulated, that were previously part of Poland but, after postwar border changes, are now located in western Ukraine. There, on 30 August 1943, the UPA massacred over 1,000 Poles and razed the villages to the ground. Similar massacres took place in many other villages, as part of an ethnic cleansing operation by the UPA to remove Poles and other minorities from what they saw as Ukrainian territory. Exhumations previously took place in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka in the 1990s, and again in 2011 and 2015, uncovering the remains of hundreds of victims. However, hundreds more are believed to remain buried. In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches for victims on its territory in response to the dismantlement of a monument to the UPA in Poland. However, in a diplomatic breakthrough last year, it allowed them to resume, including granting permission in December for work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka. In April this year, mass graves were discovered there, with exhumations then beginning in July. Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) has now announced the result of that work. They have uncovered the remains of 55 victims, 26 of them children (mostly under 12 years of age, with the youngest a few months old) and 20 women. In the Volhynia massacres as a whole, the majority of victims were women and children. The locations and conditions of the remains reveal much about the manner of their death. Most were buried “at random” without coffins, which is consistent with contemporary accounts that they were killed in a barn and then thrown into a mass burial pit, notes the IPN Most of the remains, in particular skulls, show signs of injuries that are also consistent with contemporary accounts, which said that victims were ordered to lie on the ground before being killed with farm tools, including hammers for slaughtering cattle. Material from the bones has been secured for genetic testing, which was recently used for the first time to identify massacre victims exhumed at another location in Ukraine last year. Around 300 personal items, including rosaries, crosses and clothing, were also found during the recent excavations in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka. On 30 August, the 83rd anniversary of the massacre, the newly found remains will be buried in a funeral ceremony at the cemetery in Ostrówki. The IPN believes that over 300 further victims still remain buried at unknown locations in the two former villages. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 The Volhynia massacres have long been a point of tension between Poland, which recognises them as a genocide, and Ukraine, which rejects that label. The decision by Kyiv to allow exhumations to resume last year was regarded as a major step towards reconciliation. However, that process was undermined in May this year, when Zelensky decided to name a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted an angry response from Warsaw, where President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. There have since been efforts to reach a diplomatic solution. Last month, Zelensky pointed specifically to the exhumation work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka as evidence that “Ukraine is doing its part to fairly establish the facts about those who were killed in those years”. Subsequently, he announced a five-point plan to alleviate the crisis, including allowing more exhumations and opening up historical archives. Poland welcomed the move but said that it would wait to see how it was implemented in practice. Poland has cautiously welcomed President @ZelenskyyUa's announcement of a five-point plan to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during WWII https://t.co/M3GXD9vtAr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Candidate to lead Polish state history institute rejected in rare clash between houses of parliament
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN). The nominee, Mateusz Szpytma, has served as deputy head of the IPN since 2016, including when it was under the leadership of Karol Nawrocki, who last year was elected president of Poland with the support of the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. Szpytma’s candidacy has been opposed by most of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, who argue he helped politicise the IPN under the former PiS government. However, some more conservative elements of the coalition joined the opposition in supporting Szpytma, giving him a majority in the Sejm but not the Senate. Senatorowie nie wyrazili zgody na powołanie Mateusza Szpytmy na Prezesa Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej – Komisji Ścigania Zbrodni przeciwko Narodowi Polskiemu — Senat RP 🇵🇱 (@PolskiSenat) August 6, 2026 The IPN is a body tasked with researching, documenting and educating about Poland’s tumultuous and tragic 20th-century history. It also has the power to prosecute crimes relating to the periods when the country was under Nazi and communist rule. The institute was led by Nawrocki from 2021 until August last year, when he became president of Poland. Since then, the IPN has been without a permanent head. Last October, the IPN’s council nominated Karol Polejowski, another of the institute’s deputy heads, to be its new president. But he was rejected by the Sejm, which, along with the Senate, must approve the choice. In April, the council instead recommended Szpytma, whose candidacy was approved by the Sejm last month. He received support mainly from opposition parties, including PiS and the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja). However, in a rare split within the ruling coalition, one of its junior members, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), also backed Szpytma, as did some MPs from the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050). That was enough to give him a majority. By contrast, the main ruling party, Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO), and The Left (Lewica) opposed his nomination, citing a letter signed earlier this year by 170 academics, who described Szpytma as “one of the faces of IPN’s politicisation” under the former PiS government. However, PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, who also serves as Poland’s defence minister and deputy prime minister rejected that characterisation and said that PSL had backed Szpytma because of his work commemorating historical figures from the agrarian movement in which PSL is rooted. In a rare split in the ruling coalition, MPs from two parties, PSL and Poland 2050, voted with the opposition in the Sejm for a new head of the Institute of National Remembrance. However, PM Donald Tusk says their choice will be rejected by the Senate https://t.co/0CGmbsNp4F — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 However, it was widely expected that Szpytma’s candidacy would be blocked by the upper-house Senate, where even the PSL and opposition combined do not have a majority in the 100-seat chamber. That was confirmed in a vote on Thursday, when 50 senators were opposed to Szyptma and only 38 were in favour, with one abstention. “We voted against further politicisation” of IPN and “against tolerating financial irregularities”, wrote the speaker of the Senate, Małgorzata Kidawa-Błonska of KO. The latter comment was likely a reference to a report by the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) last year which found that the IPN had, between 2022 and 2025, failed to properly manage tens of millions of zloty in spending, including various violations of regulations on the use of public funds. Szpytma told journalists that he was not surprised by the result of the vote, saying he believes his connection to Nawrocki, who is an ardent opponent of the current government and has vetoed a record number of laws, is the reason why he lost. Nie zgodziliśmy się w Senacie, by człowiek Karola Nawrockiego został prezesem IPN. Zagłosowaliśmy przeciw dalszemu upolitycznianiu Instytutu. Przeciw tolerowaniu nieprawidłowości finansowych. Pan Szpytma nie wprowadziłby żadnych zmian w funkcjonowaniu IPN. — Małgorzata Kidawa-Błońska (@M_K_Blonska) August 6, 2026 The IPN plays an important role in Polish public life, including in commemorating, investigating and prosecuting crimes that took place during the Nazi-German and Soviet occupations of Poland in World War Two, as well as during the decades of communist rule afterwards. Under Nawrocki’s leadership, the IPN accelerated the process of demolishing remaining Soviet monuments in Poland, often prompting criticism from Russia. It has also been closely involved in the exhumation of victims of the Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Poles during World War Two. During PiS’s time in power from 2015 to 2023, the IPN was accused of becoming increasingly politicised, using its activities to support the historical narratived promoted by the government. In 2021, Israel protested after a former far-right activist was appointed to head one of the IPN’s local branches. Russia has criticised the "sacrilegious" demolition of a Soviet monument in Poland, calling it a “flagrant violation” of a bilateral agreement. But Poland's @ipngovpl says it was a "propaganda object" that had to be removed under a "decommunisation" law https://t.co/73T99ZlPqU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish state energy giant Orlen posted a record profit in the first half of 2026, as turmoil in the Middle East boosted earnings in the fuel sector, despite Polish government measures to cushion the rise in consumer prices. Orlen has also this year seen its highest ever proportion of revenue from foreign markets. The results come amid a political dispute over a government plan to impose a windfall tax on excess profits from fuel sales, aimed at recouping billions spent on consumer subsidies. Orlen would be the biggest target of the tax, but the plan has been obstructed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. W pierwszym półroczu Orlen zarobił na czysto 15,8 miliarda złotych. Trzy razy więcej niż przed rokiem.https://t.co/qJS81csI0H — TVN24 BiS (@TVN24BiS) August 6, 2026 On Thursday, Orlen reported consolidated net profit of 15.9 billion zloty (€3.7 billion) for the first six months of the year, almost tripling from the 5.7 billion zloty recorded in the same period of 2025. Revenue rose to 152.2 billion zloty from 134.4 billion zloty. CEO Ireneusz Fąfara acknowledged that the figures came amid exceptional market conditions. Energy prices jumped globally in March, after the US and Israel began to attack Iran and Tehran responded by blocking the Strait of Hormuz, a key export route. Fąfara noted that, despite this, Poland had maintained some of Europe’s lowest fuel prices. He said that Orlen had prioritised fuel availability and competitive domestic prices while taking advantage of stronger margins abroad, where it brought in an “absolutely record level of revenue from foreign markets”. In the first half of 2026, foreign markets accounted for 35.7% of Orlen’s revenue, up from 33.8% a year earlier. The bulk came from Germany, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Austria, where Orlen operates petrol stations, as well as from trading activities in markets such as the Netherlands and Switzerland. Pierwsze półrocze 2026 roku ORLEN zamyka rekordowym zyskiem z rynków zagranicznych. Wynik netto całej Grupy w II kwartale wyniósł 7,7 mld zł. Wypracowane wyniki finansowe pozwoliły na wypłatę rekordowej dywidendy dla akcjonariuszy oraz dalsze finansowanie największego programu… pic.twitter.com/ohcxksuv4G — ORLEN (@GrupaORLEN) August 6, 2026 Orlen has expanded rapidly in recent years, as it has swallowed up other state-owned energy firms and sought to diversify away from its traditional focus on oil towards gas, renewables and hydrogen. In March this year, Orlen’s market valuation rose to its highest ever level of €35.2 billion, up from €7 billion in early 2022. As a result, it overtook the market capitalisation of Russian energy giant Gazprom. Mateusz Czyżkowski, an analyst at brokerage XTB, attributed Orlen’s record profits this year to “skilful balancing between geopolitical conditions and local pressures”, including government-imposed fuel price caps that squeezed margins. “The global commodities market in the second quarter of 2026 was strongly buoyed by tensions between Iran and Israel and ongoing disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz…This significant geopolitical premium boosted profits in [Orlen’s] Upstream & Supply segment,” he wrote in a note. The announcement of record profits comes as Orlen finds itself at the centre of a political dispute over the government’s proposed windfall tax, which would introduce a 60% levy on excess profits from liquid fuel sales. The measure was expected to raise around 4 billion zloty, which would have offset most of the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by, among other things, cutting VAT and introducing a maximum daily price. However, although the tax was approved by the government’s majority in parliament in July, President Nawrocki refused to sign it into law, instead referring it to the constitutional court for review – a process that has no time limit and can take years. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 According to government calculations, Orlen would account for around 60% of the tax base if the measures eventually come into force. However, at his press conference on Thursday, Fąfara emphasised that the company supports the windfall tax. “We have viewed this solution positively from the very beginning. I believe it is in the interest of the company, our customers, and the country,” he said. However, Fąfara rejected suggestions that Orlen could unilaterally reduce pump prices by sacrificing margins. “We cannot lower prices in defiance of the market and global prices…If we lowered prices below parity, there would be a shortage of fuel,” he warned, adding that artificially low prices would encourage speculative exports and fuel tourism. Prices at petrol stations jumped today in Poland after the government ended the last of the support measures introduced to cushion consumers from the energy crisis caused by the war in Iran. Some places saw prices rise by as much as 14%https://t.co/mUfWUyDMle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 1, 2026 Prime Minister Donald Tusk used Orlen’s record profit announcement to reiterate criticism of the Nawrocki for obstructing the windfall tax. “Taxing such extraordinary profits made by oil companies, not just Orlen, was intended to bring down prices at petrol stations. That is precisely what Karol Nawrocki blocked. Remember this when you’re tanking up,” Tusk wrote on social media. Nawrocki’s office has, however, rejected the idea that an increased tax on fuel companies would somehow reduce fuel prices, arguing that, if anything, it would have the opposite effect if companies pass some of the costs onto consumers. Opodatkowanie takich nadzwyczajnych zysków koncernów paliwowych, nie tylko Orlenu, miały służyć obniżeniu cen na stacjach. World.title: New Polish opposition group proposes paying parents “salary” to encourage more births
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. New Polish opposition group Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which recently broke away from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, has proposed the idea of paying a “parental salary” for the first three years of a child’s life. The idea is part of a package of proposals to tackle Poland’s dire demographic situation released on Friday by Development Plus in its first major policy announcement since leader Mateusz Morawiecki announced that the group would soon become a political party. 3600 zł miesięcznie na dziecko do 3. roku życia – jedna z wielu propozycji @RozwojPlus dla demografii! Pensja Rodzicielska wynosząca równowartość płacy minimalnej, czyli obecnie około 3600 zł netto miesięcznie przez pierwsze 3 lata życia dziecka. To ponad czterokrotnie więcej… pic.twitter.com/253pwcskNK — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) August 7, 2026 The proposed parental salary would amount to 3,600 zloty (€837) per month, the equivalent of the minimum wage after taxes. It is 4.5 times more than the current child benefit payment of 800 zloty per month that all Polish parents of children under 18 receive. Development Plus says that the parental salary could be combined with income from other work that parents undertake and that it would include contributions towards their pensions. It would end once a child turns three, after which parents would have access to normal child benefit payments. The group says that, for now, the idea is just a proposal, based on expert analysis of how to tackle Poland’s demographic crisis, and that it now wants to “refine it through dialogue with Poles” rather than “imposing top-down provisions”. Poland has long been grappling with a shrinking, ageing population. Last year, the number of births fell to a new post-war low of 238,000, while deaths totalled 406,000. That marked the 13th consecutive year in which more people died than were born in Poland. The country’s fertility rate – meaning the average number of children that are born to a woman over her lifetime – fell to a new record low of 1.068 in 2025. That is one of the lowest figures anywhere in the world and well below the so-called “replacement rate” – the figure needed to ensure that the population does not decline – which is generally defined as 2.1. Poland’s fertility rate, already one of the lowest in the world, fell to a new record low of 1.07 in 2025, deepening concerns over the country's shrinking and ageing population https://t.co/OMGC1MpA5l — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 28, 2026 Successive Polish governments have introduced various measures intended to boost the birth rate, though so far without clear success. The former PiS government, with Morawiecki as finance minister and later prime minister, introduced and expanded the current child benefit programme. While there was a brief bump in births after it was launched in 2016, numbers subsequently continued their downward trend. After PiS lost power in 2023, the current government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, continued the child benefit programme and also introduced new payments to support parents who return to work and restored funding for IVF treatment, which was previously cut by PiS. When announcing the proposed parental salary on Friday, Development Plus also outlined seven other proposed new policies to ease Poland’s demographic problems. One would allow workers to have a portion of their contributions go towards their parents’ pensions. Another pledged to provide better maternity care, including access to anaesthesia, a private hospital room and dedicated midwife, prenatal testing, and infertility treatment. Other policies promised more flexible working arrangements and mortgage repayments to prevent people from having to choose between a family or a career, as well as school hours and after-school care that “adapt to the lives of families, not the other way around”. Development Plus also proposed “granting parents the right to represent the voices of their minor children”. However, they provided no details of what this would mean in practice.
