World.title: Brazilian Summer Vibes Coming to Střelecký ostrov This Weekend
World.content:
Prague’s Střelecký ostrov will turn into a Brazilian-inspired summer spot this Friday and Saturday, with live music, DJs, food, drinks and a riverside atmosphere.

The two-day event will take place from 12 p.m. to 10 p.m. on both days, bringing Brazilian music and summer energy to one of the city’s most picturesque islands.

Visitors can expect live Brazilian music and DJ sets, alongside a selection of food and drinks. The menu will include wine, cheese, Czech dishes, cocktails, frozen margaritas and frozen daiquiris.

The event offers a relaxed way to spend the weekend in central Prague, with music, drinks and food overlooking the Vltava.

World.title: Czech Rivers Reach Record Lows as Drought Deepens
World.content:
Rivers and streams across the Czech Republic are experiencing exceptionally low flows as a prolonged drought continues to worsen, with several waterways approaching or reaching their lowest levels since records began.

According to the latest data from the Czech Hydrometeorological Institute, the vast majority of monitored rivers and streams are flowing well below their long-term averages.

Some of the country’s smallest watercourses have dried up completely, while critical conditions are emerging on several major rivers.



The Elbe is among the most affected. Its flow has fallen to one of the lowest levels ever recorded and is approaching the historic minimum for the entire period of regular observations.

The Vltava is in a somewhat better position in some sections because the reservoir system is being regulated to help stabilize water levels. But even the Vltava has reached an unprecedented low in České Budějovice, where the river is recording its lowest measured flow.

The effects of the drought are particularly visible at the Orlík Reservoir. As water levels have fallen sharply, the remains of a former hydroelectric power plant at Dubrava have emerged from beneath the reservoir.

The plant was built in 1929 but was demolished and flooded in the 1960s when the Orlík Reservoir was created. Its remains have now resurfaced as the reservoir continues to shrink.

The worsening conditions are not limited to rivers and reservoirs. Groundwater levels are also declining, affecting wells and raising concerns about the availability of water supplies in some areas.

Hydrologists are not expecting a significant improvement in the coming days. According to the medium-range weather forecast, there are currently no clear conditions that would bring a substantial recovery in river flows or groundwater levels.

World.title: How to Find a GP in Prague When Practices Aren’t Accepting New Patients
World.content:
Finding a general practitioner in Prague can look simple until the first calls begin.

One practice does not answer. Another says it is full. A third can offer an appointment, but not in English. Your insurer’s list may not show who is accepting new patients today or what kind of visit is available.

If registration is blocked, first clarify whether you need long-term GP care, a one-time consultation, a specialist, an urgent route, or a private self-paid visit.



Decide whether this is really a GP problem

A GP is often the right first contact for common health concerns, preventive care, prescription questions, basic tests, and referrals. In Czech, this doctor is called a praktický lékař.

Not every situation should wait for GP registration. For a sudden and serious health problem or a possible threat to life, call 155 for the medical emergency service or 112 for the European emergency number.

If the issue clearly belongs to a dentist, gynaecologist, or specialist, ask that provider whether direct booking is possible or a referral is required. Patients in Czechia can generally approach a specialist without a GP referral, but an individual provider, insurer, or procedure may have its own requirements.

Tell the provider if you already have results, imaging, a hospital discharge report, or a specialist recommendation, because those documents may affect the next step.

Ask your insurer for help finding a provider

If you have Czech public health insurance and cannot find a GP, contact your insurer directly. Czech health insurers are responsible for helping their members access contracted care under the applicable rules on geographical and time availability.

Ask for practical information:

• Which contracted GPs in my area should be available to new patients?

• Which providers can communicate in English?

• Does the provider have a contract for my care?

• Do I need a referral, approval, or particular documents?

Availability can change, so confirm the details with the practice before travelling there.

If you have commercial insurance, check the provider network and approval process in your policy or contact the insurer. Do not assume that a clinic visit is covered simply because the clinic appears in a search result.

Understand why a practice may say no

A practice may lawfully refuse to accept a patient into care for reasons such as capacity, operational limits, distance that prevents home visits, or the absence of a contract with the patient’s public insurer.

If a provider refuses to accept you as a patient, ask for written confirmation with the reason. This gives you something concrete to show your insurer when requesting another available provider.

Clarify whether the refusal covers long-term registration, all appointments, only publicly insured care, the requested language, or a service the practice does not provide. A limited “no” does not necessarily close every route.

Separate registration from a one-time appointment

Registration and a medical appointment are related, but they are not identical.

Registration creates a long-term relationship with a primary-care doctor. It matters for continuity and for services whose public-insurance reimbursement is linked to the registered GP.

A provider may also offer care without registering you, particularly through a one-time, self-pay appointment. The scope and payment conditions vary, so never assume that a single consultation also means registration or that public insurance will cover it.

Before booking, ask whether the offer is long-term registration, a one-time consultation, a preventive check-up, an urgent appointment, specialist care, or a self-paid visit. Do not leave a clinic assuming that one consultation means you are registered there.

Prepare the information the provider needs

Share only enough information for the provider to understand the request, and use its approved secure channel for medical documents.

Prepare:

• the main reason for the appointment;

• how long the issue has been present;

• whether the request is routine, worsening, urgent, or preventive;

• your insurer or intention to self-pay;

• your preferred language;

• current medicines and allergies;

• relevant reports, results, imaging, or referrals.

A concise request helps the provider determine whether it can help and which appointment type is appropriate.

Make sure the visit has a clear ending

Getting an appointment is only the first part of the process.

A doctor may order tests, issue a referral, prescribe medication, or recommend another consultation. It should be clear who will explain the results and arrange the next step.

Before leaving, ask:

• What happens next?

• When should I expect the results?

• Who will explain them?

• Do I need another appointment?

• Should I send anything to another doctor?

A useful appointment should leave you knowing what comes afterwards.

When coordination support can help

OpenMedical helps patients find suitable English-speaking GPs and other medical specialists in Prague, confirm current availability and appointment conditions, and coordinate the booking process. The service also helps prepare documents, communicate with selected providers, and keep follow-up steps clear.

Quick checklist when GP registration is blocked

• Decide whether the situation is an emergency or can wait for a planned appointment.

• Ask your public insurer to help identify an available contracted provider.

• Ask the practice whether its refusal applies to registration or to all appointments.

• Request written confirmation if a provider refuses to take you into care.

• Confirm language, payment route, referral requirements, and whether a one-time appointment is available.

• Keep copies of medical reports and results.

• Before leaving an appointment, confirm who will explain the results and arrange the next step.

Finding a GP in Prague can take patience. A blocked registration does not mean there is no possible way forward. It means the next route needs to be identified more precisely.

Questions to ask before confirming a GP appointment

• Are you accepting new registered patients?

• Is this a registration visit or a one-time consultation?

• Can the appointment be handled in English?

• Do you have a contract with my public health insurer?

• What is the price if the appointment is self-paid?

• Do I need a referral or prior approval?

• Which documents should I provide, and how should I send them securely?

• How will results and further steps be handled?

World.title: Prague Plans 1.9 Billion Crown Reconstruction of Kasárna Karlín
World.content:
Prague plans to invest around CZK 1.93 billion, including VAT, to transform Kasárna Karlín into a mixed-use complex with shops, offices, student housing and space for cultural and artistic activities.

The city acquired the former military complex in 2023 and has since been working on plans for its long-term redevelopment.

Prague City Council has now approved the next step, allowing the city-owned Trade Centre Prague (TCP), which manages the site, to launch a tender for the preparation of the reconstruction project.



Construction is scheduled to follow between 2027 and 2032, with the investment financed from Prague’s municipal budget.

The first stage will focus on the complex’s main building. A separate building in the courtyard, currently used by the Karlín Barracks Cultural Center, will be addressed in later phases.

Deputy Mayor for Territorial and Strategic Development Petr Hlaváček said the reconstruction should open the site to the surrounding neighborhood while preserving its historic character and protected architectural elements.

One of the main changes will be to improve access to the courtyard, which currently has just one entrance and is largely hidden from the surrounding streets.

Adam Zábranský, Prague’s councilor for property, transparency and legislation, said new passages from the street would lead into the complex, with shops and services occupying the ground floor. The arcade running alongside these commercial spaces would form part of the new circulation system through the site.

The upper levels could eventually accommodate student housing, studios and offices. Zábranský also mentioned the possibility of using some of the space for businesses such as a technology park.

The exact future use of many of the rooms has not yet been decided. According to Zábranský, the project should therefore prioritize flexible layouts that can be adapted for different purposes over time.

The initial investment will focus in particular on replacing and upgrading essential infrastructure, including water, electricity and waste systems, as well as preparing the commercial areas on the ground floor. Work on the upper floors is expected to come later.

World.title: Czechia Sees Lyme Disease Surge With 90 New Cases a Day
World.content:
Lyme disease cases are rising sharply across the Czech Republic, with more than 8,000 infections recorded since the beginning of the year.

Health officials warn that the summer peak may not have arrived yet.

A total of 8,108 cases were reported through the end of July, according to data from the Czech State Institute of Health (SZÚ). July alone accounted for 2,792 infections, meaning that roughly one in three cases recorded so far this year occurred during the month.



Doctors registered an average of about 90 new cases each day in July.

The figures are significantly higher than those seen in previous years. Between January and July, the Czech Republic typically recorded between 1,500 and 2,000 Lyme disease cases.

Part of the increase may be linked to a change in the way infectious diseases are reported.

The number of tick-borne infections depends on several factors, including tick populations and seasonal weather conditions. Climate change is also playing an increasingly important role.

The highest numbers of Lyme disease infections have so far been reported in the Central Bohemian and South Moravian regions.

The risk is not limited to forests and countryside. Prague’s parks and wooded areas can also provide suitable conditions for ticks.

“Prague’s parks and forest parks create a specific microclimate where ticks thrive, so the risk of infection is real for residents even during an ordinary walk,” said Martina Marešová, head of the anti-epidemic department at the Prague Hygiene Station.

Early treatment can prevent complications

One of the most recognizable signs of Lyme disease is an expanding red rash that develops around the site of a tick bite and may have a paler area in the center.

Anyone who develops such a rash should seek medical attention rather than waiting for it to disappear.

The most common form initially affects the skin. If left untreated, the infection can progress and cause further skin problems. More serious complications can involve the nervous system, heart or eyes.

World.title: Shella Radio Visualizes Struggling Culture Scene At National Gallery
World.content:
A radio tower installation at Prague’s National Gallery is showcasing local efforts to preserve alternative culture as the Czech government seeks to cut funding to the arts and other public sectors.

Created by members of Prague-based Shella Radio, the tower is adorned with fabrics and relics of previous parties hosted in Ankali & Planeta Za, a nightclub that has faced closure due to financial problems.

“We believe in the idea of this radio as an amplification of voices that are often neglected in other spaces,” Shania Rodriguez, a Prague-based DJ and Shella radio host, said in an interview. “Here, they can be vocal about the issues and problems within our system and also share ideas of change.”



Many artists and curators say the environment for cultural organizations has grown more challenging due to financial cuts by the new right wing government led by Andrej Babiš.

The planned budget for this year shrank by 3.9 billion crowns – an almost 20 percent decrease from the previous year, according to the Czech Ministry of Culture. The cuts sparked widespread backlash across the country in April, and many took to the streets.

Shella, an Egyptian Arabic slang word meaning “a group of friends who do things together,” hosts political talk shows, electronic music club nights, and summer markets featuring local artists.

“The idea behind our installation was to be able to transmit parts of our identity that have been fundamental in Shella Radio’s trajectory,” Rodriguez said. “This DIY approach gives us the freedom to customize and handcraft our installation and studio space using materials from our temporary home: Ankali.”

The installation is part of the Necessary Wishes exhibition at the National Gallery which brings together more than 50 collectives and artists.

The event is free of charge and ends on September 13.

By: Lili Anna Lempek, Adam Pohořilský, Milena Gevorgyan, Isabella Fattore

World.title: Where to See the Partial Solar Eclipse in Prague and Across Czechia
World.content:
Skywatchers in the Czech Republic will have two reasons to look up on the night of August 12.

A partial solar eclipse will be visible in the evening, followed by favorable conditions for watching the annual Perseid meteor shower.

The eclipse will be visible across Czechia shortly before sunset, with the Sun low over the western and northwestern horizon. In Prague, the partial eclipse is expected to begin at about 7:19 p.m., reach its maximum at 8:12 p.m. and end around 8:27 p.m.



At the height of the eclipse, the Moon will cover about 86 percent of the Sun’s disk in Prague, making the event particularly noticeable if skies are clear.

The eclipse will look different depending on where observers are located. The farther east they are, the later the eclipse will begin and the less of it will be visible. In eastern Czechia and much of Slovakia, the maximum phase will take place after sunset, when the Sun is already below the horizon.

The event will be a partial eclipse in Central Europe, while a total solar eclipse will be visible in parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain. Astronomers and eclipse enthusiasts are expected to travel to those areas to experience totality.

A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, blocking part or all of the Sun from view. In Czechia, the eclipse will be especially low on the horizon, so observers will need an unobstructed view toward the west and northwest.

Several Czech observatories are preparing public observing events. A list of locations and other information about the eclipse is available through the Czech astronomical website astro.cz.

Perseid meteor shower will follow

The same night will also offer good conditions for watching the Perseids, one of the most prominent annual meteor showers.

The shower will reach its peak during the early hours of August 13, when the Moon will be only a few hours past its new-moon phase. With virtually no moonlight in the sky, faint meteors should be easier to spot.

The Perseids are active from July 17 through August 24, but the best opportunity this year will come during the night of August 12-13.

Under dark skies and favorable weather, observers away from cities could see between 50 and 80 meteors per hour.

Light pollution will be the main obstacle for anyone hoping to see large numbers of meteors. The best locations are well away from major cities, ideally several dozen kilometers from strong sources of artificial light.

World.title: Non-Alcoholic Beer Sales Rise by More Than 25% in Czechia
World.content:
Beer remains a staple of the Czech shopping basket, but new sales data from online supermarket Rohlík shows that drinking habits are gradually changing.

Traditional lagers still dominate, while non-alcoholic beer is recording the fastest growth among the main beer categories.

The category has grown by more than a quarter over the past year, with Birell among the brands driving the increase. Birell sales alone are up by almost 20%.



Together with flavoured beers and radlers, non-alcoholic beer now accounts for close to one-third of all beer sales on Rohlík.

Beer from small and regional breweries is also gaining ground, with sales increasing by more than 11%.

The biggest decline is being recorded among craft beers grouped by style, including IPA and APA. This is currently the only major beer segment experiencing a year-on-year drop.

Czech brands continue to dominate the market. More than nine out of every 10 beers sold through Rohlík are from domestic brands.

Imported beers, however, are growing at a faster rate. Their sales have increased by 18% year-on-year.

Beer sales peak at the weekend

Friday is the busiest day for beer sales, with roughly twice as much beer sold as on Monday. Friday and Saturday together account for almost two-fifths of the category’s weekly sales.

Orders containing beer also tend to include significantly more items than orders without beer, suggesting that customers often buy it as part of a larger meal or weekend shop rather than as a standalone purchase.

Seasonal patterns have also shifted. Beer sales during this year’s summer months have reached levels comparable with the December Christmas peak.

World.title: Major changes are coming to Hungary’s 20 August celebrations this year: here’s what’s in store
World.content:
Hungary’s government is preparing a three-day programme of events for 20 August, the country’s national holiday, with this year’s celebrations set to feature a shorter fireworks display and a large-scale audiovisual show projected onto the Parliament building.

The official name of this year’s celebrations is “20 August – The Nation’s Celebration – One Thousand Years Together in Europe”. The programme will cost around HUF 4 billion (EUR 11 million), according to government spokesperson Éva Magyar, who presented details of the events at a press conference in Budapest.

While some programmes will begin as early as 19 August, events will also continue at some locations in the days following the national holiday.

Ten Budapest locations will host events

The capital will host programmes at ten main locations: Margaret Island, the Danube riverside near Budapest University of Technology, Kossuth Square, the Parliament, Szabadság Square, Várkert Bazaar, Buda Castle, City Park, St Stephen’s Square and the area around St Stephen’s Basilica.

On 20 August, the traditional flag-raising ceremony and military officer commissioning will begin the official programme at 8 AM on Kossuth Square. This will be followed by a military and air parade, which can be viewed from the Danube embankments.

Meanwhile, Margaret Island will offer family and children’s programmes during the day, followed by light installations and concerts in the evening. Performers will include Hungarian acts such as Quimby, Random Trip and Boban Marković.

The celebrations will begin already on 19 August at the riverside near the Budapest University of Technology, where an electronic music event will be held.

Kossuth Square to become a temporary “Disco Square”

Kossuth Square will combine traditional elements with more contemporary entertainment this year. After the morning flag-raising ceremony, officer commissioning and military air parade, an evening party featuring a surprise guest will be held at the square.

Government spokesperson Éva Magyar said the location would temporarily be given the name “Disco Square” for the evening.

The organisers said their aim was to create programmes appealing to several generations, from children and parents to young adults and grandparents, while retaining the best-known traditional elements of the national holiday.

Parliament to become the centre of the evening show

The main event on the evening of 20 August will be a large-scale audiovisual show projected onto the Parliament building. The approximately 30-minute production will tell a story beginning with the formation of the Carpathian Basin, using a sequence of visual effects projected onto the iconic building.

The audiovisual show will then culminate in a 10-minute fireworks display.

The fireworks will be launched from the area between Margaret Bridge and Chain Bridge and are expected to be best viewed from the Buda side of the Danube. The show will be accompanied by music from Hungarian artists Iamyank, Balázs Zságer and DJ Bootsie.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Fireworks to be shorter than usual

The fireworks will be considerably shorter than in previous years. According to Dániel Besnyő of the organising Centrum Production, he considers fireworks an outdated form of visual entertainment and had originally proposed a display lasting just three minutes.

However, fireworks and rockets had already been ordered well in advance, so the organisers ultimately decided to use them in this year’s show. The result will be a 10-minute display following the audiovisual production.

The organisers said they had only had around six weeks to put the programme together.

If you missed it: Hungary races to reorganise 20 August celebrations after contractor collapse

Free Parliament visits and cheaper refreshments

Visitors will also be able to enter the Hungarian Parliament free of charge and without prior registration during the three-day celebrations. The traditional Holy Right procession will also take place as part of the national holiday programme.

The organisers also said they would once again limit the price of beer during the celebrations, while stressing that no state subsidy would be used for this purpose. A half-litre bottle of mineral water will cost less than HUF 500, while half a litre of beer will cost less than HUF 1,000.

With family programmes, concerts, traditional ceremonies, contemporary entertainment and the shortened fireworks display combined with a major audiovisual production, this year’s 20 August celebrations are set to offer a somewhat different take on one of Hungary’s biggest annual national events.

World.title: Hungarian man arrested over plot to lure 15-year-old Danish girl to Hungary
World.content:
A 22-year-old Hungarian man has been placed in temporary extradition custody after Danish authorities issued a European Arrest Warrant over allegations that he lured a 15-year-old Danish girl to Hungary for the purpose of subjecting her to sexual offences.

The Budapest-Capital Regional Court ordered the man’s temporary detention on Tuesday. At his hearing, he consented to being handed over to Danish authorities, although he asked to retain his rights under the so-called principle of speciality. This means that, if extradited, Danish authorities may only prosecute him for the offences specified in the European Arrest Warrant. The court is expected to decide on his simplified extradition no later than 21 August.

Man allegedly met girl through social media

According to the court, the Hungarian national met the girl through social media in January 2026. Authorities allege that he exploited her young age and lack of experience to manipulate her and establish a relationship with her, using what the court described as an “exploitative position of superiority”.

On 4 August, the man and an unidentified accomplice allegedly brought the 15-year-old from Denmark to Hungary with the intention of subjecting her to sexual offences.

The Horsens City Court in Denmark issued a European Arrest Warrant for the man on suspicion of kidnapping, unlawful detention or hostage-taking, exploitation of children and child pornography. Under Danish law, the offence listed in the warrant carries a maximum sentence of 12 years in prison.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Hungarian authorities arrested him following Danish alert

The man was arrested by Hungarian police based on a so-called SIS II alert issued by Danish authorities through the Schengen Information System.

At Tuesday’s hearing, he agreed to be handed over to Denmark but did not waive his right to the principle of speciality. Consequently, if he is extradited, proceedings against him may not be launched or continued for offences other than those specified in the European Arrest Warrant, subject to the applicable legal rules.

The Budapest-Capital Regional Court has ordered his temporary extradition detention while the authorities complete the process. A decision on his simplified extradition must be made by 21 August at the latest.

World.title: Direct and safe cycling route to connect the amazing Danube Bend with Budapest
World.content:
A direct and safe cycling link between Dunakeszi and Budapest is to be created, with the route soon connecting to the northern Pest section of the international EuroVelo 6 cycleway, Dávid Vitézy, the Minister for Transport and Investment, said on Facebook on Tuesday. That means cyclists will soon be able to pedal from Budapest to the Danube Bend.

Danube Bend bike excursions from Budapest

He said that, following a government decision taken on August 7 at the ministry’s proposal, funding provided through the Integrated Transport Development Operational Programme Plus (IKOP Plus) would make it possible to build a safe and convenient cycling connection between the cycle path approaching from Dunakeszi and the asphalt-surfaced road previously constructed along the embankment, as well as between the embankment and Duna sor, MTI wrote.

“The Government is now providing funding for the construction of the two most urgently needed missing sections. This investment will finally create an uninterrupted link between the Danube Bend and Budapest,” he said.

EuroVelo extension

According to Mr Vitézy, the aim of the project is to establish a safe and fast connection as part of the EuroVelo 6 international route, linking the cycleway running through Vác and Szob all the way to the national border directly to Budapest’s inner cycling network. The development will extend the capital’s existing EuroVelo sections and complete the missing stretches along the Danube.

“Alternatives to the car bring social and environmental benefits: noise and air pollution are reduced, air quality improves and the capital’s congested roads become more liveable,” he said.

World.title: Yettel announces useful 4G and 5G mobile network development at Sziget Festival 2026
World.content:
Yettel has prepared 20 per cent more mobile network capacity for this year’s Sziget Festival than it did last year, with the additional capacity roughly equivalent to the needs of a town the size of Szombathely. The cost of building and operating the extra network has exceeded HUF 50 million, Balázs Mang, Yettel’s director of technical strategy, told a press conference at the festival on Tuesday.

30 engineers and service specialists worked on the new system

He said a team of 30 engineers and service specialists had been working on the system’s design, operation and round-the-clock monitoring since the initial planning stage. The work began in May.

For a mobile communications provider, he said, ensuring a reliable service at an event of this scale was particularly challenging because between 70,000 and 80,000 people used their devices simultaneously across an area of 0.7 square kilometres.

Festival-goers also uploaded considerably more photographs, videos and live content than they would under normal circumstances. While uploads typically account for less than 10 per cent of downloads, that figure can reach 30 per cent during the festival’s busiest hours.

Total 4G and 5G capacity increased at Sziget Festival

Working with its network infrastructure partner Cetin, Yettel has expanded last year’s 31-sector network and increased total 4G and 5G capacity by 20 per cent. Within that figure, capacity on high-speed 5G cells using the C-band frequency has risen by 40 per cent.

Mr Mang described this as particularly favourable given current energy pressures, saying that modern 4G and 5G network equipment operated far more efficiently. The latest technologies require less cooling and can handle the same volume of data while using fewer resources, he said.

The provider is supplying the additional network through 144 mobile-cell capacities at 21 locations during the festival, he added. The so-called microcells operating across the island typically cover sectors measuring between 100 and 200 metres.

He also said that, according to last year’s figures, peak-hour mobile traffic increased by 10 per cent over the previous year during the festival as a whole, with 40 per cent of it carried over the 5G network. 5G accounted for 25 per cent of total data traffic, and specialists expect that figure to approach 30 per cent this year as compatible devices become more widespread.

Free Wi-Fi zone with mobile-phone charging points

Judit Tőzsér, Yettel’s director of corporate communications, said that, as the official telecommunications partner of one of Europe’s largest music and cultural events, the company had set up a free Wi-Fi zone equipped with 15 mobile-phone charging points.

If you missed: Sziget Festival kicked off – West European police help Hungarian colleagues

Tamás Kádár, the festival’s chief organiser, said this was an exciting year for Sziget because the festival had once again come under Hungarian ownership. Its founder, Károly Gerendai, had returned, the management had become co-owners, and a group of investors with whom the organisers had worked for many years had also been brought into the festival’s ownership structure.

He added that the comfort of festival-goers would become an increasingly important consideration at European festivals, and that this included being able to use mobile phones without interruption.

Yettel was providing Sziget with extensive technological and other support in this area, he said, helping the festival deliver an outstanding experience for its guests.

World.title: New, thrilling – but deadly – routes emerge in drought-stricken Hungary
World.content:
Drought-stricken Hungary is opening up a series of intriguing new, but deadly routes even for fit and experienced hikers. Several people have already found themselves in trouble, and the latest incident came perilously close to ending in tragedy.

She almost sank into the mud

A few days ago, it was reported that a 35-year-old woman from Dunaújváros nearly disappeared into the vast expanse of mud at the shrinking Lake Velence after deciding to cross it. An off-duty police officer and a local resident eventually pulled her to safety, after which paramedics took her to hospital for further examination, the Hungarian police wrote.

The incident is a stark illustration of the dangers facing drought-stricken Hungary. As lakes and rivers recede, previously inaccessible areas are opening up, creating what may appear to be exciting new opportunities for walks and excursions. In reality, most of them are extraordinarily hazardous. Had no one nearby heard the woman’s cries for help, she would almost certainly not be alive to recount the experience as a warning to others.

Lake Velence drying out, but the mud can be extremely dangerous. Photo: Facebook/Élhető Velence Egyesület

Record-low water levels are also exposing places that had previously remained hidden, prompting magnet fishers and collectors to set out in search of discoveries. Most recently, a German Second World War motorbike was found on the banks of the Danube in Budapest, alongside various other items of equipment and human remains. Elsewhere, warships, bombs and other objects have emerged from the water – all of which may pose a danger to virtually anyone other than trained specialists.

New, but deadly routes in the Danube riverbed and in Lake Velence

Walking along the exposed banks of the shrinking Danube, or attempting to wade across Lake Velence, may seem tempting. But the receding waters have created dangers that have never previously been encountered. Experts warn that a single wrong step could put someone’s life at risk.

Entering the lakebed at Lake Velence remains prohibited, and the area becomes particularly dangerous beyond 100 metres from the shore. Although the surface may look completely dry, cracked and hard in many places, this is merely a thin crust. Beneath it, the mud may still be wet, soft and sticky.

Gábor Kürti, alias Kükü, the chairman of the Hungarian Bicycle Club, crossed the lake with special equipment he dragged with him after he studied carefully his route from the air. Photo: Facebook/Kürti Gábor Dezső

The lakebed may also contain so-called mud wells, which can be as much as two or three metres deeper than the lake’s average depth, according to Blikk.

Panic can make you even more vulnerable

Several people have already had to be rescued from the mud at Lake Velence this year. A young woman and a man from Budapest both got into difficulty; the latter was freed by water police before receiving medical attention.

One of the greatest dangers posed by the mud is the vacuum it can create around a person’s legs. The harder someone struggles and tries to move their feet, the deeper they may sink. Decomposing organic matter can also release dangerous gases, including methane and hydrogen sulphide, while the lakebed may contain shards of glass, rusty metal objects and fishing hooks.

If you missed: Did the Danube run dry in Budapest and Paks because the Slovaks diverted it?

Rescue operations are far from straightforward. Lifeguards do not approach those in trouble on foot, but use boats, ladders, planks, ropes and other equipment. Panic and unnecessary movement can make the situation even worse.

It may look dry and shallow at first

The Danube’s unusually low water level can be just as deceptive. Wide stretches of riverbank have been exposed at several points, attracting walkers and even cyclists. But the clay banks are being eroded from below by the river’s current, creating apparently solid ledges of earth that may collapse without warning, infostart.hu wrote.

The German WWII motorcycle that emerged from the record-low Danube last week. Photo: Facebook/HM Hadtörténeti Intézet és Múzeum

This is particularly dangerous because someone standing in water only a few centimetres deep could suddenly plunge into several metres of fast-flowing water. The cold can cause cramp, while the current may sweep a person away – or carry them beneath a collapsing section of riverbank.

The danger at both locations lies precisely in the false sense of security created by ground that appears dry or water that seems shallow. Experts therefore warn that exceptionally low water levels do not make a river or lakebed safer. On the contrary, they can expose hidden hazards that remain invisible under normal conditions.

Deadly new routes emerge fromt the Danube. Photo: Anadolu/Németi Róbert

World.title: Shock as young man joins women taken ill en masse at Budapest concert and recounts his ordeal
World.content:
One moment he was partying with his friends; the next, he was walking towards the toilets. After that, his next memory was of lying on a bed with a doctor standing beside him, a number marked on his stomach. This was not the opening scene of a horror film but a real-life ordeal – and it happened the day before yesterday at a Budapest on the Hajógyári Island, the site of the Sziget Festival. No one yet knows exactly what happened: were the young people drugged, or was something else behind the incidents?

Many fell ill at Budapest concert

The concert did not form part of the Sziget Festival, although it was held on the festival’s main stage, where the illnesses occurred.

Sziget organisers issued a statement on Sunday condemning what had happened, but stressed that they had nothing to do with the DJ OTI – Balázs Sebestyén – concert, which was not included in the Sziget Festival programme. The concert was nevertheless held on Sziget’s main stage, and at one of the high points of the party Balázs flew in front of a Sziget logo, leading many people to associate the two events.

Both Sziget and Balázs expressed their regret and stressed the importance of human life. Károly Gerendai, Sziget’s lead organiser, added that he and his colleagues would try to investigate exactly what had happened more thoroughly. He said he knew of 20 cases among the 100 people who had received medical attention, while tens of thousands had attended the event.

Balázs Sebestyén, alias DJ OTI, on the main stage of Sziget Festival. Source: Facebook/DJ OTI

Hours missing from his life

An affected man told Index on Tuesday how he had experienced the events. The man, who is in his thirties, said he had not drunk much alcohol, yet had ended up in a condition for which he still has little explanation: three or four hours had disappeared completely from his memory.

One moment he was partying with his friends; then he set off for the toilets and remembers nothing after that. His next memory was of lying in a room with a doctor standing beside him. He does not know how he got there, nor who helped him reach the medical facility. He assumes that, when he regained consciousness, someone may have explained what had happened to him, but none of that information remained with him.

One of the most shocking details only became clear to the man later. Once he had recovered further, he noticed that a huge number had been written on his stomach in marker pen. His pockets had been emptied, and his phone and identity documents were returned to him in a transparent plastic bag.

Professional care, followed by illness

According to Index, the number written on the skin is an identification method used at mass events. If someone is unconscious or unable to communicate, the number is used to link the patient to their medical records and to the belongings found on them.

Our previous article concerning the issue – Young women collapse one after another at Budapest concert: police investigate as victims recount same story

The man came round in the detoxification unit operating at Sziget. This is the observation area where people who are severely intoxicated or under the influence of psychoactive substances are kept under medical supervision until their condition stabilises. The festival has a fully equipped medical centre, including a triage unit, internal medicine and surgical treatment rooms, a resuscitation unit, an inpatient area and a detoxification unit, supported by an emergency team of around 50 people.

All victims received professional medical care. Photo: depositphotos.com

But the ordeal did not end with the night. The man said he felt extremely unwell throughout Sunday, adding that he had never felt so ill in his life.

Following the incident, the Budapest Police Headquarters launched an investigation on suspicion of drug possession and questioned witnesses. However, no toxicology results have yet been made public to prove that the man or anyone else was given a psychoactive substance without their consent. Many people suspect GHB – commonly known in Hungary as “gina” – but the substance leaves the body quickly, although it can be detected in hair at considerable expense.

World.title: Breaking – New Hungarian President elected: “Hungary’s future cannot be built on revenge” – read his full message below
World.content:
Hungary’s parliament elected András Baka, the former head of the Supreme Court, as President of the Republic on Tuesday. Baka, the candidate of the ruling Tisza Party, was elected head of state with 140 votes in favour and 6 against in a secret ballot. Orbán’s Fidesz and the KDNP did not participate on the vote. Baka will assume office on the eighth day following the announcement of the election result.

Hungarians cannot avoid confronting the past at the beginning of a new era, Baka, the president-elect said in a speech to parliament on Tuesday. In his address after his election, Baka emphasised the need to understand “how the nation reached this point”. The president-elect said Hungary had “wasted a generation’s worth of time, slipping from a model student during the time of the democratic transition to the ranks of lagging nations”.

He said that he had accepted the nomination “because I think that Hungary has arrived at a point in its history when it needs to seriously contemplate the operation of the state, constitutionality and the country as community.” Baka, who was the sole candidate for the post, said the National Assembly’s decision to elect him was “a great honour, recognition and exceptional trust. The candidacy itself was also unexpected, overwhelming and an honour,” he said.

Photo: MTI

Past regime failed to meet basic democratic rule-of-law requirements

Baka said that before 2026, the Hungarian state had failed to meet one of the most fundamental requirements of a democratic rule-of-law system: the genuine separation of powers and a functioning system of checks and balances.

Baka said Hungary had developed a system in which a single party had captured the state and its institutions, culminating in years of governance by decree that largely bypassed parliament. “It is the responsibility of us all to ensure such a system never emerges again in Hungary,” he said.

Expressing national unity means political neutrality, but never neutrality on values

Expressing the unity of the nation first and foremost means political neutrality, but it must never mean neutrality on values, he said. Baka said that a modern, democratic society was inherently diverse, with coexisting worldviews, political convictions, lifestyles and interests. “There may even be deep, sometimes irreconcilable divisions among them,” he said.

Here are some photos from the Parliament:

As president, Baka said, he must represent this diverse community and always acknowledge the legitimacy of differing views, as well as the right of both majority and minority positions to be heard. The president’s role, he said, was not to manufacture consensus where none exists, but to represent the idea that “citizens with differing views are equal members of the same nation.“

A democratic institution’s authority is defined by its ability to remain true to its function, even in situations of conflict, he added. A democratic institution’s authority did not come from operating without conflict, but from its ability to stay true to its mission even amid disputes. He added that he intended to uphold this principle as president.

New President Baka could stand up firmly to PM Magyar – so why is the opposition attacking him so viciously?

Constitution’s stability hinges on broad societal ownership

A constitution’s stability rests on its being regarded as belonging to the broadest sections of society, Baka said. He warned that once again drafting a constitution “solely as the document of a temporary majority” would result in repeating the mistake the consequences of which Hungary was now attempting to rectify.

Drafting a constitution required more than mere parliamentary legislation, he said. “A wide-ranging societal and expert debate, genuine political consensus, and a process that in itself reflects the democratic culture the new constitution will later be tasked with upholding” was also necessary, he said.

World.title: Inflation in Romania falls to 8.2% in July, down from 10.4% the previous month
World.content:
The annual inflation rate in Romania fell by 2.2% for the first time in the last twelve months and reached 8.2% in July, according to data from the National Institute of Statistics.

In June 2026, the annual inflation rate had fallen slightly, to 10.4%. In May 2026, the rate was 10.9%, after the indicator had already risen to 10.7% in April.

In July, the largest price increases were for services, at 13.67%. During the same period, prices of non-food goods increased by 7.93%, while food goods rose by 5.03%.

In food products, the largest price increases remained for coffee, whose price rose by 19.47% over one year. Eggs were in second place with a price increase of 13.9%, while beef became 11.67% more expensive. During the same period, cow’s milk increased in price by 11.28%, and spirits were 8.87% more expensive.

Other food price increases were recorded for bread, up 7.93%, fresh fish, up 7.54%, canned meat, up 6.77%, edible oil, up 6.57%, poultry meat, up 6.24%, and pork, up 3.4%. Beer was 7.88% more expensive, and wine by 6.66%.

There were also price reductions for several foods. Sugar fell by 0.25%, butter by 0.53%, flour by 4.3%, and cornmeal by 4.92%. The largest price decreases over one year were recorded for potatoes, down 13.68%, and fresh fruit, down 13.82%.

Among non-food goods, the most significant increases in July were for diesel, up 30.7%, followed by gasoline, up 23.15%. The electricity tariff, until last month the star of price increases over the past year, increased by only 3.39%. The electricity capping-compensation scheme ended on June 30, 2025, and from July 1, 2025, consumers returned to market prices.

Other tariff increases in this category were recorded for fuels, up 16.87%, thermal energy, up 10.70%, books, newspapers and magazines, up 10.82%, detergents, up 9.92%, and tobacco and cigarettes, up 8.51%. Hygiene products and cosmetics also became 6.80% more expensive, while medicines increased in price by 4.36% in July. During the period July 2025 – July 2026, gas prices rose by 0.97%.

In the services category, the largest price increases in July 2026 compared with the same month of 2025 were recorded for rents, which rose by 42.48%, followed by water, sewerage and sanitation tariffs, up 15.99%, car repairs, up 13.85%, and hygiene and cosmetic services, up 14.10%. Other significant increases in this category over one year were recorded for footwear and clothing manufacturing and repair services, up 14.36%.

At the same time, medical assistance became 12.48% more expensive, urban transport increased by 7.47%, and road transport by 12.21%. Air service tariffs rose by 2.3% compared with July of the previous year, but a 18.73% increase compared with June 2026 is notable. Postal service tariffs, which had been reduced in previous months, increased by 9.18% in July 2026 compared with the same month in 2025.

According to the forecast of the National Bank of Romania, the annual inflation rate will undergo a substantial downward correction in the third quarter of 2026.

World.title: Study: Business services sector contributes EUR 35.5 billion to Romania’s economy
World.content:
The local business services industry generated a gross value added of EUR 35.5 billion last year, according to the Business Services Comparative Analysis 2025 study, conducted by Deloitte Romania for the Association of Business Service Leaders Romania (ABSL).

Romania combines criteria sought by international investors, such as a large-scale market, access to a highly skilled workforce, strong foreign language capabilities, high productivity levels, competitive costs and significant expansion opportunities across multiple cities in Romania, the study shows.

Romania has one of the largest talent pools in Central and Eastern Europe among the analyzed markets, with approximately 8.3 million people in the labor force, being surpassed only by Poland. The country ranks second in the region in terms of the number of graduates and the size of its highly educated workforce. Strong foreign language capabilities are a key competitive advantage for companies with international operations.

At the same time, labor productivity, measured as the economic output generated per hour worked, places Romania among the region’s top performers. With a score of 52.1, it outperforms markets such as Poland (48.8) and Slovakia (47.6) and is close to the leaders Lithuania (54.7) and Portugal (54.4) and almost equal to Czechia (52.4), the study found.

Despite recent inflationary pressures, the study shows that Romania remains one of the most competitive European locations in terms of total employment cost. A comparison of this indicator for a mid-level General Ledger Accountant across the countries analyzed places Romania among the lowest-cost destinations, with only Bulgaria having lower costs in the region. At the opposite end of the ranking, Portugal, Czechia, Slovakia and Estonia record the highest employment costs. Simulations through 2030, taking into account effects of the forecasted inflation rates, indicate that Romania will retain its competitive edge and remain among the most cost-effective European markets for operating business services centers.

According to this simulation, in 2030, the ranking of countries with the lowest total employment costs is expected to be led by India, the Philippines and Bulgaria, but Romania would maintain its competitiveness even in the context of higher levels of inflation, ranking sixth. On the other hand, the highest total employment costs are estimated in Portugal (13th place), the Czech Republic (12th place) and Slovakia (11th place).

Regarding the expansion of the business services ecosystem beyond the capital city, the study highlights Romania’s strong potential supported by its network of ten cities with over 200,000 inhabitants, being the second European country after Poland on this indicator.

Also, more than 14 other cities with populations between 90,000 and 200,000 inhabitants offer favorable conditions for new investments or expansions of existing operations. Cities such as Cluj-Napoca, Iasi, Timisoara, Brasov, Sibiu, Oradea or Constanta provide investors with a significant labor pool, strong university graduate output, less saturated labor markets and competitive operating costs.

Romania currently hosts more than 1,000 service centers and over 280,000 employees, making it one of the most developed business services markets in Central and Eastern Europe. The sector represents 15.2% of the country’s highly educated workforce. In addition, the local sector recorded a 9.9% increase in the share of the economy's total gross value added in 2025.

The second edition of Deloitte's Business Services Comparative Analysis compares ten European countries and three Asian markets, analyzing a wide range of macroeconomic and industry-specific indicators, such as labor availability, operating costs, productivity, inflation, the real estate market, grants and incentives for investment, as well as other factors relevant to the business environment.

World.title: ARVAL ROMANIA: Less ownership, more access: how the new generation of entrepreneurs is changing the demand for corporate mobility
World.content:
News from Companies

Operational leasing intention rises to 49% in Romania, 13 points above the European average. The strongest appetite comes from small and medium-sized companies, with 54%, according to the Arval Mobility Observatory 2026 Barometer.

Arval Romania, part of the BNP Paribas Group and a major player in full-service leasing and mobility solutions for companies, presents an in-depth analysis of one of the most relevant signals captured by the 2026 edition of the Fleet and Mobility Barometer: 49% of companies in Romania intend to introduce or increase the use of operational leasing in the next three years, up from 42% in 2024 and 13 percentage points above the European average of 36%.

SMEs, the engine of operational leasing in Romania



Beyond the aggregate figure, the structure of this increase is relevant. Thus, the intention to operate leasing is more strongly supported by small (54%) and medium-sized (48%) companies than by large ones (37%), a reversal of the classic pattern, in which large corporations led the way, and SMEs followed. For years, operational leasing has been perceived as a tool for large corporate fleets, with dedicated administration departments and sophisticated procurement processes. Data from the 2026 edition show that the center of gravity of demand has shifted: the small and medium-sized business segment has become the engine of the market.



The move is even more remarkable as it takes place in a market where ownership remains the cultural norm, from housing to company assets. Against this background, the fact that Romanian entrepreneurs in the SME segment choose access over ownership when it comes to business mobility indicates a change in mentality with lasting potential, beyond immediate financial calculations.



At the same time, the general market context supports the same direction. The 2026 edition of the Barometer shows a moderate optimism of local companies regarding fleet dynamics: one in four companies expects the fleet to grow in the next three years, and 65% expect it to remain at the current level. In parallel, the electrification of fleets and adaptation to restrictive policies on combustion engines are the main challenges equally mentioned by 41% of respondents. In an environment where companies must simultaneously navigate the technological transition, regulatory uncertainty and cost pressure, formulas that transfer risk and complexity to a specialized partner are becoming increasingly attractive, and operational leasing is, by construction, such a formula.

"We see a change of mentality at the level of decision-makers. The new generation of entrepreneurs and managers in SMEs is made up of people who already operate on the logic of subscription, in personal and business life alike, from streaming services to the software through which they run their companies. The question I ask myself is no longer 'what do I own?', but 'what do I have access to and how much does it cost me monthly?'. Brought into the fleet decision, this reflex fundamentally changes the relationship to the company car: for a small business, operational leasing means access to a new fleet without capital immobilization. The cost becomes a predictable operational expense, and the money remains in the business." explains Roxana Lupescu, General Manager of Arval Romania.

The company car, from the balance sheet to the benefits package



However, the change goes beyond the scope of financing and touches the role that the car plays within the company. The barometer thus highlights a transformation of employee mobility: in 2026, companies are moving from simply expanding the available solutions to repositioning mobility as a central element in human resources and sustainability strategies. Social responsibility factors are invoked by 44% of respondents as motivation for these initiatives, and 42% mention HR aspects, namely attracting talent, improving well-being and supporting hybrid work models. In other words, the company car migrates from the balance sheet to the benefits package and becomes a tool through which the organization attracts and retains people.

"Customer requirements have changed accordingly: flexibility at the time of upgrade, digital settlement, 36 to 48-month contracts. At the same time, for employees, mobility becomes a benefit, and a benefit must be flexible, easy to manage and scalable with the team, exactly what operational leasing offers by its nature." adds Roxana Lupescu.

Less ownership, more access, a trend that is consolidating



Taken together, the data of the 2026 edition outlines a market at the beginning of a substantial transition. The demand for operational leasing is growing and changing its structure, with SMEs as the driving force; employee mobility is part of HR and sustainability strategies; and the company car redefines its role, from an asset to be managed to a service to be used and a benefit to be offered.

"The outlook remains one of growth. With an intention to use 13 points above the European average and with an SME segment that has just entered the maturity phase, the potential of operational leasing on the local market is far from being exhausted. The direction is clear, from ownership to use, and the pace of this transition is given, for the first time in the history of this market, by small and medium-sized companies." concludes Roxana Lupescu.

The Fleet and Mobility Barometer is conducted annually by the Arval Mobility Observatory. For the local market, the 2026 edition is based on over 300 interviews with decision-makers in Romania, part of a global survey carried out in 33 countries, with over 10,000 respondents.

*This is a press release.

World.title: Wizz Air opens base in Romania’s Brașov, launches four additional routes
World.content:
Budget carrier Wizz Air is opening a base at Brașov-Ghimbav International Airport with one Airbus A321neo aircraft and will add four new destinations from the central Romania city starting this winter.

Starting in December, passengers will be able to fly from Brașov to Karlsruhe/Baden-Baden, Chișinău, Barcelona and Madrid.

The Nuremberg route will resume on October 26.

Wizz Air operates flights from Brașov to London, Budapest, Dortmund, Rome, Milan, Naples, Memmingen, Warsaw and Katowice.

The airline began operating in Brașov in August 2023, shortly after the country’s newest airport opened. Since then, it has carried more than 800,000 passengers, it said.

The airline currently operates 231 routes from 14 airports in Romania, connecting passengers to 83 destinations in 26 countries.

“The opening of our tenth base in Romania is a proud moment for Wizz Air, especially after we recently celebrated 20 years of operations in the country. We are delighted to further expand our presence in Brașov by allocating a modern Airbus A321neo aircraft, launching several new routes and bringing the total number of WIZZ connections to 15,” András Radó, Head of Communications at Wizz Air, said.

Wizz Air's Romanian network began with flights from Târgu Mureș before expanding to Bucharest, Cluj-Napoca, Timișoara, Craiova, Sibiu, Iași, Constanța, Suceava, Satu Mare, Bacău, Brașov and, most recently, Oradea, where operations started in March 2026.

World.title: Romania’s land registration application e-Terra restarted after ransomware attack
World.content:
E-Terra, the application operated by the Cadastre and Land Registration Agency, or ANCPI, has been restarted in stages, beginning on Tuesday, August 11, according to an official press release. The application had been offline since mid-July after a ransomware attack.

Initially, the application will be accessed only by ANCPI personnel, the cadastre and land registration offices (OCPI), as well as public notaries.

“The restarting of the application is being carried out under the conditions established following the checks and tests performed by specialists and represents a first step towards the full resumption and normalization of cadastre and land registration activities,” the authorities said, cited by Agerpres.

The phased restart concerns exclusively the e-Terra system, the integrated IT system through which the registration, management and record-keeping of cadastre and land books are carried out at national level. The other ANCPI online platforms intended for the public remain shut down for the time being and will be brought back online gradually, with prior announcement, according to the same source.

ANCPI was targeted by a cyberattack that took the e-Terra system offline starting on July 14. Without the e-Terra system, a land registry extract could no longer be issued. As a result, real estate transactions in the country were put on hold while authorities worked to solve the problem.

Now, the registration of documents was resumed. “Personnel will have the priority task of registering documents submitted by post during the period in which the e-Terra application was not functioning; public notaries will be able to begin registering documents processed during this period and which could not be submitted through the system,” according to the statement.

“Starting Wednesday, August 12, 2026, the e-Terra application will also be available to other categories of users: persons authorized to carry out cadastre works, technical-judicial experts, judicial executors, who had access to this application before the incident occurred. For these users, user manuals and video instructional materials are being made available, intended to facilitate the resumption of activity. At the same time, working meetings and training sessions are being organized for OCPI personnel so that the resumption of activity can be carried out under the best possible conditions,” the statement mentioned.

Approximately 94,000 requests were in the process of being resolved at the time of the incident. Due to the backlog, there may be longer response times in the immediate period. To support users and provide information regarding the resumption of activity of the e-Terra application, ANCPI made dedicated Call Center telephone lines available to them. Users can get information and support at the following phone numbers: 0749012525, 0749016331, 0735 950 582.

The e-Terra application currently operates in the Government Cloud, which offers superior technical conditions compared with the infrastructure previously used.

World.title: Romania’s Constitutional Court to review biodiversity strategy law
World.content:
Romania’s Constitutional Court will review on August 12 the law implementing the National Strategy and Action Plan for Biodiversity Conservation 2026-2030, alongside the recently passed Integrity Law, with both measures linked to milestones under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR).

The biodiversity legislation was referred to the Constitutional Court by the Alliance for the Unity of Romanians (AUR) after the Parliament approved the strategy with amendments, including changes proposed by the Social Democratic Party (PSD) and criticized by environment NGOs.

Environmental organisations have criticised the final version, arguing that parliamentary amendments removed or weakened mechanisms intended to implement Romania’s biodiversity commitments.

The Federation of the Natura 2000 Coalition Romania and the Institute for Public Policies (IPP) said in a joint analysis that several amendments reduced the ambition of the strategy and, in some cases, incorrectly reproduced Romania’s existing commitments as statutory provisions.

Among the changes highlighted by the organisations is the reduction of the target for protected areas from 30% to 25%. The target for areas under strict protection was also reduced from 10% to 5%.

The amendments also changed the mechanism for removing artificial barriers from watercourses. Under the adopted version, such interventions would require a government decision and several additional approvals, according to the organisations.

The biodiversity strategy was initially approved by the government but was subsequently cancelled and transferred to Parliament following pressure from the PSD, amid concerns that the party would otherwise refer the measure to the Constitutional Court.

The Parliament adopted the National Strategy and the National Action Plan for Biodiversity Conservation 2026-2030 at the beginning of August. The legislation is considered an important PNRR milestone, with failure to complete the required reforms potentially putting associated European funding at risk.

The Constitutional Court's review comes amid wider disputes over PNRR-related legislation. The court is also examining the Integrity Law, which has been challenged over provisions concerning asset declarations by life partners and the retroactive termination of mandates held by elected officials.

World.title: Romania’s centrist parties fail to reach consensus on public sector wage law
World.content:
Romania’s centrist parliamentary parties failed to reach an agreement on the draft unitary wage law for public sector employees during talks convened by president Nicușor Dan on August 11, according to sources cited by G4Media.

The deadlock puts at risk EUR 771 million in grants under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), as the legislation is a milestone that must be adopted by August 31.

The talks brought together president Dan and the leaders of the Social Democratic Party (PSD), National Liberal Party (PNL), Save Romania Union (USR) and Democratic Alliance of Hungarians in Romania (UDMR), amid disagreements over the reform of public sector pay.

Formally, a major obstacle is the financial impact of demands made by trade unions, which are supported by the PSD, according to the cited sources. Separately, analysts argue that a more transparent and consistent framework for remuneration across the public sector could reduce the influence of trade unions, political leaders and senior public officials over discretionary bonuses and other supplements that have contributed to the complexity of the current pay structure.

The parties are continuing negotiations in an effort to find a formula that would allow the milestone to be completed by the deadline.

One option under discussion is to submit the draft law to Parliament next week or, at the latest, within two weeks, leaving limited time for its adoption before August 31.

The negotiations follow repeated warnings from the government that the deadline for completing the RRF milestone is approaching. Interim Labour Minister Dragoș Pîslaru said on August 10 that this was the final week in which a political agreement could be reached in time for the reform to be adopted and promulgated by the end of August.

World.title: Romania’s Hidroelectrica reports 62% y/y profit surge in H1
World.content:
Hidroelectrica (BVB: H2O) recorded in the first six months of 2026 operational and financial results significantly above the results recorded in the same period of 2025, against the backdrop of a normalized hydrological regime, as well as the reconfiguration of the revenue structure as a result of the increased contribution of the supply segment, the company announced on the evening of August 11 in a note to investors.

Net electricity production was 7,070 GWh, up 17% compared to H1 2025. This increase was mainly due to the hydrological conditions in the first quarter of 2026. Net profit surged by 62% y/y to RON 2.57 billion (EUR 490 million). The company's capitalisation is RON 81 bn (EUR 15.5 billion), following a 46% y/y rise in its share price.

Key results from the first semester of 2026 compared to the first semester of 2025:

Operating profit increased by 65%, up to 2,893 million RON

Net electricity production increased by 17%, to 7,070 GWh

Revenues increased by 40%, up to RON 6.05 billion

Operating margin of 48%, up 18%

Net margin of 43%, up 16%

Net profit rose by 62%, to RON 2.57 billion

Adjusted EBITDA, up 51%, to RON 3.32 billion

Earnings per share, 62% higher, at 5.72 RON/share, from 3.53 RON/share

Share price up 46% y/y to RON 180

According to the company's information, Hidroelectrica applied a prudent commercial policy, actively managed price and volume risks, and dynamically calibrated the production-purchase mix, maintaining a solid financial position and results in line with the evolution of energy markets.

"The supply portfolio continued to grow, confirming the repositioning towards a hybrid model, with stronger commercial anchoring and an expanded customer base. Market purchases increased, with market risk being managed through phased contracting and commercial discipline. Operational efficiency, optimising the production-purchase mix, developing RES and storage projects, to reduce structural exposure to hydrological variability and strengthen long-term resilience remain priorities for the group in the coming period," the report reads.

Hidroelectrica is the largest renewable energy producer in Romania, managing a portfolio of 188 hydroelectric power plants with a total capacity of 6.4 GW, as well as the Crucea wind farm, with 108 MW installed.
