“As for the legal aspect, the relevant authorities will determine that, but from a moral standpoint, what this man said is simply disgusting,” Kobakhidze said.

Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili linked Baramidze’s remarks to a broader political context. He said the opposition had previously promoted what he called a harmful narrative about Georgia’s 2008 war, and that the same was now happening with the war in Abkhazia.

Alexander Tabatadze, chairman of the parliamentary Defence and Security Committee, said Baramidze’s comments could damage Georgia’s international standing.

He argued that such remarks could be used against Georgia. Tabatadze also said the wording insulted veterans of the Abkhazia war and those who were killed in the fighting.

The opposition also criticises the remarks

Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, said Baramidze’s comments were inaccurate. However, he argued that an incorrect statement did not amount to treason.

“What was said is not true… I don’t know where this story came from. In my view, the words got ahead of the meaning, and that is not good. But treason and a crime are different things, and this is not how they are committed,” Gvaramia said.

He said he had no doubts about Baramidze’s patriotism. He described the prosecutor’s investigation as political persecution.

Shalva Kereselidze, a representative of Gakharia for Georgia, called Baramidze’s remarks politically inappropriate and unworthy of a statesman.

“This is a statement unworthy of a statesman, and it is inappropriate both politically and from a human standpoint,” Kereselidze said.

The United National Movement, meanwhile, says the investigation is entirely politically motivated. The party also pointed out that Baramidze fought in the wars in Abkhazia and Ukraine.

“While the Kremlin regards Giorgi Baramidze as an enemy and persecutes him, the Georgian Dream government is accusing the same person of treason,” the party said in a statement.

Expert: “Baramidze’s account does not match the facts”

Conflict expert and former state minister Paata Zakareishvili has questioned the factual accuracy of Baramidze’s account.

Zakareishvili himself worked on prisoner exchanges during the Abkhazia war. He said Baramidze’s account differed so sharply from the realities of the time that he initially thought Baramidze was referring to a different war.

He also disputed Baramidze’s claim that he took part in the work of the prisoner exchange commission.

“Baramidze mentions this commission, but to be honest, he did not take part in its work,” Zakareishvili said.

He noted that documents exist detailing the commission’s work, but Baramidze’s name does not appear in them.

At the same time, Zakareishvili questioned the legal grounds for the investigation. In his view, false or exaggerated statements should not provide grounds for criminal prosecution.

“I still believe that Baramidze does not deserve punishment. I will do everything I can to prove that he was not a member of the commission. His comments are simply speculation, nothing more,” Zakareishvili said.

He also said he was ready to provide the prosecutor’s office with the information he has.

How the case moved beyond the domestic political conflict

The de facto Abkhaz foreign ministry has already responded to Baramidze’s remarks.

The ministry used his comments to reinforce its own historical narrative about the conflict. Its statement described the 1992–93 war as Georgia’s armed aggression against Abkhazia.

Sukhumi also criticised the investigation into Baramidze.

“It is clear that this criminal prosecution should serve as a warning to anyone prepared to speak openly about Georgia’s armed aggression and the crimes committed during it,” the statement said.

Giorgi Baramidze case

World.title: Missed chances to save woman's life after fatal stroke misdiagnosed as migraine
World.content:
An Adelaide woman incorrectly diagnosed with a migraine was twice failed by the health system in the lead-up to her death from a stroke, according to a deputy coroner who recommended that families be given more opportunity to raise red flags when their "concerns are not being taken seriously".

Kate Marie Sylvia, a librarian for Pembroke Middle School, died in December 2021 from a cerebral venous sinus thrombosis days after she started experiencing vomiting, a stabbing head pain and slurred speech.

The 32-year-old's death was the subject of a coronial inquest which today delivered its findings, which included the "overwhelming conclusion" that her death was preventable.

Four days before Ms Sylvia died, an ambulance had taken her to an intermediate care centre at Sefton Park where a doctor gave her medication and told her to "sleep it off".

Deputy coroner Naomi Kereru found the ambulance service should have correctly assessed her symptoms and taken her straight to hospital, and that the doctor at the care centre, Lyall Henderson, should also have referred to her hospital.

"If either of those two opportunities set out above were taken, Kate would have been sent for a scan which, on the balance of probabilities, would ... then have led to an ultimate diagnosis," she said.

Kate Sylvia was incorrectly diagnosed with a migraine before she died. (Supplied)

In findings handed down today, Ms Kereru wrote that Ms Sylvia's mother Kathryn Sylvia had called the ambulance, reporting that her daughter could not "talk properly" and "sounded like a drunk person".

The deputy coroner said a paramedic who later physically assessed Ms Sylvia did "not record the speech disturbance [her mother] originally reported to the operations centre" and that, after completing his own assessment, recorded "no speech disturbance" in his clinical notes.

"He agreed that he did not have knowledge of Kate's baseline as her mother would have," the deputy coroner said.

After taking direction from the health navigator service, SA Ambulance took Ms Sylvia to an intermediate care centre at Sefton Park, which operates as one of SA Health's hospital avoidance clinics.

The deputy coroner said she was struck by the "overly complicated way in which the communication took place between the SA Ambulance Service and the hospital avoidance and supported discharge service".

"The process contributed to the loss of critical information about Kate's presentation … [and] the speech abnormalities reported by her mother," she said.

" Had this information been passed on through a more direct line of communication, evidence was heard that Kate would have been diverted to a tertiary hospital. "

The deputy coroner recounted evidence from the paramedic about his handover to the Sefton Park centre, which did not have a CT scanner.

"He said that he would be criticised if he handed over that Kate had trouble talking, but then she did not have trouble talking, so he did not mention her speech," Ms Kereru said.

Kathryn Sylvia (left) says her daughter was a beautiful soul. (ABC News: Evelyn Leckie)

Mrs Sylvia previously told the inquest her daughter was given fluids, anti-nausea medication and aspirin, before being discharged by a doctor with a migraine diagnosis.

"I said to him [the doctor], 'She doesn't normally get migraines'," she told the court.

"He said, 'She told me she gets two a year', and I said, 'No, they're not medically diagnosed migraines'."

Mrs Sylvia said when she questioned the doctor about why her daughter still sounded "groggy" and "slurry", he told her that Ms Sylvia was potentially still experiencing the "lasting effects" of green whistle pain relief medication Kate had received at the centre.

"The more fundamental issue that arose was the doctor's lack of probing on the issue of Kate's speech when specifically raised by Mrs Sylvia," Ms Kereru said.

"It is simply good medicine to take the next step of investigation to rule out the most serious condition."

'Clinicians need to listen', grieving mum says

Ms Sylvia died at the Royal Adelaide Hospital four days after her initial presentation at the Sefton Park clinic.

In her findings, Ms Kereru said Ms Sylvia was "dealing with a condition that is diagnosable on readily-available imaging and has clear treatments that have very good success rates".

The deputy coroner said that, after reviewing "competing expert evidence, the overwhelming conclusion is that Kate's death was preventable" and that two opportunities were missed.

She said that SA Ambulance should have taken Ms Sylvia straight to hospital, instead of the care centre.

"This would have involved the ambulance service correctly assessing the symptoms reported by Mrs Sylvia ... or alternatively Dr Henderson being advised of those concerning features during the intake process and declining to accept Kate," Ms Kereru said.

The deputy coroner handed down findings into Ms Sylvia's death. (ABC News: Dean Faulkner)

She said that Ms Sylvia should also have been referred to hospital from the centre.

"This would have involved Dr Henderson referring Kate to hospital after either conducting a more in-depth neurological examination than he genuinely did and detecting the severity of her condition, or alternatively probing in more detail as to whether Kate had actually been diagnosed with migraine previously, or alternatively placing sufficient weight on Mrs Sylvia's statements about Kate's condition," the coroner wrote.

The deputy coroner made several recommendations to SA Health and the SA Ambulance Service, including that "paramedics are reminded of … the importance of not filtering information about patients".

She also urged that SA Health routine training be updated, and clinicians be reminded that reports of migraine should be probed in detail and that "collateral information about a patient's presentation is valuable, particularly reports that a person being neurologically assessed is not themselves".

"SA Health should give consideration to a program to allow family members in hospitals to escalate care where they consider concerns are not being taken seriously," Ms Kereru also recommended.

Kathryn Sylvia urged clinicians to listen to family. (ABC News: Evelyn Leckie)

Outside of the SA Coroners Court today, Mrs Sylvia became emotional midway through her interview with media.

Her sister-in-law Denise Botten stepped in to support Mrs Sylvia.

"[Kate was] just a beautiful soul," Ms Botten said.

World.title: Man accused of deliberately hitting 'blameless' 12yos with ute granted bail
World.content:
A man accused of deliberately driving into two "blameless" children in Mildura's Langtree Mall has been granted bail.

Gol Gol auto electrician Andrew Brien, 56, is facing seven charges after two 12-year-old boys riding a motorised push bike were struck by a Ford ute about 11pm last Thursday night.

The charges included four counts of reckless conduct endangering life, and counts of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing injury, and driving in a dangerous manner.

On Wednesday, the Mildura Magistrates' Court heard one of the boys sustained a concussion and a sore arm after he was flung 20 metres onto a nearby street before a pole landed on him.

Andrew Brien, 56, will return to court next week for a bail application. (Supplied: Facebook)

The other boy, alleged to have been run over by the vehicle, was reported to have suffered a collapsed lung, and required surgery after breaking an arm, a leg, an ankle, his sternum, and multiple ribs, the court heard.

Court told boys not involved in incident prior to crash

The Mildura Magistrates' Court heard a business owned by Mr Brien's partner had been targeted in two criminal incidents on June 26 and 27.

In those matters, PRD Real Estate Mildura was burgled and two vehicles, keys and cash were stolen.

Police say the two young victims had not damaged any businesses on the night of the offending.

The court heard on the night of August 6, Mr Brien received a phone call from his partner who reported damage at the business about 10:30pm.

The matter was reported to police.

Police informant Detective Senior Constable Mitchell Carew told the court Mr Brien got into his car at Gol Gol, NSW, that night and drove across the border to the Mildura CBD and began patrolling the area.

Two boys seen riding a motorised pushbike down the same street the business was on were then pursued by Mr Brien.

The court heard police later examined CCTV from the business, which showed a man in his 30s with a distinctive beard and pushbike rummaging in a bin before damaging a camera at the rear of the property.

The prosecution said no attempt to brake was made before the car struck the boys' bike. (ABC News: Wade Stephens)

"I can categorically say these two boys [the victims] on this night are not involved in any offence with the business or elsewhere," Senior Constable Carew said.

'I've hit a pushbike'

Five lots of CCTV footage were shown to the Mildura Magistrates' Court, revealing what happened next.

In one video, a white Ford ute driven by Mr Brien was shown swerving to the opposite side of the road on Langtree Avenue, narrowly missing the boys and the kerbside.

The car allegedly travelled at estimated speeds of up to 79.2 kilometres per hour through Langtree Mall in Mildura. (ABC News: Wade Stephens)

Mr Brien then conducted a U-turn, pursued the bike over a speed bump and followed the pair into the pedestrian-only Langtree Mall.

Footage then showed the car driving through the mall and striking the bike at speed, moments before ramming into a light pole.

In court, the prosecution alleged no brakes were applied and that no evasive manoeuvres were taken by Mr Brien before the car struck the boys, and the ute travelled at an estimated speed of 79.2 kilometres per hour.

CCTV from after the crash showed Mr Brien stepping over a victim who was trapped under the car, and rendering no assistance.

CCTV showed the boys were followed by the white ute for about 330 metres, including through a pedestrian mall (ABC News: Wade Stephens)

The court heard the call log on Mr Brien's phone showed he had called Triple Zero (000), and then his partner.

The prosecution alleged Mr Brien told police he had run over a pushbike after claiming he had taken a wrong turn down the mall, saying "they pulled out in front of me, it's dark".

Deliberate pursuit 'grossly unjustified', court told

Prosecutor Raphael de Vietri characterised the offending as extreme and alarming, and as a deliberate pursuit that had catastrophic consequences.

"This incident in its totality is unacceptable," Mr de Vietri said.

"The actions are grossly unjustified.

"This is horrific offending, to use one's vehicle as a weapon against two 12-year-old children."

Prosecutor Raphael de Vietri argued Mr Brien was "absolutely hurtling" down Langtree Mall in a Ford ute. (ABC News: Wade Stephens)

He told the court that linking the offending to previous attacks on PRD Real Estate did the accused no favours, and "gives flavour of a deliberate, intentional, controlled act".

"This isn't a momentary snap," he said.

" He was dead set on mowing those two children down. "

Defence lawyer Paul Smallwood acknowledged Mr Brien drove in an "outrageous fashion" and that the matter was extremely serious.

Defence lawyer Paul Smallwood argued a delay in court proceedings should be part of bail considerations. (ABC News: Wade Stephens)

He argued the offending arose in a set of circumstances and that the burglaries at PRD were a relevant factor, but by no means justified the actions of his client.

Mr Smallgood argued his client was suitable for bail as he had no prior convictions, had spent his first time in custody, and a trial would likely not occur until 2028.

It was submitted Mr Brien would be highly likely too spend time in custody upon sentencing, even if acquitted of the more serious charges.

Accused to reappear in December

Magistrate Patrick Southey granted Mr Brien bail, noting he had never previously been in trouble, and was not a suspected flight risk.



He said he was largely influenced by the prospect of a lengthy delay in the court matter.

"It's outrageous, some of the commentary about the boys, who are completely blameless," Mr Southey said.



Mr Brien was bailed on the condition he not drive a car.



He must also abide by a 9pm curfew.

Andrew Brien will next appear in court in December. (Supplied: Facebook)

"It's hard to see a scenario like this arising again," Magistrate Southey said.

"If he's got any brains at all, he will keep a very, very low profile."

Several community members yelled comments outside the court precinct in protest over the bail decision.

Mr Brien will reappear before court for a committal mention on December 2.

World.title: Eli Lilly boss calls out Australia on Mounjaro and Trump over kids vaccines
World.content:
Eli Lilly pharmaceuticals CEO David Ricks says he still wants to reach an agreement with the Australian government and bring diabetes and weight loss drug Mounjaro into the Australian Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS).

The US-based pharmaceutical giant had previously walked away from a deal to have the drug listed on the PBS, due to a pricing dispute.

Despite a recommendation from the Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee (PBAC), Eli Lilly rejected that, saying the "price conditions proposed by the Australian government are unrealistic and unviable".

The April decision was one of several times Eli Lilly has attempted to have the drug added to the PBS, but the company said the price proposed was "significantly lower than any other reimbursed price globally".

Mr Ricks said Australia was not valuing the medicine properly.

"The basic problem from our standpoint is how Australia is valuing the medicine," he told 7.30.

Eli CEO Dave Ricks says a higher price is needed for Mounjaro in the Australian market. (Reuters: Antranik Tavitian)

But he did not put all the blame on the Albanese government as he called for further negotiations to help the large number of Australians with Type 2 diabetes, gain access to the drug.

"We're not [putting] all the blame on the government," he said.

"We can be flexible and think about adaptive schemes, and we're open to new schemes, but at the core of it is the value placed on the medicine.

"We definitely want Mounjaro to be listed on the PBS scheme."

Mr Ricks told 7.30 price would always be a sticking point and lowering the cost for Australia could, in his view, have global consequences.

"Australia's not an island as it comes to pricing," he said.

"So when we consider the price point, it ripples across the world and can debase the medicine everywhere, which has an effect on our ability to reinvest in R&D.

"So we're not interested in access at any price point. We think a fair price point would be good."

"There are often very robust price negotiations between big multinational drug companies and the federal government," Mr Butler said.

"That tension really and that price negotiation is a very big reason why we have such a successful and sustainable Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme."

Questions to be asked of Trump, RFK

US President Donald Trump this week issued an executive order calling for American children to be immunised against fewer diseases.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr is the US Secretary of Health and Human Services. (Reuters: Nathan Howard)

The vaccination schedule put forward by his administration recommends immunising children against 11 diseases, six fewer than what is currently recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The diseases to be dropped from the childhood immunisation schedule are: RSV, Hepatitis A, Hepatitis B, Meningococcal ACWY, Rotavirus and Influenza.

The US suffered through a large-scale Measles outbreak in 2025 and concerns have been raised about Robert F Kennedy Junior, a known vaccine sceptic being the nation's Health Secretary.

Mr Ricks said that while he was not across all the details of the executive order he hoped the US scientific community would raise concerns, especially around the notion that vaccination leads to increased rates of autism.

There is no evidence of those claims. And many people on the autism spectrum lead normal lives.

"I haven't actually read all the details of what just happened, but I would hope that the scientific community kind of raises the question," Mr Ricks said.

"Patients and parents want to know what does cause autism, that's a natural thing, but we need evidence before we take changes to the schedule.

" That would be my belief, and I'm not sure that's been produced. "

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: 'He was there': Witness rejects claim by farmer accused of triple murder
World.content:
A man who told a triple murder trial jury that he and his family were shot by Queensland cattle farmer Darryl Valroy Young has angrily rejected claims the farmer was never at the alleged shooting.

Ross Tighe, 34, was the first witness to be called in the trial of Mr Young in the Supreme Court in Townsville.

Mr Young is charged with the attempted murder of Mr Tighe and the murder of his brother Graham Tighe, mother Maree Schwarz and stepfather Mervyn Schwarz.

Mr Young has pleaded not guilty to all charges.

Mr Young is accused of killing Ross Tighe's mother, brother and stepfather. ( ABC News: Carole Howlett)

The jury trial has heard that Mr Young is accused of using a rifle to shoot the four family members when they attended the gate of his Bogie cattle property for a meeting on August 4, 2022.

Mr Young’s lawyer Anthony J Kimmins told jurors the farmer never saw the Tighes or the Schwarzes, who worked a neighbouring cattle station, on that day.

Mr Kimmins asked jurors to consider if anyone else had a motive to kill.

Mr Young's lawyer told jurors he denied ever seeing the Schwarzes or the Tighes on the day they were shot. (ABC News: Carole Howlett)

'He was there'

Mr Kimmins began his cross-examination of Ross Tighe on Tuesday afternoon and concluded it on Wednesday by suggesting Mr Young was never at the gate at the time of the alleged shooting.

“Could I suggest to you Mr Tighe that on the morning of August 4, 2022 at around 8am Darryl Young was not at the front gate of the premises but you, your brother and your parents were there?" he asked.

Defence lawyer Anthony J Kimmins (right) is representing Mr Young. (ABC News: Chloe Chomicki)

Mr Tighe raised his voice, said "he was there" and told Mr Kimmins to repeat the question.

“Darryl was at the front gate,” Mr Tighe yelled.

Earlier Mr Kimmins questioned Mr Tighe on a range of topics.

The court viewed photos of the shirt Mr Tighe was wearing on the day he said he was shot, as well as a photo of the driver's seat in the car he said he drove while wounded.

Mr Kimmins asked Mr Tighe about the absence of a bullet entry hole on his shirt and the absence of blood in the car.

“Entry holes aren’t really that big — it didn't bleed that much,” Mr Tighe said.

Mr Tighe was also asked whether he had made a civil claim against Mr Young for injuries suffered, which he confirmed.

Ross Tighe gave evidence via video link from the Mackay courthouse on Wednesday. (ABC News: Carole Howlett)

Criminal past

The court heard Mr Tighe had a history of drug use and had been charged with the possession of both cannabis and MDMA as well as obstructing police.

Mr Tighe answered questions about his criminal history but was critical of Mr Kimmins.

"Scraping the bottom of the barrel a bit," he said.

Justice Christopher Johnstone warned Mr Tighe against commenting on the line of questioning.

The court heard that after one of Mr Tighe’s convictions he lost his gun licence which he confirmed but said he could not pinpoint when that happened.

Mr Kimmins also asked Mr Tighe if he ever grew cannabis or assisted anyone to grow cannabis.

He did not answer and instead claimed legal privilege.

The Supreme Court Trial in Townsville is expected to run for three weeks. (ABC North Queensland: Rachael Merritt)

Texts shown

Text messages exchanged between Ross Tighe and his former partner, who cannot be named for legal reasons, were also shown to the court.

"What has this got to do with anything?" Mr Tighe asked.

Mr Kimmins asked if one message from Mr Tighe’s ex-girlfriend indicated the couple, who had a young child, was struggling financially while working for his family’s cattle business.

"I am stressed about having no money," the message from his then-girlfriend read.

"We were trying to save more money," Mr Tighe explained to the court.

The court was shown Mr Tighe’s tax return from 2021-22 which stated that he had earned $35,688 over 12 months with the majority of the income from his family’s business.

The court was also shown messages between the couple which made mention of physical violence and a domestic violence order (DVO).

In his evidence, Mr Tighe denied he had been physically violent towards the woman and denied that he had a DVO placed on him.

Mr Tighe finished giving evidence on Wednesday.

The trial continues.

World.title: Ex-Wallabies, league star Brian Smith dies of cancer
World.content:
Wallabies prop Angus Bell is leading the tributes for dual rugby union international and former NRL star Brian Smith, who has died aged 59.

Smith, who played six Tests for Australia in 1987 and nine for Ireland after switching allegiance, had battled cancer.

Once described by former Wallabies coach Alan Jones as one of the world's most gifted players, Smith was most recently the Head of Sport at Scots College in Sydney, where Bell and many other Wallabies graduated from.

"He was coaching at the Scots school and coached a lot of us coming through the grades and I just wanted to say it's a really sad time," Bell said from Wallabies camp in Townsville on Wednesday.

"We're wishing the best for his wife and kids. He's an avid rugby person and helped a lot of individuals in the squad and in the Wallabies today, so just sending my condolences from both the Wallabies and myself."

Australia's 999th Wallaby's Test debut Isaac Henry will run the prospect of fresh ink past his wife but is otherwise assured he can make a permanent Wallabies mark after a hard-earned debut in Osaka.

Smith, who also played 43 games for Balmain and Eastern Suburbs from 1991 to 1994, coached Bell at GPS and NSW schoolboys' level when the emerging front-rower was only 16.

"Fair to say that I wouldn't have played as good or anywhere near as good without him," Bell said.

"Me, Jeremy Williams and Will Harris from the (Western) Force were really close with him and he was a great bloke, a great father and a great coach.

"So, yeah, very sad."

After playing schoolboys' rugby for Australia, Smith made his Wallabies debut under Jones in 1987, partnering Nick Farr-Jones in the halves and bagging 18 points from a try, five conversions and a penalty in a 65-18 win over South Korea.

Australian forward Angus Bell - in Wallabies camp in Townsville - paid tribute to his former high school coach and mentor Brian Smith. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

After his playing career, Smith coached in Japan and England, where he was the national team's attack coach, and served as Australia's sevens coach.

"Brian had been very unwell in recent months and was battling an aggressive cancer," Scots College principal Dr Ian PM Lambert wrote to school colleagues.

"This is very sad news for our College community and I know it will come as a shock to many of you who knew and worked closely with him.

"Our immediate thoughts are with Brian's wife Lisa, his daughters Ruby and Santana, and his son Chilli."

AAP

World.title: Former Hurricanes cricketer jailed for abusing 15yo girl
World.content:
A former Hobart Hurricanes cricket player will serve 10 months in prison for sexually abusing a child.

WARNING: This story contains details of child sexual abuse.

Aaron William Summers, 30, pleaded guilty to two counts of penetrative sexual abuse of a young person and one count of grooming in June in the Supreme Court of Tasmania, after having previously pleaded not guilty.

In court on Wednesday, he was sentenced to two-and-a-half years in jail, suspended after 10 months, meaning he will leave prison in April next year.

Justice Helen Wood told the court that Summers met the victim at a Hobart Hurricanes cricket match in 2017.

The following month, the 15-year-old girl attended another game and spoke to Summers, who was 21 at the time.

Aaron Summers was playing for the Hobart Hurricanes when he met the 15-year-old girl. (Getty Images: Robert Prezioso)

The pair began messaging on social media, and Summers arranged to pick her up from her home later that night.

The court heard he drove her to a local primary school, laid down a blanket, and sexually abused her twice.

Justice Wood told the court that Summers knew she was under the age of 17 and at high school, but did not ask how old she was.

"She thought they were meeting to talk; in reality, she represented a sexual opportunity to him," Justice Wood said.

"She was vulnerable because of her age and innocence; he had said nothing to warn her of his real motives."

The grooming charge related to social media conversations between Summers and the girl, in which Summers sent explicit photos of himself and requested photos from her.

"As a community, we look up to sportspeople; young people are likely to admire them, see them in a positive light," Justice Woods said.

"His role as a sportsperson gave him contact with young people, and enabled the commission of his crimes; this is an aggravating factor."

In November 2021, Summers pleaded guilty to charges in the Northern Territory, including possessing and transmitting child abuse material and transmitting communication with someone under 16 with the intention of procuring the recipient to engage in, or make, sexual activity.

Summers served three years and 11 months in prison in the NT. He was arrested on the day of his release and extradited to Tasmania to face these charges.

Cricket career 'at an end'

Justice Wood said Summers had experienced social isolation, loneliness and depressive symptoms while playing cricket in Tasmania and was spending excessive time on social media.

She said once he moved to the Northern Territory, he had established a successful career playing cricket in Australia and overseas and had a high profile.

"Due to the crimes, his future as a professional cricketer is at an end," she said.

Twenty months of the sentence was suspended, meaning Aaron Summers (left) is set for release in April next year. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Justice Wood said that Summers has accepted responsibility for his crimes and understood the impact his offending has had on his victims.

In the NT, he completed an intensive sex offender treatment program, which involved over 100 sessions, in which Justice Wood told the court he engaged appropriately and gained insight into his offending.

Justice Wood said when deciding on his sentence, she considered the lengthy jail time he had already served in the NT after the Tasmanian crimes were committed, and the significant progress he has taken towards his rehabilitation.

"[The] understanding he has about the harm he has caused and he is motivated to regain his life," she said.

Justice Wood imposed a sentence of two-and-a-half years, backdated to June 28 of this year, due to the time he has spent in remand.

She suspended the last 20 months of the sentence, with strict conditions, such as obliging him to comply with his probation officers and submit to psychological treatment.

The court heard that Summers would likely return to Western Australia, where he is from and his family live, to serve out his suspended sentence once he is able to leave prison in April next year.

World.title: Coroner says off-road racing needs stronger fire safety rules
World.content:
A coroner investigating an off-road racing crash that killed two people in Victoria's north-west is recommending stronger fire safety requirements for vehicles and competitors.

On September 4, 2022, Gerald Hoekstra, 46, and Ede Taric, 50, were competing in the Desert Enduro Race at Rainbow, about 400 kilometres north-west of Melbourne, when Mr Hoekstra lost control of their vehicle and crashed into a tree.

The vehicle rolled, landed on its side and was engulfed in flames.



Two competitor teams stopped to help, and saw Mr Hoekstra attempting to exit the vehicle.

They unsuccessfully tried to douse the flames with fire extinguishers.

Both the driver, Mr Hoekstra, and passenger, Mr Taric, died at the scene.

In her investigation, Coroner Ingrid Giles explored the circumstances that caused the crash and subsequent fire, the attempts to extinguish the fire, associated safety equipment, and the ability of the men to exit their vehicle after the crash.

Ms Giles found that both men had survived the initial crash, but died when fire "rapidly engulfed the vehicle".

She found the fire could not be extinguished until the local Country Fire Authority (CFA) arrived 12 to 13 minutes later, and said that their deaths were "unspeakably tragic".

Fire extinguishers 'inadequate', coroner finds

The men had been racing in a modified Can-Am Maverick X3 side-by-side buggy, which could reach speeds of 130km/h and had been fitted with hand-held fire extinguishers as well as two auxiliary 35-litre fuel tanks.

In her report, Ms Giles said the vehicle had been inspected by a scrutineer on the Friday prior to racing, and was confirmed to be compliant with requirements laid out by Motorsport Australia (MSA).

During the investigation, Victoria Police's arson chemist, forensic officer John Kelleher, said the fire was likely caused by heat from the buggy's catalytic converter igniting fuel that had spilled around the vehicle after the crash.



"Having seen the buggy and watched the video footage of the fire starting, there is no doubt that the cause of the fire was the ignition of petrol vapour rising from the spilled fuel puddling beneath the filler," Mr Kelleher said at the time.

"The position of the catalytic converter and its location immediately above the spilled fuel raises the possibility that it was the source of ignition."

The Desert Enduro car race was held at Rainbow in north-west Victoria. (Motorsport Australia)

Ms Giles found the fuel tanks had been installed correctly, and were compliant with safety requirements at the time.

However, the tanks had a plastic fuel cap and filler neck that protruded from the buggy's safety cage, leaving them "vulnerable to damage", she said.

Upon collision, the cap detached from the filler neck on one of the tanks, which did not contain a reflux valve — a one-way valve that automatically closes if the tank is up-ended.

Ms Giles said given the filler neck was not fitted with a reflux valve, petrol flowed freely and was able to combust easily.

"I consider that, had a reflux valve been present, the fire would have most likely been prevented, in that the fuel would not have spilled freely from the tank,” she said.

MSA regulations at the time required each competing vehicle to be fitted with a hand-held fire extinguisher, which Ms Giles found to be "inadequate" given the fire could not be safely extinguished without the CFA's help.

Ms Giles said a plumbed-in fire extinguisher system may have been more effective.

“Plumbed-in systems are primarily designed to provide the occupants with an immediate extinguisher response that can increase the amount of time available to extricate from the vehicle during an incident, and limit the effect of the fire on the occupant," she said.

Decisive action

At the time of the event, MSA also required vehicles to be designed so racing crews could exit their vehicle within 10 seconds during an emergency.

However, it was up to competitors to comply with the requirement, which was "not formally assessed".

“At the time of Gerald and Ede’s collision, there was no mandatory self-extrication time frame, and no testing was performed of competitors' ability to do so," the coroner found.

Ms Giles credited MSA for making changes following Mr Hoekstra's and Mr Taric's deaths, and said its decisive action had "obviated the need for an extensive suite of coronial recommendations".

Since the incident, MSA has mandated reflux valves in fuel tanks, banned any structures protruding outside safety cage structures, and doubled the required capacity for hand-held fire extinguishers for off-road racing events.

Ms Giles said that while MSA had introduced the implementation of mandatory plumbed-in fire extinguisher systems, an extended roll-out period of three years risked competitors' lives.

"The lives of off-road racing competitors who do not already have such a system remain at greater risk in the event of a fire – and, in my view, unnecessarily so," she said.

The coroner recommended that before the end of the 2026 racing season, MSA and the Australian Auto-Sport Alliance should require all off-road vehicles participating in sanctioned off-road events to be fitted with plumbed-in fire extinguisher systems.

She recommended mandatory testing of all competitors involved in racing competitions to ensure each occupant could self-extricate within 10 seconds.

Ms Giles also recommended MSA develop improved guidance for race organisers as to what constitutes "appropriate firefighting equipment" at the paddock areas of an event.

World.title: Gun clubs should be trained to detect radicalisation, inquiry told
World.content:
Gun clubs must be better equipped to spot the signs of radicalisation in members who may risk committing violent acts, a shooting organisation official and psychologist says.

Witnesses before the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion have this week painted a picture of the tools available to disrupt someone on the path to radicalisation.

Daniel Gregg works with people at various stages of radicalisation in his work as a psychologist in New South Wales, and is also the secretary of a shooting association.

He said gun clubs were uniquely positioned to intervene early in a person's path to radicalisation, and should be trained to detect the warning signs.

"If you taught clubs to notice those things and then refer those to the more appropriate pathways that we could be preventing further radicalisation," he said.

"We don't want bad actors in our organisations … because we wear the collective consequences if something goes wrong.

"Clubs are often called to coronial inquests and the last thing I wanted to do was be called to a coronial inquest and I hadn't done enough."

People becoming radicalised in weeks, inquiry told

Mr Gregg said he had implemented a behavioural screening framework at his own gun club, which involved a prospective member being interviewed and assigned a mentor to guide them through club and legislative requirements for firearms owners.

Commissioner Virginia Bell AC SC put to Mr Gregg that further firearms restrictions may be needed as part of the response to the Bondi Beach terror attack.

"It may be that Australia would be better off if it had a more restrictive approach to people being able to obtain a licence to use, albeit at a sporting club, weapons of the kind that were used at Bondi," she said to him.

Mr Gregg disagreed more firearms restrictions were needed. (Facebook: Rothwell Professional Industry Indoor Pistol Club)

Mr Gregg said he disagreed.

"A lot of what I am seeing from those on extremist pathways is that people can come through because they are self-radicalising, they have no [criminal] background … they have no markers that law enforcement would be able to pick up," he said.

"If you had more stricter pathways, you would still have people who would meet the requirements and get through, and they'd still be vulnerable to radicalisation."

In his work as a psychologist, Mr Gregg said he had previously observed people who were recruited by an extremist network typically became radicalised over a period of 12 to 18 months.

He said that shifted post-COVID, with people who self-radicalised becoming committed to an ideology in as little as two to four weeks.

Public awareness push for support helpline

The inquiry has also considered initiatives to help people spot the signs of radicalisation in their workmates, friends and family.

Through its website and helpline, Step Together directs people to resources about violent extremism, and general services which may offer support.

Countering violent extremism expert Michelle Grossman conducted a review of the program, which is run in NSW and delivered across the country.

Professor Grossman said Step Together played an important role in the countering violent extremism landscape, but not enough people knew about its existence.

"I actually think we need a saturation campaign around violent extremism in Australia," she said.

Michelle Grossman has called for a widespread awareness campaign. (Supplied: Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion)

"Violent extremists do not arrive from another planet, they are not beamed down on a spaceship, they are ordinary people in families, in our workplaces and in our schools.

"If we do not have the public awareness to be able to recognise and take steps towards addressing harms on many levels, then I believe we are doing ourselves a national disservice."

Professor Grossman said such an awareness campaign must be widespread, instead of isolated to certain groups.

"I feel quite strongly that the softly, softly approach, that more refined targeted approach, I think we're past that point," she said.

"I think some of the tragic and horrific events that we've seen recently in Australia have really clarified that for me. I don't think that we can afford anymore to have that."

'Tunnel vision' for extremism

NSW Department of Communities and Justice director Heather Jackson said work was underway to raise the profile of Step Together.

She also discussed the role of the state's Engagement and Support program in helping people and families vulnerable to violent extremist influence.

Ms Jackson said the age of eligibility for the program had been lowered from 14 to 10 in recent years to respond to the growing demand for the service.

"Unfortunately, in the last few years the landscape was indicating that there were young people, children 10 years and above, that were indicating capacity, capability and willingness to undertake a violent extremist event," she said.

Ms Jackson said the program worked to foster a sense of connection and belonging in participants who had developed "tunnel vision" for ideologically motivated extremism.

World.title: Is 30 minutes in this room the secret to beating stress and burnout?
World.content:
NationalQueenslandStress management Is 30 minutes in this room the secret to beating stress and burnout? Courtney Kruk August 12, 2026 — 8:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The $6.8 trillion global wellness industry knows how to capitalise on a moment, and right now, it’s attuned to the fact that people are feeling increasingly stressed and burnt out. It’s why I wasn’t surprised when a video came across my feed for a new wellness clinic in Brisbane offering “Australia’s first high-tech nervous system reset studio”. Like stress and burnout, nervous system dysregulation is a hot topic, and in the information age, once a trend seeps into the collective consciousness, you know a fix is waiting in the wings. Cheatcode Playground is a new wellness studio to combat stress, burnout and fatigue in Brisbane’s Fortitude Valley. Cheatcode Playground While I’m cynical about capitalism’s encroachment on the wellness industry and the pseudoscientific claims underpinning many products and practices, I suffer from stress and am perpetually exhausted.



If 30 minutes on a vibrating chair in a dark room could make a difference, I was willing to try it. What is Cheatcode Playground? Founded by Lachy and Renee Huddy, Cheatcode Playground is described as a recovery and performance centre in Fortitude Valley that uses specialised equipment “to shift how your body and mind are operating”. Each treatment room is fitted with the same devices: a vibration chair, a light-and-sound lamp, and a cellular recovery device. These are used in combination with a guided breathing program. You don’t need any prior experience and the team will tailor the session – which runs for 18 or 30 minutes – to your needs, whether that’s stress relief, energy, or a general “reset”.



For whatever reason, Cheatcode emphasises that you stay fully clothed throughout the session. The devices The tech used isn’t new, but Lachy says his team is the first in Australia to combine these specific devices in a commercial setting. The main device – the Shiftwave vibrating chair – retails for about $10,000. Not the kind of wellness gadget the average punter can afford.



According to its makers, Shiftwave uses “pulsed pressure waves and breath-guided audio to support the body’s natural stress and recovery responses, working below conscious effort to help you feel calm, clear, or ready when it matters most”. While you can control the intensity of the vibrations, it takes a minute to get used to the feeling that you might pulsate off the chair at any moment. The audio component of Shiftwave is essentially a guided meditation with breath work – someone telling you when to breathe, and at what pace and level of intensity. The Shiftwave chair combines guided breathing with low-frequency vibroacoustic stimulation. Shiftwave This happens under a stroboscopic lamp called the “roXiva RX1”. Positioned over your face, the lamp looks like an epileptic’s worst nightmare, but the idea is to close your eyes and allow flickering lights and timed sounds to guide your brainwaves into alpha and theta states.



Depending on the program, you’ll see different colours, patterns and imagery – not dissimilar to a psychedelic experience. The final device – the “NanoVI” – delivers humidified air to speed up cellular repair. After the session, Renee, who doubles as Cheatcode’s “Beverage Alchemist” whips up a coffee with a bunch of ingredients anyone who’s stepped into a Flannerys health food store would be familiar with. What the founders say Before launching their business, Renee and Lachy managed a thoroughbred farm on the Sunshine Coast, and in 2024, they wrote, produced and acted in a feature film. The stress of making the film motivated them to create Cheatcode, which opened in June.



Travis Wesley, Cheatcode’s client flow director and front-of-house manager, has a background in theatre. Lachy says they’re not making any scientific claims about what the tech can do, but they believe they’ve created a genuine experience that can combat a range of concerns. Cheatcode Playground founders Renee and Lachy Huddy, and Client Flow Director Travis Wesley. Courtney Kruk “What we sell is the shift,” Lachy says. “The world that we have constructed is simply not good for the human nervous system. Stress is a natural part of life; constant stress is not.



“The issue is no one can switch off any more … and that’s part of what we want to address.” Related Article Perspective

Trends Neck-deep in freezing water in West End, I wanted the cold truth Renee says the beginner-friendly nature of the service is part of its appeal, with many people struggling to master activities that help them switch off. “[A lot of people] find meditation really hard. It’s one more skill to learn,” she says. “I find it funny that we have invented all of this tech to just take us back to if we lived as cavemen, not doing all of these things. That’s the state we’re trying to get to.”



Wesley adds that the $59 service (for first-time users) is accessible to those who would never otherwise afford the devices. “We want it to be accessible because everyone has burnout,” he says. What the research says Studies exploring controlled breath work practices show it can reduce stress and anxiety and improve mood. The roXiva light lamp offers drug-free psychedelic trips. It’s a fun experience but the scientific benefits are unclear. roXiva



Stroboscopic light stimulation research is emerging, but there is some evidence that consistent use can impact depression, insomnia and cognitive functions such as memory and attention. Related Article Wellbeing Beware the bad advice: With huge profits on the line, our wellness pin-ups have changed Research conducted by Shiftwave, including on police officers and first-responders, has shown positive results, with participants reporting lower work-related stress after sessions, and reduced tension. But this has not been peer-reviewed, so take it with a grain of salt. There’s no evidence for Cheatcode Playground’s approach of using all the devices in unison, only studies supporting the tech in isolation. The verdict



Parts of the session that I was sure would be uncomfortable and overstimulating – like the lamp – were pleasantly surprising. Other aspects bordered on too intense or were distracting. Related Article Mental health ‘Not snowflakes’: Severe mental disorders surge among young people At times my mind, which I had hoped would enter a blissful state of surrender, wandered incessantly, and there were moments where I felt panicked about work or things around the house that needed fixing. I felt a buzz immediately after the session, a bit like stepping off a rollercoaster, and I was grateful to be quarantined from my devices for 30 minutes. While I was optimistic that the session would result in an exceptional night’s sleep and unlock creative excellence, that wasn’t my experience, and the stress and anxiety I tried to overcome returned with a vengeance the next day.



Maybe if the schedules were reversed – a session after a particularly stressful event – the outcome would have been different. After only one session, it’s hard to deliver a concrete verdict. I’m not sure I’ll be back, but would recommend the experience to the wellness-curious crowd. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Finks sergeant-at-arms works on North East Link, court hears
World.content:
NationalVictoriaBuilding Bad Finks sergeant-at-arms works on North East Link, court hears Lachlan Abbott August 12, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The alleged sergeant-at-arms of an outlaw motorcycle gang accused of being part of a trio who threatened a man with a gun has a job working on North East Link, a court has heard. Dylan Mallia, 28, faced the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday charged with affray after a confrontation at a house in Harkness. The Finks are a notorious outlaw motorcycle gang. LUIS ENRIQUE ASCUI He applied for bail, leading to his partner testifying in court that he was employed as a machine operator for Symal on the Carroll government’s $26 billion North East Link project. Former premier Jacinta Allan previously declared there was “no evidence” bikies had cashed in on the road project as she defiantly stared down calls for a royal commission into the Big Build.



But Mallia’s partner said he had worked for Symal for “five or six years”, as his defence lawyer argued his stable employment was a reason he should be granted bail. Mallia’s partner said she was aware he was part of the Finks bikie gang. Victoria’s North East Link road project is expected to open in 2028. Jason South Police allege Mallia, Isekeli Walls and another unknown person pulled up at a house on Indigo Link in a Ford Ranger and threatened a man in the property’s driveway on June 30. A police summary of allegations read out in court said CCTV had captured the unidentified person producing a silver handgun and pointing it at the victim.



Mallia and Walls then allegedly went back to their vehicle and returned with a black bag and a glass bottle. The victim armed himself with a knife, police say. A police prosecutor said Mallia picked up a ladder from the front of the property and threatened the resident with it before the trio drove away. The special operations group arrested Mallia and Walls on Tuesday. The latter appeared at the Wyndham Magistrates’ Court earlier on Wednesday and did not apply for bail. Magistrate Gerald Lethbridge released Mallia back into the community on the grounds he could spend more time awaiting trial than a potential sentence for affray. Police had opposed bail, alleging Mallia was an unacceptable risk and was the sergeant-at-arms of the Finks’ West End chapter.



“The current offending is brazen, unsophisticated and shows a contempt for the law,” the police prosecutor said. “He simply does not care for the consequences of his actions.” Lethbridge said the prosecution “will not have a lot of difficulty” proving Mallia was at the Harkness home, but noted his defence might argue he was unaware or not complicit in his co-accused brandishing a weapon. “Of course, it’s very premature,” Lethbridge said, “but it is an overwhelming prosecution case in terms of the most serious and aggravated aspects of it.” North East Link and Symal were contacted for comment.
