World.title: ‘Are we being completely gaslit?’ The slow and then sudden demise of an A-League champion
World.content:
SportSoccerAustralian soccer ‘Are we being completely gaslit?’ The slow and then sudden demise of an A-League champion Bridget McArthur August 12, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On a cold, grey day in Melbourne, between a cow paddock and a housing estate, the dream of an A-League soccer club for the west was being dismantled piece by piece. Over the past year, Western United has rivalled Forty Winks for the number of times it has been declared on the brink of closing down, yet fans, staff and players have remained optimistic. Removalists took what they could from Western United’s home ground on Tuesday after the club was wound up in insolvency. Jason South On Tuesday, the sword of Damocles finally dropped. The club was wound up in insolvency with a liquidator appointed in Federal Court, one day after the Australian Professional Leagues (APL) terminated its licence, citing several breaches to its participation agreement. Within hours, removalists entered the club’s home ground in Tarneit, taking what they could on the instructions of receiver Alvarez and Marsal, which recently took control of Western United’s parent company, WMG Holdings, on behalf of Johnson Controls, which had lent money to the club’s owners and is now seeking to recoup costs.



Vusumizi Gumbo watched from the sidelines, shaking his head. His two sons, 16-year-old Akim and 12-year-old Amiel, were supposed to be training there that night as part of Western United’s academy – one of Victoria’s largest and most affordable elite soccer pathways – which has continued operating out of Ironbark Fields and competing in the Victorian Premier League (VPL) while the A-League men’s and women’s teams have been in hibernation. Gumbo said the club had made a positive difference in Melbourne’s multicultural western suburbs. Vusumizi Gumbo’s two sons, who are academy players for Western United, have been left in limbo after the club was wound up. Jason South “There are coaches here giving their time for free to coach these kids,” he said. “It’s not only about kicking football. They are trying to instil values that are important into the community.” In recent weeks, as things have crumbled around them, the aspiring footballers have continued to train. People involved with the club have paid from their own pockets to keep the generators running.



Senior academy player Mark Leonard said it had been a strange year, with coaches and more than a dozen teammates leaving midway through, but several had stuck it out. “I think we’re 11th, but the past couple weeks we’ve been fighting, we’ve been doing really well for the situation we’ve been put in … I don’t think anyone expected us to keep up the fight,” the 20-year-old said. When this masthead spoke to Leonard on Wednesday afternoon, he believed the team would be allowed to play out the remainder of the season, with only three matches left. But just a few hours later, academy players and their families received an email informing them they had played their last games together. Football Victoria said that, as the club was being wound up in insolvency, a number of policies and regulations had been triggered that could not be overcome or breached. “Ultimately, this means WUFC teams will not be able to play further FV competition fixtures this season or into the future, effective immediately,” Football Victoria’s chief executive Dan Birrell wrote. “We know this news marks the end of an era; but we know the friendships and bond of your football community will endure.” Reacting to the news, Gumbo said he was devastated. “Tears in my house,” he said.



Tradespeople have been busy pulling apart Ironbark Fields this week after Western United was officially wound up. Jason South Loyal staff left out of pocket Academy players, staff and fans have been in limbo this past year. While almost every external indicator has pointed to the club’s imminent collapse – the dissolution of its A-League teams, the dire financial situation of its parent company and directors – the club’s higher-ups reassured them time and again: Western United, a club that produced a champion men’s team and a grand finalist women’s team in just a few years, was here to stay. As recently as last week, current and former employees – many of whom are owed more than six months’ worth of back pay – were holding out hope that one of several wealthy white knights who had expressed interest in buying the club might pull through with a rescue deal. Even after the licence was terminated, Western United continued to push an optimistic narrative, releasing a statement on Monday saying that it marked “a significant moment in our history and the beginning of a new chapter”.



“Over recent months, we have worked closely with the APL on a pathway that gives the club the best opportunity to survive, rebuild and return to the A-League under new ownership,” it said. Western United won the 2022 A-League Men grand final. Getty Australia “This creates an opportunity for new custodians, new investment and a fresh start. The objective must now be to preserve Western United’s identity in Melbourne’s west and work towards a return to the A-League for the 2027/28 season.” Staff, however, took a less rosy view. While there is a strong possibility the APL could resell the licence to one of the buyers who had previously expressed interest, and potentially reboot Western United under the same name in the same location, former employees will remain out of pocket. Related Article A-League Men Control of A-League club stripped from businessman alleged to have stolen millions from Scott Pendlebury



The club being wound up means staff have to recover lost entitlements via the federal government’s Fair Entitlements Guarantee. Under this scheme, they are entitled to recoup up to 13 weeks in unpaid wages, annual leave, long service leave, and a capped amount of redundancy pay. It does not cover unpaid superannuation, nor workers on temporary visas. One employee, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said he had not been paid for about six months and was owed roughly $30,000, some of which he would not get back. “Thankfully, I’m still living at home,” he said. “I don’t have bills, dependants, things like that, so aside from rapidly declining mental health, living-wise, I haven’t really been impacted. But others have. There are single parents, parents of young children, who have lost significant amounts in back pay and super.” Another former staff member, also speaking on the condition of anonymity, said as much as she was frustrated by the situation, she felt Steve Horvat – the former Socceroo who founded the club and remained a director until the end – had been doing everything he could to keep the club together. “Steve is probably wearing rose-coloured glasses. His dream has been this club,” she said.



“But then, we’ve been told for months and months it would be OK, so we didn’t go to media or get lawyers involved. And it’s like, are we being completely gaslit? “And what was that statement? How can they say this isn’t the end for the club? Unless part of the plan is that Western [United] will continue under different ownership … It would be a weird situation if a billionaire takes over, and it’s bustling in the future and these 40-odd staff have just been screwed over … I feel for the fans, too. The fans we did have were so passionate … It was an important club for the west.” Downfall of a dream While Western United was Horvat’s dream, it was Jason Sourasis – then a player manager for athletes including AFL legend Scott Pendlebury – who was largely bankrolling the project, including the wider Wyndham Stadium Precinct that was central to the club’s long-term future. Pitched as a combined sporting, entertainment, health and retail precinct in Melbourne’s west, featuring a 15,000-seat soccer stadium, it secured the backing of the City of Wyndham, which owns the land.



But WMG Holdings subsequently altered the proposal to be more within its means – changes the council rejected, issuing a default notice for its failure to deliver the precinct in line with what was agreed. The redevelopment of Ironbark Fields in Tarneit was central to the club’s future. Getty Images In a statement on Tuesday, Wyndham City’s director of corporate services, Mark Rossiter, said the council had gone “above and beyond” to afford the company “significant flexibility”, but it had failed to rectify the issues, which constituted a “serious breach” of the development agreement. He said the council had made the call to terminate the deal following the APL’s decision to pull the club’s licence. With the club and precinct project both in tatters, it is still unclear exactly what went so badly wrong for the club and almost everyone affiliated with it to lose significant amounts of money. The co-directors of both parent company and club, Sourasis and Horvat, are also victims after borrowing money to prop up Western United. As of March last year, Horvat owed the ATO close to $11 million – he never filed a defence and a default judgment was entered against him – while Sourasis has been embroiled in several lawsuits with angry creditors seeking recompense including Pendlebury, who alleges Sourasis invested his money in the club without his consent.



Sourasis denies the allegations and is defending the claims. Horvat declined to comment. Western United was a dream of former Socceroo Steve Horvat, pictured here playing in a match between Scotland and Australia in 1996. Getty Images Alvarez and Marsal’s senior director of restructuring, Daniel Linaker, said the biggest asset the club owned was the licence, which was bought for about $18 million but was now worth about $10 million. With that terminated, he said, there were minimal assets that could be recovered. Related Article A-League Men ‘We are sorry’: Players released as Western United placed in A-League ‘hibernation’ mode Equipment collected from the club this week was worth up to $200,000, he said – small fry compared with the $74 million debt owed. Much of the club’s money was spent on infrastructure on council land which could not be extracted.



Linaker said it was highly likely the majority of money would not be recovered. An APL spokesman said it had given the club as much time as it could to work through its financial, governance and legal matters. He said the governing body could not share specifics about the breaches mentioned in its statement that led to the club losing its licence. As for the licence, the APL said its board was considering what to do with it. Speculation regarding South Melbourne buying it have been dismissed by sources close to the APL. The National Soccer League club – which has faced its own financial battles over the years, including a period of voluntary administration – has been agitating for a seat at the table since the A-League was established two decades ago. Despite everything that has occurred, and the ongoing questions around his team’s future, Leonard holds out hope.



“I still do have a lot of faith in that the club will return … My dream would be to play for Western United one day.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The $4 million Sydney mansion facing partial demolition after bitter council feud
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWProperty development The $4 million Sydney mansion facing partial demolition after bitter council feud Carrie Fellner August 12, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney builder Christopher Ghaleb was convinced he was onto a winner. Cap in hand, he fronted the judges on Channel Ten’s Shark Tank to spruik his start-up in 2018. Dubbed “Lifesize Plans”, it offered home owners a life-size version of their project to walk through before construction. Christopher Ghaleb and his Strathfield build on the suburb’s “golden mile”. Artwork: Monique Westermann Sporting a hot-pink hard hat as television cameras tailed him around his building site, Ghaleb explained it would resolve the same problem he encountered on almost every job: having to change things after they were already built. But fast-forward eight years, and the entrepreneurial builder’s own home on Strathfield’s “golden mile” has become a case study in the very problem he set out to avoid.



Ghaleb has agreed to demolish and rebuild parts of his dream home to resolve one arm of a court battle with Strathfield Council, which has accused him of building it without valid approvals and relying on a certifier with a conflict of interest. The increasingly bitter brawl with the council has culminated in police applying for an apprehended violence order against Ghaleb to protect a senior council officer. Christopher Ghaleb’s new home occupies an irregular shaped block on Llandilo Avenue. Sam Mooy Ghaleb, 36, has been charged with stalking and intimidating Dylan Porter, the council’s former acting director of planning and environment. It comes after a rapid rise for Ghaleb and his wife, Cindy, who have recently completed a series of high-end property redevelopments and now have a portfolio worth nearly $16 million.



The jewel in the crown is “Wellings”, labelled one of the inner west’s most significant heritage estates, bought by Cindy Ghaleb for $7.5 million in 2021. Ghaleb would not comment on the AVO application and intimidation charges while they were before the courts, but defended his actions in relation to the Llandilo Avenue property. Construction is still under way at the Llandilo Avenue site. Sam Mooy “I think a couple of heritage houses next door, they didn’t want it, so they brought a fight to me,” he told the Herald. Ghaleb said the court dispute over the development had been resolved because he had reached a compromise with the council in the Land and Environment Court in February.



Ghaleb said he agreed to “minor” changes to the home to keep the peace with the council. “We agreed to lose less than 3 per cent of the floor area,” he said. According to a court judgment, the changes include demolishing walls to increase setbacks, deleting the arch columns from the entryway, introducing additional landscaping and privacy treatments on the windows, and changing the finishes to complement the streetscape’s heritage. But a Strathfield Council spokesperson denied the matters were resolved. “The Class 4 proceedings regarding the same property have not been discontinued at this stage,” they said.



Class 4 proceedings are civil enforcement proceedings in which councils can ask the Land and Environment Court to remedy or restrain breaches of planning laws. The spokesperson noted a Building Information Certificate (BIC) had been issued for the property in June. The certificates protect unauthorised works from demolition for seven years. The saga has sparked anger and indignation on Llandilo Avenue, with several neighbours making public submissions to the council in protest. They argued the house did not sit within the heritage fabric of the street, intruded on neighbours’ privacy and retrospective approvals should not be granted legitimising unlawful works. The controversy is the latest flashpoint in an ongoing debate about whether the NSW planning regime does enough to prevent unauthorised development.



Just streets away, Strathfield Council has been fighting for years for the demolition of a mansion that was found to have been unlawfully built. Critics argue the private certification system, together with building information certificates, can allow unauthorised building work to be carried out and remain standing even when councils argue it should never have been built in the first place. Local Government NSW (LGNSW) represents the state’s councils, which are responsible for assessing the merits of BICs. LGNSW has been lobbying the state government to review the framework for BICs, arguing growing numbers of home owners are misusing them for “approving” unauthorised works. A Department of Planning spokesperson disputed that claim, saying statewide data showed no upward trend in BICs.



The spokesperson said recent reforms would ease the pressure on councils in relation to BICs by simplifying the process to make compliance easier and creating a clearer process for regulatory action and retrospective approval for unauthorised works, where appropriate. Related Article Investigation

Development outrage Fury as Sydneysiders build their mansions, then ‘ask forgiveness later’ “The reforms also introduce new offences for carrying out building work without an approval or contrary to an approval,” the spokesperson said, noting they carried maximum penalties of up to $220,000 for individuals and $1.1 million for businesses. Asked about the use of BICs, Ghaleb said he was no longer involved in development work but said it had been common for builders to use them in the past. “Builders would say, ‘I’ll do what I want,’ and then [get] a building information certificate,” he said.



“[I] wouldn’t be trying that these days, especially with Strathfield Council. They’re not there to muck around.” Purple patch While the Sharks failed to bite during Ghaleb’s television appearance, Lifesize Plans soon began to get noticed. By 2021, the business was expanding overseas, attracting glowing press coverage and had collected high-profile board members. But within a few years the company was struggling to stay afloat: it entered voluntary administration at the end of 2024 and had to be salvaged via a deed of company arrangement. In his report, administrator Daniel Frisken found the company became insolvent on June 30, 2023.



Frisken said the remaining sole director, Raymond Sheikh, had told him the business’s demise was due to the misappropriation of franchise deposits, excessive overspending, mismanagement of the company’s business and a claim brought by a creditor. Frisken said the director had not substantiated those claims with documentation, but his review of the books and records indicated the company had traded at a loss since its incorporation. Christopher Ghaleb promoting his invention on Nine News. Ghaleb has since attributed his business difficulties to severe personal trauma. In March, he told the NSW Personal Injury Commission’s review panel that he “never returned to normal and never returned to work” after developing post-traumatic stress disorder from witnessing a fatal car accident at Huntleys Point in 2019.



Ghaleb told the Herald he had stepped away from the business due to personal issues and wasn’t involved in its failure. “I wasn’t following their struggle too much at all,” he said. Sheikh said it was unfair to attribute the company’s difficulties to one individual or to characterise what occurred solely as mismanagement. He said the loss of Ghaleb’s active involvement following the accident had left those running the company with the difficult task of continuing a specialised concept “without full access to the person who had conceived [it]”. Sheikh said that, since becoming involved in 2024, he had worked to settle debts, repay franchisees and put the company on a sustainable footing, with the rebuilding process now “progressing successfully”.



Splash in the neighbourhood As his business fortunes faded, Ghaleb and his wife turned their attention to property redevelopment. In 2024, Ghaleb arrived with a splash in the neighbourhood, paying $4.1 million for a knock-down rebuild on Llandilo Avenue. Many of the street’s homes are a time capsule of the arts and crafts design era that championed natural materials and ornate details. The homes still reflect “Strathfield’s legacy as a suburb of grand homes for Sydney’s elite”, a planning document said.



Ghaleb soon set about demolishing his home, which was at the end of a long driveway and tucked behind two heritage-listed mansions, one of which was designed by renowned architect Thomas Pollard Sampson. One of the heritage-listed homes on Llandilo Avenue. Sitthixay Ditthavong To the astonishment of neighbours, a new home began to materialise where the driveway itself formerly stood. It featured a Mediterranean-inspired aesthetic, embellished with rendered white archways. Ghaleb’s consultants argued the nine-metre-wide street frontage could more than accommodate the new home, which was within a “streetscape that has undergone significant transformation due to the construction of contemporary dwellings”.



Ghaleb said he hadn’t broken any rules by relocating the house, but the decision had surprised the council. An artist’s impression of the home filed with council prior to the court verdict. “For the past 50 years [the house was] at the back,” he said. “They wouldn’t expect a house at the front.” One neighbour was blindsided. “When demolition commenced, I contacted council and was told no application for demolition or development was on record,” the neighbour said in a public submission.



The project has instead been approved by a private certifier under the state government’s fast-track complying development pathway. The rear of the house, which now extends all the way to the street front. Sam Mooy Complying development certificates (CDCs) allow straightforward projects that meet prescribed standards to bypass the traditional development application process. But Strathfield Council is now fighting to have the CDC declared invalid in the Land and Environment Court. It issued a stop work order at the site in mid-2025 and filed documents with the court that have been obtained by the Herald.



In them, the council argued the dwelling failed to meet the gross floor area and minimum setbacks allowable under a CDC and its basement amounted to an unapproved third storey. Related Article Exclusive

Development outrage Tear it down or go to jail: Council escalates fight with owner of unlawful Sydney mansion The council also alleged the CDC should be struck out because of a conflict of interest. The certifier, Sandres Markhani, and his colleague, James Wardan, both presented themselves as employees of Sydney Wide Certifiers, according to the council. However, Wardan prepared the architectural plans under a different company he owned and controlled called Syd Consulting Pty Ltd, the council alleged.



“A fair-minded observer might reasonably apprehend that because of Mr Markhani’s association with Mr Wardan, Mr Markhani might not bring an impartial mind to the determination of the application for the CDC,” the council said. Related Article Development outrage The illegal mansion, the court case and the silent witness Neither Markhani nor Wardan responded to the Herald’s request for comment. Ghaleb denied he used a certifier with a conflict of interest. “People throw 300 things at something and hope two or three stick,” he said.



Private certifiers have a responsibility to take action if they identify unauthorised work, and the NSW Building Commission can take disciplinary action against them if they fail to do so. In recent weeks, Ghaleb has been busy finishing the outstanding construction works, estimated to be worth nearly half a million dollars. The stalking and intimidation matter returns to Burwood Local Court in October. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Chiropractor who sparked outrage for cracking newborn baby’s spine now convicted sex offender
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Sarah Rose was a young aspiring ballerina, chiropractor Dr Ian Rossborough had a reputation among Melbourne’s elite dance world as a “Mr Fix-It” for injuries. She first met Rossborough for a torn hamstring when she was just 10 years old, following an injury that occurred as a result of a gruelling dance training regimen and trying to perfect her turnout. Sarah Rose, was sexually assaulted by chiropractor Dr Ian Rossborough when she was a teenager. Steven Siewert Rose says that Rossborough, who shot to prominence a decade ago when he was accused of dangerously cracking the spine of a four-day-old baby, told her he admired her discipline and maturity and said he wanted to help her achieve her dream of being a professional ballet dancer. He recommended she see him every four to six weeks for ongoing treatments and chiropractic manipulations. Rose, who gave permission for her name to be published, was one of several young Melbourne dancers who were treated by Rossborough over many years. She is also one of at least two women who have accused him of grooming and sexual abuse when they were children.



Sarah Rose was groomed and sexually assaulted by chiropractor Dr Ian Rossborough as a teenager. “He had this belief that he was very much the best and the most important in the world at what he does and we as dancers were lucky to have him in our corner and supporting us,” Rose, who is now 25, says. Last September, the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court found Rossborough guilty of four counts of sexual assault and grooming of a child aged 16 to 17 for an assault on Rose. Related Article Healthcare Call for age limit after chiropractor breaks baby's neck He was given a two-year Community Correction Order and is now a convicted sex offender. Rossborough was suspended from working as a chiropractor by the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) last year and has surrendered his registration. This masthead can reveal that another alleged victim, who was also a young dancer treated by the chiropractor, has contacted police and alleges she was groomed and sexually abused by Rossborough over a period of almost three years when she was a teenager. The woman says she was referred to Rossborough by her dance school.



Following the criminal case last year, the alleged victim, who is now in her 30s and spoke to this masthead on the condition of anonymity, submitted a 13-page statement of allegations against Rossborough to AHPRA. The national healthcare watchdog is conducting its own investigation into Rossborough. The woman hopes the matter will be referred to a civil tribunal, which examines the most severe complaints against Australian health practitioners, and will allow her to have her allegations heard. “The injustice of it really weighs on me,” she says. “I strongly believe he’s still a threat to the community, which is what prompted me to follow through with this.” Ian Rossborough was found guilty of sexual assault and grooming last year. In the statement, seen by this masthead, the woman alleges that Rossborough told her after the sexual abuse began: “You have the power to destroy me, if you ever tell anyone”. “I now feel deep discomfort and distress when I reflect on what occurred,” she wrote in her statement. “It is confronting to recognise that Ian took advantage of my youth, vulnerability, and impressionable nature.



“I was a young and emotionally vulnerable girl when I met him, and he exploited the imbalance of power.” When Sarah Rose turned 14, Rossborough gave her his personal phone number, telling her she could bypass his long waiting list whenever she needed to see him. He started texting her regularly and confided in her about his personal life and divorce. He called her his “good buddy”, and invited her to do yoga classes with him. Rose says her appointments with Rossborough were only meant to be 15 minutes, but he would often stretch them out to an hour without charging her. “All my focus was on my career. Dance was my entire identity,” Rose says.



“Dance gave me a chance to process all my emotions of the world, but it is really hard to look back now and realise how much I was ignoring and shoving down just to cope.” On the night she was assaulted, Rose was 17 and about to fly overseas for a life-changing summer program at the Washington Ballet. Sarah Rose Steven Siewert Rossborough promised to help get her body into the best physical shape before she left and, under the guise of helping her lose weight, instructed her to use the sauna in a yoga studio next to his clinic and strip completely naked before entering. About 45 minutes later, Rossborough came into the sauna took off his clothes and sexually assaulted Rose. “I just froze when it happened,” Rose says. “He was my lift home that night, so I knew no one was coming to get me, and no one was there to help. I remember thinking, ‘You have no other way home ... Just act normal. Don’t let him know you’re freaking out’.” After a video of him manipulating the spine of a newborn went viral across the world in 2016, Rossborough was temporarily banned from treating children while he was investigated by the nation’s medical watchdog.

World.title: Albanese makes deal with Taylor, denies gambling lobby had sway over reforms
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGambling Albanese makes deal with Taylor, denies gambling lobby had sway over reforms Natassia Chrysanthos and Paul Sakkal August 12, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese insists that Labor has not been swayed by gambling donations or private interests as he inches closer to a compromise deal with Opposition Leader Angus Taylor over the vexed and long-delayed issue of wagering reform. Crossbench MPs on Wednesday conceded that they may have “lost the battle” on tougher gambling advertising restrictions but would keep fighting as the major parties hashed out the fine print on amendments. Members of the crossbench will put forward their own amendments to strengthen the gambling measures – but the government is working with the Coalition. Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images Albanese and Taylor are expected to agree to tighten up gambling promotion conditions and simplify rules for streaming advertising, although a fresh sticking point has emerged over Labor’s move to ban offshore lotteries, which is dividing Coalition MPs. The Coalition sought amendments after a Senate inquiry last week heard claims that problem gamblers had been lured by VIP agents offering thousands of dollars in free bonus bets as well as hotel rooms, flights, drugs and escorts.



But Coalition MPs have this week split over the opposition’s approach, with five backbenchers urging a joint meeting of the Liberals and Nationals to do more to protect children and addicts. Four cautioned against a hardline approach, warning the Coalition could not be seen as overzealous about regulation or as pushing the industry underground. Related Article Gambling ‘Publicity-seeking extremists’: V’landys weighs in as gambling inquiry gets personal Liberal MP Zoe McKenzie on Wednesday evening said the Coalition had been asking the government to go further. “In the last week, everything has been on the table,” she said. “We will see where it lands.” But Labor’s package is likely to remain largely unchanged, aside from some action on inducements, given neither Albanese nor Taylor have an appetite for a “nanny state” debate that could be weaponised by One Nation. The laws won’t introduce a full advertising blackout, national regulator or an all-out ban on promotions – measures recommended by the bipartisan 2023 Murphy report, which has become the gold standard for reform advocates. Independents accused the government and Coalition of shying away from reform to appease private interests, pointing to this masthead’s report that donors with gambling links had reported $5 million in donations to Labor and $4.5 million to the Coalition over five years.



Independent MP Andrew Wilkie on Wednesday referred those details to the National Anti-Corruption Commission, and reported his concerns that government MPs were ignoring the public interest because they were being improperly influenced by gambling interests. “It’s not just money, it’s hospitality, it’s personal friendships. There’s a point at which the level of influence on a government and the decision that government makes is entirely improper,” Wilkie said. Independent MP Andrew Gee, a former National, claimed the major parties were beholden to their donors. “Don’t think that money doesn’t talk in this place because it does. I’m speaking as someone who has escaped a major political party,” he said. “Corporations would pay big bucks to meet with every single MP that they wanted to. So if you were an MP, you had to sit there for 15 minutes ... and after that, a bell would ring. Included on that list were gambling companies. That’s the power of money talking. They get access to politicians.” But Albanese said his position had not been influenced in the way that was being suggested, after Wilkie put the allegation to the prime minister during Wednesday’s question time.



“I don’t suggest members on any side of this debate have been influenced,” Albanese said. “People come to these issues with a genuine perspective, and we have genuine differences as well on some of these issues. But to question people’s motives is, I think, undermining the civil debate that is required on these issues. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in question time on Wednesday. Alex Ellinghausen “We will have a debate on our legislation, constructive discussions are continuing. I expect there will be amendments to the legislation that I hope to receive the support of the entire parliament.” Labor MPs including Alicia Payne and Peter Khalil on Wednesday afternoon emphasised the laws were an important first step, but there was more to be done.



Albanese, meanwhile, said he wanted to defend people’s freedom to bet while addressing problem gambling. “What we need to do in a debate like this, that can be emotional, is to make sure that we get the policy right. And our government is determined to get the policy right,” he said. Amendments hashed out this week The Coalition’s focus in negotiations has been VIP inducements and bonus bets, as well as rules for streaming services. The new rules require online platforms to have a “triple-lock” function to show unlimited gambling ads – they must register their users, prove they are over 18, and offer them an opt-out function. Some Coalition MPs want an “opt-in” function instead, although a compromise will more likely give streaming services options between the triple-lock or the same hourly ad limits as free-to-air broadcasters.



But Labor and the Coalition are at odds over one element of the bill that stops firms from offering tickets to foreign lotteries. Labor argues the measure will close a loophole that allows Australians to access foreign gambling products. Related Article Alcohol Every AFL and NRL club now sponsored by alcohol companies, research reveals But the main company in question, the Lottery Office, has challenged that basis; its chief executive Jaclyn Wood says the ban sets a “dangerous precedent” for banning industries the government doesn’t like. The Coalition also wants to preserve jobs for 50 employees at the Gold Coast-based firm, which sits in Liberal MP Leon Rebello’s seat. Rebello said Labor’s proposal was “anticompetitive behaviour dressed up as gambling reform”. The opposition’s suspicion is that Labor’s policy is designed to appease the Lottery Corporation, which dominates the market. One Nation and some Nationals MPs have sided with the legacy lottery outfit and the newsagency lobby, which also supports the ban. World.title: Now that we’ve come to our census, let’s have a NAPLAN for grown-ups
World.content:
NationalCensus Opinion Now that we’ve come to our census, let’s have a NAPLAN for grown-ups Cherie Gilmour Freelance writer August 12, 2026 — 7:30pm

August 12, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Well done, Australia. We managed to pull together on a wintry Tuesday night to declare, in the national census, our sexual identities and whether we’re practising or nominal Jedis. Now that we’ve proven our ability to answer mildly invasive questions under bureaucratic pressure, it seems logical to expand the project into tracking our emotional and social intelligence. An adults-only NAPLAN, anyone? It makes sense – we’re so busy worrying about the next generation’s declining literacy and numeracy levels, we’ve forgotten to track our own brain rot. The kids will be all right. They’ll probably have AI plugged into their skulls as superintelligent, planet-saving beings whose only weakness will be forgetting to charge themselves overnight like an EV. So that was the easy part. Now, try this quick quiz. It’s we, the adults, who doomscroll through TikTok uninhibited, knowing full well it’s turning us into Neanderthals. Here’s a sample question that could be included in the adult NAPLAN, inspired by a recent Macca’s drive-thru with my kids: When greeting a customer in a retail scenario, the correct salutation is: a) “Are you using the MyMaccas app today?” b) “Hi there! How are you?” c) “I can’t hear you, speak louder”, or d) “Are you ready to order?”



Or try these for size. A stranger strikes up a conversation in the supermarket line. You: a) Respond politely for 20 to 30 seconds; b) Give a one-word response before turning back to your phone; c) Panic internally and pretend you didn’t hear them; d) Panic internally and overshare something deeply personal about your brother-in-law’s recent gallbladder surgery and subsequent spiritual awakening. Related Article Census Immigration officers out, influencers in. These are the job changes in the Census You receive some mildly critical feedback at work. The best response is to: a) Consider it calmly and professionally; b) Feel a surge of rage, then post a long rant on social media about “toxic workplaces” and the need to “protect your peace”, accompanied by a sunset shot you took in Bali in 2019; c) Immediately consult ChatGPT for reassurance about why you’re the only emotionally intelligent person in the building; d) Immediately consult ChatGPT to help write your resignation letter using a “diplomatic” but “passive-aggressive” tone. It would be useful to track how we’re going with our devices.



You’re watching a 12-minute explanatory video for work. You should: a) Speed it up 1.5x so that you can get to your lunch break faster; b) Watch the first 30 seconds so you “get the gist”; c) Watch it all the way through and pat yourself on the back for being a meditative medieval monk; d) Keep it playing in the background while you open another three tabs and compare the nutritional information for competing brands of oat milk, which spirals into the ethics of oat farming. Related Article Opinion

AI Is your boss asking you to work with AI? Watch out for these four things You find yourself sitting in a doctor’s waiting room with no Wi-Fi. The mature response is: a) Mentally compose a blog for LinkedIn titled “What a Waiting Room Without Wi-Fi Taught Me About Being Present”; b) Sit quietly and tolerate mild boredom; c) Take an obscene interest in the infomercial on a nearby TV, showing a detailed simulation of the benefits of a new fungal cream (and wonder if you could have gotten into medical school); d) Acknowledge the dawning realisation that you’re about to embark on a very public existential crisis. Or we could even focus on something a little more recent. You are filling out the 2026 census form. Do you: a) Answer factually and accurately before getting on with another episode of The Traitors; b) Google whether underreporting the number of bedrooms in your house will be noted by the ATO; c) Put your religion as Pastafarian while muttering about government overreach; d) Consult ChatGPT about whether listing your dog as a dependent could result in a fine. (Name: Gary. Occupation: Emotional support. Highest level of education: Can sit.) If the 2026 census has shown us anything, it’s that we can still be collectively mobilised as a nation. Filling out forms was and always will be a national pastime. But rather than asking for absurdly mundane details about our lives, we should use that precious half-hour to answer more pressing questions about the state of adulthood in 2026. Can you pay attention for longer than 47 seconds? Can you engage in ordinary social interactions without panicking? Can you handle criticism without consulting ChatGPT? Can you respond to bureaucratic questions without jumping to conspiracy theories?



The results would be far more revealing than the current national tally of practising Jedis. Unless, of course, you are one. In which case: may the Force be with you. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: The Opportunity Party could decide next government, new poll shows
World.content:
The Opportunity Party has the numbers to enter Parliament - and act as kingmaker - according to the latest 1News Verian poll.

The poll, which was taken in the days leading up to the prime minister's confidence vote, has Labour in the lead, and National riding steady.

It suggests a left bloc that includes Opportunity could form a government, after Christopher Luxon ruled out working with the party.

The results of the poll:

Labour: 30 percent, down 2 (38 seats)

National: 29 percent, no change (36 seats)

Green Party: 12 percent, down 1 (15 seats)

ACT: 9 percent, up 3 (11 seats)

New Zealand First: 8 percent, down 3 (10 seats)

Opportunity: 8 percent, up 3 (9 seats)

Te Pāti Māori: 1 percent, down 1 point (6 seats)

11 percent of people said they did not know, or refused to answer.

The 1News Verian poll assumes the current Māori electorate incumbents hold their seats, meaning the poll has a 125-seat Parliament.

It means neither current bloc would have enough seats to form a majority, with Labour, the Greens, and Te Pāti Māori on 59, and National, ACT and New Zealand First on 57.

With Opportunity, the left bloc would have 68 seats - enough to govern. If Luxon changed his mind about working with Opportunity, the right bloc would have 66 seats.

Luxon ruled out working with Opportunity near the end of July, while Chris Hipkins officially ruled out New Zealand First earlier this week - earning a rebuke from Winston Peters.

The new poll comes after a bruising day for Christopher Luxon's premiership. RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

The poll was conducted from 8 to 11 August, with a sample size of 847.

Earlier on Wednesday, the poll revealed a further 1 point drop for Luxon in the preferred prime minister ratings, putting him on 17 percent.

That was still ahead of Chris Hipkins, who was on 15 percent, also down one point.

Rounding out the top three, Winston Peters was on 7 percent, down 3 points.

Chlöe Swarbrick was steady on 6 percent, David Seymour was up 1 point to 5 percent, Erica Stanford was up 1 point to 2 percent, and Kieran McAnulty was also up 1 point to 2 percent.

Another difficult day for Luxon

The new poll comes just hours after Christopher Luxon survived the second attempt to oust him in the past few months.

Luxon held an abrupt press conference on Wednesday afternoon, where he confirmed he had survived that confidence vote.

He said he had the "full support" of the National Party caucus, and was focused on the election.

Later on Wednesday, Luxon confirmed he had removed MP Chris Penk's ministerial portfolios.

"Chris Penk launched a leadership challenge this week, which resulted in today's confidence vote. This makes his role untenable and as such I have removed his portfolios," Luxon said earlier on Wednesday.

Paul Goldsmith is taking up the Defence, Veterans, Space, GCSB, and NZSIS portfolios.

Simon Watts will become Minister for Building and Construction.

World.title: Chris Penk says he will not seek re-election after losing ministerial portfolios
World.content:
Chris Penk has decided not to seek re-election in November, hours after the prime minister stripped him of his portfolios for his role in a leadership challenge.

On Wednesday, following an emergency caucus meeting, Christopher Luxon confirmed the party had undertaken a confidence vote, and he remained prime minister and leader of the National Party.

A few hours later, Luxon removed Penk's ministerial portfolios.

"Chris Penk launched a leadership challenge this week, which resulted in today's confidence vote. This makes his role untenable and as such I have removed his portfolios," Luxon said.

On Wednesday evening, Penk said he had reflected on his political future with his family, and decided not to seek re-election as an MP.

"I am a proud member of the National Party, and I fully back National and Christopher Luxon to lead the government after the election and take New Zealand forward," he said.

"It has been a privilege to serve my community of Kaipara ki Mahurangi for the last nine years, and I am proud of the progress I have contributed to as a minister this term. However, I have decided it is the time for me to seek other opportunities to serve New Zealand."

Penk's statement did not address the allegations he had launched a leadership challenge.

Paul Goldsmith will pick up the Defence, Veterans, Space, GCSB, and NZSIS portfolios.

Simon Watts will become Minister for Building and Construction.

The Prime Minister's Office told RNZ its position was that Penk was challenging for himself, not on behalf of someone else.

Earlier on Wednesday afternoon, Luxon held a press conference where he announced he had survived the second attempt to oust him this year.

In an abrupt statement to media, he said he had the full confidence of the National Party caucus before leaving without answering questions.

"Our caucus is united, and it is determined to win this election," he said.

"Our focus is on National's positive plan to fix the basics and to build the future, so that we realise the incredible potential that sits in this country, and that we set it up for our kids and our grandkids."

He was flanked by senior MPs, including Nicola Willis, Mark Mitchell and Chris Bishop.

Standing just behind them was Erica Stanford, who was rumoured to be gunning for the top job.

Chris Penk at Parliament on Wednesday. RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

Later on Wednesday evening, Bishop said rumours Penk was doing the numbers for him were "utterly incorrect," and people did not launch leadership challenges on behalf of anybody else.

"He was not doing the numbers for me. Chris Penk, as the prime minister said, launched a challenge. It didn't succeed, obviously, and any suggestion that he was involved in doing numbers for me is completely wrong.

Bishop said there was "no suggestion" Penk was doing the numbers for Stanford either.

He said it would be "tough" for Penk, saying he was talented and the two had worked closely together, but he understood why the prime minister had made the decision.

"He'll be a loss to the government, but that's what happens."

Penk, who was ranked 14th on National's list published at the weekend, had earlier denied any involvement in a leadership challenge, after Politik and the New Zealand Herald reported he was doing the numbers for an Erica Stanford bid.

Upon arriving in Wellington on Tuesday night, Penk had said he had confidence in Luxon, and would support him in any vote.

"I've always expressed confidence in the leader. Now is no different."

He would not say if anyone had called him about the leadership, saying he would not disclose private conversations, but said reports of his involvement as an instigator were "wrong".

He stuck to that position on Wednesday morning, again saying he had confidence in Luxon, and suggested people might be making up stories about him making calls for Stanford.

"I think everyone else needs to get their story straight because I'm hearing multiple different versions. None of them are true, and as I said, I'm not prepared to disclose private conversations, except only to say I have confidence in Christopher Luxon."

Penk had only been promoted to the Cabinet in April, following the retirement of Judith Collins.

He has been an MP since 2017, first in the Helensville seat, then in the redrawn Kaipara ki Mahurangi electorate.

ACT Party leader David Seymour said for Luxon to remain leader after several challenges showed he was well-positioned to stop the destabilisation in the party.

World.title: Wellington's after-hours clinic doesn't have staff to extend hours
World.content:
Wellington's after-hours medical service (WAMC) says it doesn't have the staff to extend opening hours to help it cope with a winter surge of patients.

Wellington Hopsital's emergency department had one of its busiest days in almost a year on Monday, seeing 258 patients,

Health NZ said the GP-run urgent care clinic would be extending its hours in an effort to cope with the influx. It was aiming to do this within six months of signing a contract.

But the clinic said it was still in negotiations with the agency and hadn't yet reached an agreement.

It said a new workforce model would have to be agreed before the hours could be extended and the change could take up to 15 months.

World.title: Rotorua seeks four-week extension after Head Start proposal falls apart
World.content:
Rotorua Lakes Council has asked the government for a four-week extension to enter its Head Start local government reform process.

Mayor Tania Tapsell said she had asked Local Government Minister Simon Watts for more time to resolve councillors' concerns and formally submit the proposal.

Introduced in May, Head Start gave councils three months to propose voluntary reforms, with those not progressing facing a compulsory backstop, in which the government will design the future structure for them after the 2028 elections.

The request follows the collapse of a co-ordinated plan to create three unitary authorities: Tauranga-Western Bay, Rotorua, and an Eastern Bay authority covering Whakatāne, Kawerau and Ōpōtiki.

Each would develop its own structure while the councils presented a unified regional approach through a shared cover letter.

However, the plan unravelled before the 9 August deadline.

On Thursday, Western Bay voted against Head Start, by one vote, and the Eastern Bay councils submitted their own proposal, leaving Rotorua with Tauranga as its only potential partner.

Rotorua chief executive Andrew Moraes said the council had been advised by the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport (MCERT) that it needed at least one other council to qualify for Head Start.

Rotorua Lakes Council chief executive Andrew Moraes. Andrew Warner / LDR

A Tauranga-Rotorua proposal covering a Baywide approach, minus the Eastern Bay, would have required including Western Bay despite its opposition, dividing Rotorua councillors. A proposal including only Tauranga and Rotorua would not qualify.

The council voted 6-5 against the Tauranga-Western Bay alternative and the backstop option, leaving Rotorua without an approved proposal or an obvious route into Head Start.

Tapsell said Rotorua had previously resolved to pursue a Head Start proposal, but the rejection at the final meeting on Friday left it without an "approved" final proposal.

The minister now has Rotorua's draft proposal, Tapsell said, and the council is waiting to see whether the extension will be granted.

Whakatāne Mayor Nandor Tanczos, Kawerau Mayor Faylene Tunui and Ōpōtiki Mayor David Moore present East Coast MP Dana Kirkpatrick (second from left) with their council's outline proposal for an Eastern Bay unitary council on the Beehive steps in Wellington. NZME

Whakatāne Mayor Nándor Tánczos said the Eastern Bay councils had always intended to submit their own proposal, supported by the cover letter demonstrating a co-ordinated regional approach.

"We were all committed to signing it," he said.

The Eastern Bay councils waited for Western Bay's decision before submitting, but Tánczos said there was too little time to change tack and develop a new arrangement with Rotorua.

"It's Thursday night we're talking about," he said.

The intention had been for the three sub-regions to move together, even if their proposals were submitted separately.

"We wanted it to be seen that the Bay of Plenty was coming up with a solution for the whole Bay together," Tánczos said.

He said that principle had not changed despite the collapse of the co-ordinated process.

"If there is a possibility that there's still this idea of an across-the-Bay three sub-regional authorities' approach, we'd still support that," he said.

"It still seems the best idea for the Bay of Plenty."

Tapsell said she "understood and supported" the Eastern Bay councils proceeding independently, saying it was "ultimately the best decision" for them to "determine and be part of their own future".

She said the three-authority concept reflected what the region's mayors believed was the most realistic option.

"We understood and agreed that we have three very clear and distinct sub-regions," she said.

Tapsell said she still believed the three-authority model was the best solution for the region and remained viable.

She said Tauranga and Western Bay were the most logical parts of the region to merge because of their geography and infrastructure, but Rotorua councillors had been reluctant to support a model that would effectively force Western Bay into an arrangement it had rejected.

She said the "short time frames" had contributed to the impasse.

Tánczos also questioned whether councils had been given enough time to make decisions of such magnitude, saying the process had placed enormous pressure on councils and strained relationships.

"Everyone's been put in this extremely difficult position with really impossible time frames," he said.

Local Government Minister Simon Watts. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Watts rejected the suggestion that the government's process had failed in Rotorua.

"Head Start is a voluntary process for councils that are ready and able to work together to simplify local government," he said.

Councils without a Head Start proposal proceeding to detailed design would enter the Backstop, he said, with its design to be determined by the government in 2027.

Watts declined to comment specifically on Rotorua's position but said the detailed design phase would allow successful proposals to be expanded, communities consulted, and legislation developed before the 2028 elections.

He said the government had received 18 proposals covering 48 councils by the 9 August deadline, including proposals from the Eastern Bay councils and one from Tauranga City Council, without a willing partner.

Moraes said Rotorua's options beyond Head Start remained unclear, with the government yet to set out what the Backstop process would look like.

"The Head Start process is closed," he said. "Anything that happens outside of that process will depend on future government policy announcements."

For Tapsell, that is why the extension matters.

"Head Start was the only option available to determine our own future," she said.

"I'm genuinely gutted that we're on the edge of losing this opportunity."

World.title: Kiwi dairy industry rides the Wegovy wave as  whey protein booms
World.content:
New Zealand dairy companies are cashing in on a surge in global demand for bioactive proteins found in cow's milk, like whey, off the back of the surge in weightloss drugs.

Boosting immune health or developing muscles for elderly or appetite suppressant patients were believed to be driving a recent upsurge in demand for dairy-based proteins.

Fresh cow's milk consisted mostly of water, with small fractions of lactose, fat and protein.

After dairy processors removed fat and separated the casein protein, the leftover liquid was whey, a protein-rich by-product valued for amino acids and minerals that supported human health.

This year, prices for whey powder in key market the United States were soaring.

The rural news with Gianina Schwanecke Rural News Download MP3 3m

Rabobank said in a recent agribusiness report, whey powder prices were up 76 percent in June, compared to the same time last year, with spot prices up 60 percent from the start of 2026.

The bank's senior analyst in animal proteins, Jen Corkran said high-protein yoghurt and dairy drinks containing whey were now in high demand globally.

"We've got these Gen-Zs and even your millennials in the gym, but also just everyday prioritizing protein," she said.

Do you consume whey protein, and why? Let us know monique.steele@rnz.co.nz

"We've seen this really big protein demand, and milk protein in particular benefits from this," said Corkran.

"We're seeing a lot of protein labelling, your yogurts, protein powders, and this is really adding to that demand story."

Wegovy wave

South Island dairy company Westland Milk was expanding its lactoferrin production facility in Hokitika to meet demand, advertising a number of jobs online at the West Coast facility.

Its owner, Yili Oceania's chief executive, Alex Turnbull said body builders drove early bioactive protein demand, but it was now much more mainstream, especially with the rise of GLP-1 medication use.

"Particularly with these aging populations in Western and Eastern culture," Turnbull said.

The Westland Milk Products Hokitika plant is the largest industrial coal user on the West Coast following extensive development of the site in the past decade. Greymouth Star/Brendon McMahon/

"And then, what's happened is with this crazy trend in the world for these weight loss drugs known as GLP-1, which is an appetite suppressant.

"Whatever you eat needs to be very, very nutritiously dense, because you lose a lot of muscle mass when you lose weight so quickly. And those are the casein proteins and the whey proteins."

In the United States, the use of appetite-suppressant GLP-1 medications for diabetes and weight loss had become much more widespread in recent years, with the development of brands Ozempic or Wegovy.

Turnbull said there was good demand for whey in the US, Europe and Asia.

He said people better understood the important role of proteins in the body thesedays.

"You're seeing customers putting protein into anything.

"And that's been the second catalyst to drive such enormous demand for dairy proteins, indeed throughout the world, but particularly the epicentre being in the United States of America."

Westland Milk was bought by China's Yili Group in 2019.

The whey to boost immune health

Selling the health benefits of a whey protein complex was the name of the game for Quantec, a small but longstanding company in Waikato.

It sourced milk from companies in one of the country's key dairy regions, then contract manufacturers extracted a natural mix of bioactive proteins including lactoferrin to create an ingredient that promoted immune health.

Chief executive, John Dawson said half the team were scientists who had spent years testing and working to prove the product's health benefits, like reducing the frequency of colds in children.

"We are focused on a very, very small subset of the bioactive proteins in milk. This really has carved out a unique niche for us in the dairy space," he said.

"We've been able to create a branded ingredient we call IDP, immune defense proteins, and that branded ingredient is used as an active ingredient in dietary supplements, health supplements, mainly in China, but also in other parts of the world."

Dawson said China was its top export market, that Taiwan and Japan were going well, and it was sending a little bit into Europe, with hopes to grow the US market.

123RF

"That's where the value is for us, is in building that brand supported by the science and the clinical studies. So that's a pretty narrow focus, but that's going to keep us busy for the foreseeable future."

Dawson said a focus on immune health was huge during the Covid-19 years, but had since dropped off a bit.

In addition to immune defence, he said it was exploring whey's other functional traits like anti-inflammatory or antimicrobial, as well as benefits for pets, riding on the back of the trend of owners humanising their pets.

World.title: Three arrested 45 minutes after sleeping man attacked, van and phone stolen
World.content:
Three people - including a youth - were arrested 45 minutes after a man was attacked in his van while he slept.

The attack, which left the victim with a bloody nose, happened around 2am near Lake Puketirini, Huntly, on Wednesday.

Police said the victim called from a service station, saying four people wearing balaclavas had attacked him, then stolen his van and phone.

"Responding officers located the van on Harris Street shortly after 2:30am, and set up road spikes around Tainui Bridge Road," Senior Sergeant Mary Van Dongen said.

The van was stopped on Great South Road and three occupants arrested at about 2:45am, she said, with help from a police dog unit.

"It's pleasing to have been able to locate and arrest people for this so quickly in order to hold them to account."

Two of the alleged attackers, aged 20 and 18, were due in Hamilton District Court on aggravated robbery charges, and the third in Hamilton Youth Court on an aggravated robbery charge.

World.content:
Union says Kiwis misled over Sydney bus driver jobs Nine To Noon Download MP3 18m

After being promised a Sydney beach lifestyle, a group of Kiwi bus drivers were left living in sub-standard housing and unable to return home unless they stumped up thousands of dollars.

The New South Wales transport union (RTBU) said bus company Keolis advertised jobs for New Zealand drivers promising flights, a live-by-the beach lifestyle, and attractive pay.

But a $10,000 bonding payment - holding them to the job - was sprung on workers shortly before their contracts started.

With many already having resigned from their jobs in New Zealand and sold their belongings, it was hard to turn back.

The union's secretary Toby Warnes told Nine to Noon they are aware of at least three drivers who have indicated they want to go home.

"We understand there's about 17 of them at the moment and the whole scheme allows for about 30 to be brought over."

He said the union currently had a court proceeding against Keolis, alleging the company had "duped a bunch of people to get on planes to come and work for them with this bonding arrangement in place".

Warnes indicated this arrangement could, under the Australian criminal code, amount to human trafficking and are hoping to prove the bond is not legally binding.

"Under our law over here, if you are induced to get on a plane to leave the country and come into Australia on the promise of something and that something isn't delivered, then that can carry really serious consequences."

The bus company Keolis has rejected the claims, saying the company was upfront with all contractual terms before people signed up.

Warnes said bus contracts in Sydney were funded by the taxpayer and run by private companies like Keolis.

"We, in particular, do not want to see taxpayers' money going into the pockets of private companies that are using these sort of, potentially modern slavery-like conditions on drivers that have been brought from overseas."

Warnes said bus contracts in Sydney were funded by the taxpayer. 123rf

He said the union had spoken to the transport minister about the issue, and it appeared that Keolis had not run the arrangement by the transport department.

"Which is concerning in and of itself that we could have a sort of wildcat cowboy company imposing these sorts of arrangements using taxpayer money."

Warnes said the company has also been promising an "idyllic, relaxed, laid-back lifestyle on the beach in Sydney ".

It was a lifestyle that was not reality due to the long hours, "bumper-to-bumper traffic" and the general low pay for Sydney bus drivers.

"That's why Keolis feels like it needs to try and bond these drivers to the job because they know that it's not what was promised and they know that if they don't have this kind of arrangement, these drivers are just going to get up and leave."

While the bond does scale down the longer that a driver has worked with the company, Warnes said most drivers know they want to leave within the first two weeks.

Warnes said some had brought their families with them and had been cramped into one-bedroom apartments.

Drivers were only given accommodation for their first six weeks and then had to find their own home.

"The Northern beaches of Sydney is one of the most expensive areas... on a bus driver's wage, you just simply cannot afford to live there."

Warnes said he understood the company was currently continuing with the scheme but is hoping it will come to an end with the court proceedings with the potential for government intervention.

"We think that this is the most grave of breaches of public trust... the very least the government could do is shut down this particular practice and then look at how the company responds to that and make decisions accordingly."

In a statement to Nine to Noon Keolis said employees who get relocation assistance sign an agreement detailing the support available and any repayment obligations that may apply.

"These terms are provided and agreed to before employment and relocation begin.

World.title: NZ Warriors coach Andrew Webster backs former All Blacks coach Scott Robertson for shock code switch
World.content:
NZ Warriors coach Andrew Webster has some advice for former All Blacks coach Scott Robertson, if he is to cross codes to guide a proposed South Island NRL side in the near future.

Robertson's name was surprisingly floated this week to steer Southern Orcas, a Christchurch-based bid to become the Aussie competition's 20th franchise.

Orcas president Sir Graham Lowe claimed the organisation had offered the former Crusaders maestro a four-year contract, if it was successful in winning the licence.

Robertson won seven Super Rugby crowns with the Crusaders, making him a popular choice as All Blacks coach, but his reputation took a hit, when he became the first All Blacks coach fired mid-term, after compiling a 20-win, seven-loss record over two years.

Nevertheless, Webster was impressed during his one meeting with Razor.

"I had a coffee with him, Stacey Jones and Darryl Halligan in Christchurch, when we had a trial there a couple of years ago," he recalled. "I think he had just been named All Blacks coach.

"Terrific guy, I learnt a lot off him in two hours. You could see how passionate he is about coaching and about the game."

Robertson has never coached in rugby league, but Webster didn't necessarily think that was a handicap. History is littered with examples of coaches who had switched from rugby to league or vice versa.

Australian Alan Jones coached the Wallabies from 1984-87, before linking with the Balmain Tigers for four seasons, achieving a 36 percent winning record.

Current Ireland and British & Irish Lions rugby coach Andy Farrell played rugby league most of his career, helping Wigan to seven championship crowns, before jumping codes. Webster was Farrell's guest at training last month, when the Irish faced the All Blacks at Eden Park.

Former NZ Kiwis coach David Kidwell was an NRL assistant with South Sydney Rabbitohs, Melbourne Storm, Wests Tigers and Parramatta Eels, before becoming a defensive coach with the Argentina Pumas and Japan, under former Wallabies coach Michael Cheika.

Wigan league legend Andy Farrell has made a successful coaching switch from league to rugby. PHOTOSPORT

Cheika has also flitted backwards and forward across the divide, coaching Lebanon at the Rugby League World Cup and acting as assistant coach with Sydney Roosters.

"I find, if people want to cross codes, they've got to be good man managers and I've heard that he is - he's obviously had a lot of success - and they've got to be willing to make sure they hire people who are absolute experts in their areas of the game," Webster said of Robertson.

"I'm sure Razor, if he got that opportunity - and by the way, he might not want it - I'm sure he's smart enough to realise that and get the right people. I'll leave that up to Razor, but he's a terrific guy."

The Warriors have mixed feelings about the prospect of conceding their monopoly on support on this side of the Tasman.

In June, they hosted North Queensland Cowboys at the new Te Kaha indoor stadium, attracting 25, 365 fans.

Afterwards, Webster was loathe to relinquish grip on a notoriously parochial fanbase that had taken so long to crack.

"I just struggle personally, because I really enjoy the fact that the top of the [country] to the bottom of the [country] are Warriors fans and they love their team," he said afterwards.

"We never used to have that, but we've got the whole country behind us now, not just the region.

"Will it have that same feeling if we add a team? I'm not sure."

The attempt to engage Robertson feels more like a publicity stunt in a part of the country that still fondly remembers his break-dancing victory celebrations.

Another Warrior to cross paths with him early in his career was former St Bede's College product Tanner Stowers-Smith, now an integral member of the Warriors interchange bench.

"I did a bit under Razor with the Junior Crusaders, when I was at school," he said. "Success is success and, with the amount of success he has had, I'm sure he could do something special with a league team.

"Obviously, it's a new code, but there's always room for learning and I wouldn't put it past him to excel there too, with the mindset that he's brought through the Crusaders and the amount of championships they've had under him.

World.title: 'Can't compete': Super coaches weigh into PNG Chiefs debate
World.content:
Trent Robinson won't be raging about the inequality of the tax breaks afforded to the PNG Chiefs, even if he believes the NRL's open market is no longer a "level playing field".

After Penrith winger Brian To'o became the sixth player wooed by the start-up franchise's tax-free wages, Panthers coach Ivan Cleary declared clubs "can't compete" with the bounty the Chiefs can provide from 2028.

Cleary revealed he was in tears when To'o informed him he would leave Penrith to join the Chiefs, who critics — led by South Sydney coach Wayne Bennett — have said now have an unfair advantage in attracting talent.

The salary cap has been an equaliser of talent but Bennett has claimed the NRL has eroded the competition's fairness by giving the Chiefs such an upper hand.

The Chiefs' advantages are in contrast to the few concessions afforded to the Perth Bears, who will enter the NRL next season.

Chiefs sign premiership winger To'o away from Panthers Four-time premiership-winning winger Brian To'o has become the sixth player to sign with the PNG Chiefs for their inaugural NRL season in 2028.

"It's not a level playing field and I think you can see that," said Sydney Roosters coach Robinson.

"We've got (it on) one (hand) where we feel like it's not a level playing field and the other where we feel like they need more assistance.

"We're going to debate … but do we want our game to grow?

"We're not going to stop at 19 (teams) … we should own the Pacific.

"If we want more money in the game, want to expand, we need more teams, so I think it's a positive thing — players are going to go."

Penrith were the latest club to feel that pinch when they gave To'o, who enters the last 12 months of his deal in November, a seven-day window to explore his options for 2028.

Premiership-winning Panthers Jarome Luai and Brian To'o will reunite in 2028 at the Chiefs. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The winger signed with the Chiefs without visiting PNG, joining Jarome Luai, Connor Watson, Alex Johnston and Zac Lomax in agreeing to deals with the NRL's 19th side.

Loading Instagram content

"I had a little moment the other day, just very sad that Bizza's going to be going," the usually stoic Cleary said.

"There would've been a few (tears) … It's just hard to imagine 'Biz' playing in any other jersey. But there's a few guys out there that I thought the same."

Since their rise to premiership dominance in 2020, the Panthers have become accustomed to salary cap pressure squeezing out key players.

But they are especially vulnerable after 2027, with the cashed-up Chiefs emerging just as they battle to hold on to co-captains Isaah Yeo and Nathan Cleary, as well as premiership players Paul Alamoti, Liam Martin and Moses Leota.

"I think everyone knows with the Chiefs, it's hard to match that stuff," Cleary said.

"It's not your average club, but if players want to go there, you can't compete."

Asked whether the Chiefs had unfairly skewed the player market, Cleary recalled some wisdom from Marty Gurr, who was on the coaching staff during his early playing days at Manly.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I remember when I first played 35 years ago, my first coach said to me 'rugby league isn't fair'," Cleary said.

"I think he was right. I've worked that out along the way. Whether it's fair or not, that's what the game's gone with. I can understand it."

Since overcoming the initial emotional blow of To'o's impending exit, Cleary has turned his attention to Penrith's task of retaining their stable of stars before September.

"We're very hopeful of having a few of them done (soon), you definitely don't want to be going into the finals doing this sort of stuff," he said.
